| Source | S1 | | | | | |

The freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, so the assay that anchors the cardiac use case has no opined cover, and one of five families is in appeal rather than granted. None of the five records could be verified in public patent databases in this run, and the company has no public web presence or FDA clearance record under its name; the portfolio rests entirely on the deck and should be treated as unverified until counsel's documents are read.

### Product inventory and unit economics

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer | Paid evaluation, investigational use only | Evaluation programme from 2024-03 | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) |
| Five-assay cartridge | Pilot production in Tempe | 2024 | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units |
| Contract development services | Services | Before 2025 | $0.7M | Not disclosed | None stated |
| Source | S1 | | | | |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it sells below build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received one free. The economics therefore live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which at observed use — 41 cartridges a site a month — is about $700 a site a month before service and support, against a $650 monthly analyzer fee in the evaluation programme. That covers the instrument quickly; it does not cover a direct sales force, which is why the plan's 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.

### Dependencies and readiness

The cartridge is made at a single 18-person leased plant in Tempe, Arizona, which concentrates manufacturing, quality and business-continuity risk in one site. The sealing patent is licensed from a 60%-owned related party on a 3% royalty, and reagent and optics suppliers are not disclosed. There is no cloud or model dependency; the integration work is HL7/FHIR, done in-house. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted, awaiting clearance), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), and manufacturing at 5 — a pilot line with six months of stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate and no high-volume line yet.

The strongest counter-evidence runs the other way. Creatinine and potassium matched the central laboratory in every one of 126 and 125 results, HbA1c in 99.2%, and 34 of the 37 sites in the programme for 90 days or more reordered within 90 days. A rural clinic that waits one to three days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows clinical sensitivity at the cutoff — and the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity at all, which is the missing number that would settle it. The technology is therefore plausible as a workflow product and unproven as a cardiac diagnostic; the difference is worth most of the valuation.

What would change the view: a pivotal study reporting capillary-versus-venous slope, bias and total error at each cutoff with a CV below 10% for troponin; a haemolysis-flagging capability with a published rejection rate; and a granted or allowed reader claim. What would confirm the bear case: a second additional-information request asking for capillary data, a pivotal study that reports only categorical agreement, or stability data that stops at six months.

Five questions for diligence: what are the troponin 99th-percentile value, limit of detection and share of healthy adults measurable above it; what did the August 2026 additional-information request ask for and does the answer need new clinical data; what share of pivotal finger sticks were haemolysed and does the cartridge flag haemolysis; what are line yield, cycle time and stability beyond six months; and what is the scope of the granted VD-1 claims and the grounds of the VD-2 appeal. Confidence in the technology judgement is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the 1,680 monthly cartridges behind the utilisation test are company figures, unaudited and not independently verified. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. A 13,200-site total is not the problem; utilisation is. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,280 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

::: risk-matrix
| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (company data) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (company data) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (company data) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (company data) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (company list price) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 |
:::

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US, glucose strips, blood gas and infectious disease included; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. That package is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve and the pivotal capillary study hold, and none of the three is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable concentrations above the detection limit in at least 50% of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick delivers about 40 microlitres into a capillary-fill cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator, so the clinic does no separate calibration. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. Results leave over Wi-Fi as HL7 or FHIR. The detection chemistry, troponin antibody pair, lot-to-lot calibration scheme and optics supplier are not disclosed, which caps confidence in every performance claim below [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% in whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin limit of detection | Not disclosed | 1.61 ng/L (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123 of 128), same normal/abnormal bucket | Method comparison with slope, intercept, bias and total error in cleared submissions | S1 |
| Sample volume | 40 µL | 22 µL (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Time to result | 12 minutes | About 15 minutes (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Shelf life | 9 months claimed, 6 months of data | Real-time data expected to cover the claimed expiry | S1 |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 at pilot volume | $10 at 1 million units; $7.50 at 2 million | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a chest-pain pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of about plus or minus 23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI against a conventional predicate rather than as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

### Agreement is not equivalence

A Class II cardiac submission rests on multi-level precision including the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, interference above all haemolysis, a specimen comparison and a method comparison reporting slope, intercept, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 troponin results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket as the central laboratory, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is roughly 93% to 99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results (0.9% of 640) were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — about 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary high-sensitivity troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the analyte most exposed to haemolysis, which biases it upward and produces false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes, which shows how narrow the handling window is. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Central laboratory | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 minutes | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | Venous plasma or serum | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Blood gases, electrolytes, creatinine | Full menu | S1, S70, S133 |
| Time to result | 12 minutes | About 15 minutes | Under 1 minute (vendor) | 1-3 days | S1, S70 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | Typically 2-5% CV | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA complexity | Moderate until a waiver | Not established in the sources retrieved | Moderate | High | S1, S133 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and on-board calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents needs tight tolerances and a reference channel; the granted VD-1 family covers it | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 5 | A conventional immunoassay stabilised in a dry format; Abbott and Siemens already own high-sensitivity chemistry | 1-2 years | S1 |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automated assembly, in-line quality control and yield learning from a 20,000-unit base to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1 |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Four-site pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study: 18-30 months of calendar time | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| IP and freedom to operate | 4 | One granted cartridge family, a reader family in appeal, no opinion on the troponin chemistry | 1-2 years | S1 |
| Composite | 5 | A workflow integrator's moat rather than a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

The replication test: a funded team of 50 with the published patents would need roughly two to three years to reach a cleared five-assay finger-stick panel — one to two years to build a comparable cartridge, then a pivotal study and FDA review of the size Vantelle is only now starting. The binding constraint is evidence, not invention, which is why Abbott or Siemens could close the gap faster than a start-up.

### Patent position

| Patent or application | What it covers | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03; European application pending | Core cartridge architecture; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk; design-around or narrower claims likely | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | Filed 2025-09-30; unpublished | Guards the short-fill failure mode | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin assay chemistry on dried reagents | Filed 2026-02-11; unpublished | The lead assay's chemistry; excluded from the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01; Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Freedom to operate on sealing; 3% royalty on cartridge net sales | S1 |

The freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, so the assay that anchors the cardiac use case has no opined cover, and one of five families is in appeal rather than granted. None of the five records could be verified in public patent databases in this run, and the company has no public web presence or FDA clearance record under its name; the portfolio rests entirely on the deck and should be treated as unverified until counsel's documents are read.

### Product inventory and unit economics

| Product | Stage | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer | Paid evaluation, investigational use only | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1 |
| Five-assay cartridge | Pilot production in Tempe | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1 |
| Contract development services | Services | $0.7M | Not disclosed | None stated | S1 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it sells below build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received one free. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which at observed use — 41 cartridges a site a month — is about $700 a site a month before service and support, against a $650 monthly analyzer fee. That covers the instrument quickly; it does not cover a direct sales force, which is why the plan's 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing.

### Dependencies and readiness

The cartridge is made at one leased 18-person plant in Tempe, concentrating manufacturing, quality and continuity risk in a single site. The sealing patent is licensed from a 60%-owned related party on a 3% royalty; reagent and optics suppliers are not disclosed. There is no cloud or model dependency; integration is HL7/FHIR in-house. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), and manufacturing at 5 — a pilot line with six months of stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate and no high-volume line.

The strongest counter-evidence runs the other way. Creatinine and potassium matched the central laboratory in every one of 126 and 125 results, HbA1c in 99.2%, and 34 of the 37 sites in the programme for 90 days or more reordered within 90 days. A rural clinic that waits one to three days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows clinical sensitivity at the cutoff — and the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity at all, the number that would settle it. The technology is plausible as a workflow product and unproven as a cardiac diagnostic; the difference is worth most of the valuation.

What would change the view: a pivotal study reporting capillary-versus-venous slope, bias and total error at each cutoff with troponin CV below 10%; a haemolysis-flagging capability with a published rejection rate; a granted or allowed reader claim. What would confirm the bear case: a second additional-information request asking for capillary data, a pivotal study reporting only categorical agreement, or stability data that stops at six months.

Five questions for diligence: the troponin 99th-percentile value, detection limit and share of healthy adults measurable above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked and whether the answer needs new clinical data; the share of pivotal finger sticks that were haemolysed and whether the cartridge flags haemolysis; line yield, cycle time and stability beyond six months; and the scope of the granted VD-1 claims and the grounds of the VD-2 appeal. Confidence in the technology judgement is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US, glucose strips, blood gas and infectious disease included; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and the arithmetic works only when four or five analytes are ordered and paid on the same run. Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine on the nearest priced code and $4.76 for potassium, $71.38 if all five are billed and collected. Against a $38 cartridge and a $650 monthly analyzer fee, a site running 41 cartridges a month collects $2,926.58 and pays $2,208, $718.58 of gross margin per analyzer-month before staff time and billing cost. Run only troponin and potassium, the two analytes a chest-pain patient needs, and the clinic collects $17.23 against a $38 cartridge, a loss of $20.77 per run. The company does not disclose ordered tests per cartridge, and that metric decides whether the clinic is a customer or a charity. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Until the waiver is granted, Vantelle sells into a base one-eighth the size of the one its labour-free pitch addresses, and each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024, and that is the only facility class the policy creates. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more, and the company's own clinic survey reports a median daily send-out volume far above what its evaluation sites ran. The survey and the operating data differ by an order of magnitude and only one can describe the commercial site. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, confidence in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests per cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge in the first ten billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate at the 41 evaluation sites; and whether any evaluation site sustained more than two cartridges a day per analyzer in any month. Until those are answered, the section underwrites the US cartridge market at $350M-$500M, not $2.4B, and the gap belongs in the price, not in the narrative.

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. That package is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve and the pivotal capillary study hold, and none of the three is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable concentrations above the detection limit in at least 50% of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A 40-microlitre finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator, so the clinic does no separate calibration. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. Results leave over Wi-Fi as HL7 or FHIR. The detection chemistry, troponin antibody pair, lot-to-lot calibration and optics supplier are not disclosed, which caps confidence in every performance claim below [S1].

| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin detection limit | Not disclosed | 1.61 ng/L (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error in cleared submissions | S1 |
| Sample volume and time | 40 µL and 12 minutes | 22 µL and about 15 minutes (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 | $10 target at 1 million units, $7.50 at 2 million | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of about plus or minus 23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI against a conventional predicate rather than as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II cardiac submission also rests on multi-level precision including the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, interference above all haemolysis, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, intercept, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 troponin results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket as the central laboratory, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is roughly 93% to 99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results (0.9% of 640) were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — about 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary high-sensitivity troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the analyte most exposed to haemolysis, which biases it upward and produces false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes, which shows how narrow the handling window is. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Central laboratory | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | Venous plasma | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | Full menu | S1, S70, S133 |
| Time to result | 12 minutes | About 15 minutes | Under 1 minute (vendor) | 1-3 days | S1, S70 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | Typically 2-5% CV | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA complexity | Moderate until a waiver | Not established | Moderate | High | S1, S133 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents needs tight tolerances and a reference channel; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 5 | A conventional immunoassay in dry format; Abbott and Siemens already own high-sensitivity chemistry | 1-2 years | S1 |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automated assembly and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1 |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study: 18-30 months of calendar time | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| IP and freedom to operate | 4 | One granted cartridge family, a reader family in appeal, no opinion on the troponin chemistry | 1-2 years | S1 |
| Composite | 5 | A workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

The replication test: a funded team of 50 with the published patents would need two to three years to reach a cleared five-assay finger-stick panel — one to two years for a comparable cartridge, then a pivotal study and review of the size Vantelle is only now starting. The binding constraint is evidence, not invention, which is why Abbott or Siemens could close the gap faster than a start-up.

### Patent position

| Patent or application | What it covers | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 | Capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03; Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 | Five-assay optical reader with drift correction | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 | Finger-stick sample-volume check | Filed 2025-09-30; unpublished | Guards the short-fill failure | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 | Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | Filed 2026-02-11; unpublished | Lead assay chemistry, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 | Cartridge sealing film and reagent blister | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01; Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, so the assay anchoring the cardiac use case has no opined cover, and one of five families is in appeal rather than granted. None of the five records could be verified in public patent databases in this run, and the company has no public web presence or FDA clearance record under its name; the portfolio rests entirely on the deck and is unverified until counsel's documents are read.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1 |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1 |
| Contract development services | $0.7M | Not disclosed | None stated | S1 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it sells below build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received one free. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, about $700 a site a month at the observed 41 cartridges a site, which covers the instrument quickly but not a direct sales force — the plan's 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — one leased 18-person plant, six months of stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate and no high-volume line. The roadmap runs two assays to five, moderate to waived and 20,000 cartridges a year to 2 million; the open technical debate is whether a five-assay panel from 40 µL can hold precision at the cutoff or whether integration produces the 11.8% trade-off already visible.

The strongest counter-evidence runs the other way. Creatinine and potassium matched the central laboratory in every one of 126 and 125 results, HbA1c in 99.2%, and 34 of the 37 sites in the programme for 90 days or more reordered within 90 days. A rural clinic that waits one to three days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows clinical sensitivity at the cutoff — and the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity at all, the number that would settle it. The technology is plausible as a workflow product and unproven as a cardiac diagnostic.

Diligence questions: the troponin 99th-percentile value, detection limit and share of healthy adults measurable above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked and whether the answer needs new clinical data; the share of pivotal finger sticks that were haemolysed and whether the cartridge flags haemolysis; line yield, cycle time and stability beyond six months; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and grounds of the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the monthly cartridge volumes behind the utilisation test are unverified company figures, unaudited and not independently confirmed. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. A 13,200-site total is not the problem; utilisation is. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,280 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

::: risk-matrix
| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |
:::

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US, glucose strips, blood gas and infectious disease included; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and the arithmetic works only when four or five analytes are ordered and paid on the same run. Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine on the nearest priced code and $4.76 for potassium, $71.38 if all five are billed and collected. Against a $38 cartridge and a $650 monthly analyzer fee, a site running 41 cartridges a month collects $2,926.58 and pays $2,208, $718.58 of gross margin per analyzer-month before staff time and billing cost. Run only troponin and potassium, the two analytes a chest-pain patient needs, and the clinic collects $17.23 against a $38 cartridge, a loss of $20.77 per run. The company does not disclose ordered tests per cartridge, and that metric decides whether the clinic is a customer or a charity. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico together hold 4,296 moderate-complexity laboratories and 31,720 waived ones. Until the waiver is granted, Vantelle sells into a base one-eighth the size of the one its labour-free pitch addresses, and each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024, and that is the only facility class the policy creates. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. [S81, S79, S95, S1]

::: risk-matrix
| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: Texas, Arizona, New Mexico | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA laboratories across the three states (2026) | US point-of-care 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only, no billable use | Moderate-complexity CLIA certificate and staffed quality control until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital and reference laboratories | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of the United States | $2.89B-$14.0B total US point-of-care market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR, 2026-2034 | Planned after a waiver; 300 sites targeted by end-2027 through a non-binding distributor letter of intent | Same CLIA constraint; payer coverage; no waiver before 2027 | Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Roche, Radiometer, Quest Diagnostics | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15 with no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement, distributor | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens Healthineers | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |
:::

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more, and the company's own clinic survey reports a median daily send-out volume far above what its evaluation sites ran. The survey and the operating data differ by an order of magnitude and only one can describe the commercial site. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, confidence in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests per cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any evaluation site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until those are answered, the section underwrites the US cartridge market at $350M-$500M, not $2.4B, and the gap belongs in the price, not in the narrative.

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**

The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in 2026, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model needs eight a day, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M [S1].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. That package is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve and the pivotal capillary study hold, and none of the three is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable concentrations above the detection limit in at least 50% of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A 40-microlitre finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator, so the clinic does no separate calibration. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. Results leave over Wi-Fi as HL7 or FHIR [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin detection limit | Not disclosed | 1.61 ng/L (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error in cleared submissions | S1 |
| Sample, time, shelf life, cost | 40 µL, 12 minutes, 9 months claimed on 6 months of data, $16.20 | 22 µL and about 15 minutes (i-STAT); $7.50 at 2 million units | S1, S70 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of about plus or minus 23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II cardiac submission also rests on multi-level precision including the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, interference above all haemolysis, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, intercept, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is roughly 93% to 99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results (0.9% of 640) were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — about 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary high-sensitivity troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the analyte most exposed to haemolysis, which biases it upward and produces false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes, which shows how narrow the handling window is. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA complexity | Moderate until a waiver | Not established | Moderate | S1, S133 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Troponin chemistry on dried reagents | 5 | Conventional immunoassay in dry format; Abbott and Siemens own hs chemistry | 1-2 years | S1 |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1 |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| IP and freedom to operate | 4 | One granted cartridge family, reader in appeal, no chemistry opinion | 1-2 years | S1 |
| Composite | 5 | A workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

The replication test: a funded team of 50 with the published patents would need two to three years to reach a cleared five-assay finger-stick panel — one to two years for a comparable cartridge, then a pivotal study and review of the size Vantelle is only now starting. The constraint is evidence, not invention, so Abbott or Siemens could close the gap faster than a start-up.

### Patent position

| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03; Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30; unpublished | Guards the short-fill failure | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11; unpublished | Lead assay chemistry, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01; Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, so the assay anchoring the cardiac use case has no opined cover, and one of five families is in appeal rather than granted. None of the five records could be verified in public patent databases in this run, and the company has no public web presence or FDA clearance record under its name; the portfolio rests entirely on the deck and is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1 |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1 |
| Contract development services | $0.7M | Not disclosed | None stated | S1 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it sells below build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received one free. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, about $700 a site a month at the observed 41 cartridges a site, which covers the instrument quickly but not a direct sales force — the plan's 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-bNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — one leased 18-person plant, six months of stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate and no high-volume line.

The strongest counter-evidence runs the other way. Creatinine and potassium matched the central laboratory in every one of 126 and 125 results, HbA1c in 99.2%, and 34 of the 37 sites in the programme for 90 days or more reordered within 90 days. A rural clinic that waits one to three days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows clinical sensitivity at the cutoff — and the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity at all, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin 99th-percentile value, detection limit and share of healthy adults measurable above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked and whether the answer needs new clinical data; the share of pivotal finger sticks that were haemolysed and whether the cartridge flags haemolysis; line yield, cycle time and stability beyond six months; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and grounds of the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the monthly cartridge volumes behind the utilisation test are unverified company figures, unaudited and not independently confirmed. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. A 13,200-site total is not the problem; utilisation is. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,280 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

::: risk-matrix
| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |
:::

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US, glucose strips, blood gas and infectious disease included; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and the arithmetic works only when four or five analytes are ordered and paid on the same run. Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine on the nearest priced code and $4.76 for potassium, $71.38 if all five are billed and collected. Against a $38 cartridge and a $650 monthly analyzer fee, a site running 41 cartridges a month collects $2,926.58 and pays $2,208, $718.58 of gross margin per analyzer-month before staff time and billing cost. Run only troponin and potassium, the two analytes a chest-pain patient needs, and the clinic collects $17.23 against a $38 cartridge, a loss of $20.77 per run. The company does not disclose ordered tests per cartridge, and that metric decides whether the clinic is a customer or a charity. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico together hold 4,296 moderate-complexity laboratories and 31,720 waived ones. Until the waiver is granted, Vantelle sells into a base one-eighth the size of the one its labour-free pitch addresses, and each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024, and that is the only facility class the policy creates. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. [S81, S79, S95, S1]

::: risk-matrix
| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: Texas, Arizona, New Mexico | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA laboratories across the three states (2026) | US point-of-care 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only, no billable use | Moderate-complexity CLIA certificate and staffed quality control until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital and reference laboratories | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of the United States | $2.89B-$14.0B total US point-of-care market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR, 2026-2034 | Planned after a waiver; 300 sites targeted by end-2027 through a non-binding distributor letter of intent | Same CLIA constraint; payer coverage; no waiver before 2027 | Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Roche, Radiometer, Quest Diagnostics | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15 with no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement, distributor | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens Healthineers | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |
:::

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more, and the company's own clinic survey reports a median daily send-out volume far above what its evaluation sites ran. The survey and the operating data differ by an order of magnitude and only one can describe the commercial site. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, confidence in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests per cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any evaluation site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until those are answered, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price, not in the narrative.

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**

The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in 2026, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M [S1].
:::

rows.benchmark: Truvian founded 2015, $74M raised in 2024, first FDA clearance November 2025, still private in October 2026 - about 11 years; the recommended holding period is 4-5 years from a January 2027 close.
rows.confidence: medium - precedent dates are public but the exit timing is a judgement

rows.follow_up: Would a foreign acquirer need to re-file the 510(k) or re-certify the quality system, and how long would that add?

rows.weakens: A strategic buyer could move earlier, before the waiver, if it wants the cartridge IP and can run the waiver study itself; that would shorten the hold but lower the price.

Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, no offshore holding chain and no founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at about $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out.

The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is buyer and budget owner, paying $2,900 for an analyzer (60% of evaluation sites got theirs free) and $38 a cartridge at a $33.40 average realized price in 2026. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M (evaluation program $1.1M, research-use cartridges $0.8M, contract development $0.7M). Scale depends on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent, so the next two quarters are regulatory, not commercial.

The ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the entity being priced, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and its 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Undisclosed are whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped, and the intercompany terms for Ireland. The arithmetic reproduces the deck exactly: $140.0M / 42,991,881 shares = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The "shares today" column excludes both the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% "today" is 14.89% on the actual pre-money base. The bridge converts $6.28M of principal plus 8% interest at $2.4423, 75% of the round price, into 2,571,392 shares, a 1.33x paper step-up in seven months funded by existing holders.

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted options plus the unallocated pool equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the new pool shares are worth $17.0M at the round price and are created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than a clean 15/170. The deck presents 10% as the pool when the true overhang is double that.

The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A takes $36.0M then participates at 23.75% of the residual, and seed takes $4.5M non-participating. [S100, S98]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, about $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of roughly $9.4M, or 5.5% of post-money. The net cost to the group is lower because Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty whose economics grow with cartridge volume rather than equity value. No arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate is disclosed.

The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat means no founder majority, unlike Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC settlement stripped it and required 18.9M shares returned. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20]

### Six months of cash, a loan that starts amortising, and no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to about 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29. The $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only only until 2027-03, then amortises over 30 months at about $0.167M of principal a month, so a closing slip lands with the first principal payment. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M also includes $2.4M from a stocking order that ships only on clearance, 40.7% of the year.

Six searches on the company name on 2026-10-31 returned no SEC Form D, no state registry record, no USPTO assignee record, no FDA 510(k) decision record and no news; the only near matches were Vanta Diagnostics, a different company, and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, a California LLC filed 2026-09-09. Pending 510(k)s are not published, so this does not test the filing, and absence of indexing is not wrongdoing, but every entity date, ownership percentage and IP claim here rests on company-provided material. arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. That package is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve and the pivotal capillary study hold, and none of the three is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable concentrations above the detection limit in at least 50% of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A 40-microlitre finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator, so the clinic does no separate calibration. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. Results leave over Wi-Fi as HL7 or FHIR [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin detection limit | Not disclosed | 1.61 ng/L (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error in cleared submissions | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% | No independent replication | S1 |
| Sample, time, shelf life, cost | 40 µL, 12 minutes, 9 months claimed on 6 months of data, $16.20 | 22 µL and about 15 minutes (i-STAT); $7.50 at 2 million units | S1, S70 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of about plus or minus 23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II cardiac submission also rests on multi-level precision including the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, interference above all haemolysis, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, intercept, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is roughly 93% to 99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — about 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary high-sensitivity troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the analyte most exposed to haemolysis, which biases it upward and produces false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes, which shows how narrow the handling window is. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. That package is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve and the pivotal capillary study hold, and none of the three is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable concentrations above the detection limit in at least 50% of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A 40-microlitre finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator, so the clinic does no separate calibration. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. Results leave over Wi-Fi as HL7 or FHIR [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin detection limit | Not disclosed | 1.61 ng/L (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error in cleared submissions | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of about plus or minus 23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II cardiac submission also rests on multi-level precision including the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, interference above all haemolysis, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, intercept, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is roughly 93% to 99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — about 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary high-sensitivity troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the analyte most exposed to haemolysis, which biases it upward and produces false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
