arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim, so the advantage lasts only until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships, and it cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is not a startup with better chemistry; it is the incumbent that already owns the buyer's analyser slot. [S1, S67, S104]

The buyer at a three-to-five-site urgent-care operator is choosing between four things, and only one of them is a direct competitor. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a handheld cartridge analyser whose waived menu covers creatinine, potassium, glucose and blood gases and which has carried an hs-troponin I cartridge since 2025-01-03 and an Alinity version since 2026-06-11. Direct but narrower: Siemens epoc, 13 blood-gas, electrolyte and metabolite analytes in under a minute, with no troponin or natriuretic peptide; QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel, troponin I, CK-MB and myoglobin from EDTA whole blood; Roche's cobas h 232, troponin T and NT-proBNP from heparinised venous blood; and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX for hospital emergency departments. Substitute: the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: send the chest-pain patient to the emergency department, or send the sample out and call the patient later. No US product retrieved combines troponin, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium in one finger-stick cartridge, which is the gap the company is selling into. [S104, S6, S2, S107, S108, S111, S109]

::: risk-matrix
| Competitor | Product | Technology | Regulatory status | Performance and menu | Price | Share and scale | Strengths versus Vantelle | Weaknesses versus Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and i-STAT Alinity with hs-TnI cartridge | Handheld cartridge immunoassay and electrochemical | 510(k) cleared hs-TnI on i-STAT 1 (2025-01-03) and Alinity (2026-06-11); separate manual for waived cartridges; CG8+ cleared for capillary whole blood (2023) | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c or NT-proBNP on the same cartridge | Not publicly disclosed | Point of Care line $606M in FY2025 | Waived menu, installed base, capillary claim, distributor reach | One cartridge per test group; no single five-analyte finger-stick card | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc Blood Analysis System | Handheld blood gas, electrolyte and metabolite card | 510(k) cleared; hospital point-of-care | 13 analytes in under one minute; no troponin or natriuretic peptide | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Hospital emergency-department base, informatics, 13-analyte card | No cardiac menu; laboratory-controlled | S107 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro with cardiac panel; Sofia 2 | Fluorescence immunoassay | US cardiac panel sold through waived-test distribution; Cardio3 with BNP not for US sale | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin in about 20 minutes | $599 per 25-test kit, $23.96 a test | $2.73B total FY2025; point-of-care share not disclosed | Urgent-care installed base, lowest price per test | EDTA whole blood or plasma, no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Roche | cobas h 232; LumiraDx platform | Strip immunoassay; microfluidic | cobas h 232 cleared; LumiraDx acquired 2024-07-29 | Troponin T, NT-proBNP, D-dimer, myoglobin | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Global distribution, cardiac menu, owns a finger-stick platform | Venous sample, one test per strip, no HbA1c, creatinine or potassium | S111, S91 |
| Radiometer (Danaher) | AQT90 FLEX | Point-of-care immunoassay, whole blood | Cleared for troponin I/T and NT-proBNP in hospital settings | Laboratory-quality immunoassay | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Emergency-department base and assay quality | Benchtop, laboratory staff, no metabolic panel | S109 |
| Quest Diagnostics | Reference laboratory | Central laboratory | Not applicable | Any test; one-to-three-day turnaround | Per test; $71.38 for the five codes at 2026 Medicare rates | $11.04B in FY2025 | Zero capital, payer contracts, national logistics | Turnaround time is clinically unusable for suspected myocardial infarction | S65, S85, S83, S84, S82, S86 |
:::

Abbott is the one that decides the price. It has the waived path already documented for non-laboratory staff, it cleared the CG8+ cartridge for capillary whole blood in 2023, and it extended hs-troponin from i-STAT 1 to the Alinity in June 2026, which shows it is still investing in point-of-care cardiac testing rather than harvesting it. Its global Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025 against a Rapid Diagnostics segment of $2,454M that fell 18.1% as COVID testing receded; point of care was the growing part, up 3.1%. Its analyser price, cartridge price and installed base are not disclosed in the filing, and that absence is itself a diligence gap: the company should ask its 41 evaluation sites what Abbott quoted them. [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67]

When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert. The Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement already loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% gross margin at a $33.40 realised price and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target depends on two million cartridges a year, roughly 54 times what the 41 evaluation sites consume. An incumbent that bundles a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20 to $25 with a free or nominal-cost analyser takes the account, because the clinic's alternative is to keep paying $38 and a $650 monthly fee. At that price Vantelle's cartridge margin falls from 51% to below 20% on today's cost, and it has no second product to defend the account. [S1, S67, S106]

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and which Vantelle has not yet applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent; the copyable shell is the sample type, the 12-minute run time and the menu, all of which incumbents can assemble from parts they already sell. Sight Diagnostics shows how the regulatory step separates the two: its OLO analyser runs a finger-stick CBC and was cleared in 2021, but for moderately complex rather than waived use, so a finger-stick clearance did not become a labour-free product. The base rate points the same way: LumiraDx's point-of-care platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1]

::: risk-matrix
| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Five-analyte finger-stick cardiac and metabolic panel for clinics without a laboratory | Abbott (i-STAT, waived menu and capillary claim) | Siemens Healthineers (epoc) and Roche (cobas h 232 plus LumiraDx) | QuidelOrtho (Triage cardiac) and Radiometer (AQT90 FLEX) | Sight Diagnostics (finger-stick CBC in the same clinic) and a combined cartridge from any incumbent | S104, S107, S111, S108, S109, S112 |
:::

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and a clinic that has to draw venous blood has not removed the phlebotomist that the product's economics depend on removing. That is a genuine twelve-to-twenty-four-month opening. It is not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; confidence that Vantelle keeps a price premium past 2029 is low. The diligence that would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the 41 evaluation sites today; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived and accepts capillary blood; what price Southwest Clinical Supply's letter of intent implies for 300 sites; and whether the VD-1 patent covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design.

::: evidence
**The buyer's default alternative is a waived Abbott handheld, not a reference lab.**

Abbott cleared hs-troponin for the i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and for the Alinity in June 2026, publishes a waived-test manual for i-STAT 1, and cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's counter-position is one cartridge and five analytes at $38 [S67, S6, S104, S105, S1].
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | One finger stick and one cartridge for five analytes; 12-minute run with on-board calibration; handheld 640-gram device with HL7/FHIR output; $2,900 analyser versus $15,000-$40,000 benchtops; 92% reorder rate across evaluation sites; granted US cartridge patent VD-1 | S1 |
| Weaknesses | Cartridge cost $16.20 at pilot volume against a $7.50 target that needs two million units a year; analyser placed below cost with 60% given free; three of five assays uncleared and no CLIA waiver; no HbA1c or NT-proBNP competition on incumbent handhelds cuts both ways because incumbents can add them; 41 sites and $2.6M revenue | S1 |
| Opportunities | No US product combines all five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge; 233,448 CLIA-waived laboratories and 30,756 moderate-complexity laboratories as the addressable base after a waiver; 39% of urgent-care centers hospital-affiliated but 61% independent or chain-owned; 32 Rural Emergency Hospitals with an emergency department and no inpatient laboratory; Roche's acquisition of LumiraDx shows strategic demand for finger-stick platforms | S81, S79, S95, S91 |
| Threats | Abbott, Siemens, Roche and Radiometer can each add a combined cartridge and bundle it into existing accounts; Abbott already holds a capillary claim and a waived hs-troponin menu; reference laboratories need no capital; CLIA waiver not filed before Q3 2027; LumiraDx and Cue Health set a base rate of platform failure or sale below peak value | S67, S104, S105, S2, S65, S112, S110 |

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at about $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out.

The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is buyer and budget owner, paying $2,900 for an analyzer (60% of evaluation sites got theirs free) and $38 a cartridge at a $33.40 average realized price in 2026. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M. Scale depends on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent, so the next two quarters are regulatory, not commercial.

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Source |

| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware, formed 2018-03-12; HQ Albuquerque, NM | Series B issuer, FDA submitter, owner of patents VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | S99 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona, formed 2022-05-09 | Tempe pilot line, 18 staff, plant lease | 100% parent | S99 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland, formed 2025-01-15 | Future EU regulatory entity; no staff; CE not before 2028 | 100% parent | S99 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas, formed 2016-02-01; 60% acquired 2021-04 | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed exclusively to Vantelle at a 3% royalty | 60% Vantelle; 40% founders, incl. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist at 22% | S99 |

The ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and its 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Undisclosed are whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped, and Ireland's intercompany terms; each matters because an acquirer needs the licence and inherits the put at peak fair value.

The arithmetic reproduces the deck: $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The "shares today" column excludes both the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% "today" is 14.89% on the actual pre-money base. The bridge converts $6.28M of principal plus 8% interest at $2.4423, 75% of the round price, into 2,571,392 shares, a 1.33x paper step-up in seven months.

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the new pool shares are worth $17.0M at the round price and are created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than a clean 15/170.

The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A takes $36.0M then participates at 23.75% of the residual, and seed takes $4.5M non-participating. On an analyst calculation from the deck's share counts, the founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6% of proceeds) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%). The $30M Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs about a $357M exit for 2x; the Series A's 1x participation, which appears in roughly 5% of 2025 deals, is the largest claim on a mid-range exit. [S100, S98]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, about $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of roughly $9.4M, or 5.5% of post-money. The net cost to the group is lower because Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty whose economics grow with cartridge volume rather than equity value. No arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate is disclosed.

The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat means no founder majority, unlike Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC settlement stripped it and required 18.9M shares returned. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20]

### Six months of cash, a loan that starts amortising, and no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to about 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29. arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve and the pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A 40-microlitre finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator, so the clinic does no separate calibration. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. Results leave over Wi-Fi into the clinic's record [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin detection limit | Not disclosed | 1.61 ng/L (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error in cleared submissions | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of about plus or minus 23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is roughly 93% to 99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — about 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1 |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | A workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat; the reader family is in appeal and the lead chemistry has no freedom-to-operate opinion | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

A funded team of 50 with the published patents would need two to three years to reach a cleared five-assay finger-stick panel, then a pivotal study and review of the size Vantelle is only now starting. The constraint is evidence, not invention, so Abbott or Siemens could close the gap faster than a start-up.

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03; Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30; unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11; unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01; Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. None of the five records was verifiable in public patent databases in this run; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1 |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; about $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it sells below build cost and most evaluation sites received one free. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument quickly at observed use but not a direct sales force — the plan's 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased 18-person plant, six months of stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate.

The strongest counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed almost perfectly with the central laboratory, and most sites in the programme for 90 days or more reordered. A rural clinic waiting one to three days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff — and the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity at all, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin 99th-percentile value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond six months; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim, so the advantage lasts only until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships, and it cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is not a startup with better chemistry; it is the incumbent that already owns the buyer's analyser slot. [S1, S67, S104]

The buyer at a three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options, and only one is a direct competitor. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a handheld cartridge analyser whose waived menu covers creatinine, potassium and glucose and which added an hs-troponin I cartridge in January 2025. Direct but narrower: Siemens epoc, 13 blood-gas, electrolyte and metabolite analytes in under a minute with no cardiac marker; QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel from EDTA whole blood; Roche's cobas h 232 from heparinised venous blood; and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX in hospital emergency departments. Substitute: the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call them later. No US product retrieved combines troponin, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium in one finger-stick cartridge, which is the gap the company sells into. [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109]

::: risk-matrix
| Competitor | Product | Regulatory status | Menu | Price | Scale | Strengths versus Vantelle | Weaknesses versus Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and Alinity, hs-TnI cartridge | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 (i-STAT 1) and 2026-06-11 (Alinity); waived-test manual; CG8+ cleared for capillary blood 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c or NT-proBNP on one card | Not publicly disclosed | Point of Care line $606M FY2025 | Waived menu, installed base, capillary claim, distribution | One cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc | 510(k) cleared for hospital point of care | 13 analytes in under a minute; no troponin or natriuretic peptide | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Emergency-department base, informatics | No cardiac menu, laboratory-controlled | S107 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro cardiac panel; Sofia 2 | US cardiac panel sold through waived-test distribution; Cardio3 with BNP not for US sale | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin in about 20 minutes | $599 per 25-test kit, $23.96 a test | $2.73B total FY2025; point-of-care share not disclosed | Urgent-care base, lowest price per test | EDTA blood or plasma, no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Roche | cobas h 232; LumiraDx | Cleared; LumiraDx acquired 2024-07-29 | Troponin T, NT-proBNP, D-dimer, myoglobin | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Global distribution, owns a finger-stick platform | Venous sample, one test per strip, no HbA1c, creatinine or potassium | S111, S91 |
| Radiometer (Danaher) | AQT90 FLEX | Cleared for troponin and NT-proBNP in hospitals | Laboratory-quality immunoassay | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Emergency-department base | Benchtop, laboratory staff, no metabolic panel | S109 |
| Quest Diagnostics | Reference laboratory | Not applicable | Any test; one-to-three-day turnaround | $71.38 for the five codes at 2026 Medicare rates | $11.04B FY2025 | Zero capital, payer contracts, logistics | Turnaround time unusable for suspected myocardial infarction | S65, S85, S83, S84, S82, S86 |
:::

Abbott decides the price. It documents the waived path for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026, which shows it is still investing in point-of-care cardiac testing rather than harvesting it. Its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025 while the wider Rapid Diagnostics segment fell 18.1% as COVID testing receded; point of care grew 3.1%. Analyser price, cartridge price and installed base are not disclosed in the filing, which is itself a diligence gap. [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67]

When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert. The Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% gross margin at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, about 54 times what the 41 evaluation sites consume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20 to $25 with a free analyser takes the account, because the clinic's alternative is to keep paying $38 plus $650 a month. At that price Vantelle's cartridge margin falls below 20% on today's cost, and it has no second product to defend the account. [S1, S67, S106]

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and which Vantelle has not yet applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, all assemblable from parts incumbents already sell. Sight Diagnostics shows how the regulatory step separates the two: its OLO analyser runs a finger-stick CBC and was cleared in 2021 for moderately complex rather than waived use, so a finger-stick clearance did not become a labour-free product. The base rate agrees: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1]

::: risk-matrix
| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Five-analyte finger-stick cardiac and metabolic panel for clinics without a laboratory | Abbott (i-STAT, waived menu, capillary claim) | Siemens Healthineers (epoc) and Roche (cobas h 232 plus LumiraDx) | QuidelOrtho (Triage cardiac) and Radiometer (AQT90 FLEX) | Sight Diagnostics (finger-stick CBC in the same clinic) and a combined cartridge from any incumbent | S104, S107, S111, S108, S109, S112 |
:::

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and a clinic that must draw venous blood has not removed the phlebotomist the economics depend on removing. That is a genuine twelve-to-twenty-four-month opening, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; confidence that Vantelle keeps a premium past 2029 is low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the 41 evaluation sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived and accepts capillary blood; what price Southwest Clinical Supply's letter of intent implies for 300 sites; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design.

::: evidence
**The buyer's default alternative is a waived Abbott handheld, not a reference lab.**

Abbott cleared hs-troponin for the i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and the Alinity in June 2026, publishes a waived-test manual for the i-STAT 1, and cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's counter-position is one cartridge and five analytes at $38 [S67, S6, S104, S105, S1].
:::

Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at about $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out.

The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is buyer and budget owner, paying $2,900 for an analyzer (60% of evaluation sites got theirs free) and $38 a cartridge at a $33.40 average realized price in 2026. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M. Scale depends on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent.

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

The ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and its 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Undisclosed are whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped, and Ireland's intercompany terms; each matters at exit.

The bridge converts $6.28M of principal plus 8% interest at $2.4423, 75% of the round price, into 2,571,392 shares, a 1.33x paper step-up in seven months.

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the new pool shares are worth $17.0M at the round price and are created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than a clean 15/170.

The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A takes $36.0M then participates at 23.75% of the residual, and seed takes $4.5M non-participating. On an analyst calculation from the deck's share counts, the founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6% of proceeds) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%). The $30M Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs about a $357M exit for 2x; the Series A's 1x participation, which appears in roughly 5% of 2025 deals, is the largest claim on a mid-range exit. [S100, S98]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, about $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of roughly $9.4M, or 5.5% of post-money. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty whose economics grow with cartridge volume rather than equity value. No arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate is disclosed.

The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat means no founder majority, unlike Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC settlement stripped it and required 18.9M shares returned. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20]

### Six months of cash, a loan that starts amortising, and no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to about 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29. The $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only only until 2027-03, then amortises over 30 months at about $0.167M of principal a month, so a closing slip lands with the first principal payment. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M also includes $2.4M from a stocking order that ships only on clearance, 40.7% of the year.

Six searches on the company name on 2026-10-31 returned no SEC Form D, no state registry record, no USPTO assignee record, no FDA decision and no news; the only near matches were Vanta Diagnostics, a different company, and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, a California LLC filed 2026-09-09. Pending 510(k)s are not published, so this does not test the filing, and absence of indexing is not wrongdoing, but every entity date, ownership percentage and IP claim here rests on company-provided material. Page 1 also contains a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools asserting that no verification is needed and a rating is approved; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidentiary weight. arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A 40-microlitre finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator, so the clinic does no separate calibration. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. Results leave over Wi-Fi into the clinic's record [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin detection limit | Not disclosed | 1.61 ng/L (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of about plus or minus 23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is roughly 93% to 99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — about 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1 |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | A workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat; the reader family is in appeal and the lead chemistry has no freedom-to-operate opinion | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

A funded team of 50 with the published patents would need two to three years to reach a cleared five-assay panel, then a pivotal study and review of the size Vantelle is only starting. The constraint is evidence, not invention.

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03; Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30; unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11; unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01; Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. None of the five records was verifiable in public patent databases; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1 |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; about $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it sells below build cost and most evaluation sites received one free. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force; the 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased 18-person plant, six months of stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate.

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed almost perfectly with the central laboratory, and most sites in the programme for 90 days or more reordered. A rural clinic waiting one to three days may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin 99th-percentile value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond six months; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim, so the advantage lasts only until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships, and it cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is not a startup with better chemistry; it is the incumbent that already owns the buyer's analyser slot. [S1, S67, S104]

The buyer at a three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options, and only one is a direct competitor. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a handheld cartridge analyser whose waived menu covers creatinine, potassium and glucose and which added an hs-troponin I cartridge in January 2025. Direct but narrower: Siemens epoc, 13 blood-gas, electrolyte and metabolite analytes in under a minute with no cardiac marker; QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel from EDTA whole blood; Roche's cobas h 232 from heparinised venous blood; and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX in hospital emergency departments. Substitute: the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call them later. No US product retrieved combines troponin, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium in one finger-stick cartridge, which is the gap the company sells into. [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109]

Abbott decides the price. It documents the waived path for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026, which shows it is still investing in point-of-care cardiac testing rather than harvesting it. Its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025 while the wider Rapid Diagnostics segment fell 18.1% as COVID testing receded; point of care grew 3.1%. Analyser price, cartridge price and installed base are not disclosed in the filing, which is itself a diligence gap. [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67]

When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert. The Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% gross margin at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, about 54 times what the 41 evaluation sites consume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20 to $25 with a free analyser takes the account, because the clinic's alternative is to keep paying $38 plus $650 a month. At that price Vantelle's cartridge margin falls below 20% on today's cost, and it has no second product to defend the account. [S1, S67, S106]

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and which Vantelle has not yet applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, all assemblable from parts incumbents already sell. Sight Diagnostics shows how the regulatory step separates the two: its OLO analyser runs a finger-stick CBC and was cleared in 2021 for moderately complex rather than waived use, so a finger-stick clearance did not become a labour-free product. The base rate agrees: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1]

| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Five-analyte finger-stick cardiac and metabolic panel for clinics without a laboratory | Abbott (i-STAT, waived menu, capillary claim) | Siemens Healthineers (epoc) and Roche (cobas h 232 plus LumiraDx) | QuidelOrtho (Triage cardiac) and Radiometer (AQT90 FLEX) | Sight Diagnostics (finger-stick CBC in the same clinic) and a combined cartridge from any incumbent | S104, S107, S111, S108, S109, S112 |
:::

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and a clinic that must draw venous blood has not removed the phlebotomist the economics depend on removing. That is a genuine twelve-to-twenty-four-month opening, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; confidence that Vantelle keeps a premium past 2029 is low. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at about $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out.

The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is buyer and budget owner, paying $2,900 for an analyzer (60% of evaluation sites got theirs free) and $38 a cartridge in 2026. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M. Scale depends on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent.

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona, 2022-05-09 | Tempe pilot line, 18 staff, plant lease | 100% parent | S99 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland, 2025-01-15 | Future EU regulatory entity; no staff; CE not before 2028 | 100% parent | S99 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas, 2016-02-01; 60% acquired 2021-04 | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed exclusively to Vantelle at a 3% royalty | 60% Vantelle; 40% founders, incl. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist at 22% | S99 |

The ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and its 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Undisclosed are whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped, and Ireland's intercompany terms; each matters at exit.

### The $140M pre-money is built on 42,991,881 shares, not the 36.4M shown

The arithmetic reproduces the deck: $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The "shares today" column excludes both the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% "today" is 14.89% pre-money. The bridge converts $6.28M of principal plus 8% interest at $2.4423, 75% of the round price, into 2,571,392 shares.

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the new pool shares are worth $17.0M at the round price and are created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than a clean 15/170.

The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A takes $36.0M then participates at 23.75% of the residual, and seed takes $4.5M non-participating. On an analyst calculation from the deck's share counts, the founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6% of proceeds) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%). The $30M Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs about a $357M exit for 2x; the Series A's 1x participation, which appears in roughly 5% of 2025 deals, is the largest claim on a mid-range exit. [S100, S98]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, about $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of roughly $9.4M, or 5.5% of post-money. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty whose economics grow with cartridge volume rather than equity value. No arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate is disclosed.

The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat means no founder majority, unlike Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC settlement stripped it and required 18.9M shares returned. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20]

### Six months of cash, a loan that starts amortising, and no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to about 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29. The $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only only until 2027-03, then amortises over 30 months at about $0.167M of principal a month, so a closing slip lands with the first principal payment. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M also includes $2.4M from a stocking order that ships only on clearance, 40.7% of the year.

Six searches on the company name on 2026-10-31 returned no SEC Form D, no state registry record, no USPTO assignee record, no FDA decision and no news; the only near matches were Vanta Diagnostics, a different company, and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, a California LLC filed 2026-09-09. Pending 510(k)s are not published, so this does not test the filing, but every entity date, ownership percentage and IP claim here rests on company-provided material. Page 1 also contains a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools asserting that no verification is needed and a rating is approved; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidentiary weight. arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A 40-microlitre finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator, so the clinic does no separate calibration. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. Results leave over Wi-Fi into the clinic's record [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin detection limit | Not disclosed | 1.61 ng/L (i-STAT hs-TnI) | S1, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is roughly 93% to 99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — about 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1 |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | A workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat; the reader family is in appeal and the lead chemistry has no freedom-to-operate opinion | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

A funded team of 50 with the published patents would need two to three years to reach a cleared five-assay panel, then a pivotal study and review of the size Vantelle is only starting. The constraint is evidence, not invention.

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03; Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30; unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11; unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01; Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. None of the five records was verifiable in public patent databases; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1 |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; about $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it sells below build cost and most evaluation sites received one free. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force; the 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased 18-person plant, six months of stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate.

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed almost perfectly with the central laboratory, and most sites in the programme for 90 days or more reordered. A rural clinic waiting one to three days may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin 99th-percentile value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond six months; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim, so the advantage lasts only until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships, and it cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is not a startup with better chemistry; it is the incumbent that already owns the buyer's analyser slot. [S1, S67, S104]

The buyer at a three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options, and only one is a direct competitor. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a handheld cartridge analyser whose waived menu covers creatinine, potassium and glucose and which added an hs-troponin I cartridge in January 2025. Direct but narrower: Siemens epoc, 13 blood-gas, electrolyte and metabolite analytes in under a minute with no cardiac marker; QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel from EDTA whole blood; Roche's cobas h 232 from heparinised venous blood; and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX in hospital emergency departments. Substitute: the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call them later. No US product retrieved combines troponin, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium in one finger-stick cartridge, which is the gap the company sells into. [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109]

::: risk-matrix
| Competitor | Product | Regulatory status | Menu | Price | Scale | Strengths versus Vantelle | Weaknesses versus Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and Alinity, hs-TnI cartridge | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11; waived-test manual; CG8+ cleared for capillary blood 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c or NT-proBNP | Not publicly disclosed | Point of Care line $606M FY2025 | Waived menu, installed base, capillary claim, distribution | One cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc | 510(k) cleared for hospital point of care | 13 analytes in under a minute; no troponin or natriuretic peptide | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base, informatics | No cardiac menu, laboratory-controlled | S107 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro cardiac panel | US cardiac panel sold through waived-test channels; Cardio3 with BNP not for US sale | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin in about 20 minutes | $599 per 25-test kit, $23.96 a test | $2.73B total FY2025; point-of-care share not disclosed | Urgent-care base, lowest price per test | EDTA blood or plasma, no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Roche | cobas h 232; LumiraDx | Cleared; LumiraDx acquired 2024-07-29 | Troponin T, NT-proBNP, D-dimer, myoglobin | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Global distribution, owns a finger-stick platform | Venous sample, one test per strip, no metabolic panel | S111, S91 |
| Radiometer (Danaher) | AQT90 FLEX | Cleared for troponin and NT-proBNP in hospitals | Laboratory-quality immunoassay | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base | Benchtop, laboratory staff, no metabolic panel | S109 |
| Quest Diagnostics | Reference laboratory | n/a | Any test; one-to-three-day turnaround | $71.38 for the five codes at 2026 Medicare rates | $11.04B FY2025 | Zero capital, payer contracts | Turnaround unusable for suspected MI | S65, S85, S83, S84, S82, S86 |
:::

Abbott decides the price. It documents the waived path for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026, which shows it is still investing in point-of-care cardiac testing rather than harvesting it. Its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025 while the wider Rapid Diagnostics segment fell 18.1% as COVID testing receded; point of care grew 3.1%. Analyser, cartridge and installed-base data are not disclosed, which is itself a diligence gap. [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67]

When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert. The Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% gross margin at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, about 54 times what the 41 evaluation sites consume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20 to $25 with a free analyser takes the account, because the clinic's alternative is to keep paying $38 plus $650 a month. At that price Vantelle's cartridge margin falls below 20% on today's cost, and it has no second product to defend the account. [S1, S67, S106]

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and which Vantelle has not yet applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, all assemblable from parts incumbents already sell. Sight Diagnostics shows how the regulatory step separates the two: its OLO analyser runs a finger-stick CBC and was cleared in 2021 for moderately complex rather than waived use, so a finger-stick clearance did not become a labour-free product. The base rate agrees: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1]
