arguments.markdown:
At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and the Series A's participating preference means a $30M Series B needs a $435M exit to return 3x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, all company-reported and not independently verified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho, the closest listed comparable, trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

Company-reported financing terms, not independently verified:

| Date | Round | Amount | Price/share | Post-money | Investors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75 (implied) | not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) | S1 |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.9032 | $92.5M | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) | S1 |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.9032 | $104.5M | Existing investors | S1 |
| 2024-03 | Venture term loan | $5.0M | Warrant strike $2.903 | — | Bluestem Venture Lending (400,000 warrants) | S1 |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes, 8% | $6.0M | $2.4423 on conversion | — | Existing investors | S1 |
| 2027-01 (target) | Series B | $30.0M | $3.2564 | $170.0M | Ardent Peak ($5.0M) and Juniper Rock ($3.0M); $22.0M sought | S1 |

The seed priced at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11. The headline pre-money rises 34% from the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but $13.1M of that is the option-pool refresh to 10% of the post-money: existing holders' effective pre-money is $126.9M, a 21% uplift over 2.9 years, or 6.9% a year. Existing shares fall from 100% to 69.7% of the fully diluted company — 7.7 points of pool refresh, 4.9 points of bridge and 17.6 points of new Series B — taking the founders from 30.8% to 21.5%, the seed from 16.5% to 11.5% and the Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%. Insiders are committing $8.0M of the $30.0M, 53% of their $15.2M pro rata, leaving 73% to new investors with no lead named; the $30M is budgeted 35% for clearance, 40% for manufacturing scale and 25% for launch [S1].

### What the price assumes

Our calculations on company-reported projections, which are not independently verified:

| Method | Inputs | Implied pre-money | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2025A revenue | $2.6M × 2.5x | $6.5M | S1 |
| FY2026E ex-stocking | $3.5M × 2.5x | $8.8M | S1 |
| FY2026E ex-stocking at peer median | $3.5M × 5.5x | $19.3M | S1, S28 |
| FY2028P revenue, discounted 2 years | $41.0M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25² | $65.6M | S1 |
| FY2029P revenue, discounted 3 years | $78.5M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25³ | $100.5M | S1 |
| FY2029P earnings, discounted 3 years | $9.0M × 15x ÷ 1.30³ | $61.4M | S1 |
| Capital invested | $40.5M equity + $11.0M debt | $51.5M (ask = 2.7x) | S1 |

| Company | EV | EV/Sales, TTM | P/E, TTM | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho | $1.1B | 0.4x | n/m | Closest point-of-care and cardiac comparable | S22, S23 |
| Abbott | $211.7B | 4.7x | 29.7x | i-STAT, i-STAT Alinity, Afinion | S33, S67 |
| Danaher | $184.2B | 7.2x | 38.1x | Cepheid point-of-care molecular | S34, S35 |
| Bio-Rad | $9.5B | 3.7x | 45.3x | Life-science tools | S36, S37 |
| Thermo Fisher | $295.6B | 6.2x | 36.8x | Mesa Biotech point-of-care molecular | S38, S39 |
| Peer median | — | 5.5x | 37.4x | Diversified tools, not pure-play point of care | S28 |

The methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint, 46% below the ask; the most generous assumes $78.5M of 2029 revenue at 2.5x, discounted three years at 25%, and the $140M pre-money is 2.7x the $51.5M of capital raised so far with no clearance and no waiver. The 5.5x peer median is the wrong benchmark: it is set by diversified tools companies whose point-of-care assets sit inside larger franchises, whereas QuidelOrtho, the only pure-play point-of-care cardiac franchise, has de-rated from 2.9x at FY2022 to 2.3x, 2.4x, 2.1x and 1.7x at its next four year-ends and 0.4x now. A single-product private company with two assays filed should not be underwritten above the best-capitalised public point-of-care franchise in a de-rating market. Werfen, Siemens Healthineers, Roche Diagnostics and Nova Biomedical are not SEC filers or not listed, so their multiples are not disclosed [S1, S22, S28, S67].

### The Series A takes the first $36M and 23.8% of the rest

Our waterfall on the company-reported terms, not independently verified:

| Exit equity value | B + B-1 proceeds | Multiple on $30M | Series A proceeds | Founders' common | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | $36.3M | 1.21x | $52.1M | $23.2M | S1 |
| $197M | $36.3M | 1.21x | $74.2M | $39.0M | S1 |
| $300M | $59.6M | 1.99x | $98.7M | $63.8M | S1 |
| $435M | $90.1M | 3.00x | $130.8M | $96.4M | S1 |
| $518M | $108.8M | 3.63x | $150.5M | $116.5M | S1 |
| $1,370M | $301.1M | 10.04x | $352.9M | $322.3M | S1 |

The preference stack is $76.8M, 55% of the pre-money: Series B and B-1 $36.3M at 1x non-participating and senior, Series A $36.0M at 1x participating, seed $4.5M at 1x non-participating. The new B plus B-1 hold 22.57% of 52.2M fully diluted shares, so at a $140M exit the Series B is capped at its $36.3M preference and returns 1.21x, and it stays at 1.21x up to a $197M exit because the Series A's $36.0M preference and 23.8% participation absorb the increment. At $435M the Series B receives $90.1M, 3.0x on $30M but 2.5x on the $36.3M of B plus B-1, and the Series A takes $130.8M, 30.1% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership; 3x on the full $36.3M needs $518M and 10x on the $30M needs $1.37B. The 40% Corvia minority put, payable at fair value on an acquisition, is worth an estimated $1.5-7.6M from the 3% cartridge royalty capitalised at 8x and is deducted before the stack [S1].

### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.0 per analyser per day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — an eightfold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's operating claims (revenue, 41 sites, 92% reorder rate) are company-reported and not independently verified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools asserting that no verification is needed and prescribing a rating; it is recorded as a document-integrity finding and given no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation removed or capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on 510(k) clearance and CLIA submission), pay-to-play and full pro rata rights, and a Corvia clean-up before closing. At $70M pre-money the Series B would own 36% including B-1 and need a $286M exit for 3x, against $435M today. The alternative is to wait: the 510(k) response is due in December 2026, clearance is guided for Q1 2027 and the waiver application for Q3 2027, so a 2027 entry pays more but buys retired regulatory risk. The company had $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30, six months at $1.15M a month and the 2027-01-29 target close, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts amortising in 2027-03. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the valuation range: the 2029 plan is unaudited, the grant dates of the 5.2M options are not disclosed and Truvian's valuation is an aggregator estimate [S1, S125].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out. The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is buyer and budget owner, paying $2,900 for an analyzer (60% of evaluation sites got theirs free) and $38 a cartridge in 2026. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, with scale dependent on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent. [S99]

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

The ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and its 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Undisclosed are whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped, and Ireland's intercompany terms; each matters at exit. [S99]

The arithmetic reproduces the deck: $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The "shares today" column excludes both the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% "today" is 14.89% pre-money. The bridge converts $6.28M of principal plus 8% interest at $2.4423, 75% of the round price, into 2,571,392 shares. Share counts are company-provided and unverified against the stock ledger. [S99]

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the new pool shares are worth $17.0M at the round price and are created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than 15/170. The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A takes $36.0M then participates at 23.75% of the residual, and seed takes $4.5M non-participating. On an analyst calculation from the deck's share counts, the founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6% of proceeds) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%). The $30M Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs a $357M exit for 2x; the Series A's 1x participation, present in 5% of 2025 deals, is the largest claim on a mid-range exit. [S99, S100, S98]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of $9.4M, or 5.5% of post-money. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty whose economics grow with cartridge volume rather than equity value; no arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate is disclosed. The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat means no founder majority, unlike Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC settlement stripped it and required 18.9M shares returned. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20, S99]

### Six months of cash, a loan that starts amortising, and no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29. The $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only only until 2027-03, then amortises over 30 months at $0.167M of principal a month, so a closing slip lands with the first principal payment. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M also includes $2.4M from a stocking order that ships only on clearance, 40.7% of the year. Six searches on the company name on 2026-10-31 returned no SEC Form D, no state registry record, no USPTO assignee record, no FDA decision and no news; the only near matches were Vanta Diagnostics, a different company, and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, a California LLC filed 2026-09-09. Pending 510(k)s are not published, so this does not test the filing, but every entity date, ownership percentage and IP claim here rests on company-provided material. Page 1 also contains a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools asserting that no verification is needed and a rating is approved; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidentiary weight. Three questions remain open: does the CM-1 licence survive a change of control, is Corvia's 40% put capped, and is any IP pledged to Bluestem? [S99]

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim, so the advantage lasts only until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships, and it cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is not a startup with better chemistry; it is the incumbent that already owns the buyer's analyser slot. [S1, S67, S104]

The buyer at a three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options, and only one is a direct competitor. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a handheld cartridge analyser whose waived menu covers creatinine, potassium and glucose and which added an hs-troponin I cartridge in January 2025. Direct but narrower: Siemens epoc, 13 blood-gas, electrolyte and metabolite analytes in under a minute with no cardiac marker; QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel from EDTA whole blood; Roche's cobas h 232 from heparinised venous blood; and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX in hospital emergency departments. Substitute: the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call them later. No US product retrieved combines troponin, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium in one finger-stick cartridge, which is the gap the company sells into. [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109]

::: risk-matrix
| Competitor | Product | Regulatory status | Menu | Price | Scale | Strengths versus Vantelle | Weaknesses versus Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and Alinity, hs-TnI cartridge | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11; waived-test manual; CG8+ cleared for capillary blood 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c/NT-proBNP | Not publicly disclosed | Point of Care line $606M FY2025 | Waived menu, installed base, capillary claim, distribution | One cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc | 510(k) cleared for hospital point of care | 13 analytes in under a minute; no troponin or natriuretic peptide | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base, informatics | No cardiac menu, laboratory-controlled | S107 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro cardiac panel | US cardiac panel via waived-test channels; Cardio3 with BNP not sold in the US | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin in about 20 minutes | $599 per 25-test kit, $23.96 a test | $2.73B total FY2025; point-of-care share not disclosed | Urgent-care base, lowest price per test | EDTA blood or plasma, no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Roche | cobas h 232; LumiraDx | Cleared; LumiraDx acquired 2024-07-29 | Troponin T, NT-proBNP, D-dimer, myoglobin | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Global distribution; owns LumiraDx | Venous sample, one test per strip, no metabolic panel | S111, S91 |
| Radiometer (Danaher) | AQT90 FLEX | Cleared for troponin and NT-proBNP | Laboratory-quality immunoassay | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base | Benchtop, laboratory staff, no metabolic panel | S109 |
| Quest Diagnostics | Reference laboratory | n/a | Any test; one-to-three-day turnaround | $71.38 for the five codes at 2026 Medicare rates | $11.04B FY2025 | Zero capital, payer contracts | Turnaround unusable for suspected MI | S65, S85, S83, S84, S82, S86 |
:::

Abbott decides the price. It documents the waived path for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026, which shows it is still investing in point-of-care cardiac testing. Its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025 while the wider Rapid Diagnostics segment fell 18.1% as COVID testing receded; point of care grew 3.1%. Analyser, cartridge and installed-base data are not disclosed, which is itself a diligence gap. Set against QuidelOrtho's $2.73B and Quest's $11.04B, Vantelle's $2.6M of FY2025 revenue is a 0.02% share of the smaller competitor. [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67, S22, S65]

When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert. The Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% gross margin at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, about 54 times what the 41 evaluation sites consume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20 to $25 with a free analyser takes the account, because the alternative is $38 plus $650 a month. At that price Vantelle's cartridge margin falls below 20% on today's cost, and it has no second product to defend the account. [S1, S67, S106]

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and which Vantelle has not yet applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, all assemblable from parts incumbents already sell. Sight Diagnostics shows how the regulatory step separates the two: its OLO analyser runs a finger-stick CBC and was cleared in 2021 for moderately complex rather than waived use, so a finger-stick clearance did not become a labour-free product. The base rate agrees: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1]

| Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Vantelle share | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Five-analyte finger-stick cardiac and metabolic panel for clinics without a laboratory | Abbott (i-STAT, waived menu, capillary claim) | Siemens Healthineers (epoc) and Roche (cobas h 232 plus LumiraDx) | QuidelOrtho (Triage cardiac) and Radiometer (AQT90 FLEX) | Sight Diagnostics (finger-stick CBC in the same clinic) and a combined cartridge from any incumbent | 0.3%, on $1.1M of 2025 evaluation revenue against a $368M cartridge market at observed utilisation | S104, S107, S111, S108, S109, S112, S1 |
:::

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per group, and a clinic that must draw venous blood still needs the phlebotomist. That is a genuine opening of a year or two, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; confidence that Vantelle keeps a premium beyond the plan period is low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the evaluation sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived and accepts capillary blood; what price the distributor's letter of intent implies; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design.

::: evidence
**The buyer's default alternative is a waived Abbott handheld, not a reference lab.**

Abbott cleared hs-troponin for the i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and the Alinity in June 2026, publishes a waived-test manual for the i-STAT 1, and cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's counter-position is one cartridge and five analytes at $38 [S67, S6, S104, S105, S1].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1 |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1 |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Replication test, funded team of 50 | — | Cartridge first, then a pivotal study and review of this size | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03; Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07; appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30; unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11; unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01; Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. No public patent record was retrievable; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1 |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it sells below build cost and most evaluation sites received one free, all company data. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force; the 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased 18-person plant, six months of stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate.

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, and most sites reordered. A rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin 99th-percentile value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond the data held; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Replication test, funded team of 50 | — | Cartridge first, then a pivotal study and review of this size | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. No public patent record was retrievable; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it is priced below build cost and given away to many evaluation sites. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force; the 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased 18-person plant, six months of stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate.

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, and most sites reordered. A rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the recent additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond the data held; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

arguments.markdown:
At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and the Series A's participating preference means a $30M Series B needs a $435M exit to return 3x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, all company-reported and not independently verified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho, the closest listed comparable, trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

Company-reported financing terms, not independently verified:

| Date | Round | Amount | Price/share | Post-money | Investors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75 (implied) | not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.9032 | $92.5M | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.9032 | $104.5M | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Venture term loan | $5.0M | Warrant strike $2.903 | — | Bluestem Venture Lending (400,000 warrants) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes, 8% | $6.0M | $2.4423 on conversion | — | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027-01 (target) | Series B | $30.0M | $3.2564 | $170.0M | Ardent Peak ($5.0M) and Juniper Rock ($3.0M); $22.0M sought | S1 (unverified) |

The company-reported, unverified terms show the seed priced at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11. The headline pre-money rises 34% from the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but $13.1M of that is the option-pool refresh to 10% of the post-money: existing holders' effective pre-money is $126.9M, a 21% uplift over 2.9 years, or 6.9% a year. Existing shares fall from 100% to 69.7% of the fully diluted company — 7.7 points of pool refresh, 4.9 points of bridge and 17.6 points of new Series B — taking the founders from 30.8% to 21.5%, the seed from 16.5% to 11.5% and the Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%. Insiders are committing $8.0M of the $30.0M, 53% of their $15.2M pro rata, leaving 73% to new investors with no lead named; the $30M is budgeted 35% for clearance, 40% for manufacturing scale and 25% for launch [S1].

### What the price assumes

Our calculations on company-reported projections, which are not independently verified:

| Method | Inputs | Implied pre-money | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2025A revenue | $2.6M × 2.5x | $6.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2026E ex-stocking | $3.5M × 2.5x | $8.8M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2026E ex-stocking at peer median | $3.5M × 5.5x | $19.3M | S1 (unverified), S28 |
| FY2028P revenue, discounted 2 years | $41.0M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25² | $65.6M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P revenue, discounted 3 years | $78.5M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25³ | $100.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P earnings, discounted 3 years | $9.0M × 15x ÷ 1.30³ | $61.4M | S1 (unverified) |
| Capital invested | $40.5M equity + $11.0M debt | $51.5M (ask = 2.7x) | S1 (unverified) |

| Company | EV | EV/Sales, TTM | P/E, TTM | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho | $1.1B | 0.4x | n/m | Closest point-of-care and cardiac comparable | S22, S23 |
| Abbott | $211.7B | 4.7x | 29.7x | i-STAT, i-STAT Alinity, Afinion | S33, S67 |
| Danaher | $184.2B | 7.2x | 38.1x | Cepheid point-of-care molecular | S34, S35 |
| Bio-Rad | $9.5B | 3.7x | 45.3x | Life-science tools | S36, S37 |
| Thermo Fisher | $295.6B | 6.2x | 36.8x | Mesa Biotech point-of-care molecular | S38, S39 |
| Peer median | — | 5.5x | 37.4x | Diversified tools, not pure-play point of care | S28 |

The methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint, 46% below the ask; the most generous assumes $78.5M of 2029 revenue at 2.5x, discounted three years at 25%, and the $140M pre-money is 2.7x the $51.5M of capital raised so far with no clearance and no waiver. The 5.5x peer median is the wrong benchmark: it is set by diversified tools companies whose point-of-care assets sit inside larger franchises, whereas QuidelOrtho, the only pure-play point-of-care cardiac franchise, has de-rated from 2.9x at FY2022 to 2.3x, 2.4x, 2.1x and 1.7x at its next four year-ends and 0.4x now. A single-product private company with two assays filed should not be underwritten above the best-capitalised public point-of-care franchise in a de-rating market. Werfen, Siemens Healthineers, Roche Diagnostics and Nova Biomedical are not SEC filers or not listed, so their multiples are not disclosed [S1, S22, S28, S67].

### The Series A takes the first $36M and 23.8% of the rest

Our waterfall on the company-reported terms, not independently verified:

| Exit equity value | B + B-1 proceeds | Multiple on $30M | Series A proceeds | Founders' common | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | $36.3M | 1.21x | $52.1M | $23.2M | S1 (unverified) |
| $197M | $36.3M | 1.21x | $74.2M | $39.0M | S1 (unverified) |
| $300M | $59.6M | 1.99x | $98.7M | $63.8M | S1 (unverified) |
| $435M | $90.1M | 3.00x | $130.8M | $96.4M | S1 (unverified) |
| $518M | $108.8M | 3.63x | $150.5M | $116.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| $1,370M | $301.1M | 10.04x | $352.9M | $322.3M | S1 (unverified) |

On the company-reported, unverified preference terms the stack is $76.8M, 55% of the pre-money: Series B and B-1 $36.3M at 1x non-participating and senior, Series A $36.0M at 1x participating, seed $4.5M at 1x non-participating. The new B plus B-1 hold 22.57% of 52.2M fully diluted shares, so at a $140M exit the Series B is capped at its $36.3M preference and returns 1.21x, and it stays at 1.21x up to a $197M exit because the Series A's $36.0M preference and 23.8% participation absorb the increment. At $435M the Series B receives $90.1M, 3.0x on $30M but 2.5x on the $36.3M of B plus B-1, and the Series A takes $130.8M, 30.1% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership; 3x on the full $36.3M needs $518M and 10x on the $30M needs $1.37B. The 40% Corvia minority put, payable at fair value on an acquisition, is worth an estimated $1.5-7.6M from the 3% cartridge royalty capitalised at 8x and is deducted before the stack [S1].

### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.0 per analyser per day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — an eightfold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's operating claims (revenue, 41 sites, 92% reorder rate) are company-reported and not independently verified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools asserting that no verification is needed and prescribing a rating; it is recorded as a document-integrity finding and given no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation removed or capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on 510(k) clearance and CLIA submission), pay-to-play and full pro rata rights, and a Corvia clean-up before closing. At $70M pre-money the Series B would own 36% including B-1 and need a $286M exit for 3x, against $435M today. The alternative is to wait: the 510(k) response is due in December 2026, clearance is guided for Q1 2027 and the waiver application for Q3 2027, so a 2027 entry pays more but buys retired regulatory risk. The company had $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30, six months at $1.15M a month and the 2027-01-29 target close, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts amortising in 2027-03. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the valuation range: the 2029 plan is unaudited, the grant dates of the 5.2M options are not disclosed and Truvian's valuation is an aggregator estimate [S1, S125].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim, so the advantage lasts only until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships, and it cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is not a startup with better chemistry; it is the incumbent that already owns the buyer's analyser slot. [S1, S67, S104]

The buyer at a three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options, and only one is a direct competitor. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a handheld cartridge analyser whose waived menu covers creatinine, potassium and glucose and which added an hs-troponin I cartridge in January 2025. Direct but narrower: Siemens epoc, 13 blood-gas, electrolyte and metabolite analytes in under a minute with no cardiac marker; QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel from EDTA whole blood; Roche's cobas h 232 from heparinised venous blood; and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX in hospital emergency departments. Substitute: the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call them later. No US product retrieved combines troponin, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium in one finger-stick cartridge, which is the gap the company sells into. [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109]

| Competitor | Product | Regulatory status | Menu | Price | Scale | Strengths versus Vantelle | Weaknesses versus Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and Alinity, hs-TnI cartridge | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11; waived-test manual; CG8+ cleared for capillary blood 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c/NT-proBNP | Not publicly disclosed | Point of Care line $606M FY2025 | Waived menu, installed base, capillary claim, distribution | One cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc | 510(k) cleared for hospital point of care | 13 analytes in under a minute; no troponin or natriuretic peptide | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base, informatics | No cardiac menu, laboratory-controlled | S107 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro cardiac panel | US cardiac panel via waived-test channels; Cardio3 with BNP not sold in the US | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin in about 20 minutes | $599 per 25-test kit, $23.96 a test | $2.73B total FY2025; point-of-care share not disclosed | Urgent-care base, lowest price per test | EDTA blood or plasma, no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Roche | cobas h 232; LumiraDx | Cleared; LumiraDx acquired 2024-07-29 | Troponin T, NT-proBNP, D-dimer, myoglobin | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Global distribution; owns LumiraDx | Venous sample, one test per strip, no metabolic panel | S111, S91 |
| Radiometer (Danaher) | AQT90 FLEX | Cleared for troponin and NT-proBNP | Laboratory-quality immunoassay | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base | Benchtop, laboratory staff, no metabolic panel | S109 |
| Quest Diagnostics | Reference laboratory | n/a | Any test; one-to-three-day turnaround | $71.38 for the five codes at 2026 Medicare rates | $11.04B FY2025 | Zero capital, payer contracts | Turnaround unusable for suspected MI | S65, S85, S83, S84, S82, S86 |

Abbott decides the price. It documents the waived path for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026, which shows it is still investing in point-of-care cardiac testing. Its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025 while the wider Rapid Diagnostics segment fell 18.1% as COVID testing receded; point of care grew 3.1%. Analyser, cartridge and installed-base data are not disclosed, which is itself a diligence gap. Set against QuidelOrtho's $2.73B and Quest's $11.04B, Vantelle's $2.6M of FY2025 revenue is a 0.02% share of the smaller competitor. [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67, S22, S65]

When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert. The Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% gross margin at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, about 54 times what the 41 evaluation sites consume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20 to $25 with a free analyser takes the account, because the alternative is $38 plus $650 a month. At that price Vantelle's cartridge margin falls below 20% on today's cost, and it has no second product to defend the account. [S1, S67, S106]

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and which Vantelle has not yet applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, all assemblable from parts incumbents already sell. Sight Diagnostics shows how the regulatory step separates the two: its OLO analyser runs a finger-stick CBC and was cleared in 2021 for moderately complex rather than waived use, so a finger-stick clearance did not become a labour-free product. The base rate agrees: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1]

| Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Vantelle share | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Five-analyte finger-stick cardiac and metabolic panel for clinics without a laboratory | Abbott (i-STAT, waived menu, capillary claim) | Siemens Healthineers (epoc) and Roche (cobas h 232 plus LumiraDx) | QuidelOrtho (Triage cardiac) and Radiometer (AQT90 FLEX) | Sight Diagnostics (finger-stick CBC in the same clinic) and a combined cartridge from any incumbent | 0.3%, on $1.1M of 2025 evaluation revenue against a $368M cartridge market at observed utilisation | S104, S107, S111, S108, S109, S112, S1 |

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per group, and a clinic that must draw venous blood still needs the phlebotomist. That is a genuine opening of a year or two, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; confidence that Vantelle keeps a premium beyond the plan period is low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the evaluation sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived and accepts capillary blood; what price the distributor's letter of intent implies; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design.

::: evidence
**The buyer's default alternative is a waived Abbott handheld, not a reference lab.**

Abbott cleared hs-troponin for the i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and the Alinity in June 2026, publishes a waived-test manual for the i-STAT 1, and cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's counter-position is one cartridge and five analytes at $38 [S67, S6, S104, S105, S1].
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes; 12-minute run with on-board calibration; 640-gram device with HL7/FHIR; $2,900 analyser versus $15,000-$40,000 benchtops; 92% reorder rate across evaluation sites; granted US cartridge patent VD-1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Weaknesses | Cartridge cost $16.20 at pilot volume against a $7.50 target at two million units; analyser below cost and 60% given free; three of five assays uncleared, no CLIA waiver; 41 sites and $2.6M revenue | S1 (unverified) |
| Opportunities | No US product combines all five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge; 233,448 waived and 30,756 moderate-complexity CLIA laboratories as the post-waiver base; 61% of urgent-care centers independent or chain-owned rather than hospital-affiliated; 32 Rural Emergency Hospitals; Roche's LumiraDx purchase shows strategic demand for finger-stick platforms | S81, S79, S95, S91 |

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out. The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is buyer and budget owner, paying $2,900 for an analyzer (60% of evaluation sites got theirs free) and $38 a cartridge in 2026. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, with scale dependent on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent. [S99]

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware, 2018-03-12; HQ Albuquerque, NM | Series B issuer, FDA submitter, owner of patents VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona, 2022-05-09 | Tempe pilot line, 18 staff, plant lease | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland, 2025-01-15 | Future EU regulatory entity; no staff; CE not before 2028 | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas, 2016-02-01; 60% acquired 2021-04 | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed exclusively to Vantelle at a 3% royalty | 60% Vantelle; 40% founders, incl. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist at 22% | Unverified | S99 |

Ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and its 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Undisclosed are whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped, and Ireland's intercompany terms; each matters at exit. [S99]

### The $140M pre-money is built on 42,991,881 shares, not the 36.4M shown

| Shareholder | Class | Shares post-round | % post-money | % votes | Invested | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dr. Wren Albescu | Common | 6,400,000 | 12.26% | 15.32% | n/d | S99 |
| Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist | Common | 4,800,000 | 9.19% | 11.49% | n/d | S99 |
| Juniper Rock and seed investors | Seed preferred | 6,000,000 | 11.49% | 14.36% | $4.5M (4.34x) | S99 |
| Ardent Peak and Series A investors | Series A preferred | 12,400,000 | 23.75% | 29.68% | $36.0M (1.12x) | S99 |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | Common warrants at $2.903 | 400,000 | 0.77% | 0.96% | exercise $1.16M | S99 |
| 2026 bridge noteholders | Series B-1 preferred | 2,571,392 | 4.93% | 6.15% | $6.28M (1.33x) | S99 |
| New Series B investors | Series B preferred | 9,212,627 | 17.65% | 22.05% | $30.0M (1.00x) | S99 |
| Options granted and unallocated pool | Common | 10,420,489 | 19.96% | 0% | strike n/d | S99 |
| **Total** | | **52,204,508** | **100%** | **100%** | | S99 |

The arithmetic reproduces the deck: $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The "shares today" column excludes both the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% "today" is 14.89% pre-money. The bridge converts $6.28M of principal plus 8% interest at $2.4423, 75% of the round price, into 2,571,392 shares. Share counts are unverified against the stock ledger. [S99]

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the new pool shares are worth $17.0M and are created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than 15/170. The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A takes $36.0M then participates at 23.75% of the residual, and seed takes $4.5M non-participating. On an analyst calculation from the deck's share counts, the founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6% of proceeds) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%). The $30M Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs a $357M exit for 2x; the Series A's 1x participation, present in 5% of 2025 deals, is the largest claim on a mid-range exit. [S99, S100, S98]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of $9.4M. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty whose economics grow with cartridge volume rather than equity value; no arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate is disclosed. The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat means no founder majority, unlike Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC settlement stripped it and required 18.9M shares returned. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20, S99]

### Six months of cash, a loan that starts amortising, and no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29. The $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only only until 2027-03, then amortises over 30 months at $0.167M of principal a month, so a closing slip lands with the first principal payment. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M also includes $2.4M from a stocking order that ships only on clearance, 40.7% of the year. Six searches on the company name on 2026-10-31 returned no SEC Form D, no state registry record, no USPTO assignee record, no FDA decision and no news; near matches were Vanta Diagnostics, a different company, and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, a California LLC filed 2026-09-09. Pending 510(k)s are not published, so this does not test the filing, but every entity date, ownership percentage and IP claim here rests on company-provided material. Page 1 contains a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools asserting that no verification is needed and a rating is approved; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidentiary weight. Open questions: does the CM-1 licence survive a change of control, is Corvia's 40% put capped, and is any IP pledged to Bluestem? [S99]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,734 characters)
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified [S1].

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Replication test, funded team of 50 | — | Cartridge first, then a pivotal study and review of this size | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. No public patent record was retrievable; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it is priced below build cost and given away to many evaluation sites. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force; the 8-panels-a-day assumption is load-bearing. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased 18-person plant, six months of stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate.

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, and most sites reordered. A rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the recent additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond the data held; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 4 by Valuation Analyst, 8,616 characters)
At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and the Series A's participating preference means a $30M Series B needs a $435M exit to return 3x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, all company-reported and not independently verified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho, the closest listed comparable, trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

Company-reported financing terms, not independently verified:

The company-reported, unverified terms show the seed priced at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11.
