| FY2028P revenue, discounted 2 years | $41.0M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25² | $65.6M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P revenue, discounted 3 years | $78.5M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25³ | $100.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P earnings, discounted 3 years | $9.0M × 15x ÷ 1.30³ | $61.4M | S1 (unverified) |
| Capital invested | $40.5M equity + $11.0M debt | $51.5M (ask = 2.7x) | S1 (unverified) |

| Company | EV | EV/Sales, TTM | P/E, TTM | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho | $1.1B | 0.4x | n/m | Closest point-of-care and cardiac comparable | S22, S23 |
| Abbott | $211.7B | 4.7x | 29.7x | i-STAT, i-STAT Alinity, Afinion | S33, S67 |
| Danaher | $184.2B | 7.2x | 38.1x | Cepheid point-of-care molecular | S34, S35 |
| Bio-Rad | $9.5B | 3.7x | 45.3x | Life-science tools | S36, S37 |
| Thermo Fisher | $295.6B | 6.2x | 36.8x | Mesa Biotech point-of-care molecular | S38, S39 |

The methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint, 46% below the ask; the most generous assumes $78.5M of 2029 revenue at 2.5x, discounted three years at 25%, and the $140M pre-money is 2.7x the $51.5M of capital raised so far with no clearance and no waiver. The 5.5x peer median is the wrong benchmark: it is set by diversified tools companies whose point-of-care assets sit inside larger franchises, whereas QuidelOrtho, the only pure-play point-of-care cardiac franchise, has de-rated from 2.9x at FY2022 to 2.3x, 2.4x, 2.1x and 1.7x at its next four year-ends and 0.4x now. A single-product private company with two assays filed should not be underwritten above the best-capitalised public point-of-care franchise in a de-rating market. Werfen, Siemens Healthineers, Roche Diagnostics and Nova Biomedical are not SEC filers or not listed, so their multiples are not disclosed [S1, S22, S28, S67].

### The Series A takes the first $36M and 23.8% of the rest

Our waterfall on the company-reported terms, not independently verified:

| Exit equity value | B + B-1 proceeds | Multiple on $30M | Series A proceeds | Founders' common | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | $36.3M | 1.21x | $52.1M | $23.2M | S1 (unverified) |
| $197M | $36.3M | 1.21x | $74.2M | $39.0M | S1 (unverified) |
| $300M | $59.6M | 1.99x | $98.7M | $63.8M | S1 (unverified) |
| $435M | $90.1M | 3.00x | $130.8M | $96.4M | S1 (unverified) |
| $518M | $108.8M | 3.63x | $150.5M | $116.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| $1,370M | $301.1M | 10.04x | $352.9M | $322.3M | S1 (unverified) |

On the company-reported, unverified preference terms the stack is $76.8M, 55% of the pre-money: Series B and B-1 $36.3M at 1x non-participating and senior, Series A $36.0M at 1x participating, seed $4.5M at 1x non-participating. The new B plus B-1 hold 22.57% of 52.2M fully diluted shares, so at a $140M exit the Series B is capped at its $36.3M preference and returns 1.21x, and it stays at 1.21x up to a $197M exit because the Series A's $36.0M preference and 23.8% participation absorb the increment. At $435M the Series B receives $90.1M, 3.0x on $30M but 2.5x on the $36.3M of B plus B-1, and the Series A takes $130.8M, 30.1% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership; 3x on the full $36.3M needs $518M and 10x on the $30M needs $1.37B. The 40% Corvia minority put, payable at fair value on an acquisition, is worth an estimated $1.5-7.6M from the 3% cartridge royalty capitalised at 8x and is deducted before the stack [S1].

### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.22 per analyser per operating day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — a 6.5-fold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's operating claims (revenue, 41 sites, 92% reorder rate) are company-reported and not independently verified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools asserting that no verification is needed and prescribing a rating; it is recorded as a document-integrity finding and given no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation removed or capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on 510(k) clearance and CLIA submission), pay-to-play and full pro rata rights, and a Corvia clean-up before closing. arguments.markdown:
The founders have the right clinical insight and the CTO the right technical pedigree, but the team as disclosed has not taken a cartridge product through a CLIA waiver and a 300-site launch, and the two functions that decide whether it does — regulatory/quality and finance — rest on one 11-month hire and a part-time interim CFO. Of 64 staff, 22 are in R&D, 18 in manufacturing, 9 in clinical and regulatory, 9 in sales and support and 6 in finance and administration; five executives are disclosed. Every CV below is company-provided and unverified: no public source locates any of the five in a Vantelle role. [S99]

Dr. Lindqvist's undergraduate degree is not disclosed.

| Period | Organization | Role | Achievements | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011-2018 | St. Brennan Regional Medical Center; Quillon Diagnostics | Emergency physician; medical director | Six years of emergency practice, then one year in diagnostics before founding Vantelle | Unverified | S99 |
| 2018-03 to present | Vantelle Diagnostics | CEO, co-founder, director | 8.6 years as CEO; 41 evaluation sites signed | Unverified | S99 |
| 2012-2016 / 2016-02 | Pellucid Biosystems; Corvia Microfluidics | Senior scientist, microfluidics; founder | Four years of microfluidics R&D; inventor of the CM-1 sealing patent | Unverified | S99 |
| 2018-03 to present | Vantelle Diagnostics | CTO, co-founder, director | Product and patent families VD-1 to VD-4 | Unverified | S99 |
| 2009-2025 | Meridale Medical | Regulatory affairs manager to director | 14 FDA 510(k) clearances claimed by the deck | Unverified | S99 |
| 2025-11 to present | Vantelle Diagnostics | VP Regulatory and Quality | 510(k) filed 2026-05-18; FDA additional-information request 2026-08-21 | Unverified | S99 |
| 2006-2023 | Tavora Health Systems | Sales representative to regional VP, Southwest | 17 years of Southwest health-system sales | Unverified | S99 |
| 2024-01 to present | Vantelle Diagnostics | VP Commercial | 41 sites and a non-binding 300-site distributor LOI | Unverified | S99 |
| 2014 to present | Whitcombe Advisory | Partner, fractional finance | Part-time interim CFO since 2026-03 | Unverified | S99 |

Dr. Albescu's founder-market fit is specific rather than generic: an emergency physician who practised from 2011 to 2017 and then spent a year as medical director at a diagnostics company has lived the 1-3 day reference-lab wait that the Q5 is designed to remove, and the 41-site evaluation program is evidence she can sell a pilot into clinics. The limit is that 8.6 years as CEO have not yet produced a clearance, a CLIA waiver or a commercial launch, and no prior P&L, FDA submission or distribution build is disclosed. Dr. Lindqvist supplies the technical depth the product depends on — a 2012 bioengineering PhD, four years in microfluidics at Pellucid, then Corvia and the CM-1 patent — but he is also a single point of failure: he is the inventor of the licensed sealing patent, owns 22% of the licensor and receives 0.66% of cartridge sales through it. [S99]

The regulatory function is the thinnest part of the executive bench. Grace Oyelaran joined in 2025-11 and is credited with 14 510(k) clearances across 2009-2025 at Meridale Medical, a claim public records cannot check because the FDA database lists applicants, not individuals. She owns four parallel workstreams: the troponin I and HbA1c file and its additional-information response, the ISO 13485 audit booked for Q1 2027 (not yet certified), the CLIA-waiver application planned for Q3 2027, and EU IVDR readiness through the dormant Irish entity. The FDA's own 510(k) total time to decision averaged 139 days in FY2024 and 112 days in FY2025, and QuidelOrtho describes CLIA-waiver requirements as "onerous" and increasingly costly, so a Q1 2027 clearance after a 2026-12 response and a Q3 2027 waiver are plausible only if the first AI is the last one. [S22, S101]

The commercial bench is sized for a pilot, not a launch. Luis Arrellano's 17 years at Tavora Health Systems map well onto Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, and 9 sales and support staff cover 41 sites at 4.6 sites each; 300 sites would put 33 sites on each person, a 7.2x increase, with the only bridge a non-binding distributor LOI. QuidelOrtho, by contrast, carries more than 2,500 sales, service and marketing employees and about 1,200 service staff worldwide. Manufacturing is similarly thin at the top: 18 staff run the Tempe pilot line, but no VP Manufacturing or VP Quality is named, ISO 13485 certification is still ahead, and the 9-month cartridge shelf life rests on 6 months of data. Cue Health's 2024 warning letter is the relevant precedent: unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow a failure rate above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement put its 9-month stability claim at issue after clearance, not before it. [S99, S22]

The finance and control gap is the easiest to fix and the most revealing. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO on a part-time basis since 2026-03, after the prior CFO left in 2026-02, and the deck discloses no prior operating CFO role or fundraise for him; a $30M institutional round, a $5.0M amortising loan and a $2.4M stocking order booked on a non-binding LOI are being represented by a fractional adviser. Six months of cash makes the hire urgent rather than cosmetic. [S99]

What public records confirm is narrow: the company name returns no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignee or FDA decision record, and near matches — Vanta Diagnostics and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, filed in California on 2026-09-09 — are different entities. Reference checks are therefore the only verification available: Meridale Medical for the 14 clearances and the 2025-09 predecessor's departure; Tavora Health Systems for Arrellano's quota and channel relationships; Quillon Diagnostics and St. Brennan for Albescu; Whitcombe Advisory's other clients; Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock for board behaviour; Southwest Clinical Supply for whether the 300-site LOI names sites; and two pilot-line operators for lot-release discipline at volume. [S99]

The team is a clinical-insight team that has not yet become a regulatory-and-commercial execution team. Who invents is clear — the CTO and the CM-1 patent; who sells is clear — the VP Commercial and the 41-site evaluation base; who raises is the CEO, backed by two existing investors committing $8M of the $30M. The missing hires are a full-time CFO, VP Manufacturing and Operations, VP Quality, a clinical-affairs lead for the 1,150-patient pivotal study, a payer lead and an EU PRRC for Ireland. The $15M lead check should be conditioned on the CFO and Quality hires, verified clearance history and an independent director before money moves.

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is the 41-site paid evaluation program; the strongest doubt is the manufacturing and quality bench that has to scale it.**
Cue Health's FDA warning letter of 2024-05-09 found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow commercially released cartridges to fail above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, with the 9-month shelf life specifically at issue. Vantelle is asking investors to fund a 40% manufacturing scale-up on a line whose ISO 13485 audit has not yet happened and whose shelf-life claim rests on 6 months of data. [S113]
:::

arguments.markdown:
The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 additional-information request restarts a 90-day review clock, putting the first clearance in late March 2027 at the earliest; a CLIA waiver filed in the third quarter of 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's own 150-day goal; and at the 1.35 panels a day the evaluation sites actually run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites, not the 300 the plan reaches by end-2027. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. The FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window that runs to 2027-02-17. FDA's clock resumes on receipt of that answer, so a 90-day review cannot produce a decision before late March 2027, against a 2025 average of 146-149 days. The second submission has a harder dependency: it covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until the second quarter of 2027, so a Q2 2027 filing is not physically possible and a Q3 2027 filing is the earliest realistic date [S1, S69, S92].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to the FDA request | 2026-12 (company plan) | Received 2026-08-21; not answered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 (company) | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on the answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S92 |
| Pivotal study results, four sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary-venous equivalence, intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k), NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q2 2027 (company) | Depends on pivotal results due the same quarter | Five-assay menu | S1, unverified |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 (company) | Not filed; must reference a cleared application and include flex and user studies | Waived status, the gate to urgent care | S1, S72 |
| CLIA waiver decision | No company date | 150 FDA days after filing implies Q1 2028 at the earliest | Whether 2028 revenue is reachable | S72 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use only | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset in the plan and the one scheduled latest. A waiver submission references an already cleared application and must carry a risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended sites; FDA's goal is a substantive interaction within 90 review days and a decision within 150 FDA days. Filing in Q3 2027 therefore points to a decision around the first quarter of 2028, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. Until then the panel is a moderate-complexity test that only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified, competency-assessed staff may run; a Certificate of Waiver site cannot legally run it. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are therefore hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics that make up the serviceable market in the deck. The dual 510(k) and CLIA waiver pathway used by point-of-care peers would put both decisions on one 180-day goal [S72, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: evaluation sites averaged 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites in 2026, which is 41 cartridges a site a month, or 1.35 a day. The model assumes 8 panels a day from 2028, a 5.9-fold step-change, and the site plan does not fill the gap: 300 sites at model utilisation and the $31 2029 cartridge price produce $22.3M, not $78.5M. Reaching $78.5M requires 1,055 sites at model utilisation or 5,150 at the observed rate; $41.0M in 2028 requires 551 sites at model utilisation. The 2027 line is tighter still: $16.8M with an average of 150 sites implies full 8-a-day use from the first day of the year plus the $2.4M stocking order and instrument sales — no ramp at all, and only two assays on the menu for most of it [S1].

### Two of the plan's own numbers fail a timing test

FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from the distributor that ships on 510(k) clearance, which the company itself expects in the first quarter of 2027. That is 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026 as scheduled, and it flatters the growth rate into 2027. Separately, the 61% FY2026E gross margin sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below build cost, so either an undisclosed high-margin line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic. Neither error is fatal alone; together they suggest a top-down projection [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. Start from $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, and subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of term-loan principal once the Bluestem loan starts amortising in April 2027: $10.9M remains at the end of 2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory needed for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, so the realistic path is an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1 |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1 |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1 |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1 |

The distributor relationship is the commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme, and it is a letter of intent from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner — a related-party cost that belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridge sales and contract development are revenue but second curves that consume the same engineering team; the Irish entity and a CE mark are a distraction from the only market that matters in this round.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second additional-information letter | Second letter in the first half of 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Pivotal data show capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level, troponin CV below 10% | Results reported as categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver filed after clearance with no pre-submission | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready for scale | ISO 13485 certificate issued; automation ordered for Tempe | Audit slipped, no automation order by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount still in single digits against a 300-site plan | S1 |

Counter-evidence deserves weight. The company hired a regulatory vice-president with a record of 510(k) clearances, the pipeline of paid evaluation sites and a high reorder rate is unusual for an investigational device, and if the recent request was documentation-only a Q1 2027 clearance remains possible. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the recent request asked and what evidence the pending answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual 510(k) and waiver submission; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers and what triggers the next round; and whether the distributor letter carries any minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing judgement is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel.

Dr. Albescu's founder-market fit is specific rather than generic: an emergency physician who practised from 2011 to 2017 and then spent a year as medical director at a diagnostics company has lived the 1-3 day reference-lab wait that the Q5 is designed to remove, and the 41-site evaluation program is evidence she can sell a pilot into clinics. The limit is that 8.6 years as CEO have not yet produced a clearance, a CLIA waiver or a commercial launch, and no prior P&L, FDA submission or distribution build is publicly disclosed; the CV itself is unverified. Dr. Lindqvist supplies the technical depth the product depends on — a 2012 bioengineering PhD, four years in microfluidics at Pellucid, then Corvia and the CM-1 patent — but he is also a single point of failure: he is the inventor of the licensed sealing patent, owns 22% of the licensor and receives 0.66% of cartridge sales through it. [S99]

The regulatory function is the thinnest part of the executive bench. Grace Oyelaran joined in 2025-11 and is credited with 14 510(k) clearances across 2009-2025 at Meridale Medical, a claim public records cannot check because the FDA database lists applicants, not individuals. She owns four parallel workstreams: the troponin I and HbA1c file and its additional-information response, the ISO 13485 audit booked for Q1 2027 (not yet certified), the CLIA-waiver application planned for Q3 2027, and EU IVDR readiness through the dormant Irish entity. The FDA's own 510(k) total time to decision averaged 139 days in FY2024 and 112 days in FY2025, and QuidelOrtho describes CLIA-waiver requirements as "onerous", so a Q1 2027 clearance after a 2026-12 response and a Q3 2027 waiver are plausible only if the first AI is the last one. [S22, S101]

The commercial bench is sized for a pilot, not a launch. Luis Arrellano's 17 years at Tavora Health Systems map well onto Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, and 9 sales and support staff cover 41 sites; 300 sites would put 33 sites on each person, with the only bridge a non-binding distributor LOI. QuidelOrtho, by contrast, carries more than 2,500 sales, service and marketing employees and about 1,200 service staff. Manufacturing is similarly thin at the top: 18 staff run the Tempe pilot line, but no VP Manufacturing or VP Quality is named, ISO 13485 certification is still ahead, and the 9-month cartridge shelf life rests on 6 months of data. Cue Health's 2024 warning letter is the relevant precedent: unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow a failure rate above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement put its 9-month stability claim at issue after clearance, not before it. [S99, S22]

The finance and control gap is the easiest to fix and the most revealing. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO on a part-time basis since 2026-03, after the prior CFO left in 2026-02, and the deck discloses no prior operating CFO role or fundraise for him; a $30M institutional round, a $5.0M amortising loan and a $2.4M stocking order booked on a non-binding LOI are being represented by a fractional adviser, and these terms are company-provided and unverified. Six months of cash makes the hire urgent rather than cosmetic. What public records confirm is narrow: the company name returns no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignee or FDA decision record, and near matches — Vanta Diagnostics and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, filed in California on 2026-09-09 — are different entities. Reference checks are therefore the only verification available: Meridale Medical for the 14 clearances and the 2025-09 predecessor's departure; Tavora Health Systems for Arrellano's quota and channel relationships; Quillon Diagnostics and St. Brennan for Albescu; Whitcombe Advisory's other clients; Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock for board behaviour; Southwest Clinical Supply for whether the 300-site LOI names sites; and two pilot-line operators for lot-release discipline at volume. [S99]

The team is a clinical-insight team that has not yet become a regulatory-and-commercial execution team. Who invents is clear — the CTO and the CM-1 patent; who sells is clear — the VP Commercial and the evaluation base; who raises is the CEO, backed by two existing investors. The missing hires are a full-time CFO, VP Manufacturing and Operations, VP Quality, a clinical-affairs lead for the pivotal study, a payer lead and an EU PRRC for Ireland. The lead check should be conditioned on the CFO and Quality hires, verified clearance history and an independent director before money moves.

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is the 41-site paid evaluation program; the strongest doubt is the manufacturing and quality bench that has to scale it.**
Cue Health's FDA warning letter of 2024-05-09 found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow commercially released cartridges to fail above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, with the 9-month shelf life specifically at issue. Vantelle is asking investors to fund a 40% manufacturing scale-up on a line whose ISO 13485 audit has not yet happened and whose shelf-life claim rests on 6 months of data. [S113]
:::

2. The problem
Urgent-care clinics and rural hospitals without an on-site laboratory send cardiac and metabolic blood tests to reference labs and wait 1-3 days for
results. Patients with chest pain or uncontrolled diabetes are often transferred, or sent home, before results arrive.
-  A transfer for a suspected heart attack that turns out negative costs thousands of dollars and takes a rural ambulance out of service for hours
(company estimate).
-  Benchtop analyzers that could run these tests on site need venous blood, a trained operator and daily quality control, which small clinics can't staff.
-  The clinics we surveyed send out a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels a day (company survey of 52 clinics, 2024).
Vantelle Diagnostics: Series B investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 2 of 15

--- p.3 ---
3. Our product: the Vantelle Q5
-  A handheld, cartridge-based analyzer that runs a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel from a finger-stick sample in 12 minutes.
-  The panel: high-sensitivity troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine (with eGFR) and potassium.
-  One 40-microliter drop of blood. Each cartridge holds all its reagents and an on-board calibrator, so there is no separate calibration step.
-  The analyzer weighs 640 grams, runs on a battery and sends results to the clinic's electronic health record over Wi-Fi (HL7 and FHIR).
-  Razor-and-blade model: instruments placed at or near cost; recurring revenue from single-use cartridges.
-  Cartridges keep for 9 months at room temperature (our stability data so far covers 6 months).
Vantelle Diagnostics: Series B investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 3 of 15

4. Clinical performance
-  Lab-grade accuracy: 98.7% agreement with central-lab results in our internal study of 640 samples (company data).

## Integration into the Analysis Workflow

### When to Trigger This Lens

Trigger when the company belongs to:
- Biotech/medtech/pharma → NMPA/CDE/NHSA databases
- SOE or SOE supply chain → SASAC/procurement databases
- Semiconductor/advanced manufacturing → MIIT/CNIPA databases
- AI/internet/platform → CAC algorithm registry
- Aerospace/satellite → CAAC and SASTIND databases
- Fintech/payment → PBOC/NFRA license databases
- Energy/nuclear → NEA/NNSA databases
- Any company → gsxt.gov.cn (business registration) + wenshu.court.gov.cn (litigation check) as baseline

### Workflow Steps

1. **Before research:** Identify the company's industry → map to regulatory databases using the tables above.
2. **During web search:** Include 2-3 targeted searches against each relevant public registry.
3. **If account-gated:** Emit a User Data Request using the template.
4. **If information cannot be obtained:** Explicitly note in the report: "[information type] could not be obtained from [database name]; it has [importance level] importance for [dimension of the investment judgement]. Ask the company for it in diligence."
5. **When user provides files:** Treat them as primary-source evidence (confidence: high), cite by filename and issuing agency.

### Data Hierarchy

Regulatory data ranks at the top of the evidence hierarchy:

```
1. Court judgments / regulatory filings (the root source) ← HIGHEST CONFIDENCE
2. Government-issued licenses / certificates
3. Procurement contract awards (ccgp.gov.cn)
4. Patent office records (CNIPA/USPTO)
5. Public company filings (annual reports and prospectuses via CNINFO)
   --- "hard evidence" line ---
6. Company-provided materials (pitch decks, internal reports)
7. Media reports / industry analysis
8. OCR-derived text from scanned documents ← LOWEST CONFIDENCE
```

Anything below the "hard evidence" line should be cross-verified against something above it whenever possible.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: analysis_core.md > Mandatory Evidence Gate

## Mandatory Evidence Gate

Do not draft the final report until every material section has an evidence packet in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`. Evidence may include public web sources, user-provided files, filings, databases, industry reports, patents, job posts, media interviews, customer/procurement records, or clearly labelled analyst estimates.

Minimum evidence packet per section:

| Required item | Minimum standard |
| --- | --- |
| Search work | 3-6 targeted queries unless user-provided materials are sufficient. |
| Sources opened | At least 2 independent sources; 3+ for market, competition, team, funding, financials, and risk when public data exists. |
| Source IDs | At least 2 distinct source IDs per section in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`; the final HTML should usually show 3+ distinct source IDs per major section. |
| Primary/source-of-truth check | At least 1 primary or near-primary source where available: filing, company page, registry, patent, investor announcement, regulatory record, official report, customer/procurement record. |
| Mechanism | Explain how the evidence changes economics, adoption, pricing power, risk, financing need, valuation, or exit probability. A fact without mechanism is not analysis. |
| Public-equity source-of-truth | For listed companies, use primary filings or company IR for financial statements and record market data timestamp, exchange, currency, latest price, market cap, and enterprise value if available. |
| Public-equity financial analysis | For listed companies, analyze income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, notes/accounting quality, valuation, peer comparison, and stock-price context before making a recommendation. |
| Company-claim verification | Mark material pitch-deck claims as verified, partially verified, unverified, contradicted, or not publicly disclosed. |
| Quantification | At least 2 numbers, ranges, or proxies for measurable sections; if unavailable, state what evidence is missing. |
| Comparison | At least 1 competitor, benchmark, base rate, industry norm, or historical comparable. |
| Counter-evidence | At least 1 contradicting source, weakness, adverse case, or reason the thesis may fail. |
| Investor implication | A decision-relevant conclusion: invest, pass, wait, lower valuation, add condition, or request diligence. |

The `_work/evidence_matrix.md` table is a hard gate. Each section's `Deep Evidence Table` must contain source IDs, source type, finding/fact, mechanism, benchmark or peer context, weakening evidence, investor implication, confidence, and follow-up. Do not mark a section complete by checking boxes unless those cells contain section-specific content.

Evidence gate failure rules:

- If a section has only company-provided material, write it as low-confidence and do not make a strong positive claim.
- If no independent source can verify a claim, explicitly say `not independently verified`.
- If a section lacks counter-evidence, add a red-team paragraph with the most plausible failure mode.
- If a section lacks quantification, state which metric is missing and how it affects investment confidence.
- If a section lacks peer/benchmark context, do not score it above 7/10.
- For a public-equity report, do not issue Buy/Add/Sell/Reduce before analyzing latest price/valuation, income statement quality, margin drivers, cash flow conversion, working capital, capex, balance-sheet health, accounting notes, debt/liquidity, capital allocation, and downside risk. If financial statements or price data cannot be obtained, make that the central limitation and use Watchlist/Hold off unless the user only asked for a preliminary screen.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: policy_geopolitics_lens.md

# Policy and Geopolitics Lens

Use this file when policy, national strategy, international relations, regulation, government procurement, export controls, sanctions, data security, strategic industries, or cross-border supply chains can materially affect market size, competition, valuation, risk, or exit.

Do not impose one country's policy logic on every company. First identify the relevant jurisdictions and the report's investment perspective.

## Trigger Conditions

Read this lens when any of these are true:

- The company operates in a regulated or license-dependent market.
- The industry is strategic: aerospace, defense, semiconductors, AI, energy, biotech, medtech, telecom, cybersecurity, data infrastructure, finance, transportation, agriculture, critical minerals, or advanced manufacturing.
- Customers, revenue, subsidies, procurement, or approvals depend on government budgets or policy continuity.
- The product is dual-use, export-controlled, sanction-sensitive, or dependent on foreign components, cloud, models, chips, instruments, materials, data, or IP.
- Overseas expansion, listing, M&A, financing, supply chain, or exit depends on international market access.

## Jurisdiction and Perspective Setup

Before analysis, map:

- **Company base**: incorporation, headquarters, R&D, manufacturing, data hosting, operating licenses.
- **Revenue markets**: current customers, target customers, government or enterprise budget owners.
- **Supply chain**: critical suppliers, components, cloud/models/chips, instruments, IP, and data flows.
- **Capital and exit path**: investor jurisdiction, listing venue, likely acquirers, foreign-investment review exposure.
- **Reader perspective**: domestic investor, international investor, strategic buyer, public-market investor, or primary-market investor.

Then choose the lens:

| Situation | Primary policy lens |
| --- | --- |
| China company serving China market | central policy, local implementation, procurement, industrial catalogs, subsidies, data/security reviews, domestic substitution, local-government payment risk |
| China company going global | China outbound rules plus target-market access, sanctions/export controls, tariffs, foreign-investment review, overseas compliance, brand/geopolitical perception |
| US company | federal/state regulation, procurement, export controls, CFIUS, antitrust, IRA/CHIPS/health/defense/data rules as relevant, international sales restrictions |
| European company | EU-level regulation, member-state implementation, GDPR/data, CE/MDR/EMA/energy/AI Act as relevant, state aid, procurement, trade and supply-chain rules |
| Cross-border supply chain | home market + supplier market + customer market + financing/listing market + likely acquirer market |
| Global category leader | compare US/EU/China policy regimes and ask which regime creates advantage, compliance cost, or market-access constraint |

If the company location is uncertain, state the uncertainty and analyze the jurisdictions that could materially change the conclusion.

## Analysis Questions

Answer only the questions that matter for the company:

1. **National / regional strategy fit**: Is the company aligned with national, regional, state, EU-level, or international policy priorities? Is policy support structural demand or temporary subsidy?
2. **Regulatory path**: What licenses, approvals, certifications, safety reviews, reimbursement rules, data rules, or procurement qualifications are required?
3. **Government customer / budget**: Who controls the budget, how long is procurement, how reliable is payment, and can policy changes delay revenue?
4. **International exposure**: What export controls, sanctions, tariffs, foreign investment reviews, data-transfer rules, or market-access barriers matter?
5. **Supply-chain sovereignty**: Which components, chips, instruments, materials, software, cloud services, or IP create choke points?
6. **Standards and certification**: Does the company benefit from or depend on technical standards, industry certifications, safety regimes, or international bodies?
7. **Policy upside vs. policy trap**: Does policy create a moat/catalyst, or does it inflate TAM, invite crowded competition, and reduce pricing power?
8. **Investment implication**: How should policy change valuation, timeline, probability of milestones, required diligence, downside case, and exit route?

## Evidence Sources

Prefer primary or near-primary sources:

- Laws, regulations, regulatory drafts, enforcement actions, licenses, procurement notices, official budgets, government plans, industry catalogs, standards bodies, export-control lists, sanctions lists, customs/tariff rules, official statistical releases, and stock-exchange filings.
- For China-related analysis, check central policy, provincial/local implementation, procurement catalogs, subsidies, standards, industrial parks, data/security review, and domestic-substitution rules separately. Local support is not the same as national demand.
- For US-related analysis, separate federal and state rules; check agency guidance, procurement, export controls, sanctions, CFIUS, antitrust, sector regulators, and subsidy/industrial-policy programs when relevant.
- For Europe-related analysis, separate EU-level regulation from member-state implementation; check GDPR/data transfer, product certification, sector regulators, state aid, procurement, and EU trade/supply-chain rules when relevant.
- For international exposure, compare the rules in the company's home market, target market, supplier market, financing/listing market, and likely acquirer market.

## Report Integration

Do not write a generic policy essay. Integrate findings into:

- Market and industry: TAM/SAM/SOM, adoption timing, subsidy dependence, government budget, replacement cycle.
- Competition: protected incumbents, national champions, local-content rules, foreign competitors blocked or advantaged.
- Product and technology: certification, safety, dual-use constraints, standards, export-control sensitivity.
- Business model and financials: procurement cycle, payment risk, margin pressure from policy pricing, capex/subsidy dependency.
- Risk: policy reversal, compliance breach, sanctions, data-security review, local-government payment delay, supply-chain interruption.
- Valuation and exit: policy-driven discount/premium, IPO/M&A restrictions, foreign buyer limits, lock-up or national-security review.

If the lens is not material, state briefly: `Policy and geopolitical factors: no policy or cross-border constraints material to the investment conclusion were found.`"}],"isError":false}

## The Granularity Benchmark

Professional investment analysis is defined by **specificity**, not length. A 200-page report that uses vague language is worse than a 50-page report where every claim has a number attached. The following standards are non-negotiable:

### Numbers Must Be Precise
- ❌ "approximately 45%" → ✅ "43.1373%" or "43.1%" (state source and confidence)
- ❌ "hundreds of patents" → ✅ "69 granted patents + 12 pending across US/CN/EP"
- ❌ "founded in 2023" → ✅ "2023-10-15" or "2023-10"
- ❌ "raised several hundred million" → ✅ "$75M Series B at $450M pre-money (2025-03-15)"
- ❌ "large facility" → ✅ "16,000 m², including GMP plants for Class II and III active medical devices"

### People Must Be Traceable
- ❌ "graduated from a well-known university" → ✅ "BS, University of Science and Technology of China, mechatronic engineering; MS, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, software engineering"
- ❌ "has worked at several companies" → ✅ each role: company + title + dates + specific achievements
- ❌ "industry veteran" → ✅ "69 peer-reviewed papers; previously head of clinical partnerships at Neuralink"
- Every founder bio must trace from undergraduate through highest degree
- Every key hire must have: institution + degree + year + prior employer + role + achievements

### Events Must Be Dated
- ❌ "recently completed funding" → ✅ "on 2026-06-26, phase 1 of the super factory was completed and began operating"
- ❌ "has partnerships with hospitals" → ✅ "joint laboratories with Huashan Hospital (Shanghai), Shanghai Mental Health Center and West China Hospital"
- ❌ "attended by investors" → ✅ "the ribbon cutting was attended by Ji Wei of Huaying Capital, Zhang Song of Qingsong Capital, Tang Qibo of Gobi Partners and Gu Jie of Fourier"

### If Data Is Unavailable
- State EXACTLY what is missing (e.g., "registered capital not disclosed" not "insufficient information")
- Explain how material the gap is to the investment decision
- List what source would resolve it (e.g., "needs the business registration file")
- NEVER fill the gap with vague language that sounds informative but conveys no data

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: analysis_core.md > Section Writing Contract

## Section Writing Contract

Each final section must cover the full analytical logic, but it should read like an investment memo, not a compliance checklist. Use judgement, evidence, mechanism, comparison, counter-evidence, investor implication, confidence, and diligence questions as the internal reasoning scaffold. Do not force every section to show the same subheadings such as `Judgement / Evidence / Mechanism / Benchmark / Counter-evidence / Investor implication / Open questions`.

The final report should not become pure black text on a white background. Use visual hierarchy and compact evidence displays to make dense analysis readable, while avoiding repetitive card stacks.

Internal workflow language must not appear in the final report. Never write sentences that explain how the section should be written, such as `this section must put the evidence grade ... in one logical chain`, `cannot be written as`, `rather than splitting the material into isolated facts`, or `source IDs are only used to lock down where the evidence came from`. The final report should analyze the company, not describe the report-writing rubric.

Preferred section shape:

1. Start with a short thesis sentence that states the section-level judgement.
2. Explain the evidence in narrative paragraphs, weaving in source confidence, dates, and specific numbers.
3. Show why the evidence matters economically or strategically.
4. Compare with peers, substitutes, base rates, or historical analogs where it changes the decision.
5. Bring the main weakness or contrary evidence into the same discussion rather than isolating it mechanically.
6. End with the investor implication and the most decision-relevant open questions.

Use tables, KPI strips, risk matrices, scenario tables, or short callout cards when they improve scanability. Use explicit micro-headings only when they fit the section's content, not as a repeated template. Good micro-headings are content-specific, for example `Cash flow quality is weaker than the income statement`, `The regulatory path is the source of the valuation discount`, or `Customer validation is still at the pilot stage`.

Recommended readable section pattern:

- 1 short opening judgement paragraph.
- 2-4 analytical paragraphs, each with a clear point and evidence.
- 1 compact visual element when useful: KPI dashboard, mini table, risk matrix, timeline, scenario table, or source/confidence callout.
- 1 short closing sentence or small callout for investor implication/open question.

Use visual components selectively:

- Use a KPI/dashboard strip for numbers that need comparison.
- Use a table for peers, financial trends, milestone gates, or scenario assumptions.
- Use warning/danger callouts for decision-changing risks, not every weakness.
- Use source/confidence tags inline or at paragraph ends to preserve credibility without interrupting flow.
- Use bullets only for short lists; avoid long bullet walls.

Avoid rigid writing patterns:

- Do not write `{section name} judgement`, `{section name} mechanism`, `{section name} benchmark`, `{section name} original-document priority`, `{section name} decision threshold`, or `{section name} decision checklist`.
- Do not repeat the same seven labels in every section.
- Do not make each section a stack of independent bullet cards.
- Do not replace structured cards with unbroken long paragraphs.
- Do not put evidence in one box and interpretation in another when a paragraph would read better.
- Do not add a token "benchmark" or "counter-evidence" sentence just to satisfy the form; integrate comparison and counter-evidence into the argument.
- Do not hide the recommendation until the end of a long fact list.
- Do not append the same `How investors should read this`, `Source`, `Key figures`, `Still to confirm`, or generic transaction-structure paragraph to every section. If a reader would recognize the paragraph from another section, rewrite it as section-specific analysis or delete it.
- Put full citations in one `Source Appendix` module. Inline source/confidence tags should support the most important claims, not repeat the same source list in every paragraph.

Avoid shallow claims unless evidence-backed:

- "Market space is large."
- "Team background is strong."
- "Technology has barriers."
- "Business model is scalable."
- "Competition is intense."
- "Risks are controllable."

Rewrite them into concrete questions: which market segment, which team achievement, which moat type, which scaling constraint, which competitor, and which risk-mitigation milestone.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: regulatory_database_lens.md > The User Data Request Protocol

## The User Data Request Protocol

When the analyst hits an account-gated or restricted database, do NOT silently skip it. Instead, emit a specific, actionable request to the user.

### Request Template

```markdown
### 📋 Regulatory database information request

To improve the data quality of the [company name] analysis, the following information is needed from regulatory databases:

| # | Database | What to look up | Why it matters | How to get it |
|---|--------|---------------|-----------|---------|
| 1 | [database name] | [what exactly to look up] | [effect on the investment judgement] | [how to get it: public URL, login path, permissions needed] |

**Any of these files would significantly raise the report's confidence:**
- [ ] [file name or screenshot type 1]
- [ ] [file name or screenshot type 2]
```

### Industry-Specific Request Templates

#### Biotech/Medtech

```markdown
### 📋 Drug regulator data request

These data are essential to valuing the product pipeline of [company name]:

1. **CDE review status:** log in at https://www.cde.org.cn, look up [drug name or acceptance number] under the accepted applications, and send a screenshot of its review status and timeline.
2. **Clinical trial details:** at http://www.chinadrugtrials.org.cn, search [company or drug name] and export the trial phase, enrollment, primary endpoints and status history.
3. **Medical device registration certificate:** in the NMPA's device lookup, enter [company name] and send a screenshot of the certificate number, expiry and product scope.
4. **Reimbursement list status:** search the latest NRDL and confirm whether [drug name] is listed, its negotiated price and its reimbursement ratio.

**Why it matters:** these data directly set the pipeline's valuation. The odds of a Phase III trial, a device's registration progress or a drug's reimbursement price can each move the valuation by billions.
```

#### SOE/Infrastructure

```markdown
### 📋 SASAC and government procurement data request

1. **Central SOE equity registration:** through SASAC or an equity exchange, look up [company name]'s state ownership structure and confirm the level of its actual controller.
2. **Government procurement awards:** at https://www.ccgp.gov.cn, search [company name] and export the awards of the last 3 years, with amounts and buyers.
3. **Little giant designation:** on the MIIT site, check whether [company name] is on the "little giant" list, and at which level (national or provincial).
```

#### Semiconductor

```markdown
### 📋 MIIT and intellectual property data request

1. **Integrated circuit enterprise qualification:** confirm whether [company name] is on MIIT's list of qualified integrated circuit enterprises.
2. **Big Fund investments:** check whether the portfolio of the China Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund (Big Fund phases I, II and III) includes [company name].
3. **Legal status of core patents:** at CNIPA (https://www.cnipa.gov.cn), look up the legal status (valid, invalid, pledged or licensed) of [list of patent numbers].
```

The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Replication test, funded team of 50 | — | Cartridge first, then a pivotal study and review of this size | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. No public patent record was retrievable; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |
| Medicare reimbursement, 2026 | $71.38 for all five assays; $17.23 for troponin plus potassium | Cartridge list $38 | The panel only pays if most assays are ordered | S82-S86 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it is priced below build cost and given away to many evaluation sites. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate [S1].

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, and most sites reordered. A rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the recent additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond the data held; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

For fiscal year ended 2025, Total revenues decreased to $2,730.2 million from $2,782.9 million for the prior year. Donor Screening revenue decreased 54% compared to the prior year, primarily due to the wind-down of the U.S. donor screening business. Point of Care revenue decreased 13% compared to the prior year, primarily due to decreases in sales of QUICKVUE SARS and SOFIA SARS Antigen assays. Molecular Diagnostics revenue increased 10% compared to the prior year, driven by higher SAVANNA revenue. Currency exchange rates did not significantly impact our growth rate for fiscal year ended 2025.
For fiscal year ended 2024, Total revenues decreased to $2,782.9 million from $2,997.8 million for the prior year. Immunohematology revenue increased 2% compared to the prior year, primarily due to reagent growth. Molecular Diagnostics sales decreased by $7.7 million, primarily driven by lower demand. Currency exchange rates had an unfavorable impact of approximately 60 basis points on our growth rate for fiscal year ended 2024.
The primary purposes of our capital expenditures are to invest in manufacturing capacity expansion, acquire certain of our instruments, acquire scientific equipment, purchase or develop IT and implement facility improvements. We plan to fund the capital expenditures with the cash on our balance sheet.
We are focused on expanding the number of instruments placed in the field and solidifying long-term contractual relationships with customers. In order to achieve this goal, in certain jurisdictions where it is permitted, we have leveraged a reagent rental model that has been recognized as more attractive to certain customers. We believe that the shift in our sales strategy will grow our installed base, thereby increasing sales of higher-margin assays, reagents and other consumables over the life of the customer contracts and enhancing our recurring revenue and cash flows. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out. The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is the buyer, though 39% of US urgent-care centres are hospital-owned and route send-outs to their health-system laboratory. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, with scale dependent on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent. All figures below are company-provided and unverified. [S99, S79]

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware, 2018-03-12; HQ Albuquerque, NM | Series B issuer, FDA submitter, owner of patents VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona, 2022-05-09 | Tempe pilot line, 18 staff, plant lease | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland, 2025-01-15 | Future EU regulatory entity; no staff; CE not before 2028 | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas, 2016-02-01; 60% acquired 2021-04 | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed exclusively to Vantelle at a 3% royalty | 60% Vantelle; 40% founders, incl. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist at 22% | Unverified | S99 |

Ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and its 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Unverified and undisclosed are whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped, and Ireland's intercompany terms; each matters at exit. [S99]

### The $140M pre-money is built on 42,991,881 shares, not the 36.4M shown

| Shareholder | Class | Shares post-round | % post-money | % votes | Invested | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dr. Wren Albescu | Common | 6,400,000 | 12.26% | 15.32% | n/d | Unverified | S99 |
| Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist | Common | 4,800,000 | 9.19% | 11.49% | n/d | Unverified | S99 |
| Juniper Rock and seed investors | Seed preferred | 6,000,000 | 11.49% | 14.36% | $4.5M (4.34x) | Unverified | S99 |
| Ardent Peak and Series A investors | Series A preferred | 12,400,000 | 23.75% | 29.68% | $36.0M (1.12x) | Unverified | S99 |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | Common warrants at $2.903 | 400,000 | 0.77% | 0.96% | exercise $1.16M | Unverified | S99 |
| 2026 bridge noteholders | Series B-1 preferred | 2,571,392 | 4.93% | 6.15% | $6.28M (1.33x) | Unverified | S99 |
| New Series B investors | Series B preferred | 9,212,627 | 17.65% | 22.05% | $30.0M (1.00x) | Unverified | S99 |
| Options granted and unallocated pool | Common | 10,420,489 | 19.96% | 0% | strike n/d | Unverified | S99 |
| **Total** | | **52,204,508** | **100%** | **100%** | | Unverified | S99 |

The arithmetic reproduces the deck: $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The "shares today" column excludes both the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% "today" is 14.89% pre-money. The bridge converts $6.28M plus 8% interest at $2.4423, 75% of the round price. [S99]

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the new pool shares are worth $17.0M and are created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than 15/170. The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A takes $36.0M then participates at 23.75% of the residual, and seed takes $4.5M non-participating. On an analyst calculation from the deck's share counts, the founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6% of proceeds) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%). The $30M Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs a $357M exit for 2x; the Series A's 1x participation, present in 5% of 2025 deals, is the largest claim on a mid-range exit. [S99, S100, S98]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of $9.4M. arguments.markdown:
The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 additional-information request restarts a 90-day review clock, putting the first clearance in late March 2027 at the earliest; a CLIA waiver filed in the third quarter of 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's own 150-day goal; and at the 1.35 panels a day the evaluation sites actually run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites, not the 300 the plan reaches by end-2027. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. The FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window that runs to 2027-02-17. FDA's clock resumes on receipt of that answer, so a 90-day review cannot produce a decision before late March 2027, against a 2025 average of 146-149 days. The second submission has a harder dependency: it covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until the second quarter of 2027, so a Q2 2027 filing is not physically possible and a Q3 2027 filing is the earliest realistic date [S1, S69, S92].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to the FDA request | 2026-12 (company plan) | Received 2026-08-21; not answered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 (company) | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on the answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S92 |
| Pivotal study results, four sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary-venous equivalence, intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k), NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q2 2027 (company) | Depends on pivotal results due the same quarter | Five-assay menu | S1, unverified |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 (company) | Not filed; must reference a cleared application and include flex and user studies | Waived status, the gate to urgent care | S1, S72 |
| CLIA waiver decision | No company date | 150 FDA days after filing implies Q1 2028 at the earliest | Whether 2028 revenue is reachable | S72 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use only | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset in the plan and the one scheduled latest. A waiver submission references an already cleared application and must carry a risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended sites; FDA's goal is a substantive interaction within 90 review days and a decision within 150 FDA days. Filing in Q3 2027 therefore points to a decision around the first quarter of 2028, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. Until then the panel is a moderate-complexity test that only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified, competency-assessed staff may run; a Certificate of Waiver site cannot legally run it. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are therefore hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics that make up the serviceable market in the deck. The dual 510(k) and CLIA waiver pathway used by point-of-care peers would put both decisions on one 180-day goal [S72, S81, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: evaluation sites averaged 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites in 2026, which is 41 cartridges a site a month, or 1.35 a day. The model assumes 8 panels a day from 2028, a 5.9-fold step-change, and the site plan does not fill the gap: 300 sites at model utilisation and the $31 2029 cartridge price produce $22.3M, not $78.5M. Reaching $78.5M requires 1,055 sites at model utilisation or 5,150 at the observed rate; $41.0M in 2028 requires 551 sites at model utilisation. The 2027 line is tighter still: $16.8M with an average of 150 sites implies full 8-a-day use from the first day of the year plus the $2.4M stocking order and instrument sales — no ramp at all, and only two assays on the menu for most of it [S1].

### Two of the plan's own numbers fail a timing test

Company data, unverified: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from the distributor that ships on 510(k) clearance, which the company itself expects in the first quarter of 2027. That is 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026 as scheduled. Separately, the 61% FY2026E gross margin sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below build cost, so either an undisclosed high-margin line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. Start from $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, and subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of term-loan principal once the Bluestem loan starts amortising in April 2027: $10.9M remains at the end of 2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory needed for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, so the realistic path is an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1, unverified |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1, unverified |

The distributor relationship is the commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme, and it is a letter of intent from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner — a related-party cost that belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridge sales and contract development are revenue but second curves that consume the same engineering team; the Irish entity and a CE mark are a distraction from the only market that matters in this round.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second additional-information letter | Second letter in the first half of 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Pivotal data show capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level, troponin CV below 10% | Results reported as categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver filed after clearance with no pre-submission | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready for scale | ISO 13485 certificate issued; automation ordered for Tempe | Audit slipped, no automation order by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount still in single digits against a 300-site plan | S1 |

Counter-evidence deserves weight. The company hired a regulatory vice-president with a record of FDA clearances, the pipeline of paid evaluation sites and a high reorder rate is unusual for an investigational device, and if the recent request was documentation-only a Q1 2027 clearance remains possible. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the recent request asked and what evidence the pending answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers and what triggers the next round; and whether the distributor letter carries any minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing judgement is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel.
