The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 additional-information request restarts a 90-day review clock, putting the first clearance in late March 2027 at the earliest; a CLIA waiver filed in the third quarter of 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's own 150-day goal; and at the 1.35 panels a day the evaluation sites actually run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites, not the 300 the plan reaches by end-2027. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. The FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window that runs to 2027-02-17. FDA's clock resumes on receipt of that answer, so a 90-day review cannot produce a decision before late March 2027, against a 2025 average of 146-149 days. The second submission has a harder dependency: it covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until the second quarter of 2027, so a Q2 2027 filing is not physically possible and a Q3 2027 filing is the earliest realistic date [S1, S69, S92].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to the FDA request | 2026-12 (company plan) | Received 2026-08-21; not answered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 (company) | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on the answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S92 |
| Pivotal study results, four sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary-venous equivalence, intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k), NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q2 2027 (company) | Depends on pivotal results due the same quarter | Five-assay menu | S1, unverified |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 (company) | Not filed; must reference a cleared application and include flex and user studies | Waived status, the gate to urgent care | S1, S72 |
| CLIA waiver decision | No company date | 150 FDA days after filing implies Q1 2028 at the earliest | Whether 2028 revenue is reachable | S72 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use only | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset in the plan and the one scheduled latest. A waiver submission references an already cleared application and must carry a risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended sites; FDA's goal is a substantive interaction within 90 review days and a decision within 150 FDA days. Filing in Q3 2027 therefore points to a decision around the first quarter of 2028, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. Until then the panel is a moderate-complexity test that only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified, competency-assessed staff may run; a Certificate of Waiver site cannot legally run it. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are therefore hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics that make up the serviceable market in the deck. The dual 510(k) and CLIA waiver pathway used by point-of-care peers would put both decisions on one 180-day goal [S72, S81, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: evaluation sites averaged 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites and 55 analyzers in 2026 — 41 cartridges a site a month, about 30 an analyzer, roughly 1.2 a day against the 8 a day per analyzer the model assumes from 2028. The site plan does not close a 6.5-fold gap: 300 sites at model utilisation and the $31 2029 price produce $29.9M, not $78.5M. Reaching $78.5M requires 787 sites at model utilisation or 5,150 at the observed rate; $41.0M in 2028 requires 411. The 2027 line is tighter still: $16.8M with an average of 150 sites needs close to full model utilisation from the first day plus the $2.4M stocking order — no ramp at all, and only two assays on the menu for most of it [S1].

### Two of the plan's own numbers fail a timing test

Company data, unverified: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from the distributor that ships on 510(k) clearance, which the company itself expects in the first quarter of 2027. That is 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026 as scheduled. Separately, the 61% FY2026E gross margin sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below build cost, so either an undisclosed high-margin line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. Start from $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, and subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of term-loan principal once the Bluestem loan starts amortising in April 2027: $10.9M remains at the end of 2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory needed for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, so the realistic path is an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1, unverified |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1, unverified |

The distributor relationship is the commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme, and it is a letter of intent from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner — a related-party cost that belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridge sales and contract development are revenue but second curves that consume the same engineering team; the Irish entity and a CE mark are a distraction from the only market that matters in this round.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second additional-information letter | Second letter in the first half of 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Pivotal data show capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level, troponin CV below 10% | Results reported as categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver filed after clearance with no pre-submission | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready for scale | ISO 13485 certificate issued; automation ordered for Tempe | Audit slipped, no automation order by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount still in single digits against a 300-site plan | S1, unverified |

Counter-evidence deserves weight. The company hired a regulatory vice-president with a record of FDA clearances, the pipeline of paid evaluation sites and a high reorder rate is unusual for an investigational device, and if the recent request was documentation-only a Q1 2027 clearance remains possible. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the recent request asked and what evidence the pending answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers and what triggers the next round; and whether the distributor letter carries any minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing judgement is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out. The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is the buyer, though 39% of US urgent-care centres are hospital-owned and route send-outs to their health-system laboratory. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, with scale dependent on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent. All figures below are company-provided and unverified. [S99, S79]

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware, 2018-03-12; HQ Albuquerque, NM | Series B issuer, FDA submitter, owner of patents VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona, 2022-05-09 | Tempe pilot line, 18 staff, plant lease | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland, 2025-01-15 | Future EU regulatory entity; no staff; CE not before 2028 | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas, 2016-02-01; 60% acquired 2021-04 | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed exclusively to Vantelle at a 3% royalty | 60% Vantelle; 40% founders, incl. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist at 22% | Unverified | S99 |

Ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and its 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Unverified and undisclosed are whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped, and Ireland's intercompany terms; each matters at exit. [S99]

### The $140M pre-money is built on 42,991,881 shares, not the 36.4M shown

| Shareholder | Class | Shares post-round | % post-money | % votes | Invested | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dr. Wren Albescu | Common | 6,400,000 | 12.26% | 15.32% | n/d | Unverified | S99 |
| Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist | Common | 4,800,000 | 9.19% | 11.49% | n/d | Unverified | S99 |
| Juniper Rock and seed investors | Seed preferred | 6,000,000 | 11.49% | 14.36% | $4.5M (4.34x) | Unverified | S99 |
| Ardent Peak and Series A investors | Series A preferred | 12,400,000 | 23.75% | 29.68% | $36.0M (1.12x) | Unverified | S99 |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | Common warrants at $2.903 | 400,000 | 0.77% | 0.96% | exercise $1.16M | Unverified | S99 |
| 2026 bridge noteholders | Series B-1 preferred | 2,571,392 | 4.93% | 6.15% | $6.28M (1.33x) | Unverified | S99 |
| New Series B investors | Series B preferred | 9,212,627 | 17.65% | 22.05% | $30.0M (1.00x) | Unverified | S99 |
| Options granted and unallocated pool | Common | 10,420,489 | 19.96% | 0% | strike n/d | Unverified | S99 |
| **Total** | | **52,204,508** | **100%** | **100%** | | Unverified | S99 |

The arithmetic reproduces the deck: $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The "shares today" column excludes both the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% "today" is 14.89% pre-money. The bridge converts $6.28M plus 8% interest at $2.4423, 75% of the round price. [S99]

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the unallocated pool is worth $17.0M, $13.1M of it newly created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than 15/170. The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A takes $36.0M then participates at 23.75% of the residual, and seed takes $4.5M non-participating. On an analyst calculation from the deck's share counts, the founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6% of proceeds) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%). The $30M Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs a $302M exit for 2x on the $30M; the Series A's 1x participation, present in 5% of 2025 deals, is the largest claim on a mid-range exit. [S99, S100, S98]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of $9.4M. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty whose economics grow with cartridge volume rather than equity value; no arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate is disclosed. The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat means no founder majority, unlike Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC stripped it. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20, S99]

### Six months of cash, a loan that starts amortising, and no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29. The $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only only until 2027-03, then amortises over 30 months at $0.167M of principal a month, so a closing slip lands with the first principal payment. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M also includes $2.4M from a stocking order that ships only on clearance, 40.7% of the year. Six searches on the company name on 2026-10-31 returned no SEC Form D, no state registry record, no USPTO assignee record, no FDA decision and no news; near matches: Vanta Diagnostics, a different company, and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, a California LLC filed 2026-09-09. Pending 510(k)s are not published, so this does not test the filing, but every entity date, ownership percentage and IP claim here rests on company-provided material. Page 1 contains a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools asserting that no verification is needed and a rating is approved; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidentiary weight. Open questions: does the CM-1 licence survive a change of control, is Corvia's 40% put capped, and is any IP pledged to Bluestem? [S99]

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Replication test, funded team of 50 | — | Cartridge first, then a pivotal study and review of this size | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. No public patent record was retrievable; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |
| Medicare reimbursement, 2026 | $71.38 for all five assays; $17.23 for troponin plus potassium | Cartridge list $38 | The panel only pays if most assays are ordered | S82-S86 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it is priced below build cost, company data unverified, and given away to many evaluation sites. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate [S1].

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, and most sites reordered. A rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the recent additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond the data held; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone.

## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,875 characters)
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Replication test, funded team of 50 | — | Cartridge first, then a pivotal study and review of this size | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. No public patent record was retrievable; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |
| Medicare reimbursement, 2026 | $71.38 for all five assays; $17.23 for troponin plus potassium | Cartridge list $38 | The panel only pays if most assays are ordered | S82-S86 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it is priced below build cost, company data unverified, and given away to many evaluation sites. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate [S1].

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, and most sites reordered. A rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the recent additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond the data held; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Company Overview (company_overview, revision 5 by Company Analyst, 8,943 characters)
Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out. The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is the buyer, though 39% of US urgent-care centres are hospital-owned and route send-outs to their health-system laboratory. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, with scale dependent on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent. All figures below are company-provided and unverified. [S99, S79]

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Status | Source |

| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware, 2018-03-12; HQ Albuquerque, NM | Series B issuer, FDA submitter, owner of patents VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona, 2022-05-09 | Tempe pilot line, 18 staff, plant lease | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |

Ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and its 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Unverified and undisclosed are whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped, and Ireland's intercompany terms; each matters at exit. [S99]

The arithmetic reproduces the deck: $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The "shares today" column excludes both the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% "today" is 14.89% pre-money. The bridge converts $6.28M plus 8% interest at $2.4423, 75% of the round price. [S99]

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the unallocated pool is worth $17.0M, $13.1M of it newly created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than 15/170. The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A takes $36.0M then participates at 23.75% of the residual, and seed takes $4.5M non-participating. On an analyst calculation from the deck's share counts, the founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6% of proceeds) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%). The $30M Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs a $302M exit for 2x on the $30M; the Series A's 1x participation, present in 5% of 2025 deals, is the largest claim on a mid-range exit. [S99, S100, S98]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of $9.4M. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty whose economics grow with cartridge volume rather than equity value; no arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate is disclosed. The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat means no founder majority, unlike Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC stripped it. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20, S99]

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 5 by Market Analyst, 8,920 characters)
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim, so the advantage lasts only until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships, and it cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is not a startup with better chemistry; it is the incumbent that already owns the buyer's analyser slot. [S1, S67, S104]

The buyer at a three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options, and only one is a direct competitor. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a handheld cartridge analyser whose waived menu covers creatinine, potassium and glucose and which added an hs-troponin I cartridge in January 2025. Direct but narrower: Siemens epoc, 13 blood-gas, electrolyte and metabolite analytes in under a minute with no cardiac marker; QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel from EDTA whole blood; Roche's cobas h 232 from heparinised venous blood; and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX in hospital emergency departments. Substitute: the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call them later. No US product retrieved combines troponin, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium in one finger-stick cartridge, which is the gap the company sells into. [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109]

At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and the Series A's participating preference means a $30M Series B needs a $435M exit to return 3x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, all company-reported and not independently verified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho, the closest listed comparable, trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

Company-reported financing terms, not independently verified:

| Date | Round | Amount | Price/share | Post-money | Investors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75 (implied) | not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.9032 | $92.5M | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.9032 | $104.5M | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Venture term loan | $5.0M | Warrant strike $2.903 | — | Bluestem Venture Lending (400,000 warrants) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes, 8% | $6.0M | $2.4423 on conversion | — | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027-01 (target) | Series B | $30.0M | $3.2564 | $170.0M | Ardent Peak ($5.0M) and Juniper Rock ($3.0M); $22.0M sought | S1 (unverified) |

The company-reported, unverified terms show the seed priced at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11. The headline pre-money rises 34% from the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but $13.1M of that is the option-pool refresh to 10% of the post-money: existing holders' effective pre-money is $126.9M, a 21% uplift over 2.9 years, or 6.9% a year. Existing shares fall from 100% to 69.7% of the fully diluted company — 7.7 points of pool refresh, 4.9 points of bridge and 17.6 points of new Series B — taking the founders from 30.8% to 21.5%, the seed from 16.5% to 11.5% and the Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%. Insiders are committing $8.0M of the $30.0M, 53% of their $15.2M pro rata, leaving 73% to new investors with no lead named; the $30M is budgeted 35% for clearance, 40% for manufacturing scale and 25% for launch [S1].

### What the price assumes

On the company-reported, unverified preference terms the stack is $76.8M, 55% of the pre-money: Series B and B-1 $36.3M at 1x non-participating and senior, Series A $36.0M at 1x participating, seed $4.5M at 1x non-participating. The new B plus B-1 hold 22.57% of 52.2M fully diluted shares, so at a $140M exit the Series B is capped at its $36.3M preference and returns 1.21x, and it stays at 1.21x up to a $197M exit because the Series A's $36.0M preference and 23.8% participation absorb the increment. At $435M the Series B receives $90.1M, 3.0x on $30M but 2.5x on the $36.3M of B plus B-1, and the Series A takes $130.8M, 30.1% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership; 3x on the full $36.3M needs $518M and 10x on the $30M needs $1.37B. The 40% Corvia minority put, payable at fair value on an acquisition, is worth an estimated $1.5-7.6M from the 3% cartridge royalty capitalised at 8x and is deducted before the stack [S1].

### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.22 per analyser per operating day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — a 6.5-fold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's operating claims (revenue, 41 sites, 92% reorder rate) are company-reported and not independently verified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools asserting that no verification is needed and prescribing a rating; it is recorded as a document-integrity finding and given no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation removed or capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on 510(k) clearance and CLIA submission), pay-to-play and full pro rata rights, and a Corvia clean-up before closing. At $70M pre-money the Series B would own 36% including B-1 and need a $286M exit for 3x, against $435M today. The alternative is to wait: the 510(k) response is due in December 2026, clearance is guided for Q1 2027 and the waiver application for Q3 2027, so a 2027 entry pays more but buys retired regulatory risk. The company had $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30, six months at $1.15M a month and the 2027-01-29 target close, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts amortising in 2027-03. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the valuation range: the 2029 plan is unaudited, the grant dates of the 5.2M options are not disclosed and Truvian's valuation is an aggregator estimate [S1, S125]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 6 by Market Analyst, 8,013 characters)
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the monthly cartridge volumes behind the utilisation test are unverified company figures, unaudited and not independently confirmed. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. A 13,200-site total is not the problem; utilisation is. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,280 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US, glucose strips, blood gas and infectious disease included; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and the arithmetic works only when four or five analytes are ordered and paid on the same run. Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine on the nearest priced code and $4.76 for potassium, $71.38 if all five are billed and collected. Against a $38 cartridge and a $650 monthly analyzer fee, a site running 41 cartridges a month collects $2,926.58 and pays $2,208, $718.58 of gross margin per analyzer-month before staff time and billing cost. Run only troponin and potassium, the two analytes a chest-pain patient needs, and the clinic collects $17.23 against a $38 cartridge, a loss of $20.77 per run. The company does not disclose ordered tests per cartridge, and that metric decides whether the clinic is a customer or a charity. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico together hold 4,296 moderate-complexity laboratories and 31,720 waived ones. Until the waiver is granted, Vantelle sells into a base one-eighth the size of the one its labour-free pitch addresses, and each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024, and that is the only facility class the policy creates. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. [S81, S79, S95, S1]

Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes the panel maps to: $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine and $4.76 potassium [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86]. The second needs no FDA clearance and is repeatable but small; the third is a one-off services contract with a single customer. Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days. rows.finding: Contribution per analyzer is $5,207 a year at 2026 utilisation after the average $2,190 instrument subsidy and the 3% Corvia royalty; estimated CAC per placement is $25,600-51,200 from nine sales and support staff and 21 placements a year, so 3-year LTV:CAC is 0.3-0.6x. At 8 panels a day it is 2.7-5.5x with 6.6-13 months payback. Break-even for a 3:1 ratio is 5.9 panels a day at $16.20 cost, 4.2 at the $7.50 target.
rows.follow_up: What is actual sales and marketing spend per site placed, and what margin does the distributor take?
rows.implication: Site count is not the value driver and should not be the milestone that releases capital.
rows.mechanism: A fixed sales and support cost is spread over placements and then over panels; below roughly 4-6 panels a day the cartridge gross profit cannot carry the salesforce that places the analyzer.
rows.weakens: The CAC estimate rests on an assumed fully loaded cost per head and an arbitrary 50% allocation; a distributor that carries the selling cost would cut it sharply.

rows.benchmark: Quidel's Triage MeterPro is listed free with a three-year contract, with troponin at $23.96 a test and CLIA-waived BNP at $31.56; QuidelOrtho embeds instrument cost in reagent pricing.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic, medium on clinic behaviour
rows.finding: Medicare's five codes pay $71.38 a panel; against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $37.98 before labour, but the $650 monthly fee equals 17 panels of that margin, leaving about $508 a month per analyzer at 30.5 panels and about $8,400 at 240.
rows.follow_up: What do evaluation sites say about the $650 fee, and how many would convert at a free-instrument, volume-commitment structure?

rows.mechanism: A fixed monthly fee on a variable-margin stream makes the clinic's payback worst at the utilisation where adoption starts, which slows the ramp the plan needs.
rows.weakens: Medicare is a floor, commercial payers pay more, and a 12-minute result has clinical value independent of the fee.

rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho's recurring consumables and reagent-rental revenue is the model being claimed; Vantelle's recurring share is 42% of revenue and contract-based.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: FY2025 revenue of $2.6M is $1.1M evaluation program (42%), $0.8M research-use cartridges to CROs (31%) and $0.7M contract development for one partner (27%). The evaluation line reconstructs exactly to 55 analyzers x $650 x 12 plus 20,160 cartridges x $33.40, i.e. the 2026 monthly volume is the FY2025 average and the base has not grown in a year.
rows.follow_up: What are the terms and duration of the contract development agreement, and is the CRO cartridge business growing?
rows.implication: FY2025 supports a tools-and-services multiple, not a razor-and-blade multiple.
rows.mechanism: Paid pilots plus services revenue carry no recurring product multiple; the reusable share is the evaluation line and it ends at clearance.
rows.weakens: The research-use and development lines are real cash and validate the assay chemistry with third parties.

rows.benchmark: No external benchmark for paid evaluation programmes; 92% is high against subscription retention but the unit is a one-month consumable order.
rows.confidence: high on the numbers, low on what they imply about commercial demand
rows.finding: 34 of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, but at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is roughly one month of consumption; three sites (8%) did not reorder. Concentration: Mesa Verde is 18 of 55 analyzers and 610 of 1,680 cartridges, about 15% of revenue; with the development partner the top two are roughly 42%.
rows.follow_up: What is the reorder size distribution, and what happened to the three non-reordering sites?
rows.implication: Ask for the distribution of reorder volumes, not the rate.
rows.mechanism: A reorder rate measures engagement at a price the site already accepted; it does not measure the volume a billing-enabled clinic would run.
rows.weakens: Paying sites reordering is genuine revealed preference and the strongest demand signal in the deck.

rows.benchmark: The distributor relationship is a non-binding letter of intent to stock analyzers for 300 sites; no public record of the distributor was found.
rows.confidence: medium-high
rows.finding: 300 sites by end-2027 requires 259 net adds in 12 months (21.6 a month against 1.3 a month since March 2024), 402 analyzers, $1.35M of instrument cost, and about 1.44M cartridges a year at 8 panels a day — 71 times the current 20,160 — from a pilot line with 18 staff.
rows.follow_up: What cartridge output can the Tempe line reach before new tooling, and what is the distributor's contractual commitment?
rows.implication: Make the site count a milestone with capital behind it, and diligence manufacturing capacity separately.
rows.mechanism: Distribution can accelerate placements but cannot create panels per analyzer-day; scaling cartridge output 71x on a pilot line is a separate constraint from selling sites.
rows.weakens: A national distributor with existing clinic relationships could place sites far faster than a nine-person direct team.

Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,875 characters)
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Replication test, funded team of 50 | — | Cartridge first, then a pivotal study and review of this size | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. No public patent record was retrievable; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |
| Medicare reimbursement, 2026 | $71.38 for all five assays; $17.23 for troponin plus potassium | Cartridge list $38 | The panel only pays if most assays are ordered | S82-S86 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it is priced below build cost, company data unverified, and given away to many evaluation sites. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate [S1].

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, and most sites reordered. A rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the recent additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond the data held; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone."}],"isError":false}

Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 of revenue against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy before installation or service. The cartridge then earns $17.20 at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost, less a 3% royalty on net sales to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate that licenses the sealing patent and whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer [S1]. That royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and about $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim on gross margin, not a rounding error. Cost carries the same uncertainty: $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% reduction from $16.20 on a line that has never run above roughly 2,000 units a month, and getting a five-assay cartridge to that cost is a redesign, not a learning curve.

### The acquisition cost the deck omits decides the model

Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months, about 21 a year [S1]. At an assumed $100,000-155,000 fully loaded per head that is $0.9-1.4M a year, or $43,000-66,000 per placement; charging half of it to placements — the same team sells the research-use and development revenue — gives the $25,600-51,200 range above. On that basis the 2026 placement destroys value: three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay what it cost to win. The model turns positive at about 5.9 panels a day at today's $16.20 cost and 4.2 a day at the 2029 target of $7.50, the level at which a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1, the minimum that supports a direct salesforce. Between one panel and four is the zone where Vantelle can grow and still lose money on every site it places [S1].

### The clinic's margin is real, and the fee eats it where adoption starts

Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes the panel maps to — $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine, $4.76 potassium. The research-use line needs no FDA clearance and repeats, but it is a laboratory-reagent business, not a clinical one. The development line is services revenue from one customer with no product multiple attached. Concentration follows from the mix: Mesa Verde is 12 of 41 sites, 18 of 55 analyzers and 610 of 1,680 cartridges, roughly $385,000 or 15% of revenue, and with the development partner the top two relationships are about 42%. A top line that is 27% one-off services and 15% one customer is not yet a razor-and-blade franchise.

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is about one month of consumption: the metric shows sites keep using something they already pay for, not that they would buy at commercial volume. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — about 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, which is 114% of that median: the model does not assume Vantelle wins the urgent slice, it assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month since March 2024, 402 analyzers, $1.35M of instrument cost and cartridge volume near 1.44M a year — 71 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

A clinic that collects $71.38 a panel has an incentive no evaluation site has, the reorder rate is a paying customer's behaviour, and 14 panels a day of latent send-out volume makes four panels a day credible; eight is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. For a $15M lead check, capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone rather than the measure, and the $650 fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative before launch. Confidence is high on the arithmetic — the deck's own figures reproduce to the dollar — and medium on the interpretation, because evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Vantelle's product addresses a real gap in clinic care, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts are not yet those of a company that should carry a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque. Five of six board seats are filled, with the independent seat vacant; finance has been led by a part-time interim CFO since March 2026; ISO 13485 certification has not been obtained and the audit is booked for Q1 2027; the lead 510(k) has been under an FDA additional-information request since 2026-08-21; and the deck discloses neither the HIPAA business-associate architecture for HL7/FHIR result transfer nor the IDE and IRB basis for 41 paid evaluation sites running an investigational device. Each item is fixable and several are normal at this stage; together they mean the $15M should be governance-and-milestone capital, not a single priced bet on a Q1 2027 clearance. Company figures here are unverified. [S1]

### Two founder seats are not the problem; the empty independent seat is

Two founder directors out of six is not control, and the Series A already holds a seat. The gap is the missing independent director, no disclosed audit committee and a part-time CFO at a company that will spend $30M while running an FDA submission, a CLIA-waiver study and a manufacturing scale-up. The previous CFO left in February 2026 and the interim has been part-time since March; cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, and the $5.0M Bluestem term loan begins 30 monthly principal payments in March 2027, one month after the target close. A small finance team must therefore forecast a pre-revenue ramp, manage a lender and report to a new lead. Meridian should require a mutually agreed independent director, an audit committee with a financial expert, a permanent CFO within six months of close and monthly reporting on cash, FDA correspondence and quality metrics. [S1]

### The Corvia royalty is small until it meets an exit

The 3% royalty on cartridge net sales is paid to Corvia Microfluidics, which Vantelle owns 60% of and in which CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22%; his share is therefore about 0.66% of cartridge sales. Every $10M of cartridge revenue carries $300,000 of royalty, $120,000 of which leaves the consolidated group for the 40% minority and about $66,000 of which reaches the CTO. The larger issue is the exit: Corvia's minority may put its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value on an acquisition, and capitalising the royalty at 10x the FY2029 plan implies roughly $9.4M of put value. That is a debt-like claim ahead of the Series B and a potential valuation dispute in a sale. The rate may be defensible; the process is not visible. Meridian should require disinterested-director approval and an independent fairness opinion of both the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and disclosure of the obligation in the cap table. [S1]

### Quality culture is the open file

ISO 13485 certification is absent and FDA's QMSR has required an ISO 13485-based quality system since 2026-02-02. The regulatory vice-president who prepared the 510(k) left in September 2025 and her successor joined in November 2025, two months before the filing. The 2026-08-21 additional-information request may be routine, but its content is undisclosed, so an investor cannot tell whether FDA is asking about labelling, the 640-sample analytical study or the quality system itself. The comparable enforcement record is not reassuring: FDA's 2024-05-09 warning letter to Cue Health cited device changes made without authorisation and lot-release testing that could allow a higher failure rate than the labelled performance, and required the company to stop selling. A warning letter at Vantelle before clearance would delay launch, complicate the CLIA waiver and give 41 clinic customers a reason to pause. [S1, S71, S113]

### Patient data has no visible contract

The Q5 sends results into the clinic EHR over Wi-Fi using HL7 and FHIR, which makes Vantelle a vendor that creates, receives and transmits protected health information for a covered entity. Under HHS's business-associate rules that requires a BAA with each clinic, equivalent terms with any cloud or interface subcontractor, Security Rule safeguards and breach reporting; the business associate is directly liable, not merely the clinic. The deck discloses no BAA count, no SOC 2 Type II or HITRUST report, no named privacy or security officer, no encryption or incident-response description and no cyber insurance. Silence in a fundraising deck is not proof of absence, but it is a material non-disclosure for a device that touches PHI at 41 sites. Executed BAAs, a current security report, encryption and incident-response terms and a named security owner should be closing conditions. [S1, S135]

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 41 evaluation sites run. That gap, not the $2.4B market estimate or the FDA calendar, decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. The figures are company-reported, not independently verified, but they reconcile internally to the dollar. Vantelle reports 55 analyzers across 41 sites and 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month [S1]: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month, 1.0 a day on a 30-day basis and 1.22 on the 300-operating-day convention its own market model uses. The plan assumes 8.0 from 2028. The 2029 revenue line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 of revenue against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy before installation or service. The cartridge then earns $17.20 at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty on net sales to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate that licenses the sealing patent and whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer [S1]. That royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim on gross margin, not a rounding error. Cost carries the same uncertainty: $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month, and getting a five-assay cartridge to that cost is a redesign, not a learning curve.

### The acquisition cost the deck omits decides the model

Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months, 21 a year. At an assumed $100,000-155,000 fully loaded per head that is $0.9-1.4M a year, or $43,000-66,000 per placement; charging half of it to placements — the same team sells the research-use and development revenue — gives the $25,600-51,200 range above. On that basis the 2026 placement destroys value: three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay what it cost to win. The model turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's $16.20 cost and 4.2 a day at the 2029 target of $7.50, the level at which a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1, the minimum that supports a direct salesforce. Between one panel and four is the zone where Vantelle can grow and still lose money on every site it places.

### The clinic's margin is real, and the fee eats it where adoption starts

Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes the panel maps to — $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine, $4.76 potassium. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $37.98 a panel before labour and billing. It also pays $650 a month, which is 17 panels of that margin: at 30.5 panels a month the clinic nets $508 per analyzer, at 240 panels $8,400. A fixed fee on a variable-margin stream bites hardest exactly where adoption begins, and incumbents sell the other way: Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S106, S22].
