The research-use line needs no FDA clearance and repeats, but it is a laboratory-reagent business, not a clinical one; the development line is services revenue from one customer, with no product multiple attached. Concentration follows from the mix: Mesa Verde is 12 of 41 sites, 18 of 55 analyzers and 610 of 1,680 cartridges, $385,000 or 15% of revenue, and with the development partner the top two relationships are 42%. A top line that is 27% one-off services and 15% one customer is not yet a razor-and-blade franchise.

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows sites keep using something they already pay for, not that they would buy at commercial volume. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, which is 114% of that median: the model does not assume Vantelle wins the urgent slice, it assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out. For a $15M lead check, capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone rather than the measure, and the $650 fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative before launch. 55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month — 30.5 per analyzer-month against the 240 the 2028 plan assumes; at one panel a day a placement's three-year cartridge gross profit is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1].

Vantelle's product addresses a real gap in clinic care, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts do not yet support a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque. ### Two founder seats are not the problem; the empty independent seat is

Two founder directors of six is not control. The gap is the vacant independent seat, no disclosed audit committee and a part-time CFO at a company that will spend $30M while running an FDA submission, a waiver study and a manufacturing scale-up. The 3% cartridge royalty goes to Corvia, 60% owned by Vantelle, where CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22% — about 0.66% of cartridge sales. ISO 13485 certification is absent and FDA's QMSR has required an ISO 13485-based system since 2026-02-02. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 41 evaluation sites run. That gap, not the $2.4B market estimate or the FDA calendar, decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. The figures are company-reported, not independently verified, and reconcile to the dollar. Vantelle reports 55 analyzers across 41 sites and 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month [S1]: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month, 1.0 a day on a 30-day basis and 1.22 on the 300-operating-day convention its own market model uses. The plan assumes 8.0 from 2028. The 2029 revenue line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 of revenue against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy before installation or service. The cartridge then earns $17.20 at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty on net sales to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate that licenses the sealing patent and whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer [S1]. That royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim on gross margin. Cost carries the same uncertainty: $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month, and getting a five-assay cartridge to that cost is a redesign, not a learning curve.

### The acquisition cost the deck omits decides the model

Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months, 21 a year. At an assumed $100,000-155,000 fully loaded per head that is $0.9-1.4M a year, or $43,000-66,000 per placement; charging half of it to placements — the same team sells the research-use and development revenue — gives the $25,600-51,200 range above. On that basis the 2026 placement destroys value: three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay what it cost to win. The model turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's $16.20 cost and 4.2 a day at the 2029 target of $7.50, the level at which a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1, the minimum a direct salesforce needs. The 3% cartridge royalty goes to Corvia, 60% owned by Vantelle, where CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22% — about 0.66% of cartridge sales. Every $10M of cartridge revenue carries $300,000 of royalty, $120,000 to the 40% minority and about $66,000 to the CTO. The exit is the larger issue: the minority may put its 40% at fair value on an acquisition, roughly $9.4M capitalising the royalty at 10x FY2029. That is a debt-like claim ahead of the Series B and a dispute in a sale. Require disinterested approval and a fairness opinion of both the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and disclosure in the cap table. [S1]

### Quality culture is the open file

ISO 13485 certification is absent and FDA's QMSR has required an ISO 13485-based system since 2026-02-02. The regulatory vice-president who prepared the 510(k) left in September 2025; her successor joined in November 2025, two months before filing. The 2026-08-21 request's content is undisclosed, so an investor cannot tell whether FDA is asking about labelling, the 640-sample study or the quality system. FDA's 2024-05-09 warning letter to Cue Health cited unauthorised device changes and lot-release failures, and ordered a stop-sale. A warning letter before clearance would delay launch, complicate the waiver and give 41 clinic customers pause. [S1, S71, S113]

The Q5 sends results to the clinic EHR over Wi-Fi using HL7 and FHIR, making Vantelle a vendor that creates, receives and transmits PHI for a covered entity. Under HHS rules that requires a BAA with each clinic, equivalent terms with subcontractors, Security Rule safeguards and breach reporting; the business associate is directly liable. The deck discloses no BAA count, SOC 2 or HITRUST report, named privacy officer, encryption or incident-response terms, or cyber insurance. Silence is not proof of absence, but it is material non-disclosure at 41 PHI-touching sites. Executed BAAs, a current security report and a named security owner should be closing conditions. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 41 evaluation sites run. That gap, not the $2.4B market estimate or the FDA calendar, decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. The figures are company-reported, not independently verified. Vantelle reports 55 analyzers across 41 sites and 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month [S1]: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month, 1.0 a day on a 30-day basis and 1.22 on the 300-operating-day convention its own market model uses. The plan assumes 8.0 from 2028. The 2029 revenue line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, company-reported and unverified, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 of revenue against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty on net sales to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate that licenses the sealing patent and whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer. That royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim on gross margin. Cost carries the same uncertainty: $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month, and getting a five-assay cartridge to that cost is a redesign, not a learning curve. The acquisition cost is the line the deck omits, and the headcount gives it: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months, 21 a year [S1]. At an assumed $100,000-155,000 fully loaded per head that is $0.9-1.4M a year, $43,000-66,000 per placement; charging half to placements, since the same team sells the research-use and development revenue, gives the $25,600-51,200 in the table. On that basis the 2026 placement destroys value: three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay what it cost to win. The model turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the 2029 target of $7.50, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1, the minimum a direct salesforce needs. Between one panel and four is the zone where Vantelle can grow and still lose money on every site it places.

### The clinic's margin is real, and the fee eats it where adoption starts

Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes the panel maps to — $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine, $4.76 potassium. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $37.98 a panel before labour and billing. It also pays $650 a month, which is 17 panels of that margin: at 30.5 panels a month the clinic nets $508 per analyzer, at 240 panels $8,400. A fixed fee on a variable-margin stream bites hardest where adoption begins, and incumbents sell the other way: Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S106, S22].

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| FY2025 line | $M | Share | Repeatable? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use cartridges to contract research organisations | 0.8 | 31% | Repeatable, needs no clearance, small market | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development for one diagnostics partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

The evaluation line reconstructs exactly from the deck's own inputs to the dollar, which also says the monthly volume quoted as a 2026 average is the FY2025 average: the evaluation base has not grown in a year. The research-use line needs no clearance and repeats, but it is a reagent business, not a clinical one; the development line is services revenue from one customer. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1]. A top line this concentrated is not yet a razor-and-blade franchise.

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows sites keep using something they already pay for, not that they would buy at commercial volume. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, which is 114% of that median: the model does not assume Vantelle wins the urgent slice, it assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month the evaluation program has run since 2024, 402 analyzers, $1.35M of instrument cost and cartridge volume near 1.44M a year — 71 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the five-code rate has an incentive no evaluation site has, the reorder rate is a paying customer's behaviour, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes four panels a day credible; eight is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. For a $15M lead check, capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the $650 fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic — the deck's own figures reproduce to the dollar — and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items would settle it: the monthly volume of the best evaluation site and whether any sustained more than four panels a day; the same measure for the first ten billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix ordered, since a clinic running only troponin and potassium collects less than the cartridge costs.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight, and that gap decides the 2029 plan.**

55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against the 240 the 2028 plan assumes; a placement's three-year cartridge gross profit of $15,621 does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's product addresses a real gap in clinic care, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts do not yet support a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque. Five of six board seats are filled, the independent seat is vacant; finance has been run by a part-time interim CFO since March 2026; ISO 13485 certification is absent, audit booked Q1 2027; the lead 510(k) has been under an FDA information request since 2026-08-21; and the deck discloses neither the HIPAA business-associate architecture for HL7/FHIR transfer nor the IDE/IRB basis for 41 paid evaluation sites. Geopolitics is not material: US-only revenue, dormant Irish entity. Each gap is fixable; together they make the $15M governance-and-milestone capital, not a bet on Q1 2027 clearance. Company figures are unverified. [S1]

### Two founder seats are not the problem; the empty independent seat is

Two founder directors of six is not control. The gap is the vacant independent seat, no disclosed audit committee and a part-time CFO at a company running an FDA submission, a waiver study and a scale-up. The CFO left in February 2026; the interim has been part-time since March. Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly burn, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts 30 principal payments in March 2027, a month after the target close. The gap is therefore a pricing issue, not a checklist item: Meridian is being asked to fund a company whose controls are thinner than its $170M valuation implies. Require a mutually agreed independent director, an audit committee with a financial expert, a permanent CFO within six months and monthly reporting on cash, FDA correspondence and quality metrics. These board and cash figures are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### The Corvia royalty is small until it meets an exit

The 3% cartridge royalty goes to Corvia, 60% owned by Vantelle, where CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22% — 0.66% of cartridge sales. Every $10M of cartridge revenue carries $300,000 of royalty, $120,000 to the 40% minority and $66,000 to the CTO. The exit is the larger issue: the minority may put its 40% at fair value on an acquisition, $9.4M capitalising the royalty at 10x FY2029. For the investor the put is a $9.4M claim ranking ahead of the Series B in an exit; it should reduce the price, not merely sit in a governance list. Require disinterested approval and a fairness opinion of both the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and disclosure in the cap table. The royalty and put terms are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### Quality culture is the open file

ISO 13485 certification is absent and FDA's QMSR has required an ISO 13485-based system since 2026-02-02. The regulatory vice-president who prepared the 510(k) left in September 2025; her successor joined in November 2025, two months before filing. The 2026-08-21 request's content is undisclosed, so the deficiency could be labelling, the 640-sample study or the quality system. FDA's 2024-05-09 warning letter to Cue Health cited unauthorised device changes and lot-release failures, and ordered a stop-sale. A warning letter before clearance would delay launch, complicate the waiver and give 41 clinic customers pause. [S1, S71, S113]

### Patient data has no visible contract

The Q5 sends results to the clinic EHR over Wi-Fi using HL7 and FHIR, making Vantelle a vendor that creates, receives and transmits PHI for a covered entity. Under HHS rules that requires a BAA with each clinic, equivalent terms with subcontractors, Security Rule safeguards and breach reporting; the business associate is directly liable. The deck discloses no BAA count, SOC 2 or HITRUST report, named privacy officer, encryption or incident-response terms, or cyber insurance. Silence is not proof of absence, but it is material non-disclosure at 41 PHI-touching sites. Executed BAAs, a current security report and a named security owner should be closing conditions. [S1, S135]

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 41 evaluation sites run. That gap, not the $2.4B market estimate or the FDA calendar, decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. The figures are company-reported, unverified. Vantelle reports 55 analyzers across 41 sites and 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month [S1]: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month, 1.0 a day on a 30-day basis and 1.22 on the 300-operating-day convention its own market model uses. The plan assumes 8.0 from 2028. The 2029 revenue line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, company-reported and unverified, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 of revenue against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty on net sales to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate that licenses the sealing patent and whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer. That royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim on gross margin. Cost carries the same uncertainty: $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month, and getting a five-assay cartridge to that cost is a redesign, not a learning curve. The acquisition cost is the line the deck omits, and the headcount gives it: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months, 21 a year [S1]. At an assumed $100,000-155,000 fully loaded per head that is $0.9-1.4M a year, $43,000-66,000 per placement; charging half to placements, since the same team sells the research-use and development revenue, gives the $25,600-51,200 above. On that basis the 2026 placement destroys value: three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay what it cost to win. The model turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the 2029 target of $7.50, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1, the minimum a salesforce needs. Between one panel and four is the zone where Vantelle can grow and still lose money on every site it places.

### The clinic's margin is real, and the fee eats it where adoption starts

Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes the panel maps to — $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine, $4.76 potassium. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $37.98 a panel. It also pays $650 a month, which is 17 panels of that margin: at 30.5 panels a month the clinic nets $508 per analyzer, at 240 panels $8,400. A fixed fee on a variable-margin stream bites hardest where adoption begins, and incumbents sell the other way: Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S106, S22].

The evaluation line reconstructs exactly from the deck's own inputs to the dollar, which also says the monthly volume quoted as a 2026 average is the FY2025 average: the evaluation base has not grown in a year. The research-use line needs no clearance and repeats, but it is a reagent business, not a clinical one; the development line is services revenue from one customer. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1]. A top line this concentrated is not yet a razor-and-blade franchise.

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows sites keep using something they already pay for, not that they would buy at commercial volume. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, which is 114% of that median: the model does not assume Vantelle wins the urgent slice, it assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month the evaluation program has run since 2024, 402 analyzers, $1.35M of instrument cost and cartridge volume near 1.44M a year — 71 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the five-code rate has an incentive no evaluation site has, the reorder rate is a paying customer's behaviour, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes four panels a day credible; eight is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. For a $15M lead check, capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the $650 fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic — the deck's own figures reproduce to the dollar — and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items would settle it: the monthly volume of the best evaluation site and whether any sustained more than four panels a day; the same measure for the first ten billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix ordered, since a clinic running only troponin and potassium collects less than the cartridge costs.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight, and that gap decides the 2029 plan.**

55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against the 240 the 2028 plan assumes; a placement's three-year cartridge gross profit of $15,621 does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 41 evaluation sites run. That gap, not the $2.4B market estimate or the FDA calendar, decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. The figures are company-reported, unverified. Vantelle reports 55 analyzers across 41 sites and 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month [S1]: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month, 1.0 a day on a 30-day basis and 1.22 on the 300-operating-day convention its own market model uses. The plan assumes 8.0 from 2028. The 2029 revenue line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, company-reported and unverified, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 of revenue against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty on net sales to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate that licenses the sealing patent and whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer. That royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim on gross margin. Cost carries the same uncertainty: $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month, and getting a five-assay cartridge to that cost is a redesign, not a learning curve. The acquisition cost is the line the deck omits, and the headcount gives it: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months, 21 a year [S1]. At an assumed $100,000-155,000 fully loaded per head that is $0.9-1.4M a year, $43,000-66,000 per placement; charging half to placements, since the same team sells the research-use and development revenue, gives the $25,600-51,200 above. On that basis the 2026 placement destroys value: three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay what it cost to win. The model turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the 2029 target of $7.50, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1, the minimum a salesforce needs. Between one panel and four is the zone where Vantelle can grow and still lose money on every site it places.

### The clinic's margin is real, and the fee eats it where adoption starts

Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes the panel maps to — $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine, $4.76 potassium. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $37.98 a panel. It also pays $650 a month, which is 17 panels of that margin: at 30.5 panels a month the clinic nets $508 per analyzer, at 240 panels $8,400. A fixed fee on a variable-margin stream bites hardest where adoption begins, and incumbents sell the other way: Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S106, S22].

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |

| Contract development for one diagnostics partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

The evaluation line reconstructs exactly from the deck's inputs, which also says the monthly volume quoted as a 2026 average is the FY2025 average: the evaluation base has not grown in a year. The research-use line needs no clearance and repeats, but it is a reagent business, not a clinical one; the development line is services revenue from one customer. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27% — company-reported, unverified — the top two relationships are 42% [S1]. A top line this concentrated is not yet a razor-and-blade franchise.

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows sites keep using something they already pay for, not that they would buy at commercial volume. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, which is 114% of that median: the model does not assume Vantelle wins the urgent slice, it assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month the evaluation program has run since 2024, 402 analyzers and cartridge volume near 1.44M a year — 71 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, the reorder rate is a paying customer's behaviour, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's figure is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. For a lead check of this size, capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the $650 fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic — the deck's own figures reproduce to the dollar — and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items would settle it: the monthly volume of the best evaluation site and whether any sustained more than four panels a day; the same measure for the first ten billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix ordered, since a clinic running only troponin and potassium collects less than the cartridge costs.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight, and that gap decides the 2029 plan.**

55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against the 240 the 2028 plan assumes; a placement's three-year cartridge gross profit of $15,621 does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's product addresses a real gap in clinic care, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts do not yet support a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque. Four of six board seats are filled today; the Series B seat is Meridian's and the independent seat is vacant. Finance has been run by a part-time interim CFO since March 2026; ISO 13485 certification is absent, audit booked Q1 2027; the lead 510(k) has been under an FDA information request since 2026-08-21; and the deck discloses neither the HIPAA business-associate architecture for HL7/FHIR transfer nor the IDE/IRB basis for 41 paid evaluation sites. Geopolitics is not material: US-only revenue. Each gap is fixable; together they make the $15M milestone capital, not a bet on Q1 2027 clearance. Company figures are unverified. [S1]

### Two founder seats are not the problem; the empty independent seat is

Two founder directors of six is not control. The gap is the vacant independent seat, no disclosed audit committee and a part-time CFO at a company running an FDA submission, waiver study and scale-up. The CFO left in February 2026; the interim has been part-time since March. Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly burn, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts 30 principal payments in March 2027, one month after close. The gap is a pricing issue: Meridian is being asked to fund a company whose controls are thinner than its $170M valuation implies. Require a mutually agreed independent director, an audit committee with a financial expert, a permanent CFO within six months and monthly reporting on cash, FDA correspondence and quality metrics. These figures are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### The Corvia royalty is small until it meets an exit

The 3% cartridge royalty goes to Corvia, 60% owned by Vantelle, where CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22% — 0.66% of cartridge sales. Every $10M of cartridge revenue carries $300,000 of royalty, $120,000 to the 40% minority and $66,000 to the CTO. The exit is the larger issue: the minority may put its 40% at fair value on an acquisition, $9.4M capitalising 3% of FY2029 plan revenue at 10x. It ranks ahead of the Series B and should reduce the price. Require disinterested approval and a fairness opinion of the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and cap-table disclosure. These terms are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### Quality culture is the open file

ISO 13485 certification is absent and FDA's QMSR has required an ISO 13485-based system since 2026-02-02. The regulatory vice-president who prepared the 510(k) left in September 2025; her successor joined in November 2025, two months before filing. The 2026-08-21 request's content is undisclosed, so the deficiency could be labelling, the 640-sample study or the quality system. FDA's 2024-05-09 warning letter to Cue Health cited unauthorised device changes and lot-release failures, and ordered a stop-sale. A warning letter before clearance would delay launch, complicate the waiver and give 41 clinic customers pause. [S1, S71, S113]

### Patient data has no visible contract

The Q5 sends results to the clinic EHR over Wi-Fi using HL7 and FHIR, making Vantelle a vendor that creates, receives and transmits PHI for a covered entity. Under HHS rules that requires a BAA with each clinic, equivalent terms with subcontractors, Security Rule safeguards and breach reporting; the business associate is directly liable. The deck discloses no BAA count, SOC 2 or HITRUST report, named privacy officer, encryption or incident-response terms, or cyber insurance. Silence is not proof of absence, but it is material non-disclosure at 41 PHI sites. Executed BAAs, a current security report and a named security owner should be closing conditions. [S1, S135]

Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 41 evaluation sites run. That gap, not the $2.4B market estimate or the FDA calendar, decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. The figures are company-reported, unverified. Vantelle reports 55 analyzers across 41 sites and 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month [S1]: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month, 1.0 a day on a 30-day basis and 1.22 on the 300-operating-day convention its own market model uses. The plan assumes 8.0 from 2028. The 2029 revenue line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, company-reported and unverified, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 of revenue against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty on net sales to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate that licenses the sealing patent and whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer. That royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim on gross margin. Cost carries the same uncertainty: $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month, and getting a five-assay cartridge to that cost is a redesign, not a learning curve. The acquisition cost is the line the deck omits, and the headcount gives it: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months, 21 a year [S1]. At an assumed $100,000-155,000 fully loaded per head that is $0.9-1.4M a year, $43,000-66,000 per placement; charging half to placements, since the same team sells the research-use and development revenue, gives the $25,600-51,200 above. On that basis the 2026 placement destroys value: three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay what it cost to win. The model turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the 2029 target of $7.50, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1, the minimum a salesforce needs. Between one panel and four is the zone where Vantelle can grow and still lose money on every site it places.

### The clinic's margin is real, and the fee eats it where adoption starts

Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes the panel maps to — $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine, $4.76 potassium. The research-use line needs no clearance and repeats, but it is a reagent business, not a clinical one; the development line is services revenue from one customer. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27% — company-reported, unverified — the top two relationships are 42% [S1]. A top line this concentrated is not yet a razor-and-blade franchise.

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows sites keep using something they already pay for, not that they would buy at commercial volume. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, which is 114% of that median: the model does not assume Vantelle wins the urgent slice, it assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month the evaluation program has run since 2024, 402 analyzers and cartridge volume near 1.44M a year — 71 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, the reorder rate is a paying customer's behaviour, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's figure is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. For a lead check of this size, capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the $650 fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic — the deck's own figures reproduce to the dollar — and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items would settle it: the monthly volume of the best evaluation site and whether any sustained more than four panels a day; the same measure for the first ten billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix ordered, since a clinic running only troponin and potassium collects less than the cartridge costs.

**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight, and that gap decides the 2029 plan.**

55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against the 240 the 2028 plan assumes; a placement's three-year cartridge gross profit of $15,621 does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1].

Vantelle's product addresses a real gap in clinic care, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts do not yet support a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque. Four of six board seats are filled today; the Series B seat is Meridian's and the independent seat is vacant. Finance has been run by a part-time interim CFO since March 2026; ISO 13485 certification is absent, audit booked Q1 2027; the lead 510(k) has been under an FDA information request since 2026-08-21; and the deck discloses neither the HIPAA business-associate architecture for HL7/FHIR transfer nor the IDE/IRB basis for 41 paid evaluation sites. Geopolitics is not material: US-only revenue. Each gap is fixable; together they make the $15M milestone capital, not a bet on Q1 2027 clearance. Company figures are unverified. [S1]

### Two founder seats are not the problem; the empty independent seat is

Two founder directors of six is not control. The gap is the vacant independent seat, no disclosed audit committee and a part-time CFO at a company running an FDA submission, waiver study and scale-up. The CFO left in February 2026; the interim has been part-time since March. Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly burn, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts 30 principal payments in March 2027, one month after close. The gap is a pricing issue: Meridian is being asked to fund a company whose controls are thinner than its $170M valuation implies. Require a mutually agreed independent director, an audit committee with a financial expert, a permanent CFO within six months and monthly reporting on cash, FDA correspondence and quality metrics. These figures are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### The Corvia royalty is small until it meets an exit

The 3% cartridge royalty goes to Corvia, 60% owned by Vantelle, where CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22% — 0.66% of cartridge sales. Every $10M of cartridge revenue carries $300,000 of royalty, $120,000 to the 40% minority and $66,000 to the CTO. The exit is the larger issue: the minority may put its 40% at fair value on an acquisition, $9.4M capitalising 3% of FY2029 plan revenue at 10x. It ranks ahead of the Series B and should reduce the price. Require disinterested approval and a fairness opinion of the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and cap-table disclosure. These terms are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's product addresses a real gap in clinic care, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts do not yet support a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque. Four of six board seats are filled today; the Series B seat is Meridian's and the independent seat is vacant. Finance has been run by a part-time interim CFO since March 2026; ISO 13485 certification is absent, audit booked Q1 2027; the lead 510(k) has been under an FDA information request since 2026-08-21; and the deck discloses neither the HIPAA business-associate architecture for HL7/FHIR transfer nor the IDE/IRB basis for 41 paid evaluation sites. Geopolitics is not material: US-only revenue. Labour and environmental exposure is not material at 64 employees and a pilot line. Each gap is fixable; together they make the $15M milestone capital, not a Q1 2027 bet. Company figures are unverified. [S1]

### Two founder seats are not the problem; the empty independent seat is

Two founder directors of six is not control. The gap is the vacant independent seat, no disclosed audit committee and a part-time CFO at a company running an FDA submission, waiver study and scale-up. The CFO left in February 2026; the interim has been part-time since March. Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly burn, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts 30 principal payments in March 2027, one month after close. The gap is a pricing issue: the controls are thinner than the $170M valuation implies. Require a mutually agreed independent director, an audit committee with a financial expert, a permanent CFO within six months and monthly reporting on cash, FDA correspondence and quality metrics. These figures are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### The Corvia royalty is small until it meets an exit

The 3% cartridge royalty goes to Corvia, 60% owned by Vantelle, where CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22% — 0.66% of cartridge sales. Every $10M of cartridge revenue carries $300,000 of royalty, $120,000 to the 40% minority and $66,000 to the CTO. The exit is the larger issue: the minority may put its 40% at fair value on an acquisition, $9.4M capitalising 3% of FY2029 plan revenue at 10x. It ranks ahead of the Series B and should reduce the price. Require disinterested approval and a fairness opinion of the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and cap-table disclosure. These terms are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### Quality culture is the open file

ISO 13485 certification is absent and FDA's QMSR has required an ISO 13485-based system since 2026-02-02. The regulatory vice-president who prepared the 510(k) left in September 2025; her successor joined in November 2025, two months before filing. The 2026-08-21 request's content is undisclosed, so the deficiency could be labelling, the 640-sample study or the quality system. FDA's 2024-05-09 warning letter to Cue Health cited unauthorised device changes and lot-release failures, and ordered a stop-sale. A warning letter before clearance would delay launch, complicate the waiver and give 41 clinic customers pause. [S1, S71, S113]

### Patient data has no visible contract

The Q5 sends results to the clinic EHR over Wi-Fi using HL7 and FHIR, making Vantelle a vendor that creates, receives and transmits PHI for a covered entity. Under HHS rules that requires a BAA with each clinic, equivalent terms with subcontractors, Security Rule safeguards and breach reporting; the business associate is directly liable. The deck discloses no BAA count, SOC 2 or HITRUST report, named privacy officer, encryption or incident-response terms, or cyber insurance. Silence is not proof, but it is material non-disclosure at 41 PHI sites. Executed BAAs, a current security report and a named security owner should be closing conditions. [S1, S135]

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. On the company's projections, the $22.5M of net losses in 2027-2028 plus the capital spending and working capital a launch requires exceed the $32.3M the round would leave at close, so Vantelle needs about $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. The arithmetic starts at $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30 and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months of cushion — left at the 2027-01-29 target close. The burn is also understated today: $1.15M a month is $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M, so it is the P&L loss with no capex and no working capital in it, which are exactly the two items a launch adds.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the entire investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue, which is 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or about 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each — more than twice the 300 sites targeted for the end of 2027. Capital efficiency is poor against the stage: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E on reported revenue, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x and a common threshold that above 1.5x is inefficient at scale [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

Only two audited-looking years, FY2024 and FY2025, plus nine months to 2026-09-30 with $2.7M of revenue, are disclosed; FY2023 and quarterly statements are not, and the projections are management's, unverified. That is a weaker history than a Series B usually carries, and it is why every figure below is tied to a source rather than an auditor.

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027, under a letter of intent the deck itself calls non-binding. At $33.40 a cartridge the order is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month shelf-life claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M, and with $2.7M booked in the first nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point from the other side: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to about 52%, cutting gross profit by roughly $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's allocation of 35% to clearance, 40% to manufacturing and 25% to launch has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply about $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% the interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and post-March-2027 debt service is about $210,000 a month, 18% of today's burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting into 2.571M shares [S1, S22].

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of about $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's roughly $12.0M outflow takes it to about negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit, and the shortfall is $8-10M. The stress case moves clearance to Q3 2027 — a 175-day chemistry-panel review average plus an information-request pause makes Q1 2027 the optimistic end of the range, not the middle — puts the CLIA waiver in 2028 and halves utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with operating cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M fully diluted count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S92].

The variable that moves the outcome is panels per analyzer-day, not sites, price or the clearance date: clearance moves the clock and utilisation sets the level, and the level is set in the plan at eight. Everything else in the model is a second-order adjustment to that number. What would change the judgement is evidence from billing-enabled sites, and the diligence list is short and specific: the Bluestem loan agreement for its rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor agreement for payment terms, return and rotation rights and the wholesale price behind the $2.4M order; the Tempe line's capacity, yield and cost roll-up, since $16.20 a cartridge sits against 18 manufacturing staff and a pilot line that has never exceeded 2,000 units a month; and the Corvia minority put, which is payable at fair value on an acquisition and sits ahead of the equity. Confidence is high on the arithmetic, which reconciles to the deck's own numbers, and medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates with no auditor, no quarterly statements and no covenant disclosure behind them.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. On the company's projections, the $22.5M of net losses in 2027-2028 plus the capital spending and working capital a launch requires exceed the $32.3M the round would leave at close, so Vantelle needs about $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. The arithmetic starts at $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30 and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months of cushion — left at the 2027-01-29 target close. The burn is also understated today: $1.15M a month is $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M, so it is the P&L loss with no capex and no working capital in it, which are exactly the two items a launch adds.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the entire investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue, which is 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or about 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each — more than twice the 300 sites targeted for the end of 2027. Capital efficiency is poor against the stage: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E on reported revenue, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x and a common threshold that above 1.5x is inefficient at scale [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

| Line item, $M | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | FY2029P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 1.1 | 2.6 | 5.9 | 16.8 | 41.0 | 78.5 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue growth | — | 136% | 127% | 185% | 144% | 91% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Gross margin | 49% | 58% | 61% | 63% | 67% | 71% | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.5 | 1.5 | 3.6 | 10.6 | 27.5 | 55.7 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Net loss | (9.8) | (12.4) | (14.0) | (16.5) | (6.0) | 9.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Implied operating cost | 10.3 | 13.9 | 17.6 | 27.1 | 33.5 | 46.7 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Revenue excluding the stocking order | — | — | 3.5 | — | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash at year end | 21.0 | 11.3 | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |
| Net burn a month | — | — | 1.15 | — | — | — | S1 (unverified) |

Only FY2024 and FY2025, plus nine months to 2026-09-30 with $2.7M of revenue, are disclosed; FY2023 and quarterly statements are not, and the projections are management's, unverified.

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027, under a letter of intent the deck itself calls non-binding. At $33.40 a cartridge the order is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month shelf-life claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M, and with $2.7M booked in the first nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point from the other side: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to about 52%, cutting gross profit by roughly $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's allocation of 35% to clearance, 40% to manufacturing and 25% to launch has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply about $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% the interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and post-March-2027 debt service is about $210,000 a month, 18% of today's burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting into 2.571M shares [S1, S22].

| Metric | FY2025 | FY2026E | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Operating cost / revenue | 535% | 299% | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Net margin | (477%) | (237%) | QuidelOrtho (41.5%) | S1 (unverified), S22 |
| Revenue per dollar raised | $0.05 | $0.11 | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Burn multiple | 8.3x | 4.2x, or 15.6x ex-stocking order | Series B median 1.4x | S1 (unverified), S134 |
| ROE and ROIC | not meaningful | not meaningful | — | Accumulated deficit of at least $36.2M against $40.5M of equity raised |
| Receivable days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 55.7 days | S22 |
| Inventory days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 145 days | S22 |
| Cash conversion | Burn equals net loss: $13.8M against $14.0M | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of about $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's roughly $12.0M outflow takes it to about negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit, and the shortfall is $8-10M. The stress case moves clearance to Q3 2027 — a 175-day chemistry-panel review average plus an information-request pause makes Q1 2027 the optimistic end of the range, not the middle — puts the CLIA waiver in 2028 and halves utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with operating cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M fully diluted count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S92].

| Item | Base | Stress | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) clearance | Q1 2027 | Q3 2027 | S1 (unverified), S92 |
| CLIA waiver | applied Q3 2027 | 2028 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day, 2028 | 8.0 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue, FY2027 / 2028 / 2029 | 16.8 / 41.0 / 78.5 | 5.0 / 14.0 / 32.0 | S1 (unverified); analyst estimate |
| Cumulative net loss, 2027-2029 | (13.5) | (55.3) | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash at the 2027-01-29 close | 32.3 | 32.3 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash trough | (4.7) in 2028 | below (25) in 2029 | calculated |
| Additional capital needed, $M | 8-10 | 25-40 | calculated |
| Dilution at half the Series B price | none | 23-32% | calculated |

The variable that moves the outcome is panels per analyzer-day, not sites, price or the clearance date: clearance moves the clock and utilisation sets the level, and the level is set in the plan at eight. What would change the judgement is evidence from billing-enabled sites, and the diligence list is short and specific: the Bluestem loan agreement for its rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor agreement for payment terms, return and rotation rights and the wholesale price behind the $2.4M order; the Tempe line's capacity, yield and cost roll-up, since $16.20 a cartridge sits against 18 manufacturing staff and a pilot line that has never exceeded 2,000 units a month; and the Corvia minority put, which is payable at fair value on an acquisition and sits ahead of the equity. Confidence is high on the arithmetic, which reconciles to the deck's own numbers, and medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates with no auditor, no quarterly statements and no covenant disclosure behind them.

::: info danger
**The largest single line of FY2026 revenue cannot be delivered in FY2026 and has no evidence of pull-through.**

$2.4M of the $5.9M projection is an opening stocking order from a distributor whose commitment is a non-binding letter of intent; it ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the company dates to Q1 2027, it equals 71,856 cartridges or 3.6 years of current volume, and the product carries six months of stability data against a claimed nine-month shelf life [S1].
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,875 characters)
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. What is genuinely different is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve and pivotal capillary study hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator. The reader (the VD-2 family) measures an optical signal and corrects for drift; a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line. That can be acceptable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity; it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck labels the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes. On this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's [S68, S70].

A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error. The internal study reports none of these: 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed, and the 95% interval at that sample size is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia. Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens: the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma; un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Replication test, funded team of 50 | — | Cartridge first, then a pivotal study and review of this size | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion covers the cartridge and stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover while the reader family sits in appeal. No public patent record was retrievable; the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |
| Medicare reimbursement, 2026 | $71.38 for all five assays; $17.23 for troponin plus potassium | Cartridge list $38 | The panel only pays if most assays are ordered | S82-S86 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product: it is priced below build cost, company data unverified, and given away to many evaluation sites. The economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate [S1].

Counter-evidence runs the other way. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, and most sites reordered. A rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff; the deck reports no sensitivity or specificity, the number that would settle it.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the recent additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability beyond the data held; and the scope of the VD-1 claims and the VD-2 appeal. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing and IP judgements rest on company disclosure alone."}],"isError":false}
