{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 6 by Market Analyst, 8,013 characters)
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the monthly cartridge volumes behind the utilisation test are unverified company figures, unaudited and not independently confirmed. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. A 13,200-site total is not the problem; utilisation is. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,280 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US, glucose strips, blood gas and infectious disease included; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and the arithmetic works only when four or five analytes are ordered and paid on the same run. Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine on the nearest priced code and $4.76 for potassium, $71.38 if all five are billed and collected. Against a $38 cartridge and a $650 monthly analyzer fee, a site running 41 cartridges a month collects $2,926.58 and pays $2,208, $718.58 of gross margin per analyzer-month before staff time and billing cost. Run only troponin and potassium, the two analytes a chest-pain patient needs, and the clinic collects $17.23 against a $38 cartridge, a loss of $20.77 per run. The company does not disclose ordered tests per cartridge, and that metric decides whether the clinic is a customer or a charity. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico together hold 4,296 moderate-complexity laboratories and 31,720 waived ones. Until the waiver is granted, Vantelle sells into a base one-eighth the size of the one its labour-free pitch addresses, and each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024, and that is the only facility class the policy creates. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. [S81, S79, S95, S1]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: Texas, Arizona, New Mexico | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA laboratories across the three states (2026) | US point-of-care 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only, no billable use | Moderate-complexity CLIA certificate and staffed quality control until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital and reference laboratories | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of the United States | $2.89B-$14.0B total US point-of-care market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR, 2026-2034 | Planned after a waiver; 300 sites targeted by end-2027 through a non-binding distributor letter of intent | Same CLIA constraint; payer coverage; no waiver before 2027 | Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Roche, Radiometer, Quest Diagnostics | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15 with no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement, distributor | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens Healthineers | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more, and the company's own clinic survey reports a median daily send-out volume far above what its evaluation sites ran. The survey and the operating data differ by an order of magnitude and only one can describe the commercial site. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, confidence in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests per cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any evaluation site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until those are answered, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price, not in the narrative.

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**

The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in 2026, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M [S1].
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 5 by Market Analyst, 8,920 characters)
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim, so the advantage lasts only until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships, and it cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is not a startup with better chemistry; it is the incumbent that already owns the buyer's analyser slot. [S1, S67, S104]

The buyer at a three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options, and only one is a direct competitor. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a handheld cartridge analyser whose waived menu covers creatinine, potassium and glucose and which added an hs-troponin I cartridge in January 2025. Direct but narrower: Siemens epoc, 13 blood-gas, electrolyte and metabolite analytes in under a minute with no cardiac marker; QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel from EDTA whole blood; Roche's cobas h 232 from heparinised venous blood; and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX in hospital emergency departments. Substitute: the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call them later. No US product retrieved combines troponin, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium in one finger-stick cartridge, which is the gap the company sells into. [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109]

| Competitor | Product | Regulatory status | Menu | Price | Scale | Strengths versus Vantelle | Weaknesses versus Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and Alinity, hs-TnI cartridge | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11; waived-test manual; CG8+ cleared for capillary blood 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c/NT-proBNP | Not publicly disclosed | Point of Care line $606M FY2025 | Waived menu, installed base, capillary claim, distribution | One cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc | Marketed for hospital point-of-care use | 13 analytes in under a minute; no troponin or natriuretic peptide | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base, informatics | No cardiac menu, laboratory-controlled | S107 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro cardiac panel | US cardiac panel via waived-test channels; Cardio3 with BNP not sold in the US | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin in about 20 minutes | $599 per 25-test kit, $23.96 a test | $2.73B total FY2025; point-of-care share not disclosed | Urgent-care base, lowest price per test | EDTA blood or plasma, no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Roche | cobas h 232; LumiraDx | Marketed; LumiraDx acquired 2024-07-29 | Troponin T, NT-proBNP, D-dimer, myoglobin | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Global distribution; owns LumiraDx | Venous sample, one test per strip, no metabolic panel | S111, S91 |
| Radiometer (Danaher) | AQT90 FLEX | Marketed for troponin I/T and NT-proBNP | Laboratory-quality immunoassay | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base | Benchtop, laboratory staff, no metabolic panel | S109 |
| Quest Diagnostics | Reference laboratory | n/a | Any test; one-to-three-day turnaround | $71.38 for the five codes at 2026 Medicare rates | $11.04B FY2025 | Zero capital, payer contracts | Turnaround unusable for suspected MI | S65, S85, S83, S84, S82, S86 |

Abbott decides the price. It documents the waived path for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026, which shows it is still investing in point-of-care cardiac testing. Its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025 while the wider Rapid Diagnostics segment fell 18.1% as COVID testing receded; point of care grew 3.1%. Analyser, cartridge and installed-base data are not disclosed, which is itself a diligence gap. Set against QuidelOrtho's $2.73B and Quest's $11.04B, Vantelle's $2.6M of FY2025 revenue is a 0.02% share of the smaller competitor. [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67, S22, S65]

When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert. The Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% gross margin at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, about 54 times what the 41 evaluation sites consume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20 to $25 with a free analyser takes the account, because the alternative is $38 plus $650 a month. At that price Vantelle's cartridge margin falls below 20% on today's cost, and it has no second product to defend the account. [S1, S67, S106]

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and which Vantelle has not yet applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, all assemblable from parts incumbents already sell. Sight Diagnostics shows how the regulatory step separates the two: its OLO analyser runs a finger-stick CBC and was cleared in 2021 for moderately complex rather than waived use, so a finger-stick clearance did not become a labour-free product. The base rate agrees: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1]

| Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Vantelle share | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Five-analyte finger-stick cardiac and metabolic panel for clinics without a laboratory | Abbott (i-STAT, waived menu, capillary claim) | Siemens Healthineers (epoc) and Roche (cobas h 232 plus LumiraDx) | QuidelOrtho (Triage cardiac) and Radiometer (AQT90 FLEX) | Sight Diagnostics (finger-stick CBC in the same clinic) and a combined cartridge from any incumbent | 0.3%, on $1.1M of 2025 evaluation revenue against a $368M cartridge market at observed utilisation | S104, S107, S111, S108, S109, S112, S1 |

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per group, and a clinic that must draw venous blood still needs the phlebotomist. That is a genuine opening of a year or two, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; confidence that Vantelle keeps a premium beyond the plan period is low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the evaluation sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived and accepts capillary blood; what price the distributor's letter of intent implies; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design.

::: evidence
**The buyer's default alternative is a waived Abbott handheld, not a reference lab.**

Abbott cleared hs-troponin for the i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and the Alinity in June 2026, publishes a waived-test manual for the i-STAT 1, and cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's counter-position is one cartridge and five analytes at $38 [S67, S6, S104, S105, S1].
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 5 by Valuation Analyst, 8,625 characters)
At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and the Series A's participating preference means a $30M Series B needs a $435M exit to return 3x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, all company-reported and not independently verified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho, the closest listed comparable, trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

Company-reported financing terms, not independently verified:

The company-reported, unverified terms show the seed priced at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11. The headline pre-money rises 34% from the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but $13.1M of that is the option-pool refresh to 10% of the post-money: existing holders' effective pre-money is $126.9M, a 21% uplift over 2.9 years, or 6.9% a year. Existing shares fall from 100% to 69.7% of the fully diluted company — 7.7 points of pool refresh, 4.9 points of bridge and 17.6 points of new Series B — taking the founders from 30.8% to 21.5%, the seed from 16.5% to 11.5% and the Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%. ### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. The alternative is to wait: the 510(k) response is due in December 2026, clearance is guided for Q1 2027 and the waiver application for Q3 2027, so a 2027 entry pays more but buys retired regulatory risk. The company had $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30, six months at $1.15M a month and the 2027-01-29 target close, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts amortising in 2027-03. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 3 by Valuation Analyst, 8,438 characters)
The realistic buyer set is five point-of-care incumbents, and the most recent cleared-and-waived platform sold for $100M in April 2026; at $140M pre-money the Series B needs a $435M exit for 3x, a price only a strategic paying for the platform rather than the plan can justify. The asset being bought is not the 64-person team or the evaluation programme but the cartridge IP — the granted on-board-calibrator patent (VD-1) and the exclusively licensed Corvia sealing film (CM-1) — plus the two-assay 510(k), the CLIA-waiver path and 41 evaluation sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico (company-reported, unverified). QuidelOrtho, Abbott, Roche Diagnostics and Werfen all sell point-of-care instruments into US urgent-care or hospital channels, and none sells a five-analyte finger-stick panel run by clinic staff. Abbott's i-STAT and Afinion platforms cover blood gas, chemistries and cardiometabolic tests; QuidelOrtho's Triage and Sofia cover cardiac and rapid immunoassay; Roche bought LumiraDx's multi-assay platform in 2024; Werfen's acute-care line sits beside hemostasis and autoimmunity. Each has a gap Vantelle would fill, but each also has a platform to protect [S22, S67, S91, S119, S126].

### Who buys, for which asset and when

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale (asset) | Timing | Likelihood (our judgement) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | QuidelOrtho | Triage and Sofia installed base in urgent care; bought LEX for $100M in 2026-04 | 2029-2031 | Medium-low | S22, S126 |
| Trade sale | Abbott | i-STAT and Afinion base; needs a staff-run finger-stick cardiac panel | 2029-2031 | Medium | S67 |
| Trade sale | Roche Diagnostics | LumiraDx platform since 2024; primary-care immunoassay menu | 2029-2031 | Low-medium | S91 |
| Trade sale | Werfen | Acute-care and hemostasis channel; paid $2.0B for Immucor in 2023 | 2029-2031 | Low | S119 |
| Trade sale | Thermo Fisher or Hologic | Molecular point-of-care only (Mesa $450M, Mobidiag $795M) | 2029-2031 | Low | S120, S122 |
| IPO | Nasdaq | Needs $100M+ revenue and a waived menu | 2030 or later | Low | S125 |
| Distressed asset sale | Financial or strategic buyer | IP and 510(k) only, no commercial franchise | 2027-2028 if the waiver fails | Medium in the failure case | S117, S126 |

The strongest fit is QuidelOrtho, which owns Triage and Sofia in exactly the urgent-care channel Vantelle targets and paid $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics in April 2026 — but it also carries $1.1B of enterprise value and negative free cash flow, and it has just bought the molecular platform it wanted. Abbott is the largest and most able payer, with i-STAT Alinity and Afinion already placed in clinics, yet that installed base gives it a build-or-buy option that argues for a lower price. Roche and Werfen are European buyers with no US ownership limits in diagnostics, but Roche has owned a LumiraDx platform since 2024 and Werfen's recent acquisitions have been in transfusion and hemostasis. The practical conclusion is a five-buyer, not a competitive, auction. The strategic logic is scale economics: a waived five-analyte cartridge at $38 lets an incumbent serve the 11,400 US urgent-care sites that cannot staff a laboratory, and the clinic bills the payer under existing test codes rather than to Vantelle. The counter-evidence is that Abbott or QuidelOrtho can add a waived cardiac assay to its own installed analyser and reach the same sites without buying Vantelle, and that a pre-clearance asset carries 510(k) and CLIA risk an acquirer can wait out at no cost. That substitution risk, not the number of buyers, is the central threat to a $435M exit [S22, S67, S91, S119, S126].

### The precedent record prices a cleared platform well below the ask

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho–LEX Diagnostics | 2026 | $100M cash | not disclosed; platform pre-commercial | S126 |
| Roche–LumiraDx point-of-care platform | 2023-24 | $295M plus up to $55M | ~3.4x annualised H1 2023 revenue of $86.4M | S91, S117 |
| Quidel–Ortho Clinical Diagnostics | 2021-22 | ~$6.0B | ~3.3x 2020 revenue of $1.8B | S121, S123 |
| Werfen–Immucor | 2022-23 | ~$2.0B | not disclosed | S119 |
| Roche–GenMark Diagnostics | 2021 | $1.8B | not disclosed | S118 |
| Hologic–Mobidiag | 2021 | $795M enterprise value | not disclosed | S122 |
| Thermo Fisher–Mesa Biotech | 2021 | $450M plus up to $100M | not disclosed | S120 |
| LumiraDx de-SPAC listing | 2021 | $3.0B valuation, cut from $5.0B | sold for $295M in 2023-24 | S130, S131 |
| Cue Health Chapter 7 | 2024 | zero equity value | after $480M+ raised | S129, S132 |

The 2026 clearing price is $100M for a platform that already had FDA clearance and a CLIA waiver when it was sold; LumiraDx, a commercial multi-assay platform with 30 assays and H1 2023 revenue of $43.2M, sold its point-of-care technology for $295M after its lenders took control. The larger 2021 prices — $450M plus milestones for Mesa, $795M for Mobidiag, $1.8B for GenMark — were set in the COVID-era liquidity window, and the market has since re-rated: QuidelOrtho itself trades at 0.4x EV/Sales, down 50.9% over 12 months. A $435M exit would be 4.4x the LEX price and 1.5x the LumiraDx assets, a 2021-style price in a 2026 market [S117, S118, S120, S121, S122, S123, S126].

### What the company must be worth after preferences and the minority put

| Entry pre-money | Series B and B-1 ownership | Exit needed for 3x on $30M | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | 22.6% | $435M | S1 (unverified) |
| $100M | 28.5% | $352M | S1 (unverified) |
| $70M | 36% | $286M | S1 (unverified) |
| $50M | 44% | $241M | S1 (unverified) |

At $140M pre-money the Series B needs $435M for 3x on $30M, $518M for 3x on the $36.3M of B plus B-1 and $1.37B for 10x; the 40% Corvia minority put, worth an estimated $1.5-7.6M, is deducted before the stack. The company's own unverified FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue at a 2.5x multiple gives a $196M enterprise value, which returns 1.2x to the Series B — below the 4.93% yield on the 10-year Treasury on 2026-10-30. Only a 2031 bull case of $150M revenue at 25% EBITDA and 12x EV/EBITDA reaches about $450M, and that is the 3x threshold five years out, a 24.6% internal rate of return. Entry price is the first lever: at $70M pre-money the Series B owns 36% and 3x needs $286M; at $50M it owns 44% and 3x needs $241M. The Series A's participation is the second: it takes $130.8M, 30.1% of a $435M exit, on 23.8% ownership [S1].

### The base rate is poor and the IPO is not a route

LumiraDx listed at a $3B de-SPAC valuation in September 2021 after cutting the deal from $5B, then sold its technology for $295M; Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after raising $480M+; Truvian, the best-capitalised private comparable, raised $294M, cleared 12 analytes by 2026-01-12 and is still private in October 2026, eleven years after founding. An IPO is not a route before 2029-2030: the company has two assays filed, no CLIA waiver and $3.5M of normalised FY2026 revenue (company-reported, unverified), while the 2025 US medtech IPO market absorbed eight deals raising $1.8B in total. The realistic holding period is 4-5 years — 510(k) clearance in Q1 2027, a waiver decision in 2028, commercial scale in 2028-2029 and a sale in 2030-2031 [S124, S125, S127, S129, S130, S131, S132].

### Policy tests and liquidity

No US foreign-ownership limit applies to diagnostics, so Werfen (Spain) or Roche (Switzerland) would face HSR antitrust review and FDA quality-system scrutiny but not CFIUS on national-security grounds; sanctions and export controls do not bind, and the binding constraints are the 510(k) and the CLIA waiver. The Corvia put and the 3% related-party royalty to a company 22%-owned by the CTO are closing frictions an acquirer will price and may require to be cleaned up before signing. Liquidity: a $15M cheque at $140M pre-money buys 8.8% of the company; a 3x return is $45M, which on a $300-500M IPO with a 25-30% float would be 30-60% of the tradable stock, so an IPO exit would require a discounted block trade after the 180-day lock-up. A trade sale pays cash at closing, typically with 10-15% escrow and an earn-out. At $140M the entry is incompatible with the exit evidence; the same company at $60-80M pre-money, with the Series A participation capped and the cheque tranched, is a defensible wait-for-milestone investment [S1, S119, S125]."}],"isError":false}

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. On the company's projections, the $22.5M of net losses in 2027-2028 plus the capital spending and working capital a launch requires exceed the $32.3M the round would leave at close, so Vantelle needs about $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. The arithmetic starts at $6.9M of cash, company-reported on 2026-09-30, and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months of cushion — left at the 2027-01-29 target close. The burn is also understated today: $1.15M a month is $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M, so it is the P&L loss with no capex and no working capital in it, which are exactly the two items a launch adds.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the entire investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue, which is 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each — more than twice the 300 sites targeted for the end of 2027. Capital efficiency is poor against the stage: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E on reported revenue, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x and a common threshold that above 1.5x is inefficient at scale [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

| Line item, $M | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | FY2029P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 1.1 | 2.6 | 5.9 | 16.8 | 41.0 | 78.5 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue growth | — | 136% | 127% | 185% | 144% | 91% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Gross margin | 49% | 58% | 61% | 63% | 67% | 71% | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.5 | 1.5 | 3.6 | 10.6 | 27.5 | 55.7 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Net loss | (9.8) | (12.4) | (14.0) | (16.5) | (6.0) | 9.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Implied operating cost | 10.3 | 13.9 | 17.6 | 27.1 | 33.5 | 46.7 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Revenue excluding the stocking order | — | — | 3.5 | — | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash at year end | 21.0 | 11.3 | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |
| Net burn a month | — | — | 1.15 | — | — | — | S1 (unverified) |

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027, under a letter of intent the deck itself calls non-binding. At $33.40 a cartridge the order is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month shelf-life claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M, and with $2.7M booked in the first nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point from the other side: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's allocation of 35% to clearance, 40% to manufacturing and 25% to launch has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% the interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and post-March-2027 debt service is $210,000 a month, 18% of today's burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting into 2.571M shares [S1, S22].

| Metric | FY2025 | FY2026E | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Operating cost / revenue | 535% | 299% | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Net margin | (477%) | (237%) | QuidelOrtho (41.5%) | S1 (unverified), S22 |
| Revenue per dollar raised | $0.05 | $0.11 | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Burn multiple | 8.3x | 4.2x, or 15.6x ex-stocking order | Series B median 1.4x | S1 (unverified), S134 |
| ROE and ROIC | not meaningful | not meaningful | — | S1 (unverified); accumulated deficit of at least $36.2M against $40.5M of equity raised |
| Receivable days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 55.7 days | S22 |
| Inventory days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 145 days | S22 |
| Cash conversion | Burn equals net loss: $13.8M against $14.0M | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's $12.0M outflow takes it to negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit, and the shortfall is $8-10M. The stress case moves clearance to Q3 2027 — a 175-day chemistry-panel review average plus an information-request pause makes Q1 2027 the optimistic end of the range, not the middle — puts the CLIA waiver in 2028 and halves utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with operating cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M fully diluted count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S92].

| Item | Base | Stress | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) clearance | Q1 2027 | Q3 2027 | S1 (unverified), S92 |
| CLIA waiver | applied Q3 2027 | 2028 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day, 2028 | 8.0 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue, FY2027 / 2028 / 2029 | 16.8 / 41.0 / 78.5 | 5.0 / 14.0 / 32.0 | S1 (unverified); analyst estimate |
| Cumulative net loss, 2027-2029 | (13.5) | (55.3) | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash at the 2027-01-29 close | 32.3 | 32.3 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash trough | (4.7) in 2028 | below (25) in 2029 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Additional capital needed, $M | 8-10 | 25-40 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Dilution at half the Series B price | none | 23-32% | S1 (unverified); calculated |

The variable that moves the outcome is panels per analyzer-day, not sites, price or the clearance date: clearance moves the clock, utilisation sets the level, and the level is set at the plan's launch-year assumption. The counter-case is that the burn is discretionary — a company that cut operating cost sharply and slowed the site ramp would close most of the base-case gap, and a distributor that finances inventory would remove much of the working-capital need — so the shortfall describes this plan rather than the company's ability to survive. For the check, the implication is that the round should be sized larger or tranched, with the second tranche released on clearance and on a utilisation milestone, and that the price should assume a further financing before breakeven. Evidence from billing-enabled sites would change the judgement, and the diligence list is short: the Bluestem loan agreement for its rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor agreement for payment terms, return and rotation rights and the wholesale price behind the stocking order; the Tempe line's capacity, yield and cost roll-up, since the cartridge cost sits against a manufacturing team of eighteen on a pilot line that has never run at launch volumes; and the Corvia minority put, payable at fair value on an acquisition and ahead of the equity. Confidence is high on the arithmetic, which reconciles to the deck's own numbers, and medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates with no auditor, no quarterly statements and no covenant disclosure behind them.

Company-reported and unverified: $2.4M of the $5.9M projection is an opening stocking order from a distributor whose commitment is a non-binding letter of intent; it ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the company dates to Q1 2027, it equals 71,856 cartridges or 3.6 years of current volume, and the product carries six months of stability data against a claimed nine-month shelf life [S1].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. On the company's projections, the $22.5M of net losses in 2027-2028 plus the capital spending and working capital a launch requires exceed the $32.3M the round would leave at close, so Vantelle needs $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. The arithmetic starts at $6.9M of cash, company-reported on 2026-09-30, and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months of cushion — left at the 2027-01-29 target close. The burn is also understated: $1.15M a month is $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M, so it is the P&L loss with no capex and no working capital in it.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the entire investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue, which is 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each — more than twice the 300 sites targeted for the end of 2027. Capital efficiency is poor against the stage: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E on reported revenue, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x and a common threshold that above 1.5x is inefficient at scale [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027, under a letter of intent the deck itself calls non-binding. At $33.40 a cartridge the order is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month shelf-life claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M, and with $2.7M booked in the first nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's allocation of 35% to clearance, 40% to manufacturing and 25% to launch has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% the interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and post-March-2027 debt service is $210,000 a month, 18% of burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting into 2.571M shares [S1, S22].

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's $12.0M outflow takes it to negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit, and the shortfall is $8-10M. The stress case moves clearance to Q3 2027 — a 175-day chemistry-panel review average plus an information-request pause makes Q1 2027 the optimistic end of the range, not the middle — puts the CLIA waiver in 2028 and halves utilisation to 4 panels a day. 2. The problem
Urgent-care clinics and rural hospitals without an on-site laboratory send cardiac and metabolic blood tests to reference labs and wait 1-3 days for
results. Patients with chest pain or uncontrolled diabetes are often transferred, or sent home, before results arrive.
-  A transfer for a suspected heart attack that turns out negative costs thousands of dollars and takes a rural ambulance out of service for hours
(company estimate).
-  Benchtop analyzers that could run these tests on site need venous blood, a trained operator and daily quality control, which small clinics can't staff.
-  The clinics we surveyed send out a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels a day (company survey of 52 clinics, 2024).
Vantelle Diagnostics: Series B investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 2 of 15

--- p.3 ---
3. Our product: the Vantelle Q5
-  A handheld, cartridge-based analyzer that runs a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel from a finger-stick sample in 12 minutes.
-  The panel: high-sensitivity troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine (with eGFR) and potassium.
-  One 40-microliter drop of blood. Each cartridge holds all its reagents and an on-board calibrator, so there is no separate calibration step.
-  The analyzer weighs 640 grams, runs on a battery and sends results to the clinic's electronic health record over Wi-Fi (HL7 and FHIR).
-  Razor-and-blade model: instruments placed at or near cost; recurring revenue from single-use cartridges.
-  Cartridges keep for 9 months at room temperature (our stability data so far covers 6 months).
Vantelle Diagnostics: Series B investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 3 of 15

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. On the company's projections, the $22.5M of net losses in 2027-2028 plus the capital spending and working capital a launch requires exceed the $32.3M the round would leave at close, so Vantelle needs $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. The arithmetic starts at $6.9M of cash, company-reported on 2026-09-30, and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months of cushion — left at the 2027-01-29 target close. The burn is also understated: $1.15M a month is $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M, so it is the P&L loss with no capex and no working capital in it.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue, which is 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each — more than twice the 300 sites targeted for the end of 2027. Capital efficiency is poor against the stage: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E on reported revenue, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x and a common threshold that above 1.5x is inefficient at scale [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 1.1 | 2.6 | 5.9 | 16.8 | 41.0 | 78.5 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue growth | — | 136% | 127% | 185% | 144% | 91% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Gross margin | 49% | 58% | 61% | 63% | 67% | 71% | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.5 | 1.5 | 3.6 | 10.6 | 27.5 | 55.7 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Net loss | (9.8) | (12.4) | (14.0) | (16.5) | (6.0) | 9.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Implied operating cost | 10.3 | 13.9 | 17.6 | 27.1 | 33.5 | 46.7 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Revenue excluding the stocking order | — | — | 3.5 | — | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash at year end | 21.0 | 11.3 | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |
| Net burn a month | — | — | 1.15 | — | — | — | S1 (unverified) |

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027, under a letter of intent the deck itself calls non-binding. At $33.40 a cartridge the order is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month shelf-life claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M, and with $2.7M booked in the first nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's use of funds has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% the interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and post-March-2027 debt service is $210,000 a month, 18% of burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting into 2.571M shares [S1, S22].

| Net margin | (477%) | (237%) | QuidelOrtho (41.5%) | S1 (unverified), S22 |
| Revenue per dollar raised | $0.05 | $0.11 | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Burn multiple | 8.3x | 4.2x, or 15.6x ex-stocking order | Series B median 1.4x | S1 (unverified), S134 |
| ROE and ROIC | not meaningful | not meaningful | Accumulated deficit above $36.2M against $40.5M of equity raised | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Receivable days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 55.7 days | S22 |
| Inventory days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 145 days | S22 |

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's $12.0M outflow takes it to negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit, and the shortfall is $8-10M. The stress case moves clearance to Q3 2027 — a 175-day chemistry-panel review average plus an information-request pause makes Q1 2027 the optimistic end of the range, not the middle — puts the CLIA waiver in 2028 and halves utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with operating cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M fully diluted count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S92].

| Item | Base | Stress | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) clearance | Q1 2027 | Q3 2027 | S1 (unverified), S92 |
| CLIA waiver | applied Q3 2027 | 2028 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day, 2028 | 8.0 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue, FY2027 / 2028 / 2029 | 16.8 / 41.0 / 78.5 | 5.0 / 14.0 / 32.0 | S1 (unverified); analyst estimate |
| Cumulative net loss, 2027-2029 | (13.5) | (55.3) | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash trough | (4.7) in 2028 | below (25) in 2029 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Additional capital needed, $M | 8-10 | 25-40 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Dilution at half the Series B price | none | 23-32% | S1 (unverified); calculated |

These are capital-intensive instrument economics: growth is bought with placed hardware and funded receivables, so the faster Vantelle sells, the more cash it consumes before the cartridge annuity arrives. The variable that moves the outcome is panels per analyzer-day, not sites, price or the clearance date: clearance moves the clock, utilisation sets the level, and the level is set in the plan. The counter-case is that the burn is discretionary: a company that cut cost sharply and slowed the site ramp would close most of the gap, and a distributor that finances inventory would remove much of the working-capital need, so the shortfall is about this plan, not survival. For the check, the implication is that the round should be sized larger or tranched, the second tranche released on clearance and utilisation, and the price should assume a further financing before breakeven. The diligence list is short: the Bluestem loan agreement for its rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor agreement for payment terms, return and rotation rights and the wholesale price behind the stocking order; the Tempe line's capacity, yield and cost roll-up, with cartridge cost set by a manufacturing team of eighteen on a pilot line that has never run at launch volumes; and the Corvia minority put, payable at fair value on an acquisition and ahead of the equity. Confidence is high on the arithmetic, which reconciles to the deck's own numbers, and medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates with no auditor, no quarterly statements and no covenant disclosure behind them.

::: info danger
**The largest single line of FY2026 revenue cannot be delivered in FY2026 and has no evidence of pull-through.**

Company-reported and unverified: $2.4M of the $5.9M projection is an opening stocking order from a distributor whose commitment is a non-binding letter of intent; it ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the company dates to Q1 2027, it equals 71,856 cartridges or 3.6 years of current volume, and the product carries six months of stability data against a claimed nine-month shelf life [S1].
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,983 characters)
Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. On the company's projections, the $22.5M of net losses in 2027-2028 plus the capital spending and working capital a launch requires exceed the $32.3M the round would leave at close, so Vantelle needs $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. The arithmetic starts at $6.9M of cash, company-reported on 2026-09-30, and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months of cushion — left at the 2027-01-29 target close. The burn is also understated: $1.15M a month is $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M, so it is the P&L loss with no capex and no working capital in it.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue, which is 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each — more than twice the 300 sites targeted for the end of 2027. Capital efficiency is poor against the stage: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E on reported revenue, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x and a common threshold that above 1.5x is inefficient at scale [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027, under a letter of intent the deck itself calls non-binding. At $33.40 a cartridge the order is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month shelf-life claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M, and with $2.7M booked in the first nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's use of funds has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% the interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and post-March-2027 debt service is $210,000 a month, 18% of burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting into 2.571M shares [S1, S22].

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's $12.0M outflow takes it to negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit, and the shortfall is $8-10M. The stress case moves clearance to Q3 2027 — a 175-day chemistry-panel review average plus an information-request pause makes Q1 2027 the optimistic end of the range, not the middle — puts the CLIA waiver in 2028 and halves utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with operating cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M fully diluted count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S92].

These are capital-intensive instrument economics: growth is bought with placed hardware and funded receivables, so the faster Vantelle sells, the more cash it consumes before the cartridge annuity arrives. The variable that moves the outcome is panels per analyzer-day, not sites, price or the clearance date: clearance moves the clock, utilisation sets the level, and the level is set in the plan. The counter-case is that the burn is discretionary: a company that cut cost sharply and slowed the site ramp would close most of the gap, and a distributor that finances inventory would remove much of the working-capital need, so the shortfall is about this plan, not survival. For the check, the implication is that the round should be sized larger or tranched, the second tranche released on clearance and utilisation, and the price should assume a further financing before breakeven. The diligence list is short: the Bluestem loan agreement for its rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor agreement for payment terms, return and rotation rights and the wholesale price behind the stocking order; the Tempe line's capacity, yield and cost roll-up, with cartridge cost set by a manufacturing team of eighteen on a pilot line that has never run at launch volumes; and the Corvia minority put, payable at fair value on an acquisition and ahead of the equity. Confidence is high on the arithmetic, which reconciles to the deck's own numbers, and medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates with no auditor, no quarterly statements and no covenant disclosure behind them.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,935 characters)
The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 additional-information request restarts a 90-day review clock, putting the first clearance in late March 2027 at the earliest; a CLIA waiver filed in the third quarter of 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's own 150-day goal; and at the 1.35 panels a day the evaluation sites actually run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites, not the 300 the plan reaches by end-2027. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. The FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window that runs to 2027-02-17. FDA's clock resumes on receipt of that answer, so a 90-day review cannot produce a decision before late March 2027, against a 2025 average of 146-149 days. The second submission has a harder dependency: it covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until the second quarter of 2027, so a Q2 2027 filing is not physically possible and a Q3 2027 filing is the earliest realistic date [S1, S69, S92].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to the FDA request | 2026-12 (company plan) | Received 2026-08-21; not answered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 (company) | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on the answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S92 |
| Pivotal study results, four sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary-venous equivalence, intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k), NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q2 2027 (company) | Depends on pivotal results due the same quarter | Five-assay menu | S1, unverified |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 (company) | Not filed; must reference a cleared application and include flex and user studies | Waived status, the gate to urgent care | S1, S72 |
| CLIA waiver decision | No company date | 150 FDA days after filing implies Q1 2028 at the earliest | Whether 2028 revenue is reachable | S72 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use only | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset in the plan and the one scheduled latest. A waiver submission references an already cleared application and must carry a risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended sites; FDA's goal is a substantive interaction within 90 review days and a decision within 150 FDA days. Filing in Q3 2027 therefore points to a decision around the first quarter of 2028, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. Until then the panel is a moderate-complexity test that only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified, competency-assessed staff may run; a Certificate of Waiver site cannot legally run it. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are therefore hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics that make up the serviceable market in the deck. The dual 510(k) and CLIA waiver pathway used by point-of-care peers would put both decisions on one 180-day goal [S72, S81, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: evaluation sites averaged 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites and 55 analyzers in 2026 — 41 cartridges a site a month, about 30 an analyzer, roughly 1.2 a day against the 8 a day per analyzer the model assumes from 2028. The site plan does not close a 6.5-fold gap: 300 sites at model utilisation and the $31 2029 price produce $29.9M, not $78.5M. Reaching $78.5M requires 787 sites at model utilisation or 5,150 at the observed rate; $41.0M in 2028 requires 411. The 2027 line is tighter still: $16.8M with an average of 150 sites needs close to full model utilisation from the first day plus the $2.4M stocking order — no ramp at all, and only two assays on the menu for most of it [S1].

### Two of the plan's own numbers fail a timing test

Company data, unverified: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from the distributor that ships on 510(k) clearance, which the company itself expects in the first quarter of 2027. That is 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026 as scheduled. Separately, the 61% FY2026E gross margin sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below build cost, so either an undisclosed high-margin line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. Start from $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, and subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of term-loan principal once the Bluestem loan starts amortising in April 2027: $10.9M remains at the end of 2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory needed for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, so the realistic path is an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1, unverified |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1, unverified |

The distributor relationship is the commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme, and it is a letter of intent from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner — a related-party cost that belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridge sales and contract development are revenue but second curves that consume the same engineering team; the Irish entity and a CE mark are a distraction from the only market that matters in this round.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second additional-information letter | Second letter in the first half of 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Pivotal data show capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level, troponin CV below 10% | Results reported as categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver filed after clearance with no pre-submission | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready for scale | ISO 13485 certificate issued; automation ordered for Tempe | Audit slipped, no automation order by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount still in single digits against a 300-site plan | S1, unverified |

Counter-evidence deserves weight. The company hired a regulatory vice-president with a record of FDA clearances, the pipeline of paid evaluation sites and a high reorder rate is unusual for an investigational device, and if the recent request was documentation-only a Q1 2027 clearance remains possible. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the recent request asked and what evidence the pending answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers and what triggers the next round; and whether the distributor letter carries any minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing judgement is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,935 characters)
The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 additional-information request restarts a 90-day review clock, putting the first clearance in late March 2027 at the earliest; a CLIA waiver filed in the third quarter of 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's own 150-day goal; and at the 1.35 panels a day the evaluation sites actually run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites, not the 300 the plan reaches by end-2027. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. The FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window that runs to 2027-02-17. FDA's clock resumes on receipt of that answer, so a 90-day review cannot produce a decision before late March 2027, against a 2025 average of 146-149 days. The second submission has a harder dependency: it covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until the second quarter of 2027, so a Q2 2027 filing is not physically possible and a Q3 2027 filing is the earliest realistic date [S1, S69, S92].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to the FDA request | 2026-12 (company plan) | Received 2026-08-21; not answered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 (company) | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on the answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S92 |
| Pivotal study results, four sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary-venous equivalence, intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k), NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q2 2027 (company) | Depends on pivotal results due the same quarter | Five-assay menu | S1, unverified |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 (company) | Not filed; must reference a cleared application and include flex and user studies | Waived status, the gate to urgent care | S1, S72 |
| CLIA waiver decision | No company date | 150 FDA days after filing implies Q1 2028 at the earliest | Whether 2028 revenue is reachable | S72 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use only | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset in the plan and the one scheduled latest. A waiver submission references an already cleared application and must carry a risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended sites; FDA's goal is a substantive interaction within 90 review days and a decision within 150 FDA days. Filing in Q3 2027 therefore points to a decision around the first quarter of 2028, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. Until then the panel is a moderate-complexity test that only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified, competency-assessed staff may run; a Certificate of Waiver site cannot legally run it. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are therefore hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics that make up the serviceable market in the deck. The dual 510(k) and CLIA waiver pathway used by point-of-care peers would put both decisions on one 180-day goal [S72, S81, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: evaluation sites averaged 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites and 55 analyzers in 2026 — 41 cartridges a site a month, about 30 an analyzer, roughly 1.2 a day against the 8 a day per analyzer the model assumes from 2028. The site plan does not close a 6.5-fold gap: 300 sites at model utilisation and the $31 2029 price produce $29.9M, not $78.5M. Reaching $78.5M requires 787 sites at model utilisation or 5,150 at the observed rate; $41.0M in 2028 requires 411. The 2027 line is tighter still: $16.8M with an average of 150 sites needs close to full model utilisation from the first day plus the $2.4M stocking order — no ramp at all, and only two assays on the menu for most of it [S1].

### Two of the plan's own numbers fail a timing test

Company data, unverified: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from the distributor that ships on 510(k) clearance, which the company itself expects in the first quarter of 2027. That is 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026 as scheduled. Separately, the 61% FY2026E gross margin sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below build cost, so either an undisclosed high-margin line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. Start from $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, and subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of term-loan principal once the Bluestem loan starts amortising in April 2027: $10.9M remains at the end of 2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory needed for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, so the realistic path is an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1, unverified |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1, unverified |

The distributor relationship is the commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme, and it is a letter of intent from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner — a related-party cost that belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridge sales and contract development are revenue but second curves that consume the same engineering team; the Irish entity and a CE mark are a distraction from the only market that matters in this round.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second additional-information letter | Second letter in the first half of 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Pivotal data show capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level, troponin CV below 10% | Results reported as categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver filed after clearance with no pre-submission | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready for scale | ISO 13485 certificate issued; automation ordered for Tempe | Audit slipped, no automation order by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount still in single digits against a 300-site plan | S1, unverified |

Counter-evidence deserves weight. The company hired a regulatory vice-president with a record of FDA clearances, the pipeline of paid evaluation sites and a high reorder rate is unusual for an investigational device, and if the recent request was documentation-only a Q1 2027 clearance remains possible. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the recent request asked and what evidence the pending answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers and what triggers the next round; and whether the distributor letter carries any minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing judgement is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel."}],"isError":false}

That gap, not the $2.4B market estimate or the FDA calendar, decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. The figures are company-reported, unverified. Vantelle reports 55 analyzers across 41 sites and 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month [S1]: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month, 1.0 a day on a 30-day basis and 1.22 on the 300-operating-day convention its own market model uses. The plan assumes 8.0 from 2028. The 2029 revenue line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, company-reported and unverified, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 of revenue against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty on net sales to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate that licenses the sealing patent and whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer. That royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim on gross margin. Cost carries the same uncertainty: $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month, and getting a five-assay cartridge to that cost is a redesign, not a learning curve. The acquisition cost is the line the deck omits, and the headcount gives it: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months, 21 a year [S1]. At an assumed $100,000-155,000 fully loaded per head that is $0.9-1.4M a year, $43,000-66,000 per placement; charging half to placements, since the same team sells the research-use and development revenue, gives the $25,600-51,200 above. On that basis the 2026 placement destroys value: three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay what it cost to win. The model turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the 2029 target of $7.50, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1, the minimum a salesforce needs. Between one panel and four is the zone where Vantelle can grow and still lose money on every site it places.

### The clinic's margin is real, and the fee eats it where adoption starts

Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes the panel maps to — $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine, $4.76 potassium. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $37.98 a panel. It also pays $650 a month, which is 17 panels of that margin: at 30.5 panels a month the clinic nets $508 per analyzer, at 240 panels $8,400. A fixed fee on a variable-margin stream bites hardest where adoption begins, and incumbents sell the other way: Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S106, S22].
