The evaluation line reconstructs exactly from the deck's inputs, which also says the monthly volume quoted as a 2026 average is the FY2025 average: the evaluation base has not grown in a year. The research-use line needs no clearance and repeats, but it is a reagent business, not a clinical one; the development line is services revenue from one customer. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27% — company-reported, unverified — the top two relationships are 42% [S1]. A top line this concentrated is not yet a razor-and-blade franchise.

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows sites keep using something they already pay for, not that they would buy at commercial volume. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, which is 114% of that median: the model does not assume Vantelle wins the urgent slice, it assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month the evaluation program has run since 2024, 402 analyzers and cartridge volume near 1.44M a year — 71 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, the reorder rate is a paying customer's behaviour, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. For a lead check this size, capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic — the deck's own figures reproduce to the dollar — and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items would settle it: the monthly volume of the best evaluation site and whether any sustained a materially higher run rate; the same measure for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix ordered, since a clinic running only troponin and potassium collects less than the cartridge costs.

**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight, and that gap decides the 2029 plan.**

Let's compute: 1.2 panels/analyzer-day on 300 operating days = 360 cartridges/analyzer/year. At the 300-site / 402-analyzer placement plan by end-2027, that's 402 × 360 = 144,720 cartridges a year — 7.2% of the 2 million needed for the $7.50 cost target. Even at 8 panels/day: 402 × 2,400 = 964,800 cartridges — still only 48% of 2M, so even the base plan doesn't reach the 2M volume that justifies $7.50 cartridge cost! That's a very strong finding. Let me check: 2029 revenue $78.5M. At $31 average price and ~$7.50 cost, gross margin 76% on cartridges. But the blended gross margin in the plan is 71%. Hmm. 78.5M / 31 = 2.53M cartridges. Ah — so 2029 revenue implies 2.53M cartridges, above the 2M threshold. But that requires ~1,050 analyzers at 2,400/year. Right; my breakeven calc said 884 analyzers for $65.8M revenue. 78.5/31 = 2.53M cartridges = 1,055 analyzers at 2,400. So the 2M volume and $7.50 cost are internally consistent with the 2029 revenue target, but only if the company gets to >1,000 analyzers and 8 panels/day. At 1.2 panels/day you'd need ~7,000 analyzers to reach 2M cartridges (2M/360 = 5,556 analyzers). That is a striking number: at observed utilisation, reaching the 2M-cartridge volume that delivers $7.50 cost needs 5,556 analyzers — 14x the 402 planned by end-2027 — or 13.8x the 2027 site plan.

That is the "fixed-cost absorption and 2029 cost target" test. Let me compute precisely:
- 1.2 panels/analyzer-day × 300 days = 360 cartridges/analyzer/year.
- 2,000,000 / 360 = 5,556 analyzers.
- Against 402 analyzers at 300 sites by end-2027 → 13.8x.
- At 8 panels/day: 2,400/analyzer/year → 833 analyzers. Hmm, 2M/2400 = 833. So even the base plan's 2029 revenue of $78.5M at $31 implies 2.53M cartridges → 1,055 analyzers. Consistent-ish.
- At 2029 revenue of $78.5M and 1.2 panels/day, you'd need 2.53M/360 = 7,032 analyzers. That's 17.5x the 300-site plan (assuming ~1.34 analyzers/site → 5,248 sites).

So the 2029 cost target is not a learning curve but a volume threshold that the deployment plan cannot deliver at observed utilisation. At 1.2/day, cartridge cost stays at $16.20 (or wherever volume-based pricing puts it at 144,720 units — probably far above $7.50). Gross margin at $31 - $16.20 = 47.7%, not 76%. That destroys the 71% blended 2029 margin and hence the profit.

rows.finding: Vantelle's troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, above the IFCC <10% high-sensitivity definition and more than twice Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI (<5.2% CV whole blood, 1.61 ng/L LoD).
rows.mechanism: A high-sensitivity troponin is defined by imprecision at the decision limit; at 11.8% CV a true value on the cutoff spreads roughly +/-23% at 95%, so results cross the line and rule-out pathways built on hs-TnI cannot be replicated.
rows.benchmark: IFCC/AACC <10% CV at the 99th percentile; Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% CV.
rows.weakens: Company may be measuring CV at a different level or with a different sample matrix; neither the cutoff value nor the LoD is disclosed, so the comparison is to a claim, not a verified dataset.
rows.implication: Price the assay as conventional cTnI, not hs-TnI; require the cutoff, LoD and precision profile before the round closes.
rows.confidence: high on the gap, medium on magnitude because the dataset is company-reported and partial.
rows.follow_up: What is the 99th-percentile value, the LoD and the full precision profile at each decision level?

rows.finding: The 640-sample, 128-patient method comparison is venous blood, run by company staff, at a single urgent-care site; it reports 96.1% categorical agreement (123/128) with six exclusions for insufficient sample or cartridge error, and no capillary data.
rows.mechanism: Categorical agreement hides direction and magnitude of error; a false negative on troponin is the error that matters. The exclusions and the venous, staff-run design remove exactly the variables (capillary collection, untrained operators, short fills) that a 510(k) specimen comparison and CLIA flex studies test.
rows.benchmark: Class II cardiac assay submissions require multi-level precision, LoB/LoD/LoQ, linearity, haemolysis interference, specimen comparison and method comparison with slope, bias and total error.
rows.weakens: Categorical agreement of 96.1% is respectable for a first feasibility set; the 95% interval (93-99%) does not exclude acceptable performance, and the pivotal study is designed to answer the gap.
rows.implication: Treat the pivotal capillary study, not the existing dataset, as the binary risk; the section's confidence cannot rise until it reports.
rows.confidence: high - the design limitations are stated in the company's own materials.
rows.follow_up: What were the six excluded results, and what were the five discordant troponin results and their direction?

rows.finding: A CLIA Waiver by Application must reference an already cleared or approved application and include flex studies plus a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended-use sites; FDA's goal is a substantive interaction at 90 days and a MDUFA decision at 150 FDA days (180 for a dual 510(k)+CW), and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days.
rows.mechanism: The waiver is a second validation exercise with its own evidence standard, not paperwork appended to a clearance; it cannot start until the 510(k) is cleared, so a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028.
rows.benchmark: Company plan: waiver application Q3 2027.
rows.weakens: A dual submission filed with the second 510(k) would collapse both clocks into one 180-day goal and could decide in late 2027; the company has not said it will use that pathway.
rows.implication: Model waived-site revenue from 2028, not 2027; ask whether the company will convert to a dual submission.
rows.confidence: high - published FDA review goals.
rows.follow_up: Will Vantelle file the waiver as a dual submission with the second 510(k), and has it pre-submitted the flex and user-study protocols?

rows.finding: No point-of-care troponin system reviewed carries waived status: Abbott's i-STAT publishes a separate waived-test manual for chemistry and blood-gas cartridges, its hs-TnI cartridge launched 2025-01-03 as a moderate-complexity test, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for i-STAT cTnI on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is listed moderate (its Cardio3 panel is not sold in the U.S.).
rows.mechanism: Waived cardiac testing has no established precedent to copy; a five-analyte waived panel would need its own user study and flex data, and the closest analog proves the opposite - the market leader sells troponin as moderate complexity.
rows.benchmark: Abbott i-STAT waived chemistry/blood-gas menu; Quidel Triage MeterPro troponin moderate complexity.
rows.weakens: Abbott's waived menu changes with new clearances, and the PulseAid list is a secondary rendering of the FDA CLIA database; a future waiver by a competitor would not help Vantelle but would prove feasibility.
rows.implication: The waiver is the highest-risk, least-precedented regulatory step and the gate to the urgent-care customer set; the plan must fund a waiver study it has not described.
rows.confidence: high on Abbott and CMS documents; medium on completeness of the troponin list.
rows.follow_up: Which intended users and sites will run the waiver study, and what flex studies are planned for haemolysis and short fills?

rows.finding: The cartridge costs $16.20 at pilot volume against $10 at 1 million units and $7.50 at 2 million, on an 18-person pilot line with six months of stability data against a nine-month claimed shelf life.
rows.mechanism: The margin case depends on yield and line speed that only volume production proves; stability is the gating variable for a distributed, inventory-held consumable, and a six-month dataset cannot support a nine-month claim to a reviewer.
rows.benchmark: Peer point-of-care consumables are sold at $10-20 with validated shelf lives of 12 months or more; the company's own cost targets.
rows.weakens: If the device is manufactured at low volume for evaluation only, unit cost is not yet meaningful; automation could deliver the curve faster than a linear read-across suggests.
rows.implication: Treat the scale-up budget ($12.0M of the $30M) as the real test; a yield or stability miss converts the gross-margin story into a working-capital problem.
rows.confidence: medium - company data, no independent manufacturing evidence.
rows.follow_up: What is line yield at the pilot line, what cycle time is assumed at 1 million units, and what stability data exist at 6, 9 and 12 months?

rows.finding: One patent family is granted (2023-03), the five-assay reader application received a final rejection in 2026-07 with an appeal under consideration, two families are unpublished, and the licensed Corvia sealing patent is the only opined freedom to operate - the opinion excludes the troponin chemistry.
rows.mechanism: Without an opined route on the lead assay, the company's defensibility rests on trade secrets and manufacturing know-how, which are weaker against a funded competitor and do not stop a design-around.
rows.benchmark: Typical point-of-care cartridge portfolios hold 5-15 granted families; a single granted family plus one licensed patent is thin for a platform claim.
rows.weakens: Pending and unpublished applications may mature into granted claims; the rejection is appealable and the company says it is contesting it.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite an IP moat on the troponin assay; require the file wrappers and the FTO opinion's scope before closing.
rows.confidence: medium - no public patent record was retrievable, so all patent facts are unverified company statements.
rows.follow_up: Can the company produce the file wrappers and the FTO opinion, and what claims survive the reader rejection?

plan.comparison_set: Abbott i-STAT (hs-TnI <5.2% CV, waived chemistry menu, troponin moderate), Siemens epoc (moderate complexity), Quidel Triage MeterPro (troponin moderate), Roche and Nova capillary chemistry; IFCC/AACC high-sensitivity definition as the analytical benchmark; CLIA Waiver by Application as the regulatory benchmark.
plan.counter_evidence: 96.1% categorical agreement and a high reorder rate show clinical usefulness; the pivotal 1,150-patient capillary study may close the gap; a dual 510(k)+CW submission would accelerate the waiver; Abbott's waived menu may expand.
plan.decision_question: Is the five-analyte finger-stick panel technically proven and defensible, or is the evidence a venous feasibility study run by the company's own staff?
plan.mechanism: Analytical imprecision at the decision limit determines whether the assay can support high-sensitivity rule-out pathways; the CLIA waiver determines which sites can legally run it; the cartridge cost curve determines gross profit per site; the patent position determines whether a competitor can copy the package.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, about/many/various counts, any reference to how the report is written or to team tools and records.
plan.thesis_sentence: The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance: its troponin fails the high-sensitivity standard on the company's own data, its evidence is venous and company-run, and its most valuable asset - a waived cardiac panel - has no point-of-care precedent.
plan.visual: Performance metrics table plus the CLIA-status row of the technology comparison table, with the evidence component carrying the 11.8% CV claim.
plan.why_different: This section judges whether the technology works and can be defended; market sizes the opportunity, financials models the P&L, and strategy tests the sequence of milestones.

The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the monthly cartridge volumes behind the utilisation test are unverified company figures, unaudited and not independently confirmed. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. A 13,200-site total is not the problem; utilisation is. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,280 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US, glucose strips, blood gas and infectious disease included; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. The 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine and $4.76 for potassium: $71.38 for all five, $61.67 for a chest-pain workup of troponin, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, and $51.73 for troponin plus NT-proBNP, each covering the $38 cartridge before the $650 monthly analyzer fee. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes cap at $32.12, below both the $38 list price and the $33.40 average realised price, and a metabolic-only visit of HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collects $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 of gross margin before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation then supports $222M, not $368M. Medicare is the only public price benchmark; commercial and cash prices are not disclosed and could loosen the constraint. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S79, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico together hold 4,296 moderate-complexity laboratories and 31,720 waived ones. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 cannot produce a decision before Q1 2028 under FDA's 150-day goal, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so a waiver is a 2028 event at the earliest; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must therefore be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base the pitch addresses. Until then each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024, and that is the only facility class the policy creates. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. [S81, S79, S95, S72, S1]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: Texas, Arizona, New Mexico | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA laboratories across the three states (2026) | US point-of-care 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only, no billable use | Moderate-complexity CLIA certificate and staffed quality control until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital and reference laboratories | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of the United States | $2.89B-$14.0B total US point-of-care market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR, 2026-2034 | Blocked until a waiver decision in 2028; 300 sites targeted by end-2027 through a non-binding distributor letter of intent, necessarily as moderate-complexity customers | Same CLIA constraint; payer coverage; no waiver decision before Q1 2028 | Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Roche, Radiometer, Quest Diagnostics | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15 with no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement, distributor | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens Healthineers | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more, and the company's own 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, far above what its evaluation sites ran. The survey and the operating data differ by an order of magnitude and only one can describe the commercial site; Medicare is also the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, confidence in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests per cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any evaluation site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until those are answered, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price, not in the narrative.

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in 2026, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 fee schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge [S1, S85].

The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The genuine difference is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve, the pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader measures the optical signal and corrects for drift, and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a single result whose true value sits on the cutoff has a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line; that can pass for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity, but it cannot support the guideline-recommended high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck calls the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor can tell which decision level the figure describes, and on this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI rather than as an hs-TnI against Abbott's. A Class II submission rests on multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the internal study reports none of these, 96.1% of 128 results fell in the same normal/abnormal bucket, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed and the 95% interval at that sample size is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative, and the six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15, S68, S70].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood to be run within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens, so the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma, un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate today; waiver planned Q3 2027 (company) | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate complexity | Moderate complexity | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

A CLIA waiver is not paperwork layered on a clearance. The application must reference an already cleared product and carry risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended-use sites, and FDA's goal is a decision 150 FDA days after filing, with an additional-information request adding up to 180 days [S72]. That standard is a user study, which is precisely what a venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not. Nor is there a point-of-care precedent to copy: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for its chemistry and blood-gas cartridges, its high-sensitivity troponin cartridge launched on 2025-01-03 as a moderate-complexity test, and CMS ended the pandemic discretion that had let the older cTnI cartridge run in non-waived laboratories on 2026-03-30 [S104, S145, S146]. Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is likewise moderate complexity on the FDA-derived list, and its Cardio3 panel is not sold in the United States [S108, S142]. A waived five-analyte panel with troponin would therefore be first-of-kind among the systems reviewed, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028, not 2027 [S72].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat; a funded team of 50 needs 2-3 years to match the cartridge and evidence base | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

One granted family, one reader family in appeal, two unpublished applications and a licensed sealing patent are thin cover for a platform. The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry, leaving the lead assay without opined cover; no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |
| Medicare reimbursement, 2026 | $71.38 for all five assays; $17.23 for troponin plus potassium | Cartridge list $38 | The panel only pays if most assays are ordered | S82-S86 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product, and the economics live entirely in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate [S1].

Counter-evidence deserves weight. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, most evaluation sites reordered, and a rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff — a number the deck does not report and the one that would settle the assay's clinical use.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability data beyond the six months held; and whether the company will file the CLIA waiver as a dual submission with the second 510(k). Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's published process.

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The genuine difference is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, an on-board calibrator, a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve, the pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader measures the optical signal and corrects for drift, and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards the short fills that are the commonest failure mode of capillary devices. This is the company's description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a result whose true value sits on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional troponin used as a rule-out aid with demonstrated sensitivity, not for the high-sensitivity pathways, which assume imprecision a fraction of this. The deck calls the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor knows which decision level the figure describes; on this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none of these. The 96.1% is categorical agreement over 128 results, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed and the 95% interval is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative, and the six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15, S68, S70].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Capillary hs-troponin verification is only now being published, and potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and whole-blood potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens, so the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma, un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate today; waiver planned Q3 2027 (company) | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate complexity | Moderate complexity | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

A CLIA waiver is not paperwork layered on a clearance. The application must reference an already cleared product and carry risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended-use sites; FDA's goal is a decision 150 FDA days after filing, and an additional-information request can add 180 days [S72]. That is a user study, which a venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not. Nor is there a point-of-care precedent to copy: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood-gas cartridges, its high-sensitivity troponin launched on 2025-01-03 as a moderate-complexity test, and CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30 [S104, S145, S146]; Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate complexity on the FDA-derived list and its Cardio3 panel is not sold in the United States [S108, S142]. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind among the systems reviewed, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028, not 2027 [S72].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 units to 2 million | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat; a funded team of 50 needs 2-3 years | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

One granted family, one reader family in appeal, two unpublished applications and a licensed sealing patent are thin cover for a platform. The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry, and no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |
| Medicare reimbursement, 2026 | $71.38 for all five assays; $17.23 for troponin plus potassium | Cartridge list $38 | The panel only pays if most assays are ordered | S82-S86 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c sit at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate [S1].

Counter-evidence deserves weight. The other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, most evaluation sites reordered, and a rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff — a number the deck does not report and the one that would settle the assay's clinical use.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability data beyond the six months held; and whether the waiver will be filed as a dual submission with the second 510(k). Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's published process.

arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the monthly cartridge volumes behind the utilisation test are unverified company figures, unaudited and not independently confirmed. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,280 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. The 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine and $4.76 for potassium: $71.38 for all five, $61.67 for a chest-pain workup of troponin, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, and $51.73 for troponin plus NT-proBNP, each covering the $38 cartridge before the $650 monthly analyzer fee. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes cap at $32.12, below both the $38 list price and the $33.40 average realised price, and a metabolic-only visit of HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collects $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 of gross margin before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation then supports $222M, not $368M. Medicare is the only public price benchmark; commercial and cash prices are not disclosed and could loosen the constraint. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S79, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico together hold 4,296 moderate-complexity laboratories and 31,720 waived ones. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 cannot produce a decision before Q1 2028 under FDA's 150-day goal, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so a waiver is a 2028 event at the earliest; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must therefore be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base the pitch addresses. Until then each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. [S81, S79, S95, S72, S1]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: Texas, Arizona, New Mexico | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA laboratories across the three states (2026) | US point-of-care 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only, no billable use | Moderate-complexity CLIA certificate and staffed quality control until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital and reference laboratories | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of the United States | $2.89B-$14.0B total US point-of-care market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR, 2026-2034 | Blocked until a waiver decision in 2028; 300 sites targeted by end-2027 through a non-binding distributor letter of intent, necessarily as moderate-complexity customers | Same CLIA constraint; payer coverage; no waiver decision before Q1 2028 | Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Roche, Radiometer, Quest Diagnostics | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15 with no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement, distributor | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens Healthineers | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more, and the company's own 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, far above what its evaluation sites ran. Medicare is also the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, confidence in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests per cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any evaluation site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until those are answered, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price, not in the narrative.

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in 2026, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 fee schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge [S1, S85].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The difference is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick and a 12-minute result. It is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve, the pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader measures the optical signal and corrects for drift, and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills. This is the company's description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | NT-proBNP 98.4%, HbA1c 99.2%, creatinine 100%, potassium 100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a result whose true value sits on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways, which assume far tighter imprecision. The deck calls the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so neither a reviewer nor an investor knows which decision level the figure describes; on this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference, a specimen comparison and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none of these. The 96.1% is categorical agreement over 128 results, the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed and the 95% interval is 93-99%. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative, and the six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15, S68, S70].

### The capillary question is the investment case

There is no capillary-versus-venous data in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia, and Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, capillary HbA1c and whole-blood potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens, so the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge, not the finger stick [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood or plasma, un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate today; waiver planned Q3 2027 (company) | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate complexity | Moderate complexity | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

A CLIA waiver is not paperwork layered on a clearance. The application must reference an already cleared product and carry risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended-use sites; FDA's goal is a decision 150 FDA days after filing, and an additional-information request can add 180 days [S72]. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. Nor is there a point-of-care precedent to copy: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood-gas cartridges, its high-sensitivity troponin launched on 2025-01-03 as a moderate-complexity test, and CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30 [S104, S145, S146]; Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate complexity on the FDA-derived list [S142]. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind among the systems reviewed, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028, not 2027 [S72].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL with dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat; a funded team of 50 needs 2-3 years to match the cartridge and the evidence | 2-3 years | Analyst assessment |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge with on-board calibrator) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay optical reader with drift correction) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry, and no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | Part of $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |
| Medicare reimbursement, 2026 | $71.38 for all five assays; $17.23 for troponin plus potassium | Cartridge list $38 | The panel only pays if most assays are ordered | S82-S86 |

The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c at technology readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — leased plant, limited stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate [S1].

Counter-evidence: the other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory, most evaluation sites reordered, and a rural clinic waiting days for a send-out may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff — the number the deck does not report.

Diligence questions: the troponin cutoff value, detection limit and share of healthy adults above it; what the August 2026 additional-information request asked; the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks and whether the cartridge flags it; line yield and stability data beyond the six months held; and whether the waiver will be filed as a dual submission with the second 510(k). Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in the company's own data, while the manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's published process.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. On the company's projections, the $22.5M of net losses in 2027-2028 plus the capital spending and working capital a launch requires exceed the $32.3M the round would leave at close, so Vantelle needs $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halved. The arithmetic starts at $6.9M of cash, company-reported on 2026-09-30, and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months of cushion — left at the 2027-01-29 target close. The burn is understated too: $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M is the P&L loss with no capex or working capital in it.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue — 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each, twice the 300 sites targeted for end-2027. The cost target fails the same test. Two million cartridges a year is what buys the $7.50 cost; at the 1.2 panels a day the 41 evaluation sites actually ran, an analyzer consumes about 360 cartridges a year, so that volume needs 5,500 analyzers, and the 402 analyzers behind the 300-site plan produce 147,000 cartridges, 7% of it, where the only disclosed cost is $16.20 and the margin 48%, not 76%. Capital efficiency is poor against the stage: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x, where above 1.5x is inefficient at scale [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

| Gross margin | 49% | 58% | 61% | 63% | 67% | 71% | S1 (unverified) |

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, dated Q1 2027 in the deck, under a letter of intent the deck calls non-binding. At $33.40 a cartridge the order is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month shelf-life claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M, and with $2.7M booked in the first nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's use of funds has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and debt service after 2027-03 is $210,000 a month, 18% of burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting at 75% of the $3.2564 round price into 2,571,392 shares, 4.9% of the post-round count [S1, S22].

| Burn multiple | 8.3x | 4.2x, or 15.6x ex-stocking order | Series B median 1.4x | S1 (unverified), S134 |
| ROE and ROIC | not meaningful | not meaningful | Accumulated deficit above $36.2M against $40.5M of equity raised | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Receivable days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 55.7 days | S22 |
| Inventory days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 145 days | S22 |

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's $12.0M outflow takes it to negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit and the shortfall is $8-10M. The stress case moves clearance to Q3 2027 — a 175-day chemistry-panel review average plus an information-request pause makes Q1 2027 the optimistic end of the range, not the middle — puts the CLIA waiver in 2028 and halves utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with operating cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M: a two-quarter slip moves the shortfall from $8-10M to $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M post-round count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S92].

| Item | Base | Stress | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) clearance | Q1 2027 | Q3 2027 | S1 (unverified), S92 |
| CLIA waiver | applied Q3 2027 | 2028 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day, 2028 | 8.0 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue, FY2027 / 2028 / 2029 | 16.8 / 41.0 / 78.5 | 5.0 / 14.0 / 32.0 | S1 (unverified); analyst estimate |
| Cumulative net loss, 2027-2029 | (13.5) | (55.3) | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash trough | (4.7) in 2028 | below (25) in 2029 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Additional capital needed, $M | 8-10 | 25-40 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Dilution at half the Series B price | none | 23-32% | S1 (unverified); calculated |

These are capital-intensive instrument economics: growth is bought with placed hardware and funded receivables, so the faster Vantelle sells, the more cash it consumes before the cartridge annuity arrives. The variable that moves the outcome is panels per analyzer-day, not sites, price or the clearance date: clearance moves the clock, utilisation sets the level, and the level is set in the plan. The counter-case is that the burn is discretionary: a company that cut cost sharply and slowed the site ramp would close most of the gap, and a distributor that finances inventory would remove much of the working-capital need, so the shortfall is about this plan, not survival. For the check, the implication is that the round should be sized larger or tranched, the second tranche released on clearance and utilisation, and the price should assume a further financing before breakeven. The diligence list is short: the Bluestem agreement for its rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor's payment, return and pricing terms; and the Tempe line's cost and yield at 150,000-500,000 cartridges. Confidence is high on the arithmetic, which reconciles to the deck's own numbers, and medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates with no auditor, no quarterly statements and no covenant disclosure behind them.

::: info danger
**The largest single line of FY2026 revenue cannot be delivered in FY2026 and has no evidence of pull-through.**

Company-reported and unverified: $2.4M of the $5.9M projection is an opening stocking order from a distributor whose commitment is a non-binding letter of intent; it ships only on 510(k) clearance, which the company dates to Q1 2027, it equals 71,856 cartridges, 3.6 years of current volume, on a product with six months of stability data against a nine-month claim [S1].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the monthly cartridge volumes behind the utilisation test are unverified company figures, unaudited and not independently confirmed. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,280 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. Its own survey of 52 clinics reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. The 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine and $4.76 for potassium: $71.38 for all five, $61.67 for a chest-pain workup of troponin, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, and $51.73 for troponin plus NT-proBNP, each covering the $38 cartridge before the $650 monthly analyzer fee. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes cap at $32.12, below both the $38 list price and the $33.40 average realised price, and a metabolic-only visit of HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collects $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 of gross margin before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation then supports $222M, not $368M. Medicare is the only public price benchmark; commercial and cash prices are not disclosed and could loosen the constraint. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S79, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico together hold 4,296 moderate-complexity laboratories and 31,720 waived ones. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 cannot produce a decision before Q1 2028 under FDA's 150-day goal, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so a waiver is a 2028 event at the earliest; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must therefore be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base the pitch addresses. Until then each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. [S81, S79, S95, S72, S1]

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: Texas, Arizona, New Mexico | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA laboratories across the three states (2026) | US point-of-care 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only, no billable use | Moderate-complexity CLIA certificate and staffed quality control until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital and reference laboratories | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of the United States | $2.89B-$14.0B total US point-of-care market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR, 2026-2034 | Blocked until a waiver decision in 2028; 300 sites targeted by end-2027 through a non-binding distributor letter of intent, necessarily as moderate-complexity customers | Same CLIA constraint; payer coverage; no waiver decision before Q1 2028 | Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Roche, Radiometer, Quest Diagnostics | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15 with no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement, distributor | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens Healthineers | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more. Medicare is also the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, confidence in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests per cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any evaluation site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until those are answered, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price, not in the narrative.

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in 2026, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 fee schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge [S1, S85].
:::
