arguments.analogs: LumiraDx (cautionary, 2021-2024): listed at a $3.0B de-SPAC valuation after cutting the deal from $5.0B and sold its point-of-care technology to Roche for $295M after lenders took control — a multi-assay platform with revenue still went for a fifth of its listing value. Cue Health (cautionary, 2021-2024): raised $480M+ and reached a $2.3B valuation, then filed Chapter 7 in 2024 after an FDA warning letter on unauthorised device changes and lot-release failures — the closest precedent to Vantelle's quality-system gap. QuidelOrtho-LEX Diagnostics (pricing, 2026): $100M cash for a platform already cleared and CLIA-waived, the current clearing price for the asset Vantelle will hold in 2028. Truvian Sciences (cautionary, 2015-2026): raised $294M, cleared 12 analytes by 2026-01-12 and remains private eleven years after founding — the base rate for finger-stick platforms reaching commercial scale late and at a discount. The decision rule: a cleared, waived, revenue-generating point-of-care platform transacts at $100-300M in this market, so entry must leave room for a 3x return below that band.
arguments.capital_efficiency: $51.5M of equity and debt has produced $2.6M of FY2025 revenue, $0.05 of revenue per dollar raised and a burn multiple of 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E and 15.6x excluding the $2.4M stocking order, against a Series B median near 1.4x. The 2029 profit assumes $46.7M of operating cost carrying $78.5M of revenue; breakeven at the 71% target margin needs $65.8M of revenue, 884 analyzers at 2,400 panels a year, twice the sites targeted for end-2027. Two million cartridges, the volume behind the $7.50 cost, needs 5,500 analyzers at observed use; the 402 analyzers behind 300 sites produce 147,000 cartridges, 7% of it, at a disclosed cost of $16.20 and a 48% margin. Capital needed is $40M on the company's own plan and $55-70M in the stress case, against a $30M round.

consensus.consensus: The company and the $140M pre-money assume 8 panels per analyzer-day, a Q1 2027 clearance, a 2027 CLIA waiver, $78.5M of 2029 revenue and a point-of-care market of $2.4B; the insider $8M commitment implies existing investors accept that timeline.
consensus.evidence: The deck's own operating data contradict the utilisation assumption: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers is 1.22 per operating day, a 6.5x gap, and at that rate the same 13,200 sites and $38 price support $368M, not $2.4B [S1, S79]. FDA's clocks put a Q3 2027 waiver filing into 2028, and no troponin-I system appears on the waived list [S72, S104, S145]. The 2026 clearing price for a cleared, waived platform was $100M [S126].
consensus.our_view: The need is real and the packaging lead is genuine for 12-24 months, but the plan is priced as if clearance, waiver and 8-panel utilisation all land on schedule. We would invest only at $60-80M pre-money, with the Series A participation capped, the $30M tranched on clearance and the Corvia terms cleaned up; at $140M the evidence supports waiting.
consensus.proof_event: The first four quarters of billing-enabled cartridge use at the initial commercial sites after clearance, reported as panels per analyzer-day and collected revenue per cartridge.

one_question.question: At the first billing-enabled sites after 510(k) clearance, how many five-analyte cartridges does each analyzer run per day, and what revenue does the site collect per cartridge?
one_question.why: This single measure decides the case. At 1.22 panels a day the three-year cartridge gross profit of $15,621 does not repay the $25,600-51,200 cost of winning a placement, and $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites rather than 300. At 6 or more, the LTV:CAC clears 3:1, the 300-site plan produces $30-60M and a $300M+ exit comes back into view. Every other variable — clearance date, waiver, cartridge cost — moves the timing or the margin; utilisation sets the level, and no evidence in the file yet shows it at a billing-enabled site.

arguments.position_sizing: Private company: do not lead at $140M pre-money. If Meridian invests, cap the entry at $70M pre-money, where $15M buys about 17.6% and a 3x return needs a $286M exit, and tranche it $7.5M at close and $7.5M on 510(k) clearance with a waiver milestone attached. Reserve one times the initial cheque ($15M) for the 2029 follow-on the plan itself requires, for a $30M total exposure; maximum loss is the full $15M if the waiver fails and the IP sells at the $50-100M distressed range, where the Series B preference of $36.3M is covered only partially. Downside recovery in the bear case is 0.3-0.8x; the base case is 1.0-1.5x, below the venture hurdle; only the bull case clears 3x.

arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the monthly cartridge volumes behind the utilisation test are unverified company figures, unaudited and not independently confirmed. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. Its own survey of 52 clinics reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. The 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine and $4.76 for potassium: $71.38 for all five, $61.67 for a chest-pain workup of troponin, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, and $51.73 for troponin plus NT-proBNP, each covering the $38 cartridge before the $650 monthly analyzer fee. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes cap at $32.12, below both the $38 list price and the $33.40 average realised price, and a metabolic-only visit of HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collects $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 of gross margin before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation then supports $222M, not $368M. Medicare is the only public price benchmark; commercial and cash prices are not disclosed and could loosen the constraint. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S79, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico together hold 4,296 moderate-complexity laboratories and 31,720 waived ones. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 faces FDA's 150-day decision goal from the filing date and a 180-day window to answer any information request, so a decision in 2027 is unlikely and no waiver before 2028 is the realistic case; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must therefore be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base the pitch addresses. Until then each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. [S81, S79, S95, S72, S1]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: Texas, Arizona, New Mexico | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA laboratories across the three states (2026) | US point-of-care 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only, no billable use | Moderate-complexity CLIA certificate and staffed quality control until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital and reference laboratories | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of the United States | $2.89B-$14.0B total US point-of-care market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR, 2026-2034 | Blocked until a waiver decision in 2028; 300 sites targeted by end-2027 through a non-binding distributor letter of intent, necessarily as moderate-complexity customers | Same CLIA constraint; payer coverage; no waiver before 2028 | Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Roche, Radiometer, Quest Diagnostics | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15 with no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement, distributor | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens Healthineers | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more. Medicare is also the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, confidence in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests per cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any evaluation site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until those are answered, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price, not in the narrative.

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in 2026, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 fee schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge [S1, S85].
:::

At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and with the Series A's uncapped participating preference the $30M Series B needs $546M of exit proceeds to return 3x and $1.74B to return 10x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, all company-reported and not independently verified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

[table]

The company-reported, unverified terms show the seed at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11. The headline pre-money rises 34% from the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but $13.1M of that is the option-pool refresh to 10% of the post-money: existing holders' effective pre-money is $126.9M, a 21% uplift over 2.9 years, or 6.9% a year. Existing shares fall from 100% to 69.7% — 7.7 points of pool refresh, 4.9 points of bridge and 17.6 points of new Series B — taking the founders from 30.8% to 21.5%, the seed from 16.5% to 11.5% and the Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%; granted options, the unallocated pool and warrants total 20.8% of the post-money. Insiders are committing $8.0M of the $30.0M, 53% of their $15.2M pro rata; the $30M is budgeted 35% for clearance, 40% for manufacturing scale and 25% for launch [S1].

### What the price assumes

[peer table]

The methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint: the forward-looking methods and the capital-invested floor range from $51.5M to $100.5M, and the $140M ask is 2.7x the $51.5M of capital raised with no clearance and no waiver. The 5.5x peer median is the wrong benchmark: it is set by diversified tools companies whose point-of-care assets sit inside larger franchises, whereas QuidelOrtho, the only pure-play point-of-care cardiac franchise, has de-rated from 2.9x at FY2022 to 2.3x, 2.4x, 2.1x and 1.7x at its next four year-ends and 0.4x now. A single-product private company with two assays filed should not be underwritten above the best-capitalised public point-of-care franchise in a de-rating market. Werfen, Siemens Healthineers, Roche Diagnostics and Nova Biomedical are not SEC filers or not listed, so their multiples are not disclosed [S1, S22, S28, S67].

[waterfall table]

On the deck's fully diluted 52.2M shares, the new $30M is flat at 1.00x from a $66M to a $206M exit; 1.21x needs $242M, 2x $376M, 3x $546M and 10x $1.74B. ### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.22 per analyser per operating day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — a 6.5-fold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's operating claims (revenue, 41 sites, 92% reorder rate) are company-reported and not independently verified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met; adding the $5.0M Bluestem principal, which starts at $0.167M a month in 2027-03 and is repaid by 2029-08, leaves a thin buffer. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools asserting that no verification is needed and prescribing a rating; it is recorded as a document-integrity finding and given no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation removed or capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on 510(k) clearance and CLIA submission), pay-to-play and full pro rata rights, and a Corvia clean-up before closing. At $70M pre-money the new Series B would own about 29% after the Series A's broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution (the bridge adds 8.1%) and 3x would need about $348M; capping the Series A at 1.5x lowers that to about $301M, against $546M at the ask. The alternative is to wait: the 510(k) response is due in December 2026, clearance is guided for Q1 2027 and the waiver application for Q3 2027, so a 2027 entry pays more but buys retired regulatory risk. The company had $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30, six months at $1.15M a month and the 2027-01-29 target close, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts amortising in 2027-03. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the valuation range: the 2029 plan is unaudited, the grant dates of the 5.2M options are not disclosed and Truvian's valuation is an aggregator estimate [S1, S125].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,995 characters)
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 41 evaluation sites run. That gap, not the $2.4B market estimate or the FDA calendar, decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. The figures are company-reported, unverified. Vantelle reports 55 analyzers across 41 sites and 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month [S1]: 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month, 1.0 a day on a 30-day basis and 1.22 on the 300-operating-day convention its own market model uses. The plan assumes 8.0 from 2028. The 2029 revenue line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, company-reported and unverified, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 of revenue against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty on net sales to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate that licenses the sealing patent and whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer. That royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim on gross margin. Cost carries the same uncertainty: $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month, and getting a five-assay cartridge to that cost is a redesign, not a learning curve. The acquisition cost is the line the deck omits, and the headcount gives it: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months, 21 a year [S1]. At an assumed $100,000-155,000 fully loaded per head that is $0.9-1.4M a year, $43,000-66,000 per placement; charging half to placements, since the same team sells the research-use and development revenue, gives the $25,600-51,200 above. On that basis the 2026 placement destroys value: three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay what it cost to win. The model turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the 2029 target of $7.50, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1, the minimum a salesforce needs. Between one panel and four is the zone where Vantelle can grow and still lose money on every site it places.

| Line | 2026 actual | 2028 model | 2029 target | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day (300 days) | 1.0 | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit per cartridge, after 3% royalty | $16.20 | $19.84 | $22.57 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Analyzer subsidy, amortised over three years | ($730) | ($730) | ($730) | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Contribution per analyzer-year, before CAC | $5,207 | $46,886 | $53,438 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| CAC per analyzer placed (estimate) | $25,600-51,200 | same | same | S1 (unverified) headcount; analyst estimate |
| Three-year LTV | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels a day for a 3:1 ratio | 5.9 at $16.20 cost; 4.2 at $7.50 | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| CAC payback | over 48 months | 6.6-13 months | 5.7-11.5 months | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### The clinic's margin is real, and the fee eats it where adoption starts

Medicare's 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes the panel maps to — $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine, $4.76 potassium. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $37.98 a panel. It also pays $650 a month, which is 17 panels of that margin: at 30.5 panels a month the clinic nets $508 per analyzer, at 240 panels $8,400. A fixed fee on a variable-margin stream bites hardest where adoption begins, and incumbents sell the other way: Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S106, S22].

| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | $2.71 a panel at 240 panels | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage cardiac panel (troponin, CK-MB), 25 tests | $699 | $27.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage BNP, CLIA-waived, 25 tests | $789 | $31.56 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| FY2025 line | $M | Share | Repeatable? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use cartridges to contract research organisations | 0.8 | 31% | Repeatable, needs no clearance, small market | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development for one diagnostics partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

The evaluation line reconstructs exactly from the deck's inputs, which also says the monthly volume quoted as a 2026 average is the FY2025 average: the evaluation base has not grown in a year. The research-use line needs no clearance and repeats, but it is a reagent business, not a clinical one; the development line is services revenue from one customer. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27% — company-reported, unverified — the top two relationships are 42% [S1]. A top line this concentrated is not yet a razor-and-blade franchise.

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows sites keep using something they already pay for, not that they would buy at commercial volume. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, which is 114% of that median: the model does not assume Vantelle wins the urgent slice, it assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month the evaluation program has run since 2024, 402 analyzers and cartridge volume near 1.44M a year — 71 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, the reorder rate is a paying customer's behaviour, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. For a lead check this size, capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic — the deck's own figures reproduce to the dollar — and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items would settle it: the monthly volume of the best evaluation site and whether any sustained a materially higher run rate; the same measure for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix ordered, since a clinic running only troponin and potassium collects less than the cartridge costs.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight, and that gap decides the 2029 plan.**

55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against the 240 the 2028 plan assumes; a placement's three-year cartridge gross profit of $15,621 does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 5 by Valuation Analyst, 8,625 characters)
At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and the Series A's participating preference means a $30M Series B needs a $435M exit to return 3x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, all company-reported and not independently verified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho, the closest listed comparable, trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

Company-reported financing terms, not independently verified:

| Date | Round | Amount | Price/share | Post-money | Investors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75 (implied) | not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.9032 | $92.5M | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.9032 | $104.5M | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Venture term loan | $5.0M | Warrant strike $2.903 | — | Bluestem Venture Lending (400,000 warrants) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes, 8% | $6.0M | $2.4423 on conversion | — | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027-01 (target) | Series B | $30.0M | $3.2564 | $170.0M | Ardent Peak ($5.0M) and Juniper Rock ($3.0M); $22.0M sought | S1 (unverified) |

The company-reported, unverified terms show the seed priced at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11. The headline pre-money rises 34% from the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but $13.1M of that is the option-pool refresh to 10% of the post-money: existing holders' effective pre-money is $126.9M, a 21% uplift over 2.9 years, or 6.9% a year. Existing shares fall from 100% to 69.7% of the fully diluted company — 7.7 points of pool refresh, 4.9 points of bridge and 17.6 points of new Series B — taking the founders from 30.8% to 21.5%, the seed from 16.5% to 11.5% and the Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%. Insiders are committing $8.0M of the $30.0M, 53% of their $15.2M pro rata, leaving 73% to new investors with no lead named; the $30M is budgeted 35% for clearance, 40% for manufacturing scale and 25% for launch [S1].

### What the price assumes

Our calculations on company-reported projections, which are not independently verified:

| Method | Inputs | Implied pre-money | Source |

| FY2025A revenue | $2.6M × 2.5x | $6.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2026E ex-stocking | $3.5M × 2.5x | $8.8M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2026E ex-stocking at peer median | $3.5M × 5.5x | $19.3M | S1 (unverified), S28 |
| FY2028P revenue, discounted 2 years | $41.0M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25² | $65.6M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P revenue, discounted 3 years | $78.5M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25³ | $100.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P earnings, discounted 3 years | $9.0M × 15x ÷ 1.30³ | $61.4M | S1 (unverified) |
| Capital invested | $40.5M equity + $11.0M debt | $51.5M (ask = 2.7x) | S1 (unverified) |

| Company | EV | EV/Sales, TTM | P/E, TTM | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho | $1.1B | 0.4x | n/m | Closest point-of-care and cardiac comparable | S22, S23 |
| Abbott | $211.7B | 4.7x | 29.7x | i-STAT, i-STAT Alinity, Afinion | S33, S67 |
| Danaher | $184.2B | 7.2x | 38.1x | Cepheid point-of-care molecular | S34, S35 |
| Bio-Rad | $9.5B | 3.7x | 45.3x | Life-science tools | S36, S37 |
| Thermo Fisher | $295.6B | 6.2x | 36.8x | Mesa Biotech point-of-care molecular | S38, S39 |
| Peer median | — | 5.5x | 37.4x | Diversified tools, not pure-play point of care | S28 |

The methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint, 46% below the ask; the most generous assumes $78.5M of 2029 revenue at 2.5x, discounted three years at 25%, and the $140M pre-money is 2.7x the $51.5M of capital raised so far with no clearance and no waiver. The 5.5x peer median is the wrong benchmark: it is set by diversified tools companies whose point-of-care assets sit inside larger franchises, whereas QuidelOrtho, the only pure-play point-of-care cardiac franchise, has de-rated from 2.9x at FY2022 to 2.3x, 2.4x, 2.1x and 1.7x at its next four year-ends and 0.4x now. A single-product private company with two assays filed should not be underwritten above the best-capitalised public point-of-care franchise in a de-rating market. Werfen, Siemens Healthineers, Roche Diagnostics and Nova Biomedical are not SEC filers or not listed, so their multiples are not disclosed [S1, S22, S28, S67].

### The Series A takes the first $36M and 23.8% of the rest

Our waterfall on the company-reported terms, not independently verified:

| Exit equity value | B + B-1 proceeds | Multiple on $30M | Series A proceeds | Founders' common | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | $36.3M | 1.21x | $52.1M | $23.2M | S1 (unverified) |
| $197M | $36.3M | 1.21x | $74.2M | $39.0M | S1 (unverified) |
| $300M | $59.6M | 1.99x | $98.7M | $63.8M | S1 (unverified) |
| $435M | $90.1M | 3.00x | $130.8M | $96.4M | S1 (unverified) |
| $518M | $108.8M | 3.63x | $150.5M | $116.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| $1,370M | $301.1M | 10.04x | $352.9M | $322.3M | S1 (unverified) |

On the company-reported, unverified preference terms the stack is $76.8M, 55% of the pre-money: Series B and B-1 $36.3M at 1x non-participating and senior, Series A $36.0M at 1x participating, seed $4.5M at 1x non-participating. The new B plus B-1 hold 22.57% of 52.2M fully diluted shares, so at a $140M exit the Series B is capped at its $36.3M preference and returns 1.21x, and it stays at 1.21x up to a $197M exit because the Series A's $36.0M preference and 23.8% participation absorb the increment. At $435M the Series B receives $90.1M, 3.0x on $30M but 2.5x on the $36.3M of B plus B-1, and the Series A takes $130.8M, 30.1% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership; 3x on the full $36.3M needs $518M and 10x on the $30M needs $1.37B. The 40% Corvia minority put, payable at fair value on an acquisition, is worth an estimated $1.5-7.6M from the 3% cartridge royalty capitalised at 8x and is deducted before the stack [S1].

### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.22 per analyser per operating day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — a 6.5-fold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's operating claims (revenue, 41 sites, 92% reorder rate) are company-reported and not independently verified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools asserting that no verification is needed and prescribing a rating; it is recorded as a document-integrity finding and given no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation removed or capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on 510(k) clearance and CLIA submission), pay-to-play and full pro rata rights, and a Corvia clean-up before closing. Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. On the company's projections, the $22.5M of net losses in 2027-2028 plus the capital spending and working capital a launch requires exceed the $32.3M the round would leave at close, so Vantelle needs $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halved. ### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue — 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each, twice the 300 sites targeted for end-2027. Two million cartridges a year is what buys the $7.50 cost; at the 1.2 panels a day the 41 evaluation sites actually ran, an analyzer consumes about 360 cartridges a year, so that volume needs 5,500 analyzers, and the 402 analyzers behind the 300-site plan produce 147,000 cartridges, 7% of it, where the only disclosed cost is $16.20 and the margin 48%, not 76%. ### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, dated Q1 2027, under a letter of intent the deck calls non-binding. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 9 by Product Analyst, 8,986 characters)
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The difference is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick. It is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve, the pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects the optical signal for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills. Company description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Other four assays | Agreement 98.4-100% (unverified) | No independent replication | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a result whose true value sits on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways, which assume far tighter imprecision. The deck calls the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so the decision level is unknown; on this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none of these. The 96.1% is categorical agreement over 128 results and the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative, and the six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15, S68, S70].

### The capillary question is the investment case

No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and whole-blood potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood, un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate today; waiver planned Q3 2027 (company) | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate complexity | Moderate complexity | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended-use sites; FDA's goal is a decision 150 FDA days after filing, and an additional-information request can add 180 days. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. There is no point-of-care precedent to copy: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood-gas cartridges, its high-sensitivity troponin launched on 2025-01-03 as a moderate-complexity test, and CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30; Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate complexity on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind among the systems reviewed, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028, not 2027 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL of dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Composite | 5 | Workflow integrator's moat, not a science moat; a funded team of 50 needs 2-3 years | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |

### Patent position

| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; nominal term to 2040 | S1 |

| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry; no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost; $700 gross profit a site a month at observed use | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |
| Medicare reimbursement, 2026 | $71.38 for all five assays; $17.23 for troponin plus potassium | Cartridge list $38 | The panel only pays if most assays are ordered | S82-S86 |

Company data, unverified: the analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c at readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — leased plant, limited stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate. The questions that would settle the analytical case are the troponin cutoff and detection limit, what the pending FDA request asked, the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks, line yield and stability beyond the data held, and whether the waiver will be filed as a dual submission alongside the second clearance [S1].

Counter-evidence, company data unverified: the other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory and sites reordered; a rural clinic may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff, which the deck omits.

Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in company data, while the manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's published process."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 10 by Market Analyst, 8,938 characters)
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites deliver, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the monthly cartridge volumes behind the utilisation test are unverified company figures, unaudited and not independently confirmed. [S1, S67]

The site count is the only input in the build-up that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% of them owned by or affiliated with a hospital or health system and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 centers in September 2024, of which 2,300 were private-equity backed. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the independent range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base that independent counts put near 2,400. The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap, and the gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at a $31 realised price, almost exactly the model's eight and six times what the sites run. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M. It has 41. Its own survey of 52 clinics reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used. [S79, S80, S78, S1]

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Half the model, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | $1.20B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics, the broadest TAM, was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% CAGR to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% CAGR to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. The company's $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17% to 83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M SOM implied by observed utilisation is still 60% of it. The sharper comparator is Abbott: its global Point of Care line, i-STAT, Afinion and every other point-of-care product it sells in every country, generated $606M in FY2025. The claimed US SAM is four times that. [S93, S94, S96, S67]

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. The 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine and $4.76 for potassium: $71.38 for all five, $61.67 for a chest-pain workup of troponin, NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, and $51.73 for troponin plus NT-proBNP, each covering the $38 cartridge before the $650 monthly analyzer fee. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes cap at $32.12, below both the $38 list price and the $33.40 average realised price, and a metabolic-only visit of HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collects $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 of gross margin before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation then supports $222M, not $368M. Medicare is the only public price benchmark; commercial and cash prices are not disclosed and could loosen the constraint. [S85, S83, S84, S82, S86, S79, S1]

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico together hold 4,296 moderate-complexity laboratories and 31,720 waived ones. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 faces FDA's 150-day decision goal from the filing date and a 180-day window to answer any information request, so a decision in 2027 is unlikely and no waiver before 2028 is the realistic case; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must therefore be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base the pitch addresses. Until then each site must hold or obtain a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff. Ownership consolidation compounds this: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated, and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024. The market systems sit in one country: home, revenue, supplier, comparable and capital are US, exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents, and the EU is a blocked expansion market, not a second revenue base, until CE marking after 2028. [S81, S79, S95, S72, S1]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: Texas, Arizona, New Mexico | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA laboratories across the three states (2026) | US point-of-care 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only, no billable use | Moderate-complexity CLIA certificate and staffed quality control until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital and reference laboratories | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of the United States | $2.89B-$14.0B total US point-of-care market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR, 2026-2034 | Blocked until a waiver decision in 2028; 300 sites targeted by end-2027 through a non-binding distributor letter of intent, necessarily as moderate-complexity customers | Same CLIA constraint; payer coverage; no waiver before 2028 | Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Roche, Radiometer, Quest Diagnostics | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15 with no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement, distributor | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens Healthineers | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more. Medicare is also the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, confidence in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests per cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any evaluation site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until those are answered, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price, not in the narrative.

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in 2026, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 fee schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge [S1, S85].
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 7 by Market Analyst, 8,916 characters)
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim, so the advantage lasts only until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships, and it cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is not a startup with better chemistry; it is the incumbent that already owns the buyer's analyser slot. [S1, S67, S104]

The buyer at a three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options, and only one is a direct competitor. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a handheld cartridge analyser whose waived menu covers creatinine, potassium and glucose and which added an hs-troponin I cartridge in January 2025. Direct but narrower: Siemens epoc, 13 blood-gas, electrolyte and metabolite analytes in under a minute with no cardiac marker; QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel from EDTA whole blood; Roche's cobas h 232 from heparinised venous blood; and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX in hospital emergency departments. Substitute: the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call them later. No US product retrieved combines troponin, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium in one finger-stick cartridge, which is the gap the company sells into. [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109]

| Competitor | Product | Regulatory status | Menu | Price | Scale | Strengths versus Vantelle | Weaknesses versus Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and Alinity, hs-TnI cartridge | hs-TnI cleared 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11; waived-test manual; CG8+ cleared for capillary blood 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c/NT-proBNP | Not publicly disclosed | Point of Care line $606M FY2025 | Waived menu, installed base, capillary claim, distribution | One cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc | Marketed for hospital point-of-care use | 13 analytes in under a minute; no troponin or natriuretic peptide | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base, informatics | No cardiac menu, laboratory-controlled | S107 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro cardiac panel | US cardiac panel via waived-test channels; Cardio3 with BNP not sold in the US | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin in about 20 minutes | $599 per 25-test kit, $23.96 a test | $2.73B total FY2025; point-of-care share not disclosed | Urgent-care base, lowest price per test | EDTA blood or plasma, no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Roche | cobas h 232; LumiraDx | Marketed; LumiraDx acquired 2024-07-29 | Troponin T, NT-proBNP, D-dimer, myoglobin | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | Global distribution; owns LumiraDx | Venous sample, one test per strip, no metabolic panel | S111, S91 |
| Radiometer (Danaher) | AQT90 FLEX | Marketed for troponin I/T and NT-proBNP | Laboratory-quality immunoassay | Not publicly disclosed | Not disclosed | ED base | Benchtop, laboratory staff, no metabolic panel | S109 |
| Quest Diagnostics | Reference laboratory | n/a | Any test; one-to-three-day turnaround | $71.38 for the five codes at 2026 Medicare rates | $11.04B FY2025 | Zero capital, payer contracts | Turnaround unusable for suspected MI | S65, S85, S83, S84, S82, S86 |

Abbott decides the price. It documents the waived path for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026, which shows it is still investing in point-of-care cardiac testing. Its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025 while the wider Rapid Diagnostics segment fell 18.1% as COVID testing receded; point of care grew 3.1%. Analyser, cartridge and installed-base data are not disclosed, which is itself a diligence gap. Set against QuidelOrtho's $2.73B and Quest's $11.04B, Vantelle's $2.6M of FY2025 revenue is a 0.1% share of the smaller competitor. [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67, S22, S65]

When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert. The Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% gross margin at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, about 100 times what the 41 evaluation sites consume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20 to $25 with a free analyser takes the account, because the alternative is $38 plus $650 a month. At that price Vantelle's cartridge margin falls to 19-35% on today's cost, and it has no second product to defend the account. [S1, S67, S106]

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and which Vantelle has not yet applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, all assemblable from parts incumbents already sell. Sight Diagnostics shows how the regulatory step separates the two: its OLO analyser runs a finger-stick CBC and was cleared in 2021 for moderately complex rather than waived use, so a finger-stick clearance did not become a labour-free product. The base rate agrees: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1]

| Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Vantelle share | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Five-analyte finger-stick cardiac and metabolic panel for clinics without a laboratory | Abbott (i-STAT, waived menu, capillary claim) | Siemens Healthineers (epoc) and Roche (cobas h 232 plus LumiraDx) | QuidelOrtho (Triage cardiac) and Radiometer (AQT90 FLEX) | Sight Diagnostics (finger-stick CBC in the same clinic) and a combined cartridge from any incumbent | 0.3%, on $1.1M of 2025 evaluation revenue against a $368M cartridge market at observed utilisation | S104, S107, S111, S108, S109, S112, S1 |

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per group, and a clinic that must draw venous blood still needs the phlebotomist. That is a genuine opening of a year or two, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; confidence that Vantelle keeps a premium beyond the plan period is low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the evaluation sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived and accepts capillary blood; what price the distributor's letter of intent implies; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design.

::: evidence
**The buyer's default alternative is a waived Abbott handheld, not a reference lab.**
Abbott cleared hs-troponin for the i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and the Alinity in June 2026, publishes a waived-test manual for the i-STAT 1, and cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's counter-position is one cartridge and five analytes at $38 [S67, S6, S104, S105, S1].
:::

| Weaknesses | Cartridge cost $16.20 at pilot volume against a $7.50 target at two million units; analyser below cost and 60% given free; three of five assays uncleared, no CLIA waiver; 41 sites and $2.6M revenue | S1 (unverified) |
| Opportunities | No US product combines all five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge; 233,448 waived and 30,756 moderate-complexity CLIA laboratories as the post-waiver base; 61% of urgent-care centers independent or chain-owned rather than hospital-affiliated; 32 Rural Emergency Hospitals; Roche's LumiraDx purchase shows strategic demand for finger-stick platforms | S81, S79, S95, S91 |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,978 characters)
The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 additional-information request restarts a 90-day review clock, putting the first clearance in late March 2027 at the earliest; a CLIA waiver filed in the third quarter of 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's own 150-day goal; and at the 1.35 panels a day per site the evaluation sites actually run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites, not the 300 the plan reaches by end-2027. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. The FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window that runs to 2027-02-17. FDA's clock resumes on receipt of that answer, so a 90-day review cannot produce a decision before late March 2027, against a 2025 average of 146-149 days. The second submission has a harder dependency: it covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until the second quarter of 2027, so a Q2 2027 filing is not physically possible and a Q3 2027 filing is the earliest realistic date [S1, S69, S92].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to the FDA request | 2026-12 (company plan) | Received 2026-08-21; not answered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 (company) | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on the answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S92 |
| Pivotal study results, four sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary-venous equivalence, intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k), NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q2 2027 (company) | Depends on pivotal results due the same quarter | Five-assay menu | S1, unverified |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 (company) | Not filed; must reference a cleared application and include flex and user studies | Waived status, the gate to urgent care | S1, S72 |
| CLIA waiver decision | No company date | 150 FDA days after filing implies Q1 2028 at the earliest | Whether 2028 revenue is reachable | S72 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use only | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset in the plan and the one scheduled latest. A waiver submission references an already cleared application and must carry a risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended sites; FDA's goal is a substantive interaction within 90 review days and a decision within 150 FDA days. Filing in Q3 2027 therefore points to a decision around the first quarter of 2028, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. Until then the panel is a moderate-complexity test that only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified, competency-assessed staff may run; a Certificate of Waiver site cannot legally run it. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are therefore hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics that make up the serviceable market in the deck. The dual 510(k) and CLIA waiver pathway used by point-of-care peers would put both decisions on one 180-day goal [S72, S81, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: evaluation sites averaged 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites and 55 analyzers in 2026 — 41 cartridges a site a month, or 1.35 a site a calendar day, and 30 an analyzer, about 1.2 an analyzer operating day against the 8 a day the model assumes from 2028. The site plan does not close a 6.5-fold gap: 300 sites at model utilisation and the $31 2029 price produce $29.9M, not $78.5M. Reaching $78.5M requires 787 sites at model utilisation or 5,150 at the observed rate; $41.0M in 2028 requires 411. The 2027 line is tighter still: $16.8M with an average of 150 sites needs close to full model utilisation from the first day plus the $2.4M stocking order — no ramp at all, and only two assays on the menu for most of it [S1].

### Two of the plan's own numbers fail a timing test

Company data, unverified: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from the distributor that ships on 510(k) clearance, which the company itself expects in the first quarter of 2027. That is 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026 as scheduled. Separately, the 61% FY2026E gross margin sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below build cost, so either an undisclosed high-margin line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. Start from $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, and subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of term-loan principal once the Bluestem loan starts amortising in April 2027: $10.9M remains at the end of 2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory needed for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, so the realistic path is an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1, unverified |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1, unverified |

The distributor relationship is the commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme, and it is a letter of intent from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner — a related-party cost that belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridge sales and contract development are revenue but second curves that consume the same engineering team; the Irish entity and a CE mark are a distraction from the only market that matters in this round.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second additional-information letter | Second letter in the first half of 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Pivotal data show capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level, troponin CV below 10% | Results reported as categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver filed after clearance with no pre-submission | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready for scale | ISO 13485 certificate issued; automation ordered for Tempe | Audit slipped, no automation order by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount still in single digits against a 300-site plan | S1, unverified |

Counter-evidence deserves weight. The company hired a regulatory vice-president with a record of FDA clearances, the pipeline of paid evaluation sites and a high reorder rate is unusual for an investigational device, and if the recent request was documentation-only a Q1 2027 clearance remains possible. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the recent request asked and what evidence the pending answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers and what triggers the next round; and whether the distributor letter carries any minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing judgement is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel."}],"isError":false}

Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money. At $140M pre-money the operating business is priced at $126.9M once the new 10% pool is stripped out. The customer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a laboratory; the clinic is the buyer, though 39% of US urgent-care centres are hospital-owned and route send-outs to their health-system laboratory. Vantelle grows by placing instruments and selling consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers and 1,680 cartridges a month in 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, with scale dependent on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor letter of intent. ### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

The pool is the larger dilution. Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against a 10-15% typical range at Series B; the unallocated pool is worth $17.0M, $13.1M of it newly created inside the pre-money, so Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% of post-money rather than 15/170. The $30M Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs a $302M exit for 2x on the $30M; the Series A's 1x participation, present in 5% of 2025 deals, is the largest claim on a mid-range exit. ### The related-party royalty is small in percentage terms and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66% of sales, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; capitalising the royalty at 10x on the FY2029 plan implies a put liability of $9.4M. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty whose economics grow with cartridge volume rather than equity value; no arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate is disclosed. The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat means no founder majority, unlike Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC stripped it. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29. The $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only only until 2027-03, then amortises over 30 months at $0.167M of principal a month, so a closing slip lands with the first principal payment. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M also includes $2.4M from a stocking order that ships only on clearance, 40.7% of the year. Six searches on the company name on 2026-10-31 returned no SEC Form D, no state registry record, no USPTO assignee record, no FDA decision and no news; near matches: Vanta Diagnostics, a different company, and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, a California LLC filed 2026-09-09. Page 1 contains a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools asserting that no verification is needed and a rating is approved; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidentiary weight.
