Dr. Albescu's founder-market fit is specific rather than generic: an emergency physician who practised from 2011 to 2017 and then spent a year as medical director at a diagnostics company has lived the 1-3 day reference-lab wait that the Q5 is designed to remove, and the 41-site evaluation program is evidence she can sell a pilot into clinics. The limit is that 8.6 years as CEO have not yet produced a clearance, a CLIA waiver or a commercial launch, and no prior P&L, FDA submission or distribution build is publicly disclosed; the CV itself is unverified. Dr. Lindqvist supplies the technical depth the product depends on — a 2012 bioengineering PhD, four years in microfluidics at Pellucid, then Corvia and the CM-1 patent — but he is also a single point of failure: he is the inventor of the licensed sealing patent, owns 22% of the licensor and receives 0.66% of cartridge sales through it. [S99]

The regulatory function is the thinnest part of the executive bench. Grace Oyelaran joined in 2025-11 and is credited with 14 510(k) clearances across 2009-2025 at Meridale Medical, a claim public records cannot check because the FDA database lists applicants, not individuals. She owns four parallel workstreams: the troponin I and HbA1c file and its additional-information response, the ISO 13485 audit booked for Q1 2027 (not yet certified), the CLIA-waiver application planned for Q3 2027, and EU IVDR readiness. The FDA's own 510(k) total time to decision averaged 139 days in FY2024 and 112 days in FY2025, and QuidelOrtho describes CLIA-waiver requirements as "onerous", so a Q1 2027 clearance after a 2026-12 response and a Q3 2027 waiver are plausible only if the first AI is the last one. [S22, S101]

The commercial bench is sized for a pilot, not a launch. Luis Arrellano's 17 years at Tavora Health Systems map well onto Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, and 9 sales and support staff cover 41 sites; 300 sites would put 33 sites on each person, with the only bridge a non-binding distributor LOI. QuidelOrtho, by contrast, carries more than 2,500 sales, service and marketing employees. Manufacturing is similarly thin at the top: 18 staff run the Tempe pilot line, but no VP Manufacturing or VP Quality is named, ISO 13485 certification is still ahead, and the 9-month cartridge shelf life rests on 6 months of data. Cue Health's 2024 warning letter is the relevant precedent: unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow a failure rate above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement put its 9-month stability claim at issue after clearance, not before it. [S99, S22]

The finance and control gap is the easiest to fix and the most revealing. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO on a part-time basis since 2026-03, after the prior CFO left in 2026-02, and the deck discloses no prior operating CFO role or fundraise for him; a $30M institutional round, a $5.0M amortising loan and a $2.4M stocking order booked on a non-binding LOI are being represented by a fractional adviser, and these terms are company-provided and unverified. Six months of cash makes the hire urgent. What public records confirm is narrow: the company name returns no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignee or FDA decision record, and near matches — Vanta Diagnostics and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, filed in California on 2026-09-09 — are different entities. Reference checks are therefore the only verification available: Meridale Medical for the 14 clearances and the 2025-09 predecessor's departure; Tavora Health Systems for Arrellano's quota and channel relationships; Quillon Diagnostics and St. Brennan for Albescu; Whitcombe Advisory's other clients; Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock for board behaviour; Southwest Clinical Supply for whether the 300-site LOI names sites; and two pilot-line operators for lot-release discipline at volume. [S99]

The team is a clinical-insight team that has not yet become a regulatory-and-commercial execution team. Who invents is clear — the CTO and the CM-1 patent; who sells is clear — the VP Commercial and the evaluation base; who raises is the CEO. The missing hires are a full-time CFO, VP Manufacturing and Operations, VP Quality, a clinical-affairs lead for the pivotal study, a payer lead and an EU PRRC for Ireland. The lead check should be conditioned on the CFO and Quality hires, verified clearance history and an independent director before money moves.

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The difference is the package: five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick. It is defensible only if the cartridge, the cost curve, the pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects the optical signal for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills. Company description, unverified.

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | <10% for the IFCC high-sensitivity definition; i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Shelf life and cartridge cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a result whose true value sits on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share of measurements land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways, which assume far tighter imprecision. The deck calls the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff, so the decision level is unknown; on this data the assay is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none of these. The 96.1% is categorical agreement over 128 results and the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. For troponin the error that matters is a false negative, and the six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15, S68, S70].

### The capillary question is the investment case

No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and whole-blood potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood, un-anticoagulated within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary whole blood | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin precision at cutoff | 11.8% CV (unverified) | Below 5.2% CV | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate today; waiver planned Q3 2027 (company) | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate complexity | Moderate complexity | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended-use sites; FDA's goal is a decision 150 FDA days after filing, and an additional-information request can add 180 days. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. There is no point-of-care precedent to copy: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood-gas cartridges, its high-sensitivity troponin launched on 2025-01-03 as a moderate-complexity test, and CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30; Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate complexity on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind among the systems reviewed, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028, not 2027 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL of dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |

A funded team of 50 needs two to three years to match the combination, and the binding constraint is evidence, not chemistry: every constituent assay already exists at the point of care [S70, S74, S133].

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay reader) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal under consideration | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (finger-stick sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry on dried reagents) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (cartridge sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, exclusively licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry; no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational use) | $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot production, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |

### Reimbursement pays the panel only if the expensive assays are ordered

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| Five-code total | | $71.38 | S154 |

Two codes — troponin and potassium, the minimum a chest-pain visit needs — pay $17.23 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised price. Four codes, the cardiac and renal workup without HbA1c, pay $61.67; all five pay $71.38. Drop NT-proBNP, which carries $39.26 of the $71.38, and the other four pay $32.12, below the list price. The cartridge economics therefore depend on the clinic ordering the natriuretic peptide on most panels, not on the panel's existence; CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts the chemistry codes and takes the five-code total to $60.67, 15% lower [S149, S154].

### Supply chain and the antibody are undisclosed

The deck names no bill of materials, no supplier, no second source and no antibody licence. The only licensed component it identifies is the Corvia CM-1 sealing patent (exclusive, 3% royalty); the troponin antibody's supplier, licence terms and assignability on a change of control are not disclosed, which is a gap because the assay is the regulated product and a sole-source antibody would be a launch constraint. What would settle it: the cartridge and reader bills of materials with supplier sites, the antibody licence and supply agreement (including change-of-control and transfer rights), second-source qualification records, and the unredacted freedom-to-operate opinion [S1].

Company data, unverified: the analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c at readiness level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal study enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — leased plant, limited stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate. The questions that would settle the analytical case are the troponin cutoff and detection limit, what the pending FDA request asked, the haemolysis rate in pivotal finger sticks, line yield and stability beyond the data held, and whether the waiver will be filed as a dual submission alongside the second clearance [S1].

Counter-evidence, company data unverified: the other four assays agreed closely with the central laboratory and sites reordered; a rural clinic may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff, which the deck omits. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in company data, while the manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's published process.

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. On the company's own data its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The package is five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, and it is defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve, pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood, with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills (company description, unverified).

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | IFCC high-sensitivity <10%; i-STAT hs-TnI <5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Shelf life and cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. The deck calls the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff; on this data it is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI, not as an hs-TnI against Abbott's. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none. The 96.1% is categorical agreement over 128 results and the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. The error that matters is a false negative, and the six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15, S68, S70].

### The capillary question is the investment case

No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in the second quarter of 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and whole-blood potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | Below 5.2% | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate; waiver planned Q3 2027 | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate | Moderate | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is 150 FDA days, and an additional-information request can add 180. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. There is no point-of-care precedent: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood-gas cartridges, its hs-TnI launched on 2025-01-03 as moderate complexity, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind among the systems reviewed, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL of dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |

A funded team of 50 needs two to three years to match the combination; the binding constraint is evidence, not chemistry, because every constituent assay already exists at the point of care [S70, S74, S133].

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |

The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. Its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. ::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values above the detection limit in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit. |---|---|---|---|

| Shelf life and cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. Its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The package is five analytes from one 40-microlitre finger stick, defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve, pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit; Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills (company description, unverified).

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | IFCC high-sensitivity <10%; i-STAT hs-TnI <5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Shelf life and cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. The deck calls the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff; on this data it is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none. The 96.1% is categorical agreement over 128 results and the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. The error that matters is a false negative, and the six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15, S68, S70].

### The capillary question is the investment case

No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in Q2 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and whole-blood potassium are already sold by Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary | S1, S70, S74 |
| Menu | 5 assays | 1 assay | Gases, electrolytes, creatinine | S1, S70, S133 |
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | Below 5.2% | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate; waiver planned Q3 2027 | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate | Moderate | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is 150 FDA days, and an additional-information request can add 180. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. There is no point-of-care precedent: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood gas, its hs-TnI launched on 2025-01-03 as moderate complexity, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind among the systems reviewed, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL of dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |

A funded team of 50 needs two to three years; the constraint is evidence, not chemistry [S70, S74, S133].

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay reader) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal pending | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770 (sample-volume check) | Filed 2025-09-30 (unverified); unpublished | Guards short fills | S1 |
| PCT/US2026/014022 (troponin chemistry) | Filed 2026-02-11 (unverified); unpublished | Lead assay, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry; no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational) | $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |

### Reimbursement pays the panel only if the expensive assays are ordered

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| Five-code total | | $71.38 | S154 |

Two codes — troponin and potassium, the minimum a chest-pain visit needs — pay $17.23 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised price. Four codes without HbA1c pay $61.67; all five pay $71.38. Drop NT-proBNP, which carries $39.26 of the total, and the other four pay $32.12, below the list price. The economics therefore depend on the clinic ordering the natriuretic peptide on most panels; CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts the chemistry codes and takes the five-code total to $60.67, 15% lower [S149, S154].

### Supply chain and the antibody are undisclosed

The deck names no bill of materials, no supplier, no second source and no antibody licence. The only licensed component it identifies is the Corvia CM-1 sealing patent (exclusive, 3% royalty); the troponin antibody's supplier, licence terms and assignability on a change of control are not disclosed — a gap because the assay is the regulated product and a sole-source antibody would be a launch constraint. What would settle it: the bills of materials with supplier sites, the antibody licence and supply agreement (including change-of-control and transfer rights), second-source qualification records, and the unredacted FTO opinion [S1].

Company data, unverified: the analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, not a product, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c at level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — leased plant, limited stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate. The open questions are the troponin cutoff and detection limit, what the FDA request asked, haemolysis in pivotal finger sticks, line yield and stability beyond the data held, and whether the waiver is filed alongside the second clearance [S1].

Counter-evidence, company data unverified: the other four assays agreed closely and sites reordered; a rural clinic may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in company data, while manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's process.

The founders have the right clinical insight and the CTO the right technical pedigree, but the team as disclosed has not taken a cartridge product through a CLIA waiver and a 300-site launch, and the two functions that decide whether it does — regulatory/quality and finance — rest on one 11-month hire and a part-time interim CFO. | 2006-2023 | Tavora Health Systems | Sales representative to regional VP, Southwest | 17 years of Southwest health-system sales | Unverified | S99 |

Dr. Albescu's founder-market fit is specific: an emergency physician who practised from 2011 to 2017 and then spent a year as medical director at a diagnostics company has lived the 1-3 day reference-lab wait the Q5 is designed to remove, and the 41-site evaluation program shows she can sell a pilot into clinics. But 8.6 years as CEO have not produced a clearance, a CLIA waiver or a launch, and no prior P&L, FDA submission or distribution build is publicly disclosed; the CV itself is unverified. Dr. Lindqvist supplies the technical depth — a 2012 bioengineering PhD, four years in microfluidics at Pellucid, then Corvia and the CM-1 patent — but he is a single point of failure: inventor of the licensed sealing patent, owner of 22% of the licensor and recipient of 0.66% of cartridge sales through it. [S99]

The regulatory function is the thinnest part of the executive bench. Grace Oyelaran joined in 2025-11 and is credited with 14 510(k) clearances across 2009-2025 at Meridale Medical, a claim public records cannot check because the FDA database lists applicants, not individuals. She owns four parallel workstreams: the troponin I and HbA1c file and its additional-information response, the ISO 13485 audit booked for Q1 2027 (not yet certified), the CLIA-waiver application planned for Q3 2027, and EU IVDR readiness. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report gives one 510(k) series, total time to decision: 127 days in FY2023 against a 128-day goal and 139 days in FY2024 against a 124-day goal (missed); the FY2025 goal is 112 days and that cohort was still pending at 2025-09-30. The 90-day clock is FDA days and stops while an additional-information request is open, so a December 2026 answer plus 90 FDA days is late March 2027 at the earliest, while the FY2024 total-time average of 139 days points to mid-May 2027; the 175-day Chemistry-panel figure used elsewhere in this report is a 510(k)-database average, not FDA's. QuidelOrtho describes CLIA-waiver requirements as "onerous", so a Q1 2027 clearance after a 2026-12 response and a Q3 2027 waiver are plausible only if the first AI is the last one. [S97, S92, S22]

The commercial bench is sized for a pilot, not a launch. Luis Arrellano's 17 years at Tavora Health Systems map onto Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, but 9 sales and support staff cover 41 sites; 300 sites would put 33 on each person, with only a non-binding distributor LOI as bridge. QuidelOrtho carries more than 2,500 sales, service and marketing employees. Manufacturing is thin at the top: 18 staff run the Tempe pilot line, no VP Manufacturing or VP Quality is named, ISO 13485 certification is ahead, and the 9-month shelf life rests on 6 months of data. Cue Health's 2024 warning letter found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow a failure rate above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, putting its 9-month stability claim at issue after clearance, not before it. [S99, S22]

The finance and control gap is the easiest to fix and the most revealing. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO on a part-time basis since 2026-03, after the prior CFO left in 2026-02, and the deck discloses no prior operating CFO role or fundraise for him; a $30M institutional round, a $5.0M amortising loan and a $2.4M stocking order booked on a non-binding LOI are being represented by a fractional adviser, and these terms are company-provided and unverified. Six months of cash makes the hire urgent. What public records confirm is narrow: the company name returns no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignee or FDA decision record, and near matches — Vanta Diagnostics and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, filed in California on 2026-09-09 — are different entities. Reference checks are therefore the only verification available: Meridale Medical for the 14 clearances and the 2025-09 departure; Tavora Health Systems for Arrellano's quota; Quillon Diagnostics for Albescu; Whitcombe Advisory's other clients; Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock for board behaviour; Southwest Clinical Supply on whether the LOI names sites; and two pilot-line operators on lot-release discipline. [S99]

The team is a clinical-insight team that has not yet become a regulatory-and-commercial execution team. Who invents is clear — the CTO and the CM-1 patent; who sells is clear — the VP Commercial and the evaluation base; who raises is the CEO. The missing hires are a full-time CFO, VP Manufacturing and Operations, VP Quality, a clinical-affairs lead for the pivotal study, a payer lead and an EU PRRC for Ireland. The lead check should be conditioned on the CFO and Quality hires, verified clearance history and an independent director before money moves.

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is the 41-site paid evaluation program; the strongest doubt is the manufacturing and quality bench that has to scale it.**
Cue Health's FDA warning letter of 2024-05-09 found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow released cartridges to fail above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, with the 9-month shelf life at issue. Vantelle asks investors to fund a 40% manufacturing scale-up on a line whose ISO 13485 audit has not happened and whose shelf-life claim rests on 6 months of data. [S113]
:::

The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites delivered in the 2026 year to date, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the cartridge volume behind it are company-provided, unaudited and not independently confirmed [S1, S67].

The site count is the only input that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% hospital-owned or affiliated and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 in September 2024. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of that range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base near 2,400 [S79, S80, S78, S1]. The volume is dated precisely: deck p.7 heads its column "Cartridges a month, 2026 average", and with all figures as of 2026-09-30 that is a 2026 year-to-date average, not an FY2025 average; FY2025 monthly volume is not disclosed. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, so 1,680 is roughly double the program-to-date rate, not a flat line. Across 55 analyzers it is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days, or 1.35 per site-day; the model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap. That gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at $31 realised, almost exactly the model's eight and six times the observed rate. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M; it has 41. Its 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used [S1].

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Observed utilisation, one analyzer | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | 1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | 1.22 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | $0.18B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. A $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17%-83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M figure is still 60% of the smallest estimate. Abbott's global Point of Care line generated $606M in FY2025, four times the claimed US SAM [S93, S94, S96, S67].

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. CMS's CY2026 national limitation amounts pay $71.38 for all five codes; without the natriuretic peptide the other four cap at $32.12, below the $38 list and the $33.40 realised price. HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collect $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; troponin plus potassium collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation supports $222M, not $368M. Medicare is the only public benchmark; commercial and cash prices are not disclosed [S154, S79, S1].

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| All five codes | — | $71.38 | S154 |
| Four codes excluding 83880 | — | $32.12 | S154 |
| Troponin plus potassium | — | $17.23 | S154 |

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico hold 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived laboratories [S81]. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 faces FDA's 150-day decision goal from filing and a 180-day window to answer an information request, so no waiver before 2028 is the realistic case; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base the pitch addresses [S72, S1]. The first 510(k), filed 2026-05-18, drew an additional-information request on 2026-08-21 with a response planned for December 2026; FDA's own series reports average total time to decision of 127 days in FY2023 and 139 days in FY2024 against goals of 128 and 124, with FY2025 pending at 2025-09-30, so Q1 2027 clearance is plausible but company-provided [S97, S1]. Ownership consolidation compounds the friction: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024 [S79, S95]. The market systems are US; exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents; the EU is blocked until CE marking after 2028 [S1].

The commercial path is unproven at each step. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation program two and a half years later; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. The deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, installed EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price evidence. What would settle it: signed contracts with start dates, the first ten sites' CLIA certificates and EHR go-live dates, and collected revenue per cartridge by payer [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more. Medicare is the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until then, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price, not the narrative.

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: TX, AZ, NM | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA labs (2026) | US POC 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only | Moderate-complexity certificate and staffed QC until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital labs | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of US | $2.89B-$14.0B US POC market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR | Blocked until a 2028 waiver; 300 sites by end-2027 via non-binding LOI, as moderate-complexity customers | CLIA; payer coverage | Abbott, Siemens, Roche, Radiometer, Quest | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15, no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in the 2026 year-to-date average month across 55 analyzers, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge [S1, S154].
:::

The founders have the right clinical insight and the CTO the right technical pedigree, but the team as disclosed has not taken a cartridge product through a CLIA waiver and a 300-site launch, and the two functions that decide whether it does — regulatory/quality and finance — rest on one 11-month hire and a part-time interim CFO. Of 64 staff, 22 are in R&D, 18 in manufacturing, 9 in clinical and regulatory, 9 in sales and support and 6 in finance and administration; five executives are disclosed. Dr. Albescu's founder-market fit is specific: an emergency physician who practised from 2011 to 2017 and then spent a year as medical director at a diagnostics company has lived the 1-3 day reference-lab wait the Q5 is designed to remove, and the 41-site evaluation program shows she can sell a pilot into clinics. But 8.6 years as CEO have not produced a clearance, a CLIA waiver or a launch, and no prior P&L, FDA submission or distribution build is publicly disclosed; the CV itself is unverified. Dr. Lindqvist supplies the technical depth — a 2012 bioengineering PhD, four years in microfluidics at Pellucid, then Corvia and the CM-1 patent — but he is a single point of failure: inventor of the licensed sealing patent, owner of 22% of the licensor and recipient of 0.66% of cartridge sales through it. [S99]

The regulatory function is the thinnest part of the executive bench. Grace Oyelaran joined in 2025-11 and is credited with 14 510(k) clearances across 2009-2025 at Meridale Medical, a claim public records cannot check because the FDA database lists applicants, not individuals. She owns four parallel workstreams: the troponin I and HbA1c file and its additional-information response, the ISO 13485 audit booked for Q1 2027 (not yet certified), the CLIA-waiver application planned for Q3 2027, and EU IVDR readiness. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report gives one 510(k) series, total time to decision: 127 days in FY2023 against a 128-day goal and 139 days in FY2024 against a 124-day goal (missed); the FY2025 goal is 112 days and that cohort was still pending at 2025-09-30. The 90-day clock is FDA days and stops while an additional-information request is open, so a December 2026 answer plus 90 FDA days is late March 2027 at the earliest, while the FY2024 total-time average of 139 days points to mid-May 2027; the 175-day Chemistry-panel figure used elsewhere in this report is a 510(k)-database average, not FDA's. QuidelOrtho describes CLIA-waiver requirements as "onerous", so a Q1 2027 clearance after a 2026-12 response and a Q3 2027 waiver are plausible only if the first AI is the last one. [S97, S92, S22]

The commercial bench is sized for a pilot, not a launch. Luis Arrellano's 17 years at Tavora Health Systems map onto Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, but 9 sales and support staff cover 41 sites; 300 sites would put 33 on each person, with only a non-binding distributor LOI as bridge. QuidelOrtho carries more than 2,500 sales, service and marketing employees. Manufacturing is thin at the top: 18 staff run the Tempe pilot line, no VP Manufacturing or VP Quality is named, ISO 13485 certification is ahead, and the 9-month shelf life rests on 6 months of data. Cue Health's 2024 warning letter found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow a failure rate above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, putting its 9-month stability claim at issue after clearance, not before it. [S99, S22]

The finance and control gap is the easiest to fix and the most revealing. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO on a part-time basis since 2026-03, after the prior CFO left in 2026-02, and the deck discloses no prior operating CFO role or fundraise for him; a $30M round, a $5.0M amortising loan and a $2.4M stocking order on a non-binding LOI are represented by a fractional adviser, unverified. Six months of cash makes the hire urgent. What public records confirm is narrow: the company name returns no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignee or FDA decision record, and near matches — Vanta Diagnostics and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, filed in California on 2026-09-09 — are different entities. Reference checks are therefore the only verification available: Meridale Medical for the 14 clearances and the 2025-09 departure; Tavora Health Systems for Arrellano's quota; Quillon Diagnostics for Albescu; Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock for board behaviour; Southwest Clinical Supply on whether the LOI names sites. [S99]

The team is a clinical-insight team that has not yet become a regulatory-and-commercial execution team. Who invents is clear — the CTO and the CM-1 patent; who sells is clear — the VP Commercial and the evaluation base; who raises is the CEO. The missing hires are a full-time CFO, VP Manufacturing and Operations, VP Quality, a clinical-affairs lead for the pivotal study, a payer lead and an EU PRRC for Ireland. The lead check should be conditioned on the CFO and Quality hires, verified clearance history and an independent director before money moves.

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is the 41-site paid evaluation program; the strongest doubt is the manufacturing and quality bench that has to scale it.**
Cue Health's FDA warning letter of 2024-05-09 found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow released cartridges to fail above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, with the 9-month shelf life at issue. Vantelle asks investors to fund a 40% manufacturing scale-up on a line whose ISO 13485 audit has not happened and whose shelf-life claim rests on 6 months of data. [S113]
:::

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. Its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The package is five analytes from one finger stick, defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve, pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit; Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills (company description, unverified).

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | IFCC high-sensitivity <10%; i-STAT hs-TnI <5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Troponin agreement | 96.1% (123/128), same normal/abnormal bucket (unverified) | Method comparison with slope, bias and total error | S1 |
| Shelf life and cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. The deck calls the assay high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff; on this data it is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none. The 96.1% is categorical agreement and the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15, S68, S70].

### The capillary question is the investment case

No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in Q2 2027 — is the first test of the two variables that matter: capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and potassium already exist from Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary | S1, S70, S74 |
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | Below 5.2% | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate; waiver planned Q3 2027 | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate | Moderate | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is 150 FDA days, and an additional-information request can add 180. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. No point-of-care precedent exists: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood gas, its hs-TnI launched on 2025-01-03 as moderate complexity, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind among the systems reviewed, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL of dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |

A funded team of 50 needs two to three years; the constraint is evidence, not chemistry [S70, S74, S133].

### Patent position

|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay reader) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal pending | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770; PCT/US2026/014022 (unpublished) | Filed 2025-09-30 and 2026-02-11 (unverified) | Sample-volume check; troponin chemistry, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |

The freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry; no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation, investigational) | $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot, Tempe) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |

### Reimbursement pays the panel only if the expensive assays are ordered

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| Five-code total | | $71.38 | S154 |

Two codes — troponin and potassium, the minimum a chest-pain visit needs — pay $17.23 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised price. Four codes without HbA1c pay $61.67; all five pay $71.38. Drop NT-proBNP, which carries $39.26 of the total, and the other four pay $32.12, below the list price. The economics therefore depend on the clinic ordering the natriuretic peptide on most panels; CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts the chemistry codes and takes the five-code total to $60.67, 15% lower [S149, S154].

### Supply chain and the antibody are undisclosed

The deck names no bill of materials, no supplier, no second source and no antibody licence. The only licensed component it identifies is the Corvia CM-1 sealing patent (exclusive, 3% royalty); the troponin antibody's supplier, licence terms and assignability on a change of control are not disclosed — a launch and exit constraint because the assay is the regulated product. What would settle it: the bills of materials with supplier sites, the antibody licence and supply agreement (including change-of-control and transfer rights), second-source qualification records, and the unredacted FTO opinion [S1].

Company data, unverified: the analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c at level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — leased plant, limited stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate. The open questions are the troponin cutoff and detection limit, what the FDA request asked, haemolysis in pivotal finger sticks, line yield and stability beyond the data held, and whether the waiver is filed alongside the second clearance [S1].

Counter-evidence, company data unverified: the other four assays agreed closely and sites reordered; a rural clinic may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in company data, while manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's process.

arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites delivered in the 2026 year to date, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the cartridge volume behind it are company-provided, unaudited and not independently confirmed [S1, S67].

The site count is the only input that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% hospital-owned or affiliated and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 in September 2024. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of that range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base near 2,400 [S79, S80, S78, S1]. The volume is dated precisely: deck p.7 heads its column "Cartridges a month, 2026 average", and with all figures as of 2026-09-30 that is a 2026 year-to-date average, not an FY2025 average; FY2025 monthly volume is not disclosed. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, so 1,680 is roughly double the program-to-date rate, not a flat line. Across 55 analyzers it is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days, or 1.35 per site-day; the model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap. That gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at $31 realised, almost exactly the model's eight and six times the observed rate. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M; it has 41. Its 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used [S1].

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. A $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17%-83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M figure is still 60% of the smallest estimate. Abbott's global Point of Care line generated $606M in FY2025, four times the claimed US SAM [S93, S94, S96, S67].

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. CMS's CY2026 national limitation amounts pay $71.38 for all five codes; without the natriuretic peptide the other four cap at $32.12, below the $38 list and the $33.40 realised price. HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collect $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; troponin plus potassium collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation supports $222M, not $368M [S154, S79, S1].

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| All five codes | — | $71.38 | S154 |
| Four codes excluding 83880 | — | $32.12 | S154 |
| Troponin plus potassium | — | $17.23 | S154 |

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico hold 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived laboratories [S81]. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 faces FDA's 150-day decision goal from filing and a 180-day window to answer an information request, so no waiver before 2028 is the realistic case; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base the pitch addresses [S72, S1]. The first 510(k), filed 2026-05-18, drew an additional-information request on 2026-08-21 with a response planned for December 2026; FDA's own series reports average total time to decision of 127 days in FY2023 and 139 days in FY2024 against goals of 128 and 124, with FY2025 pending at 2025-09-30, so Q1 2027 clearance is plausible but company-provided [S97, S1]. Ownership consolidation compounds the friction: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024 [S79, S95]. The market systems are US; exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents; the EU is blocked until CE marking after 2028 [S1].

The commercial path is unproven at each step. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation program two and a half years later; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. The deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, installed EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price evidence. What would settle it: signed contracts with start dates, the first ten sites' CLIA certificates and EHR go-live dates, and collected revenue per cartridge by payer [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more. Medicare is the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until then, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price, not the narrative.

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: TX, AZ, NM | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA labs (2026) | US POC 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only | Moderate-complexity certificate and staffed QC until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital labs | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of US | $2.89B-$14.0B US POC market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR | Blocked until a 2028 waiver; 300 sites by end-2027 via non-binding LOI, as moderate-complexity customers | CLIA; payer coverage | Abbott, Siemens, Roche, Radiometer, Quest | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15, no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens | S1 (unverified) |
| Other regions | Not addressed | n/a | Not planned | n/a | n/a | S1 (unverified) |

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in the 2026 year-to-date average month across 55 analyzers, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge [S1, S154].
:::

The founders have the right clinical insight and the CTO the right technical pedigree, but the team as disclosed has not taken a cartridge product through a CLIA waiver and a 300-site launch, and the two functions that decide whether it does — regulatory/quality and finance — rest on one 11-month hire and a part-time interim CFO. Of 64 staff, 22 are in R&D, 18 in manufacturing, 9 in clinical and regulatory, 9 in sales and support and 6 in finance and administration; five executives are disclosed. Every CV below is company-provided and unverified: no public source locates any of the five in a Vantelle role. [S99]

Dr. Lindqvist's undergraduate degree is not disclosed.

| 2011-2018 | St. Brennan Regional Medical Center; Quillon Diagnostics | Emergency physician; medical director | Six years of emergency practice, then one year in diagnostics | Unverified | S99 |
| 2018-03 to present | Vantelle Diagnostics | CEO, co-founder, director | 8.6 years as CEO; 41 evaluation sites signed | Unverified | S99 |
| 2012-2016 / 2016-02 | Pellucid Biosystems; Corvia Microfluidics | Senior scientist, microfluidics; founder | Four years of microfluidics R&D; inventor of the CM-1 sealing patent | Unverified | S99 |
| 2018-03 to present | Vantelle Diagnostics | CTO, co-founder, director | Product and patent families VD-1 to VD-4 | Unverified | S99 |
| 2009-2025 | Meridale Medical | Regulatory affairs manager to director | 14 FDA 510(k) clearances claimed by the deck | Unverified | S99 |
| 2025-11 to present | Vantelle Diagnostics | VP Regulatory and Quality | 510(k) filed 2026-05-18; FDA additional-information request 2026-08-21 | Unverified | S99 |
| 2006-2023 | Tavora Health Systems | Sales representative to regional VP, Southwest | 17 years of Southwest health-system sales | Unverified | S99 |
| 2024-01 to present | Vantelle Diagnostics | VP Commercial | 41 sites and a non-binding 300-site distributor LOI | Unverified | S99 |
| 2014 to present | Whitcombe Advisory | Partner, fractional finance | Part-time interim CFO since 2026-03 | Unverified | S99 |

Dr. Albescu's founder-market fit is specific: an emergency physician who practised from 2011 to 2017 and then spent a year as medical director at a diagnostics company has lived the 1-3 day reference-lab wait the Q5 is designed to remove, and the 41-site evaluation program shows she can sell a pilot into clinics. But 8.6 years as CEO have not produced a clearance, a CLIA waiver or a launch, and no prior P&L, FDA submission or distribution build is publicly disclosed; the CV itself is unverified. Dr. Lindqvist supplies the technical depth — a 2012 bioengineering PhD, four years in microfluidics at Pellucid, then Corvia and the CM-1 patent — but he is a single point of failure: inventor of the licensed sealing patent, owner of 22% of the licensor and recipient of 0.66% of cartridge sales through it. [S99]

The regulatory function is the thinnest part of the executive bench. Grace Oyelaran joined in 2025-11 and is credited with 14 510(k) clearances across 2009-2025 at Meridale Medical, a claim public records cannot check because the FDA database lists applicants, not individuals. She owns four parallel workstreams: the troponin I and HbA1c file and its additional-information response, the ISO 13485 audit booked for Q1 2027 (not yet certified), and the CLIA-waiver application planned for Q3 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report gives one 510(k) series, total time to decision: 127 days in FY2023 against a 128-day goal and 139 days in FY2024 against a 124-day goal (missed); the FY2025 goal is 112 days and that cohort was still pending at 2025-09-30. The 90-day clock is FDA days and stops while an additional-information request is open, so a December 2026 answer plus 90 FDA days is late March 2027 at the earliest, while the FY2024 total-time average of 139 days points to mid-May 2027; the 175-day Chemistry-panel figure used elsewhere in this report is a 510(k)-database average, not FDA's. QuidelOrtho describes CLIA-waiver requirements as "onerous", so a Q1 2027 clearance after a 2026-12 response and a Q3 2027 waiver are plausible only if the first AI is the last one. [S97, S92, S22]

The commercial bench is sized for a pilot, not a launch. Luis Arrellano's 17 years at Tavora Health Systems map onto Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, but 9 sales and support staff cover 41 sites; 300 sites would put 33 on each person, with only a non-binding distributor LOI as bridge. QuidelOrtho carries more than 2,500 sales, service and marketing employees. Manufacturing is thin at the top: 18 staff run the Tempe pilot line, no VP Manufacturing or VP Quality is named, ISO 13485 certification is ahead, and the 9-month shelf life rests on 6 months of data. Cue Health's 2024 warning letter found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow a failure rate above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, putting its 9-month stability claim at issue after clearance, not before it. [S99, S22]

The finance and control gap is the easiest to fix and the most revealing. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO on a part-time basis since 2026-03, after the prior CFO left in 2026-02, and the deck discloses no prior operating CFO role or fundraise for him; a $30M round, a $5.0M amortising loan and a $2.4M stocking order on a non-binding LOI are represented by a fractional adviser, unverified. Six months of cash makes the hire urgent. What public records confirm is narrow: the company name returns no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignee or FDA decision record, and near matches — Vanta Diagnostics and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, filed in California on 2026-09-09 — are different entities. Reference checks are therefore the only verification available: Meridale Medical for the 14 clearances and the 2025-09 departure; Tavora Health Systems for Arrellano's quota; Quillon Diagnostics for Albescu; Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock for board behaviour; Southwest Clinical Supply on whether the LOI names sites. [S99]

The team is a clinical-insight team that has not yet become a regulatory-and-commercial execution team. Who invents is clear — the CTO and the CM-1 patent; who sells is clear — the VP Commercial and the evaluation base; who raises is the CEO. The missing hires are a full-time CFO, VP Manufacturing and Operations, VP Quality, a clinical-affairs lead for the pivotal study, a payer lead and an EU PRRC for Ireland. The lead check should be conditioned on the CFO and Quality hires, verified clearance history and an independent director before money moves.

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is the 41-site paid evaluation program; the strongest doubt is the manufacturing and quality bench that has to scale it.**
Cue Health's FDA warning letter of 2024-05-09 found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow released cartridges to fail above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, with the 9-month shelf life at issue. Vantelle asks investors to fund a 40% manufacturing scale-up on a line whose ISO 13485 audit has not happened and whose shelf-life claim rests on 6 months of data. [S113]
:::
