arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. Its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The package is five analytes from one finger stick, defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve, pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit; Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills (company description, unverified).

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | IFCC high-sensitivity <10%; i-STAT hs-TnI <5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Shelf life and cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### What 11.8% at the cutoff does to a reviewer and a pathway

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. The deck calls it high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff; on this data it is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none. The 96.1% is categorical agreement; the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress [S1, S13, S15, S68, S70].

### The capillary question is the investment case

No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck. The four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in Q2 2027 — is the first test of capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and potassium already exist from Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S16, S21, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary | S1, S70, S74 |
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | Below 5.2% | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate; waiver planned Q3 2027 | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate | Moderate | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is 150 FDA days, and an additional-information request can add 180. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. No point-of-care precedent exists: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood gas, its hs-TnI launched on 2025-01-03 as moderate complexity, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL of dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |

A funded team of 50 needs two to three years; the constraint is evidence, not chemistry [S70, S74, S133].

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay reader) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal pending | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770; PCT/US2026/014022 (unpublished) | Filed 2025-09-30 and 2026-02-11 (unverified) | Sample-volume check; troponin chemistry, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry; no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation) | $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |

### Reimbursement pays the panel only if the expensive assays are ordered

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| Five-code total | | $71.38 | S154 |

Two codes — troponin and potassium, the minimum a chest-pain visit needs — pay $17.23 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised price. Four codes without HbA1c pay $61.67; all five pay $71.38. Drop NT-proBNP, which carries $39.26 of the total, and the other four pay $32.12, below the list price. The economics depend on the clinic ordering the natriuretic peptide on most panels; CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts the chemistry codes and takes the five-code total to $60.67, 15% lower [S149, S154].

### Supply chain and the antibody are undisclosed

The deck names no bill of materials, no supplier, no second source and no antibody licence. The only licensed component it identifies is the Corvia CM-1 sealing patent (exclusive, 3% royalty); the troponin antibody's supplier, licence terms and assignability on a change of control are not disclosed — a launch and exit constraint because the assay is the regulated product. What would settle it: the bills of materials with supplier sites, the antibody licence and supply agreement (including change-of-control and transfer rights), second-source qualification records, and the unredacted FTO opinion [S1].

Company data, unverified: the analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force. Readiness is uneven: troponin I and HbA1c at level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal enrolling), manufacturing at 5 — leased plant, limited stability data, no ISO 13485 certificate. The open questions are the troponin cutoff and detection limit, what the FDA request asked, haemolysis in pivotal finger sticks, line yield and stability beyond the data held, and whether the waiver is filed alongside the second clearance [S1].

Counter-evidence, company data unverified: the other four assays agreed closely and sites reordered; a rural clinic may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in company data, while manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's process.

arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites delivered in the 2026 year to date, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the cartridge volume behind it are company-provided, unaudited and not independently confirmed [S1, S67].

The site count is the only input that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% hospital-owned or affiliated and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 in September 2024. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of that range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base near 2,400 [S79, S80, S78, S1]. The volume is dated precisely: deck p.7 heads its column "Cartridges a month, 2026 average", and with all figures as of 2026-09-30 that is a 2026 year-to-date average, not an FY2025 average; FY2025 monthly volume is not disclosed. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, so 1,680 is roughly double the program-to-date rate. Across 55 analyzers it is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days, or 1.35 per site-day; the model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap. That gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at $31 realised, almost exactly the model's eight and six times the observed rate. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M; it has 41. Its 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used [S1].

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. A $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17%-83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M figure is still 60% of the smallest estimate. Abbott's global Point of Care line generated $606M in FY2025, four times the claimed US SAM [S93, S94, S96, S67].

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. CMS's CY2026 national limitation amounts pay $71.38 for all five codes; without the natriuretic peptide the other four cap at $32.12, below the $38 list and the $33.40 realised price. HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collect $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; troponin plus potassium collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation supports $222M, not $368M [S154, S79, S1].

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| All five codes | — | $71.38 | S154 |
| Four codes excluding 83880 | — | $32.12 | S154 |
| Troponin plus potassium | — | $17.23 | S154 |

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico hold 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived laboratories [S81]. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 faces FDA's 150-day decision goal from filing and a 180-day window to answer an information request, so no waiver before 2028 is the realistic case; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base [S72, S1]. The first 510(k), filed 2026-05-18, drew an additional-information request on 2026-08-21 with a response planned for December 2026; FDA's own series reports average total time to decision of 127 days in FY2023 and 139 days in FY2024 against goals of 128 and 124, with FY2025 pending at 2025-09-30, so Q1 2027 clearance is plausible but company-provided [S97, S1]. Ownership consolidation compounds the friction: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024 [S79, S95]. The market systems are US; exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents; the EU is blocked until CE marking after 2028 [S1].

The commercial path is unproven at each step. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation program two and a half years later; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. The deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, installed EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price evidence. What would settle it: signed contracts with start dates, the first ten sites' CLIA certificates and EHR go-live dates, and collected revenue per cartridge by payer [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more. Medicare is the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until then, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price.

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: TX, AZ, NM | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA labs (2026) | US POC 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only | Moderate-complexity certificate and staffed QC until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital labs | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of US | $2.89B-$14.0B US POC market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR | Blocked until a 2028 waiver; 300 sites by end-2027 via non-binding LOI, as moderate-complexity customers | CLIA; payer coverage | Abbott, Siemens, Roche, Radiometer, Quest | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15, no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens | S1 (unverified) |

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in the 2026 year-to-date average month across 55 analyzers, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge [S1, S154].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. Its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The package is five analytes from one finger stick, defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve, pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit; Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills (company description, unverified).

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | IFCC high-sensitivity <10%; i-STAT hs-TnI <5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Shelf life and cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### Precision and capillary collection decide the label

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. The deck calls it high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff; on this data it is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none. The 96.1% is categorical agreement; the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress. No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck: the four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in Q2 2027 — is the first test of capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and potassium already exist from Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S1, S13, S15, S16, S21, S68, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary | S1, S70, S74 |
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | Below 5.2% | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate; waiver planned Q3 2027 | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate | Moderate | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is 150 FDA days, and an additional-information request can add 180. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. No point-of-care precedent exists: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood gas, its hs-TnI launched on 2025-01-03 as moderate complexity, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL of dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |

A funded team of 50 needs two to three years; the constraint is evidence, not chemistry.

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay reader) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal pending | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770; PCT/US2026/014022 (unpublished) | Filed 2025-09-30 and 2026-02-11 (unverified) | Sample-volume check; troponin chemistry, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry; no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation) | $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |

### Reimbursement pays the panel only if the expensive assays are ordered

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| Five-code total | | $71.38 | S154 |

Two codes — troponin and potassium, the minimum a chest-pain visit needs — pay $17.23 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised price. Four codes without HbA1c pay $61.67; all five pay $71.38. Drop NT-proBNP, which carries $39.26 of the total, and the other four pay $32.12, below the list price. The economics depend on the clinic ordering the natriuretic peptide on most panels; CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts the chemistry codes and takes the five-code total to $60.67, 15% lower [S149, S154].

### Supply chain and the antibody are undisclosed

Company data, unverified: the deck names no bill of materials, no supplier, no second source and no antibody licence; the only licensed component it identifies is the Corvia CM-1 sealing patent (exclusive, 3% royalty), and the troponin antibody's supplier, licence terms and assignability on a change of control are not disclosed — a launch and exit constraint because the assay is the regulated product. What would settle it: the bills of materials with supplier sites, the antibody licence and supply agreement (including change-of-control and transfer rights), second-source qualification records, and the unredacted FTO opinion. The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force; readiness is uneven — troponin I and HbA1c at level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal enrolling), manufacturing at 5, with a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate. The open questions are the troponin cutoff and detection limit, what the FDA request asked, haemolysis in pivotal finger sticks, line yield and stability beyond the data held, and whether the waiver is filed alongside the second clearance [S1].

Counter-evidence, company data unverified: the other four assays agreed closely and sites reordered; a rural clinic may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in company data, while manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's process.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money — all company-provided and unverified. The buyer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a lab; 39% of US urgent-care centres are hospital-owned and send send-outs to their health-system lab. Vantelle places instruments and sells consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers, 1,680 cartridges a month and FY2025 revenue of $2.6M are unverified; scale depends on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor LOI. [S99, S79]

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware, 2018-03-12; HQ Albuquerque, NM | Series B issuer, FDA submitter, owner of VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona, 2022-05-09 | Tempe pilot line, 18 staff, plant lease | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland, 2025-01-15 | Future EU regulatory entity; no staff; CE not before 2028 | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas, 2016-02-01; 60% acquired 2021-04 | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed exclusively to Vantelle at 3% royalty | 60% Vantelle; 40% founders, incl. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist at 22% | Unverified | S99 |

Ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and 18 employees, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability rather than US assets. Whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped and Ireland's intercompany terms are not publicly disclosed. [S99]

### The $140M pre-money is built on 42,991,881 shares, not the 36.4M shown

| Shareholder | Class | Shares post-round | % post-money | % votes | Invested | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dr. Wren Albescu | Common | 6,400,000 | 12.26% | 15.32% | n/d | Unverified | S99 |
| Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist | Common | 4,800,000 | 9.19% | 11.49% | n/d | Unverified | S99 |
| Juniper Rock and seed investors | Seed preferred | 6,000,000 | 11.49% | 14.36% | $4.5M (4.34x) | Unverified | S99 |
| Ardent Peak and Series A investors | Series A preferred | 12,400,000 | 23.75% | 29.68% | $36.0M (1.12x) | Unverified | S99 |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | Common warrants at $2.903 | 400,000 | 0.77% | 0.96% | exercise $1.16M | Unverified | S99 |
| 2026 bridge noteholders | Series B-1 preferred | 2,571,392 | 4.93% | 6.15% | $6.28M (1.33x) | Unverified | S99 |
| New Series B investors | Series B preferred | 9,212,627 | 17.65% | 22.05% | $30.0M (1.00x) | Unverified | S99 |
| Options granted and unallocated pool | Common | 10,420,489 | 19.96% | 0% | strike n/d | Unverified | S99 |
| **Total** | | **52,204,508** | **100%** | **100%** | | Unverified | S99 |

The arithmetic reproduces the deck's unverified share counts: $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The deck's "shares today" column excludes the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% is 14.89% pre-money (unverified). The bridge converts at $2.4423, 75% of the round price; the note is not disclosed, so those terms are unverified. [S99]

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against the 10% post-money pool this round itself creates; no primary NVCA or Cooley survey publishes a Series B option-pool median this report could retrieve, so the overhang is scored warn rather than critical. The top-up lifts the unallocated pool from 1,200,000 shares to 5,220,489, adding 4,020,489 shares — 7.7 points of post-money and $13.1M at $3.2564 — dilution borne entirely by existing holders inside the pre-money. $15M is 8.82% of the $170.0M post-money and 10.7% of the $140.0M pre-money; the refresh dilutes existing holders, not the new money. The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value on the unverified share counts: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A $36.0M then 23.75% of the residual, and seed $4.5M non-participating. The founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6%) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%) on the deck's share counts; the $30M Series B returns 1.0x at $170M and needs $376M for 2x. Cooley's Q2 2026 survey of 166 financings found 96.4% non-participating preferred and 95.8% at 1x, so the Series A's 1x participation is a 3.6% structure and the largest mid-range claim. [S99, S159]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66%, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M — company-provided and unverified. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; 10x the FY2029 royalty implies a $9.4M put liability, an analyst estimate on unverified inputs. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty paid per cartridge rather than per dollar of equity value; no arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate and no Corvia LLC agreement is publicly disclosed. The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat; unlike Theranos, Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC stripped it. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20, S99]

### Six months of cash, a loan amortising, no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close (company figures, unverified). The $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only until 2027-03, then amortises at $0.167M a month, so a closing slip lands on the first payment (unverified; any IP security is not publicly disclosed). FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes $2.4M from a stocking order that ships only on clearance, 40.7% of the year (unverified). Searches on 2026-10-31 found no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignee, FDA decision or news. Pending 510(k)s are not published, so this does not test the filing; every entity date, ownership percentage and IP claim here rests on company-provided material. Page 1 carries a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools asserting no verification is needed and a rating approved; a document-integrity finding. Open questions: does the CM-1 licence survive a change of control, is Corvia's 40% put capped, and is any IP pledged to Bluestem? [S99]

The 112 days often quoted for FY2025 is the MDUFA V goal for FY2025-FY2027, not a measured outcome; FY2025 is preliminary and open. rows.mechanism: Review time is FDA days plus the company's own response time; an additional-information request stops the clock and the response resumes it, so a file's date depends on how long the company takes to answer as much as on FDA throughput.
rows.weakens: The FY2024 closed-cohort average is a lagging indicator; Vantelle's file is a two-assay 510(k) with an AI request, not the average submission.

rows.benchmark: The 180-day response window and 90-day clock are FDA policy; the company's December 2026 plan is inside both.

rows.mechanism: The AI hold is company time, not FDA time; a December answer is three months faster than the deadline but still leaves a second-cycle risk because the average 510(k) needs more than one review cycle.
rows.weakens: If the December answer is incomplete, the FDA can issue another AI request and the Q3 2027 stress becomes the base.

rows.benchmark: Series B burn multiple median near 1.4x; Vantelle is 4.2x in FY2026E and 15.6x excluding the stocking order.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates

rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025; Vantelle discloses neither.

rows.finding: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order that ships only on clearance; excluding it, revenue is $3.5M, or $2.7M booked in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. The 61% blended gross margin is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts to a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M. arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. Its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The package is five analytes from one finger stick, defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve, pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit; Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills (company description, unverified).

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | IFCC high-sensitivity <10%; i-STAT hs-TnI <5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Shelf life and cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### Precision and capillary collection decide the label

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share land on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. The deck calls it high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff; on this data it is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none. The 96.1% is categorical agreement; the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress. No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck: the four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in Q2 2027 — is the first test of capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and potassium already exist from Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S1, S13, S15, S16, S21, S68, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary | S1, S70, S74 |
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | Below 5.2% | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate; waiver planned Q3 2027 | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate | Moderate | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is 150 FDA days, and an additional-information request can add 180. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. No point-of-care precedent exists: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood gas, its hs-TnI launched on 2025-01-03 as moderate complexity, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL of dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Replication test | — | A funded team of 50 needs 2-3 years across all three barriers; the constraint is evidence, not chemistry | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay reader) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal pending | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770; PCT/US2026/014022 (unpublished) | Filed 2025-09-30 and 2026-02-11 (unverified) | Sample-volume check; troponin chemistry, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry; no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation) | $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |

### Reimbursement pays the panel only if the expensive assays are ordered

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| Five-code total | | $71.38 | S154 |

Two codes — troponin and potassium, the minimum a chest-pain visit needs — pay $17.23 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised price. Four codes without HbA1c pay $61.67; all five pay $71.38. Drop NT-proBNP, which carries $39.26 of the total, and the other four pay $32.12, below the list price. The economics depend on the clinic ordering the natriuretic peptide on most panels; CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts the chemistry codes and takes the five-code total to $60.67, 15% lower [S149, S154].

### Supply chain and the antibody are undisclosed

Company data, unverified: the deck names no bill of materials, no supplier, no second source and no antibody licence; the only licensed component it identifies is the Corvia CM-1 sealing patent (exclusive, 3% royalty), and the troponin antibody's supplier, licence terms and assignability on a change of control are not disclosed — a launch and exit constraint because the assay is the regulated product. What would settle it: the bills of materials with supplier sites, the antibody licence and supply agreement (including change-of-control and transfer rights), second-source qualification records, and the unredacted FTO opinion. The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force; readiness is uneven — troponin I and HbA1c at level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal enrolling), manufacturing at 5, with a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate. The open questions are the troponin cutoff and detection limit, what the FDA request asked, haemolysis in pivotal finger sticks, line yield and stability beyond the data held, and whether the waiver is filed alongside the second clearance [S1].

Counter-evidence, company data unverified: the other four assays agreed closely and sites reordered; a rural clinic may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in company data, while manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's process.

arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites delivered in the 2026 year to date, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the cartridge volume behind it are company-provided, unaudited and not independently confirmed [S1, S67].

The site count is the only input that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% hospital-owned or affiliated and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 in September 2024. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of that range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base near 2,400 [S79, S80, S78, S1]. The volume is dated precisely: deck p.7 heads its column "Cartridges a month, 2026 average", and with all figures as of 2026-09-30 that is a 2026 year-to-date average, not an FY2025 average; FY2025 monthly volume is not disclosed. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, so 1,680 is roughly double the program-to-date rate. Across 55 analyzers it is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days, or 1.35 per site-day; the model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap. That gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at $31 realised, almost exactly the model's eight and six times the observed rate. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M; it has 41. Its 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used [S1].

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. A $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17%-83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M figure is still 60% of the smallest estimate. Abbott's global Point of Care line generated $606M in FY2025, four times the claimed US SAM [S93, S94, S96, S67].

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. CMS's CY2026 national limitation amounts pay $71.38 for all five codes; without the natriuretic peptide the other four cap at $32.12, below the $38 list and the $33.40 realised price. HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collect $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; troponin plus potassium collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation supports $222M, not $368M [S154, S79, S1].

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| All five codes | — | $71.38 | S154 |
| Four codes excluding 83880 | — | $32.12 | S154 |
| Troponin plus potassium | — | $17.23 | S154 |

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico hold 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived laboratories. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 faces FDA's 150-day decision goal from filing and a 180-day window to answer an information request, so no waiver before 2028 is the realistic case; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base. The first 510(k), filed 2026-05-18, drew an additional-information request on 2026-08-21 with a response planned for December 2026; FDA's own series reports average total time to decision of 127 days in FY2023 and 139 days in FY2024 against goals of 128 and 124, with FY2025 pending at 2025-09-30, so Q1 2027 clearance is plausible but company-provided. Ownership consolidation compounds the friction: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024. The market systems are US; exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents; the EU is blocked until CE marking after 2028 [S81, S72, S97, S95, S1].

The commercial path is unproven at each step, on company-provided and unverified evidence. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation program two and a half years later; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. The $22.5M of net losses in 2027-2028 plus launch capex and working capital exceed the $32.3M the round leaves at close, so the plan needs $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. It starts at $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30 and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months — left at the 2027-01-29 target close. The burn is understated: $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M is the P&L loss with no capex or working capital in it.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue — 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each, twice the 300 sites targeted for end-2027. The cost target fails the same test. Two million cartridges a year is what buys the $7.50 cost; at the 1.2 panels a day the 41 evaluation sites actually ran, an analyzer consumes about 360 cartridges a year, so that volume needs 5,500 analyzers, and the 402 analyzers behind the 300-site plan produce 147,000 cartridges, 7% of it, where the only disclosed cost is $16.20 and the margin 48%, not 76%. Capital efficiency is poor against the stage: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x, where above 1.5x is inefficient at scale [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, dated Q1 2027, under a non-binding letter of intent. At $33.40 a cartridge the order is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month shelf-life claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M; with $2.7M booked in nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's use of funds has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and debt service after 2027-03 is $210,000 a month, 18% of burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting at 75% of the $3.2564 round price into 2,571,392 shares, 4.9% of the post-round count [S1, S22].

| Burn multiple | 8.3x | 4.2x, or 15.6x ex-stocking order | Series B median 1.4x | S1 (unverified), S134 |

| Receivable days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 55.7 days | S22 |
| Inventory days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 145 days | S22 |

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's $12.0M outflow takes it to negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit and the shortfall is $8-10M. The base keeps clearance in Q1 2027, consistent with the one review-time series in the FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report: average total time to decision (FDA days plus company time) was 127 days for the FY2023 receipt cohort and 139 days for FY2024, the most recent closed cohort; the 112 days often quoted for FY2025 is the MDUFA V goal, not a measured outcome, and FY2025 is preliminary and open [S97]. Vantelle's file is slower than average already: the FDA's additional-information request of 2026-08-21 stops the clock, the company plans to answer in December 2026 within the 180-day limit that runs to 2027-02-17, and the response resumes the 90-day FDA clock [S140]. That leaves a first-cycle decision in Q1 2027; the stress case adds a second information request and a full 90-day review cycle, moves clearance to Q3 2027, puts the CLIA waiver in 2028 and halves utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with operating cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M: a two-quarter slip moves the shortfall from $8-10M to $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M post-round count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S97, S140].

| 510(k) clearance | Q1 2027 (first AI cycle) | Q3 2027 (second AI cycle) | S1 (unverified), S97, S140 |
| CLIA waiver | applied Q3 2027 | 2028 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day, 2028 | 8.0 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue, FY2027 / 2028 / 2029 | 16.8 / 41.0 / 78.5 | 5.0 / 14.0 / 32.0 | S1 (unverified); analyst estimate |
| Cumulative net loss, 2027-2029 | (13.5) | (55.3) | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash trough | (4.7) in 2028 | below (25) in 2029 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Additional capital needed, $M | 8-10 | 25-40 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Dilution at half the Series B price | none | 23-32% | S1 (unverified); calculated |

These are capital-intensive instrument economics: growth is bought with placed hardware and funded receivables, so the faster Vantelle sells, the more cash it consumes before the cartridge annuity arrives. The variable that moves the outcome is panels per analyzer-day, not sites, price or the clearance date: clearance moves the clock, utilisation sets the level. The counter-case is that the burn is discretionary: a company that cut cost and slowed the site ramp would close most of the gap, and a distributor that finances inventory would remove much of the working-capital need, so the shortfall is about this plan, not survival. The round should be sized larger or tranched, the second tranche released on clearance and utilisation, and the price should assume a further financing before breakeven. The diligence list: the Bluestem agreement for its rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor's payment, return and pricing terms; and the Tempe line's cost and yield at launch volumes. Confidence is high on the arithmetic, which reconciles to the deck's numbers, and medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates with no auditor, no quarterly statements and no covenant disclosure behind them.

arguments.markdown:
The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 additional-information request restarts a 90-FDA-day review clock, putting the first clearance in April 2027 at the earliest, not the first quarter; a CLIA waiver filed in the third quarter of 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's own 150-FDA-day goal; and at the 1.35 cartridges a site a day the evaluation sites actually run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs about 5,150 sites, not the 300 the plan reaches by end-2027. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72, S97].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. The FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window that runs to 2027-02-17. The review clock resumes on receipt of that answer, and FDA's goal is 90 FDA days — about 18 weeks once weekends are excluded — so a December answer points to an April 2027 decision, not Q1 2027. FDA's one all-device series is the MDUFA average total time to decision: 127 days in FY2023 against a 128-day goal, met, and 139 days in FY2024 against a 124-day goal, missed; the FY2025 cohort was not complete at 2025-09-30. Those are calendar days including information holds, not FDA days, so they cannot be added to the post-answer clock. The 175-day Chemistry-panel and 337-day denied-submission figures used elsewhere are third-party panel averages of total time [S92], not the MDUFA series [S97].

The second submission has a harder dependency: it covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until Q2 2027, so the company's Q2 2027 filing is not physically possible; a Q3 2027 filing followed by 90 FDA days gives a Q1 2028 decision, and a second information request would push it to mid-2028. The five-assay menu is therefore a 2028 product, not a 2027 one [S1, S97].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to the FDA request | 2026-12 (company) | Received 2026-08-21; not answered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027 (company); April 2027 at 90 FDA days after a December answer | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on the answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S97 |
| Pivotal results, four sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary-venous equivalence; intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k), NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q3 2027 filing; Q1 2028 decision | Needs pivotal results due Q2 2027 | Five-assay menu | S1, S97 |

| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use only; two assays for most of the year | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset in the plan and the one scheduled latest. A waiver submission references an already cleared application and must carry a risk analysis, flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended sites; FDA's goal is a decision within 150 FDA days. Filing in Q3 2027 therefore points to a decision in Q2 2028, and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. A five-assay waiver cannot be filed until the second 510(k) clears in 2028, which puts it in 2029. Until then the panel is a moderate-complexity test that only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified, competency-assessed staff may run; a Certificate of Waiver site cannot legally run it. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are therefore hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics that make up the serviceable market in the deck. The dual 510(k) and CLIA waiver pathway used by point-of-care peers would put both decisions on one 180-day goal [S72, S81, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: the deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month as its "2026 average" across 41 sites and 55 analyzers (p.7) and repeats 41 cartridges a site a month for 2026 (p.9). The deck does not state the months covered; its figures are as of 2026-09-30, so the average cannot cover more than January-September 2026, and neither 2026 unit volume nor FY2025 cartridge units are disclosed, so no growth rate can be computed. On the disclosed average, 1,680 cartridges is 41.0 a site a month, or 1.35 a site a calendar day, and 30.5 an analyzer-month, or 1.02 an analyzer a calendar day (1.22 on a 300-operating-day basis) against the 8 a day the model assumes from 2028. At 1.35 a site a day and $31 a cartridge, a site produces $15,275 a year, so $78.5M needs about 5,150 sites, not 300; at the model's two analyzers and eight panels, 300 sites produce $44.6M and $78.5M needs 528 sites. The 2028 line is further away: $41.0M needs 2,680 sites at observed use or 276 at full model utilisation, against 300 planned by end-2027 [S1].

### Two of the plan's own numbers fail a timing test

Company data, unverified: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from the distributor that ships on 510(k) clearance, which the company expects in Q1 2027 and which, on the 90-FDA-day clock, is an April 2027 event at the earliest. That is 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026 as scheduled. Separately, the 61% FY2026E gross margin sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below build cost, so either an undisclosed high-margin line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. Start from $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, and subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of term-loan principal once the Bluestem loan starts amortising in April 2027: $10.9M remains at the end of 2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory needed for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, so the realistic path is an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1, unverified |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1, unverified |

The distributor relationship is the commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme, and it is a letter of intent from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner — a related-party cost that belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridge sales and contract development are revenue but second curves that consume the same engineering team; the Irish entity and a CE mark are a distraction from the only market that matters in this round.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second additional-information letter | Second letter in the first half of 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Pivotal data show capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level, troponin CV below 10% | Results reported as categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver filed after clearance with no pre-submission | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready for scale | ISO 13485 certificate issued; automation ordered for Tempe | Audit slipped, no automation order by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount still in single digits against a 300-site plan | S1, unverified |

Counter-evidence deserves weight. The company hired a regulatory vice-president with a record of FDA clearances, the pipeline of paid evaluation sites and a high reorder rate is unusual for an investigational device, and if the recent request was documentation-only a faster decision remains possible. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the recent request asked and what evidence the pending answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers and what triggers the next round; and whether the distributor letter carries any minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing judgement is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel.

Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money — all company-provided and unverified. The buyer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a lab; 39% of US urgent-care centres are hospital-owned and send send-outs to a health-system lab. Vantelle places instruments and sells consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers, 1,680 cartridges a month and FY2025 revenue of $2.6M are unverified; scale depends on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor LOI. [S99, S79]

### One issuer holds the IP and the FDA file; the minority sits around the core patent

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Status | Source |

| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware, 2018-03-12; HQ Albuquerque, NM | Series B issuer, FDA submitter, owner of VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders below | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona, 2022-05-09 | Tempe pilot line, 18 staff, plant lease | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland, 2025-01-15 | Future EU regulatory entity; no staff; CE not before 2028 | 100% parent | Unverified | S99 |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas, 2016-02-01; 60% acquired 2021-04 | Owns CM-1 sealing patent, licensed exclusively to Vantelle at 3% royalty | 60% Vantelle; 40% founders, incl. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist at 22% | Unverified | S99 |

Ring-fencing works where it exists: patents and the FDA dossier sit in the priced entity, the Arizona LLC carries the lease and 18 staff, and the Irish shell would carry future EU product liability, not US assets. Whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control, whether Corvia's 40% put is capped and Ireland's intercompany terms are not publicly disclosed. [S99]

### The $140M pre-money is built on 42,991,881 shares, not the 36.4M shown

The arithmetic reproduces the deck's unverified counts: $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564, and 52,204,508 shares at that price = $170.0M post-money. The deck's "shares today" excludes the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% is 14.89% pre-money (unverified). The bridge converts at $2.4423, 75% of the round price; the note is not disclosed, so those terms are unverified. [S99]

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against the 10% post-money pool this round itself creates; no primary NVCA or Cooley survey publishes a Series B option-pool median, so the overhang is scored warn rather than critical. The top-up lifts the unallocated pool from 1,200,000 shares to 5,220,489, adding 4,020,489 shares — 7.7 points of post-money and $13.1M at $3.2564 — dilution borne entirely by existing holders inside the pre-money. $15M is 8.82% of the $170.0M post-money and 10.7% of the $140.0M pre-money; the refresh dilutes existing holders, not the new money. The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value on the unverified share counts: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A $36.0M then 23.75% of the residual, and seed $4.5M non-participating. The founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6%) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%); the $30M Series B returns 1.0x at $170M and needs $376M for 2x. Cooley's Q2 2026 survey of 166 financings found 96.4% non-participating preferred and 95.8% at 1x, so the Series A's 1x participation is a 3.6% structure and the largest mid-range claim. [S99, S159]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66%, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M — company-provided and unverified. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; 10x the FY2029 royalty implies a $9.4M put liability, an analyst estimate. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty paid per cartridge; no arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate and no Corvia LLC agreement is publicly disclosed. The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat; unlike Theranos, Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC stripped it. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. [S20, S99]

### Six months of cash, a loan amortising, no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close (unverified). The $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only until 2027-03, then amortises at $0.167M a month, so a closing slip lands on the first payment (unverified; any IP security is not publicly disclosed). FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes $2.4M from a stocking order that ships only on clearance, 40.7% of the year (unverified). Searches on 2026-10-31 found no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignee, FDA decision or news. Pending 510(k)s are not published, so this does not test the filing; every entity date, ownership percentage and IP claim here rests on company-provided material. Page 1 carries a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools asserting no verification is needed and a rating approved; a document-integrity finding. Open questions: does the CM-1 licence survive a change of control, is Corvia's 40% put capped, and is any IP pledged to Bluestem? [S99]
