arguments.markdown:
The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A late-December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 request restarts a 90-FDA-day clock, putting the first clearance at late March 2027 at the earliest and mid-May 2027 at the FY2024 average total time to decision, against a company plan of Q1 2027; a waiver filed in Q3 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's 150-FDA-day goal; and at the 1.35 cartridges a site a day the evaluation sites run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites, not 300. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72, S97].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window to 2027-02-17. The review clock resumes on receipt, and FDA's goal is 90 FDA days; a late-December answer therefore puts the floor in late March 2027, and the FY2024 average total time to decision of 139 days points to mid-May 2027 if this file behaves like the average. Those are calendar days; the MDUFA series is 127 days in FY2023 against a 128-day goal, met, and 139 days in FY2024 against a 124-day goal, missed, with the FY2025 cohort incomplete at 2025-09-30. The 175-day Chemistry-panel and 337-day denial figures used elsewhere are third-party total-time averages, not FDA's series [S92, S97].

The second submission covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until Q2 2027, so a Q2 2027 filing is impossible; a Q3 2027 filing plus 90 FDA days gives a Q4 2027 decision and the FY2024 average points to Q1 2028. The five-assay menu is at best a Q4 2027 product, not the Q2 2027 the plan assumes [S1, S97].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to FDA request | 2026-12 (company) | Received 2026-08-21; unanswered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance | Late March 2027 (90-day goal); mid-May 2027 (FY2024 average) | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S97 |
| Pivotal results, 4 sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary equivalence; intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k): NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q3 2027 filing; Q4 2027-Q1 2028 decision | Needs pivotal results due Q2 2027 | Five-assay menu | S1, S97 |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 (company); first two assays | Not filed; needs cleared application, flex and user studies | Waived status for two assays | S1, S72 |
| CLIA waiver decision | Q1 2028 at 150 FDA days; mid-2028 with a hold; five-assay waiver 2028-2029 | No company date | Whether 2028 revenue is reachable | S72, S97 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset and the one scheduled latest. A submission references an already cleared application and must carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is a decision within 150 FDA days. A Q3 2027 filing therefore decides in Q1 2028, and an information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. A five-assay waiver cannot be filed until the second 510(k) clears, which puts its decision in 2028 at the earliest and 2029 if the second file slips. Until then the panel is moderate complexity: only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified staff may run it, and a Certificate of Waiver site cannot. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics in the market model [S72, S81, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: the deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month as its "2026 average" across 41 sites and 55 analyzers (p.7) and repeats 41 a site a month for 2026 (p.9). The deck does not state the months covered; with figures as of 2026-09-30 the average cannot cover more than January-September 2026, and neither 2026 unit volume nor FY2025 cartridge units is disclosed, so no growth rate can be computed. On that average, 1,680 cartridges is 41.0 a site a month (1.35 a site a calendar day) and 30.5 an analyzer-month (1.02 a calendar day; 1.22 on 300 operating days) against the 8 a day the model assumes from 2028. At 1.35 a site a day and $31 a cartridge, a site produces $15,275 a year, so $78.5M needs 5,150 sites, not 300; at the model's two analyzers and eight panels, 300 sites produce $44.6M and $78.5M needs 528. The 2028 line needs 2,680 sites at observed use or 276 at full model utilisation, against 300 planned by end-2027. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order that ships on clearance, a late-March 2027 event at the earliest — 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026; the 61% FY2026E gross margin also sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below cost, so either an undisclosed line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. From $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of Bluestem principal from April 2027: $10.9M remains at end-2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, pointing to an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1, unverified |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1, unverified |
| Corvia related-party terms | 3% royalty on cartridge net sales; the CTO owns 22% of Corvia | — | Related-party cost in gross margin | S1, unverified |

Company data, unverified: the distributor letter is the only commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme; it is non-binding, from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner, so it belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridges and contract development are second curves consuming the same engineering team; the Irish entity and CE mark are a distraction.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second request | Second request in H1 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level; CV below 10% | Categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver after clearance | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready | ISO 13485 certificate; automation ordered | Audit slipped; no automation by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount in single digits against 300 sites | S1, unverified |

Counter-evidence deserves weight: the regulatory vice-president has a record of FDA clearances, the evaluation pipeline and reorder rate are unusual for an investigational device, and a documentation-only request could clear faster. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the FDA request asked and what the answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers; and whether the distributor letter carries a minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel.

arguments.markdown:
The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A late-December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 request restarts a 90-FDA-day clock, putting the first clearance at late March 2027 at the earliest and mid-May 2027 at the FY2024 average total time to decision, against a company plan of Q1 2027; a waiver filed in Q3 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's 150-FDA-day goal; and at the 1.35 cartridges a site a day the evaluation sites run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites, not 300. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72, S97].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window to 2027-02-17. The review clock resumes on receipt, and FDA's goal is 90 FDA days; a late-December answer therefore puts the floor in late March 2027, and the FY2024 average total time to decision of 139 days points to mid-May 2027 if this file behaves like the average. Those are calendar days; the MDUFA series is 127 days in FY2023 against a 128-day goal, met, and 139 days in FY2024 against a 124-day goal, missed, with the FY2025 cohort incomplete at 2025-09-30. The 175-day Chemistry-panel and 337-day denial figures used elsewhere are third-party total-time averages, not FDA's series [S92, S97].

The second submission covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until Q2 2027, so a Q2 2027 filing is impossible; a Q3 2027 filing plus 90 FDA days gives a Q4 2027 decision and the FY2024 average points to Q1 2028. The five-assay menu is at best a Q4 2027 product, not the Q2 2027 the plan assumes [S1, S97].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to FDA request | 2026-12 (company) | Received 2026-08-21; unanswered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance | Late March 2027 (90-day goal); mid-May 2027 (FY2024 average) | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S97 |
| Pivotal results, 4 sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary equivalence; intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k): NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q3 2027 filing; Q4 2027-Q1 2028 decision | Needs pivotal results due Q2 2027 | Five-assay menu | S1, S97 |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 (company); first two assays | Not filed; needs cleared application, flex and user studies | Waived status for two assays | S1, S72 |
| CLIA waiver decision | Q1 2028 at 150 FDA days; mid-2028 with a hold; five-assay waiver 2028-2029 | No company date | Whether 2028 revenue is reachable | S72, S97 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset and the one scheduled latest. A submission references an already cleared application and must carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is a decision within 150 FDA days. A Q3 2027 filing therefore decides in Q1 2028, and an information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. A five-assay waiver cannot be filed until the second 510(k) clears, which puts its decision in 2028 at the earliest and 2029 if the second file slips. Until then the panel is moderate complexity: only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified staff may run it, and a Certificate of Waiver site cannot. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics in the market model [S72, S81, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: the deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month as its "2026 average" across 41 sites and 55 analyzers (p.7) and repeats 41 a site a month for 2026 (p.9). The deck does not state the months covered; with figures as of 2026-09-30 the average cannot cover more than January-September 2026, and neither 2026 unit volume nor FY2025 cartridge units is disclosed, so no growth rate can be computed. On that average, 1,680 cartridges is 41.0 a site a month (1.35 a site a calendar day) and 30.5 an analyzer-month (1.02 a calendar day; 1.22 on 300 operating days) against the 8 a day the model assumes from 2028. At 1.35 a site a day and $31 a cartridge, a site produces $15,275 a year, so $78.5M needs 5,150 sites, not 300; at the model's two analyzers and eight panels, 300 sites produce $44.6M and $78.5M needs 528. The 2028 line needs 2,680 sites at observed use or 276 at full model utilisation, against 300 planned by end-2027. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order that ships on clearance, a late-March 2027 event — 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026; the 61% FY2026E gross margin also sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below cost, so either an undisclosed line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. From $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of Bluestem principal from April 2027: $10.9M remains at end-2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, pointing to an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1, unverified |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1, unverified |
| Corvia related-party terms | 3% royalty on cartridge net sales; the CTO owns 22% of Corvia | — | Related-party cost in gross margin | S1, unverified |

Company data, unverified: the distributor letter is the only commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme; it is non-binding, from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner, so it belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridges and contract development are second curves consuming the same engineering team; the Irish entity and CE mark are a distraction.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second request | Second request in H1 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level; CV below 10% | Categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver after clearance | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready | ISO 13485 certificate; automation ordered | Audit slipped; no automation by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount in single digits against 300 sites | S1, unverified |

Counter-evidence deserves weight: the regulatory vice-president has a record of FDA clearances, the evaluation pipeline and reorder rate are unusual for an investigational device, and a documentation-only request could clear faster. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the FDA request asked and what the answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers; and whether the distributor letter carries a minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. The figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day on 30 days and 1.22 on 300, against 8.0 in 2028. The 2029 revenue line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for; the 58% below is reproducible only if the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers sits outside cost of sales. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan, a related-party claim on gross margin. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. The deck omits acquisition cost: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded per head with half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that. The model turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | $0.43M fees; 20,160 cartridges at $33.40/$16.20; analyzer cost excluded |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | 23,952 cartridges at the only disclosed price and cost |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | residual cost; not disclosed |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | deck p.10; bridge closes only on the 2026-average volume |

Expensing the 55 analyzers would raise cost to $1.28M and cut the margin to 51%; three-year capitalisation gives $61,417 a year and 56%. The deck states neither the policy nor the volume, so the 58% is consistent but unverified.

| Line | 2026 actual | 2028 model | 2029 target | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day (300 days) | 1.0 | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year LTV | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels a day for a 3:1 ratio | 5.9 at $16.20; 4.2 at $7.50 | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| CAC per analyzer placed (estimate) | $25,600-51,200 | same | same | S1 (unverified); analyst estimate |

### The clinic's margin exists only at full five-test use

Medicare's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets national limitation amounts of $12.47 for troponin (84484), $24.84 for natriuretic peptide (83880), $4.76 for HbA1c (83036), $9.71 for creatinine (82570) and $5.18 for potassium (84132) — $56.96 for the five-test panel. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $23.56 a panel. A two-test troponin/HbA1c clinic collects $17.23 and loses $16.17 a cartridge; a four-test clinic without natriuretic peptide collects $32.12 and loses $1.28. The $650 monthly fee equals 27.6 panels of the five-test margin: at 30.5 panels a month the clinic nets $68.58 per analyzer, at 240 panels $5,004. The fee consumes 90% of the clinic's margin at observed use and bites hardest where adoption begins. Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S154, S106, S22].

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 27.6 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage BNP, CLIA-waived, 25 tests | $789 | $31.56 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| FY2025 line | $M | Share | Repeatable? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use cartridges to CROs | 0.8 | 31% | Repeatable, needs no clearance, small market | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development for one partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, and about 567 before 2026 if 2026 ran at 1,680. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer cartridge use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume and whether any sustained a higher run rate; the same for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix, since troponin and potassium alone collect less than the cartridge costs.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the clinic keeps $68.58 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $56.96, so the $650 fee equals 27.6 panels of margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim and Boditech sells a six-test fingertip immunoassay menu. The advantage lasts until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships and cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is the incumbent owning the buyer's analyser slot [S1, S67, S104, S157].

A three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a waived handheld that added hs-troponin I in January 2025; Siemens epoc, QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel, Roche's cobas h 232 and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX. Adjacent: Boditech's AFIAS-6 (six immunoassays including troponin I, NT-proBNP and HbA1c from fingertip blood), Truvian's TruVerus (12 cleared tests, no cardiac marker) and Babson's BetterWay (retail-pharmacy collection routed to a central lab). Substitute: Quest Diagnostics, the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call later. No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge, the gap the company sells into [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109, S157, S127, S158, S156, S65].

| Competitor | Product and status | Menu | Price | Scale and distribution | Advantage / gap vs Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1, Alinity; hs-TnI 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11; waived manual; CG8+ capillary 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c or NT-proBNP | Not disclosed | POC line $606M FY2025; hospital and laboratory channel; installed base not disclosed | Waived slot and capillary claim; one cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro | Waived cardiac panel; EDTA blood | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin | $599 per 25 tests, $23.96 a test | $2.73B FY2025; urgent-care base | Lowest cost per test; no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Siemens/Radiometer/Roche | epoc; AQT90 FLEX; cobas h 232 | Marketed; venous or moderate-complexity | Blood gas; troponin and NT-proBNP separately | Not disclosed | Hospital emergency and laboratory base | Laboratory-quality assays; benchtop, trained staff | S107, S109, S111 |
| Boditech | AFIAS-6 | 510(k) cleared; CLIA waiver not stated | Troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c; six tests a run; fingertip C-tip | Not disclosed | Hospitals, emergency rooms and clinics; US distribution not disclosed | Menu breadth and Asian cost base; no creatinine or potassium, no US waiver | S157 |
| Truvian | TruVerus | 510(k) K251058 and nine analytes 2026-01-12; waiver not stated | 12 tests including creatinine, glucose and lipids; no troponin, natriuretic peptide or HbA1c | Not disclosed | Benchtop; waitlist, distribution not disclosed | Multimodal whole blood; no cardiac menu or waiver | S127 |
| Babson | BetterWay | 510(k) for a collection component; not a clinic analyser; no waiver claimed | Retail-pharmacy finger-stick collection with central-lab testing | Not disclosed | 20+ Austin pharmacies and a national retailer | Removes the venous draw; still a one-to-three-day turnaround | S158, S156 |
| Waived readers | Roche cobas b 101; Nova StatSensor | Near-patient capillary; single-analyte waiver categories | HbA1c, lipids and CRP; creatinine and eGFR | Reader under $1,000 (company claim) | Pharmacy and medical distributors | Low cost; one analyte, no cardiac panel | S73, S77, S90, S1 |

Abbott decides the price. It publishes a waived-test manual for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026. Its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's $2.6M of FY2025 revenue is a 0.1% share of QuidelOrtho's $2.73B in FY2025. Analyser, cartridge, installed-base and per-test prices are undisclosed. When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert: the Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% margin at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, 100 times current volume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20-$25 with a free analyser takes the account against $38 plus $650 a month; Vantelle's cartridge margin falls to 19-35% on today's cost and it has no second product. Boditech's AFIAS-6 shows the menu is assemblable: six immunoassays, including troponin I and NT-proBNP, from a fingertip [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67, S1, S157].

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and Vantelle has not applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, assemblable from parts incumbents already sell. Sight Diagnostics' OLO finger-stick CBC was cleared in 2021 as moderately complex. LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024 [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1].

The funnel is unproven. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation program two years later; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. The company-provided, unverified deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, completed EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price evidence. What would settle it: signed contracts, the first sites' CLIA certificates and EHR go-live dates, and collected revenue per cartridge by payer [S1].

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, and Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per group. That is an opening of a year or two, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; that Vantelle keeps a premium beyond the plan period is low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the evaluation sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived and accepts capillary blood; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

No US competitor retrieved sells a waived five-analyte finger-stick panel; Boditech's AFIAS-6 comes closest with three of the five analytes. Source: S67, S6, S104, S105, S157, S1.
:::

| Weaknesses | Cartridge cost $16.20 against a $7.50 target at two million units; analyser below cost and 60% given free; three of five assays uncleared; no CLIA waiver; 41 sites and $2.6M revenue | S1 (unverified) |

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day on 30 days and 1.22 on 300, against 8.0 in 2028. The 2029 line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for; the 58% below is reproducible only if the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers sits outside cost of sales. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan, a related-party claim on gross margin. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. The deck omits acquisition cost: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded per head with half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that. It turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | $0.43M fees; 20,160 cartridges at $33.40/$16.20; analyzer cost excluded |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | 23,952 cartridges at the only disclosed price and cost |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | residual cost; not disclosed |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | deck p.10; bridge closes only on the 2026-average volume |

Expensing the 55 analyzers would raise cost to $1.28M and cut the margin to 51%; three-year capitalisation gives $61,417 a year and 56%. The deck states neither the policy nor the volume, so the 58% is consistent but unverified.

| Line | 2026 actual | 2028 model | 2029 target | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day (300 days) | 1.0 | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year LTV | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels a day for a 3:1 ratio | 5.9 at $16.20; 4.2 at $7.50 | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| CAC per analyzer placed (estimate) | $25,600-51,200 | same | same | S1 (unverified); analyst estimate |

### The clinic's margin exists only at full five-test use

Medicare's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets national limitation amounts of $12.47 for troponin (84484), $24.84 for natriuretic peptide (83880), $4.76 for HbA1c (83036), $9.71 for creatinine (82570) and $5.18 for potassium (84132) — $56.96 for the five-test panel. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $23.56 a panel. A two-test troponin/HbA1c clinic collects $17.23 and loses $16.17 a cartridge; a four-test clinic without natriuretic peptide collects $32.12 and loses $1.28. The $650 monthly fee equals 27.6 panels of the five-test margin: at 30.5 panels a month the clinic nets $68.58 per analyzer, at 240 panels $5,004. The fee consumes 90% of the clinic's margin at observed use and bites hardest where adoption begins. Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S154, S106, S22].

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 27.6 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage BNP, CLIA-waived, 25 tests | $789 | $31.56 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| FY2025 line | $M | Share | Repeatable? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use cartridges to CROs | 0.8 | 31% | Repeatable, needs no clearance, small market | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development for one partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, and about 567 before 2026 if 2026 ran at 1,680. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer cartridge use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume and whether any sustained a higher run rate; the same for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix, since troponin and potassium alone collect less than the cartridge costs.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the clinic keeps $68.58 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $56.96, so the $650 fee equals 27.6 panels of margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. Its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The package is five analytes from one finger stick, defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve, pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit; Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills (company description, unverified).

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | IFCC high-sensitivity <10%; i-STAT hs-TnI <5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Shelf life and cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### Precision and capillary collection decide the label

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share lands on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. The deck calls it high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff; on this data it is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none. The 96.1% is categorical agreement; the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress. No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck: the four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in Q2 2027 — is the first test of capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and potassium already exist from Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S1, S13, S15, S16, S21, S68, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary | S1, S70, S74 |
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | Below 5.2% | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate; waiver planned Q3 2027 | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate | Moderate | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is 150 FDA days, and an additional-information request can add 180. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. No point-of-care precedent exists: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood gas, its hs-TnI launched on 2025-01-03 as moderate complexity, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### The moat is manufacturing and workflow, not the assay

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridge metering and calibration | 6 | Five assays from 40 µL of dried reagents; VD-1 covers it | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| Manufacturing cost curve | 7 | $16.20 to $7.50 needs automation and yield learning from 20,000 to 2 million units | 2-4 years | S1, unverified |
| Clinical and regulatory evidence | 6 | Pivotal study, two 510(k)s and a first-of-kind waiver study | 2-3 years | S1, S69, unverified |
| Replication test | — | A funded team of 50 needs 2-3 years across all three barriers; the constraint is evidence, not chemistry | 2-3 years | S1, S69 |

### Patent position

| Patent or application | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| US 16/884,327 (capillary-fill cartridge) | Filed 2020-05-28; granted 2023-03 (unverified); Europe pending | Core cartridge; term to 2040 | S1 |
| US 17/662,019 (five-assay reader) | Filed 2022-05-04; final rejection 2026-07 (unverified); appeal pending | Reader claims at risk | S1 |
| US 19/318,770; PCT/US2026/014022 (unpublished) | Filed 2025-09-30 and 2026-02-11 (unverified) | Sample-volume check; troponin chemistry, outside the FTO opinion | S1 |
| US 15/707,915 (sealing film and blister) | Filed 2017-09-18; granted 2021-01 (unverified); Corvia-owned, licensed | Sealing freedom to operate; 3% royalty | S1 |

The freedom-to-operate opinion stops short of the troponin chemistry; no public patent record was retrievable, so the portfolio is unverified.

### Products, unit economics and readiness

| Product | Revenue (FY2025) | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 analyzer (paid evaluation) | $1.1M evaluation revenue | Negative: $2,900 list against $3,350 build | 510(k) clearance (company: Q1 2027) | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay cartridge (pilot) | $0.8M research-use cartridges | 51% at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost | Cost below $10 at 1 million units | S1, unverified |

### Reimbursement pays the panel only if the expensive assays are ordered

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| Five-code total | | $71.38 | S154 |

Two codes — troponin and potassium, the minimum a chest-pain visit needs — pay $17.23 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised price. Four codes without HbA1c pay $61.67; all five pay $71.38. Drop NT-proBNP, which carries $39.26 of the total, and the other four pay $32.12, below the list price. The economics depend on the clinic ordering the natriuretic peptide on most panels; CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts the chemistry codes and takes the five-code total to $60.67, 15% lower [S149, S154].

### Supply chain and the antibody are undisclosed

Company data, unverified: the deck names no bill of materials, no supplier, no second source and no antibody licence; the only licensed component it identifies is the Corvia CM-1 sealing patent (exclusive, 3% royalty), and the troponin antibody's supplier, licence terms and assignability on a change of control are not disclosed — a launch and exit constraint because the assay is the regulated product. What would settle it: the bills of materials with supplier sites, the antibody licence and supply agreement (including change-of-control and transfer rights), second-source qualification records, and the unredacted FTO opinion. The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force; readiness is uneven — troponin I and HbA1c at level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal enrolling), manufacturing at 5, with a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate. The open questions are the troponin cutoff and detection limit, what the FDA request asked, haemolysis in pivotal finger sticks, line yield and stability beyond the data held, and whether the waiver is filed alongside the second clearance [S1].

Counter-evidence, company data unverified: the other four assays agreed closely and sites reordered; a rural clinic may accept a conventional troponin if the pivotal study shows sensitivity at the cutoff. Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in company data, while manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's process.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 6 by Valuation Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,919 characters)
The realistic buyer set is five point-of-care incumbents, and the most recent cleared-and-waived platform sold for $100M in April 2026; at $140M pre-money the Series B needs $546M of exit proceeds for 3x, a price only a strategic paying for the platform rather than the plan can justify. The asset being bought is not the 64-person team or the evaluation programme but the cartridge IP — the granted on-board-calibrator patent (VD-1) and the exclusively licensed Corvia sealing film (CM-1) — plus the two-assay 510(k), the CLIA-waiver path and 41 evaluation sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico (company-reported, unverified). QuidelOrtho, Abbott, Roche Diagnostics and Werfen all sell point-of-care instruments into US urgent-care or hospital channels, and none sells a five-analyte finger-stick panel run by clinic staff. Abbott's i-STAT and Afinion platforms cover blood gas, chemistries and cardiometabolic tests; QuidelOrtho's Triage and Sofia cover cardiac and rapid immunoassay; Roche bought LumiraDx's multi-assay platform in 2024; Werfen's acute-care line sits beside hemostasis and autoimmunity. Each has a gap Vantelle would fill, but each also has a platform to protect [S22, S67, S91, S119, S126].

### Who buys, for which asset and when

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale (asset) | Timing | Likelihood (our judgement) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | QuidelOrtho | Triage and Sofia installed base in urgent care; bought LEX for $100M in 2026-04 | 2029-2031 | Medium-low | S22, S126 |
| Trade sale | Abbott | i-STAT and Afinion base; needs a staff-run finger-stick cardiac panel | 2029-2031 | Medium | S67 |
| Trade sale | Roche Diagnostics | LumiraDx platform since 2024; primary-care immunoassay menu | 2029-2031 | Low-medium | S91 |
| Trade sale | Werfen | Acute-care and hemostasis channel; paid $2.0B for Immucor in 2023 | 2029-2031 | Low | S119 |
| Trade sale | Thermo Fisher or Hologic | Molecular point-of-care only (Mesa $450M, Mobidiag $795M) | 2029-2031 | Low | S120, S122 |
| IPO | Nasdaq | Needs $100M+ revenue and a waived menu | 2030 or later | Low | S125 |
| Distressed asset sale | Financial or strategic buyer | IP and 510(k) only, no commercial franchise | 2027-2028 if the waiver fails | Medium in the failure case | S117, S126 |

The strongest fit is QuidelOrtho, which owns Triage and Sofia in exactly the urgent-care channel Vantelle targets and paid $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics in April 2026 — but it also carries $1.1B of enterprise value and negative free cash flow, and it has just bought the molecular platform it wanted. Abbott is the largest and most able payer, with i-STAT Alinity and Afinion already placed in clinics, yet that installed base gives it a build-or-buy option that argues for a lower price. Roche and Werfen are European buyers with no US ownership limits in diagnostics, but Roche has owned a LumiraDx platform since 2024 and Werfen's recent acquisitions have been in transfusion and hemostasis. The practical conclusion is a five-buyer, not a competitive, auction. The strategic logic is scale economics: a waived five-analyte cartridge at $38 lets an incumbent serve the 11,400 US urgent-care sites that cannot staff a laboratory, and the clinic bills the payer under existing test codes rather than to Vantelle. The counter-evidence is that Abbott or QuidelOrtho can add a waived cardiac assay to its own installed analyser and reach the same sites without buying Vantelle, and that a pre-clearance asset carries 510(k) and CLIA risk an acquirer can wait out at no cost. That substitution risk, not the number of buyers, is the central threat to a $546M exit [S2, S22, S67, S91, S119, S126].

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho–LEX Diagnostics | 2026 | $100M cash | not disclosed; platform pre-commercial | S126 |
| Roche–LumiraDx point-of-care platform | 2023-24 | $295M plus up to $55M | ~3.4x annualised H1 2023 revenue of $86.4M | S91, S117 |
| Quidel–Ortho Clinical Diagnostics | 2021-22 | ~$6.0B | ~3.3x 2020 revenue of $1.8B | S121, S123 |
| Werfen–Immucor | 2022-23 | ~$2.0B | not disclosed | S119 |
| Roche–GenMark Diagnostics | 2021 | $1.8B | not disclosed | S118 |
| Hologic–Mobidiag | 2021 | $795M enterprise value | not disclosed | S122 |
| Thermo Fisher–Mesa Biotech | 2021 | $450M plus up to $100M | not disclosed | S120 |
| LumiraDx de-SPAC listing | 2021 | $3.0B valuation, cut from $5.0B | sold for $295M in 2023-24 | S130, S131 |

The larger 2021 prices — $450M plus milestones for Mesa, $795M for Mobidiag, $1.8B for GenMark — were set in the COVID-era liquidity window, and the market has since re-rated: QuidelOrtho itself trades at 0.4x EV/Sales, down 50.9% over 12 months. | Entry pre-money | New Series B ownership | Exit needed for 3x on $30M | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | 17.6% | $546M | S1 (unverified) |
| $100M | 22.8% | $431M | S1 (unverified) |
| $70M | 28.9% | $348M | S1 (unverified) |
| $50M | 35.5% | $289M | S1 (unverified) |

The thresholds use the new B's 17.6% at $140M; B and B-1 together own 22.6%. At $140M pre-money the new Series B needs $546M for 3x, $518M for 3x on the $36.28M class (the B-1's 25% discount makes the class cheaper to return than the new money) and $1.74B for 10x; the $546M corrects an earlier $435M that credited the B-1 preference to the new $30M. The 40% Corvia minority put, estimated at $9.4M and ranking ahead of the Series B, is deducted before the stack, as is any remaining Bluestem debt (nil by 2029-08, $4-5M in a 2027-28 sale). The company's own unverified FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue at a 2.5x multiple gives a $196M enterprise value; after the Corvia put, the new Series B returns 1.0x, below the 4.93% yield on the 10-year Treasury on 2026-10-30. Only a 2031 bull case of $150M revenue at 25% EBITDA and 12x EV/EBITDA reaches $450M, and that returns 2.4x, an 18.9% internal rate of return, not the 24.6% a 3x return needs over five years. Entry price is the first lever: at $70M pre-money the Series B owns 28.9% after anti-dilution and 3x needs $348M; capping the Series A at 1.5x lowers that to $301M. LumiraDx listed at a $3B de-SPAC valuation in September 2021 after cutting the deal from $5B, then sold its technology for $295M; Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after raising $480M+; Truvian, the best-capitalised private comparable, raised $294M, cleared 12 analytes by 2026-01-12 and is still private in October 2026, eleven years after founding. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028. The 2029 line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for; the 58% is reproducible only if the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers sits outside cost of sales. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. The deck omits acquisition cost: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded per head and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that. It turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | $0.43M fees; 20,160 cartridges at $33.40/$16.20; analyzer cost excluded | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | 23,952 cartridges at the only disclosed price and cost | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | residual cost; not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | deck p.10; bridge closes only on the 2026-average volume | S1 (unverified) |

Expensing the analyzers would raise cost to $1.28M and cut the margin to 51%; three-year capitalisation gives $61,417 a year and 56%. The deck states neither policy nor volume, so the 58% is consistent but unverified [S1].

| Line | 2026 actual | 2028 model | 2029 target | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day (300 days) | 1.0 | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year LTV | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels a day for a 3:1 ratio | 5.9 at $16.20; 4.2 at $7.50 | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### The clinic's margin exists only at full five-test use

Medicare's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets national limitation amounts of $12.47 for troponin (84484), $24.84 for natriuretic peptide (83880), $4.76 for HbA1c (83036), $9.71 for creatinine (82570) and $5.18 for potassium (84132) — $56.96 for the five-test panel. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $23.56 a panel. A two-test troponin/HbA1c clinic collects $17.23 and loses $16.17 a cartridge; a four-test clinic without natriuretic peptide collects $32.12 and loses $1.28. $650 a month equals 27.6 panels of the five-test margin: at 30.5 panels the clinic nets $68.58 per analyzer, at 240 panels $5,004. The fee consumes 90% of the clinic's margin at observed use and bites hardest where adoption begins. Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S154, S106, S22].

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 27.6 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage BNP, CLIA-waived, 25 tests | $789 | $31.56 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| FY2025 line | $M | Share | Repeatable? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use cartridges to CROs | 0.8 | 31% | Repeatable, needs no clearance, small market | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development for one partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, and about 567 before 2026 if 2026 ran at 1,680. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume and whether any sustained a higher run rate; the same for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix, since troponin and potassium alone collect less than the cartridge.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the clinic keeps $68.58 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $56.96, so the $650 fee equals 27.6 panels of margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154].
:::

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, and about 567 before 2026 if 2026 ran at 1,680. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume and whether any sustained a higher run rate; the same for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix, since troponin and potassium alone collect less than the cartridge.

55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $56.96, so the $650 fee equals 27.6 panels of margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154].

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy.
