arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028. The 2029 line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for; the 58% is reproducible only if the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers sits outside cost of sales. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. The deck omits acquisition cost: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded per head and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that. It turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1. Expensing all 55 analyzers would cut the 58% below to 51%; three-year capitalisation gives 56%.

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | $0.43M fees; 20,160 cartridges at $33.40/$16.20; analyzer cost excluded | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | 23,952 cartridges at the only disclosed price and cost | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | residual cost; not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | deck p.10; bridge closes only on the 2026-average volume | S1 (unverified) |

| Line | 2026 actual | 2028 model | 2029 target | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day (300 days) | 1.0 | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year LTV | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels a day for a 3:1 ratio | 5.9 at $16.20; 4.2 at $7.50 | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### The clinic's margin exists only at full five-test use

Medicare's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets national limitation amounts of $12.47 for troponin (84484), $24.84 for natriuretic peptide (83880), $4.76 for HbA1c (83036), $9.71 for creatinine (82570) and $5.18 for potassium (84132) — $56.96 for the five-test panel. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $23.56 a panel. A two-test troponin/HbA1c clinic collects $17.23 and loses $16.17 a cartridge; a four-test clinic without natriuretic peptide collects $32.12 and loses $1.28. The five-test contribution is $718.58 a month at 30.5 panels; $650 a month equals 27.6 panels of it, leaving the clinic $68.58 per analyzer, or $5,004 at 240 panels. The fee consumes 90% of the clinic's margin at observed use and bites hardest where adoption begins. Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S154, S106, S22].

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 27.6 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage BNP, CLIA-waived, 25 tests | $789 | $31.56 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| FY2025 line | $M | Share | Repeatable? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use cartridges to CROs | 0.8 | 31% | Repeatable, needs no clearance, small market | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development for one partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, and about 567 before 2026 if 2026 ran at 1,680. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume and whether any sustained a higher run rate; the same for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix, since troponin and potassium alone collect less than the cartridge.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the clinic keeps $68.58 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $56.96, so the $650 fee equals 27.6 panels of margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154].
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 10 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,885 characters)
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028. The 2029 line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for; the 58% is reproducible only if the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers sits outside cost of sales. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. The deck omits acquisition cost: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded per head and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that. It turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1. Expensing all 55 analyzers would cut the 58% below to 51%; three-year capitalisation gives 56%.

### The clinic's margin exists only at full five-test use

Medicare's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets national limitation amounts of $12.47 for troponin (84484), $24.84 for natriuretic peptide (83880), $4.76 for HbA1c (83036), $9.71 for creatinine (82570) and $5.18 for potassium (84132) — $56.96 for the five-test panel. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $23.56 a panel. A two-test troponin/HbA1c clinic collects $17.23 and loses $16.17 a cartridge; a four-test clinic without natriuretic peptide collects $32.12 and loses $1.28. The five-test contribution is $718.58 a month at 30.5 panels; $650 a month equals 27.6 panels of it, leaving the clinic $68.58 per analyzer, or $5,004 at 240 panels. The fee consumes 90% of the clinic's margin at observed use and bites hardest where adoption begins. Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S154, S106, S22].

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, and about 567 before 2026 if 2026 ran at 1,680. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume and whether any sustained a higher run rate; the same for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix, since troponin and potassium alone collect less than the cartridge.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 10 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,885 characters)
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028. The 2029 line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for; the 58% is reproducible only if the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers sits outside cost of sales. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. The deck omits acquisition cost: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded per head and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that. It turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1. Expensing all 55 analyzers would cut the 58% below to 51%; three-year capitalisation gives 56%.

### The clinic's margin exists only at full five-test use

Medicare's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets national limitation amounts of $12.47 for troponin (84484), $24.84 for natriuretic peptide (83880), $4.76 for HbA1c (83036), $9.71 for creatinine (82570) and $5.18 for potassium (84132) — $56.96 for the five-test panel. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $23.56 a panel. A two-test troponin/HbA1c clinic collects $17.23 and loses $16.17 a cartridge; a four-test clinic without natriuretic peptide collects $32.12 and loses $1.28. The five-test contribution is $718.58 a month at 30.5 panels; $650 a month equals 27.6 panels of it, leaving the clinic $68.58 per analyzer, or $5,004 at 240 panels. The fee consumes 90% of the clinic's margin at observed use and bites hardest where adoption begins. Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S154, S106, S22].

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, and about 567 before 2026 if 2026 ran at 1,680. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume and whether any sustained a higher run rate; the same for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix, since troponin and potassium alone collect less than the cartridge.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 5 by Lead Analyst, 7,094 characters)
Meridian should not lead Vantelle's Series B at $140M pre-money. The company has the strongest clinical wedge in the file — a five-analyte finger-stick panel aimed at clinics that cannot staff a laboratory, 41 paid evaluation sites and a 92% reorder rate — and a first-of-kind packaging position that incumbents would pay for. It also has the weakest operating proof: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the FY2025 monthly average on deck p.7, with 2026 volume not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day against the eight its 2028 plan needs; troponin runs at 11.8% CV against the IFCC's <10% standard; the 510(k) is under an information request and a CLIA waiver has no cardiac precedent; and $6.9M of cash is six months at the current burn. Evidence confidence is medium on the regulatory calendar and low on the commercial plan, because every operating figure is company-reported and no public record of the company, its 510(k) or its patents exists [S1].

The price is the second problem. Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint against the $140M ask and $170M post-money. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — and the Series A then participates at 23.75% of value above it, so the $30M Series B needs $546M of proceeds for 3x and $376M for 2x, while the April 2026 clearing price for a cleared, waived platform was $100M. The company's own 2029 plan, at 2.5x revenue, is worth $196M and returns the new money 1.0x. Only a strategic premium to $400-500M makes the bull case work, and that is 4-5x the clearing price [S126].

The consensus — the company plan, the $8M insider commitment, a Q1 2027 clearance and a 2027 waiver — is not the report's view. We differ on utilisation and price, not on the need: a first billing cohort above six panels a day and a waiver path accepted by FDA would re-rate the asset, while a second information request, a capillary troponin failure or a refused cardiac waiver would take most of the equity value. If Meridian wants exposure before the proofs arrive, the only defensible structure is a lower pre-money, a tranched cheque, a capped Series A participation and a capped or converted Corvia put [S72].

Three risks decide the outcome: utilisation staying near the evaluation rate, the capillary troponin study failing at the cutoff, and a waiver refused or deferred for the cardiac analyte. Each has an early warning in the sensitivity analysis and none is priced at the ask. The immediate financial risk is the six months of cash against a close that still has to be signed.

Before any cheque, Meridian's diligence list should obtain the FDA letter and the pivotal protocol, the Corvia LLC agreement and its change-of-control clause, the Bluestem rate and covenants, the distributor's purchase terms, and the first billing cohort's panels per day and collected revenue per cartridge. Those items, not another meeting with management, decide whether the price is defensible or zero.

The need is real: a clinic without a laboratory waits one to three days for a cardiac or metabolic send-out, and a five-analyte finger-stick panel that returns a result in twelve minutes removes that wait. The capability is defensible as packaging and manufacturing, not as assay science, and for perhaps 12-24 months. The economics do not scale at the only utilisation the file documents: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the FY2025 average on deck p.7, with 2026 volume not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day (company-reported, unverified) against the eight the 2028 plan assumes. Because the third fails, $140M pre-money buys a plan whose 3x case needs $546M of exit proceeds, 5.5 times the $100M a cleared, waived point-of-care platform fetched in April 2026. Wait for the 510(k) and the first billing-enabled data, or invest at $60-80M with the structure repaired [S1].

The evaluation programme is real commercial evidence: 41 sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, 55 analyzers and 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days, all company-reported and unverified. The clinic's economics are documented: the CY2026 fee schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes, against $33.40 realised, leaving $37.98 a panel before the $650 monthly fee. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts Chemistry 16%, taking the five-code panel to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029 and the clinic's contribution to $10.43, when the fee equals 62 panels of margin [S154, S149].

No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge, and that packaging is worth something: Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and the granted on-board-calibrator patent runs to 2040 (company-reported, unverified). The assay evidence is weaker. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, against the IFCC's <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%; the study is 640 venous samples from 128 patients, run by company staff at one site, with six excluded results and no capillary-versus-venous comparison. The deck's own operating data undo the revenue plan. Fifty-five analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in the average FY2025 month (deck p.7; 2026 volume is not disclosed) — 30.5 per analyzer-month, 1.22 a day on the 300-operating-day convention the market model uses — against 8.0 assumed from 2028, a 6.5-fold gap. Vantelle scores below the threshold for a lead at the ask and inside the range for a wait-for-milestone position. The score is not a verdict on the technology: the need and the team sit in the middle of the scale. It is a verdict on evidence — a product short of its own menu, a regulatory path with no waived cardiac precedent, and unit economics that fail at the company's own utilisation. The recommendation is Wait for milestone: no cheque at the ask, a conditional offer at a lower pre-money, and a re-underwrite when clearance, the waiver pre-submission and the first billing cohort report.

The weighted average is 3.9 (0.9 + 0.8 + 0.6 + 0.45 + 0.3 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.1) [S1]. Two dimensions can re-rate the company quickly. A clearance certificate and an accepted waiver pre-submission would lift regulatory from 3 to 6-7; a first billing cohort above 5.9 panels a day would lift unit economics from 3 to 7 and the composite by roughly two points. Conversely, a second information request or a capillary troponin failure takes product and regulatory to 2 and the composite down by about a point and a half. The asymmetry is why price matters more than the score: on company-reported terms (unverified), the probability-weighted return is 1.35x over 4.5 years at the ask and 2.0x at $70M, a 6.9% versus 16.4% IRR. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores 7 at most, and none of these has one that supports more.

### How the recommendation changes under the downside

The base case carries a 45% weight: clearance in H2 2027, a waiver in 2028-29, 2-4 panels a day and a $150-250M sale in 2031 returning 1.0-1.5x. The bear case carries 40%: a second request or a capillary-troponin deficiency, a refused or deferred waiver, and a $50-100M distressed sale in 2028 that still covers the $36.3M senior preference on company-reported terms, unverified, and returns 1.0-1.2x [S126].

### The branches that change the recommendation

The recommendation becomes Pass if the waiver is refused for the cardiac analyte or the pivotal study misses the cutoff, because both remove the chest-pain use case and 50-65% of equity value. It becomes Invest with conditions at a lower pre-money if clearance arrives and the first billing cohort exceeds four panels a day. It becomes Invest now only if the FDA letter proves documentation-only and a billing cohort prints above six panels — neither of which is in the file today [S68].

### Position sizing and what can be lost

Private company sizing: no capital at the ask. At a lower pre-money, split the cheque between close and clearance, with a follow-on reserve sized to the plan's funding gap rather than to the initial cheque. The maximum loss is not the full commitment: a distressed sale still covers the senior preference, and a full loss needs no sale at all or a price below the preference stack after the Bluestem loan and the Corvia put. The terms that make the cheque worth writing are a board seat, pay-to-play, full pro-rata, a utilisation covenant tied to the second tranche and disinterested approval of the Corvia royalty and put.

### Next diligence and conditions

The diligence list decides the re-underwrite: the FDA information request; the pivotal protocol and any capillary-versus-venous data; the Corvia LLC agreement and the change-of-control clause; the Bluestem rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor's purchase, payment and return terms; the first billing sites' panels per day and collected revenue per cartridge; and the quality-system certificate. The conditions for any cheque are a price at or below the agreed cap, the tranche structure, the Series A participation capped, the Corvia put capped or converted, a permanent CFO and an independent director before closing, and the certificate before launch. A clearance slip or a later waiver filing reopens the price, not just the timetable.

The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle. The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 per analyzer-month and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers and 610 cartridges, and the one independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme running point-of-care chemistry and haematology at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months from three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight — the top of the supported range, not its centre — with 40% on the bear and 15% on the bull. ### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024, against a 124-FDA-day goal it missed, and sets a 112-FDA-day goal for FY2025 with the cohort still pending at 2025-09-30; a December 2026 answer plus the 139-day average points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry-panel figure is the 510(k) database's total time from acceptance to decision, a different series, not FDA days. The bear case's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request; the base rate alone points to May 2027. A second request pushes the decision into the second half of 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 at the earliest and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster, on one 180-day goal. I put 45-55% on clearance later than June 2027 and 30% on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a pre-submission answer accepting a troponin panel, and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due in Q2 2027, is the first test of the two variables that caused the exclusions. Meridian should not lead Vantelle's Series B at $140M pre-money. The company has the strongest clinical wedge in the file — a five-analyte finger-stick panel aimed at clinics that cannot staff a laboratory, 41 paid evaluation sites and a 92% reorder rate — and a first-of-kind packaging position that incumbents would pay for. The price is the second problem. Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint against the $140M ask and $170M post-money. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — and the Series A then participates at 23.75% of value above it, so the $30M Series B needs $546M of proceeds for 3x and $376M for 2x, while the April 2026 clearing price for a cleared, waived platform was $100M. The company's own 2029 plan, at 2.5x revenue, is worth $196M and returns the new money 1.0x. Only a strategic premium to $400-500M makes the bull case work, and that is 4-5x the clearing price [S126].

The consensus — the company plan, the $8M insider commitment, a Q1 2027 clearance and a 2027 waiver — is not the report's view. We differ on utilisation and price, not on the need: a first billing cohort above six panels a day and a waiver path accepted by FDA would re-rate the asset, while a second information request, a capillary troponin failure or a refused cardiac waiver would take most of the equity value. If Meridian wants exposure before the proofs arrive, the only defensible structure is a lower pre-money, a tranched cheque, a capped Series A participation and a capped or converted Corvia put [S72].

Three risks decide the outcome: utilisation staying near the evaluation rate, the capillary troponin study failing at the cutoff, and a waiver refused or deferred for the cardiac analyte. Each has an early warning in the sensitivity analysis and none is priced at the ask. The immediate financial risk is the six months of cash against a close that still has to be signed.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle clears the first test and fails the third. The need is real: a clinic without a laboratory waits one to three days for a cardiac or metabolic send-out, and a five-analyte finger-stick panel that returns a result in twelve minutes removes that wait. The capability is defensible as packaging and manufacturing, not as assay science, and for perhaps 12-24 months. The economics do not scale at the only utilisation the file documents: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series and FY2025 volume not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day (company-reported, unverified) against the eight the 2028 plan assumes. Because the third fails, $140M pre-money buys a plan whose 3x case needs $546M of exit proceeds, 5.5 times the $100M a cleared, waived point-of-care platform fetched in April 2026. Wait for the 510(k) and the first billing-enabled data, or invest at $60-80M with the structure repaired [S1].

The evaluation programme is real commercial evidence: 41 sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, 55 analyzers and 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days, all company-reported and unverified. The clinic's economics are documented: the CY2026 fee schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes, against $33.40 realised, leaving $37.98 a panel before the $650 monthly fee. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle clears the first test and fails the third. The need is real: a clinic without a laboratory waits one to three days for a cardiac or metabolic send-out, and a five-analyte finger-stick panel that returns a result in twelve minutes removes that wait. The capability is defensible as packaging and manufacturing, not as assay science, and for perhaps 12-24 months. The economics do not scale at the only documented utilisation: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day (company-reported, unverified) against the eight the 2028 plan assumes. Because the third fails, $140M buys a plan whose 3x case needs $546M of exit proceeds, 5.5 times the $100M a cleared, waived point-of-care platform fetched in April 2026. Wait for the 510(k) and the first billing-enabled data, or invest at $60-80M with the structure repaired [S1].

The evaluation programme is real commercial evidence: 41 sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, 55 analyzers and 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days, all company-reported and unverified. The clinic's economics are documented: the CY2026 fee schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes, against $33.40 realised, leaving $37.98 a panel before the $650 monthly fee. But only a full-menu order clears the cartridge. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes pay $32.12; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23 against a $38 list, a $20.77 loss. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts Chemistry 16%, taking the five-code panel to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029 and the clinic's contribution to $10.43, when the fee equals 62 panels of margin [S154, S149].

No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge: Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and the granted on-board-calibrator patent runs to 2040 (company-reported, unverified). The assay evidence is weaker. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, against the IFCC's <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%; the study is 640 venous samples from 128 patients, run by company staff at one site, with six excluded results and no capillary-versus-venous comparison. The five-assay reader patent received a final rejection in 2026-07 and is on appeal, and the freedom-to-operate opinion excludes the troponin chemistry [S68].

The deck's own operating data undo the revenue plan. Fifty-five analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in the January-September 2026 average (deck p.7; FY2025 volume not disclosed) — 30.5 per analyzer-month, 1.22 a day on 300 operating days — against 8.0 assumed from 2028, a 6.5-fold gap. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month, so the 2026 rate is roughly double, and the step to $3.5M normalised FY2026 revenue reflects a larger installed base, not per-analyzer growth. Three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 per placement, against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site; the model needs 5.9 panels a day at today's cost, 4.2 at the $7.50 target, for a 3:1 LTV:CAC. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so the 300-site plan is a marketing cost, not a franchise. The counter-case is that evaluation analyzers are investigational and results never reach care, so their use is a floor; a billing-enabled clinic has a reason to run more. The first commercial quarter must prove it [S1, S148].

Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint: 2.5x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M is $8.8M; the FY2029 plan at 2.5x discounted three years is $100.5M; capital invested is $51.5M, or 2.7x the ask. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — with the Series A participating at 23.75% above the stack, and the Corvia 40% put adds $9.4M ahead of the B. The new $30M is flat at 1.00x to a $206M exit, needs $376M for 2x, $546M for 3x and $1.74B for 10x. QuidelOrtho paid $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics on 2026-04-20, Roche paid $295M plus up to $55M for LumiraDx, and QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales [S126].

The company, the $140M pre-money and the $8M insider commitment assume a Q1 2027 clearance, a 2027 waiver, eight panels a day and a $2.4B market. Our view differs on the variables that set the level rather than the timing: utilisation and price. The evidence is internal — 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in the January-September 2026 average, a $368M cartridge market at observed use rather than $2.4B, a 139-day FY2024 average to decision against a 124-day goal, and a waiver pathway with no troponin-I precedent. The thesis is consensus on the need and the strategic logic, non-consensus on price. The decision tree has four branches. Invest now at $140M: no, because the expected return is 1.35x over 4.5 years, a 6.9% IRR. Pass: only if the waiver is refused for the cardiac analyte, which would leave a four-analyte heart-failure product and take 50-65% off equity value. Wait for milestone: yes, the default — the December 2026 answer, clearance, a waiver pre-submission accepted and ten billing sites' panels per day would retire the three unknowns. Invest with conditions: at $60-80M pre-money, $15M at close and $15M on clearance, the Series A capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior B, pay-to-play and full pro-rata, the Corvia put capped or converted, and a permanent CFO, independent director and ISO 13485 certificate before closing; at $70M the new money owns 28.9% and 3x needs $348M, or $301M with the Series A capped [S149, S126, S97].

arguments.markdown:
The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle. Three risks decide the outcome — utilisation, capillary troponin and the CLIA waiver — and the recommendation prices the last two while assuming the first.

### A placement returns value only above five panels a day

The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers; the independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme running point-of-care chemistry and haematology at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months from three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight — the top of the supported range, not its centre — with 40% on the bear and 15% on the bull. The mechanism is the placement: three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site, four panels a day reaches only 1.1-2.3x LTV:CAC against the 3:1 a direct salesforce needs, and the 3:1 arrives at 5.9. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so 402 analyzers would consume $4.0-14.3M of the round — the plan's 300 sites are a marketing cost, not yet a franchise. [S1, S148]

### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024, against a 124-day goal it missed, and sets a 112-day goal for FY2025; a December 2026 answer plus the 139-day average points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry-panel figure is the 510(k) database's total time, not FDA days. The bear case's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request; the base rate alone points to May 2027. A second request pushes the decision into the second half of 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 at the earliest and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster, on one 180-day goal. I put 45-55% on clearance later than June 2027 and 30% on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a troponin-panel pre-submission answer and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. [S97, S92, S69, S72, S147]

### The pivotal study is the first honest test of the assay

The only clinical evidence is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, with six results excluded for insufficient sample or cartridge error and 96.1% categorical agreement with no direction for the five discordant troponin results. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, so a true value on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of ±23%. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due in Q2 2027, is the first test of the two variables that caused the exclusions. I put 30-40% on it failing to show acceptable agreement at the cutoff and 15-20% on outright failure; failure removes troponin, the chest-pain use case and the $12.47 code, takes 50-65% off equity value and leaves a four-analyte heart-failure product, not the acute-cardiac platform the price assumes. [S1, S68, S70]

### Reimbursement is priced at 2026 rates everywhere in this report

CMS's preliminary calendar-2027 fee schedule lowers 1,171 of 1,528 laboratory codes, with Chemistry 16% lower and cuts phased at no more than 15% a year through 2029. On that path the five-code panel falls from $71.38 to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029, and the clinic's contribution per $33.40 cartridge falls from $37.98 to $10.43; the $650 monthly fee then costs 62 panels of contribution rather than 17. That is a demand risk worth -15% to -25% of equity value, and it compounds with CLIA: until a waiver, the 300 sites planned for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity laboratories, not urgent-care clinics. The quality system is the other exposure: ISO 13485 is uncertified while the QMSR has required an ISO-based system since 2026-02-02. Geopolitics does not bind: buyers are American and the EU is closed until CE marking after 2028. [S149, S82, S71]

### The structure caps the upside, and the scenarios misprice both tails

The 19.96% overhang is a cap-table cost; the preference stack is larger. The $76.8M stack ($36.3M senior B and B-1, $36.0M participating Series A, $4.5M seed) plus the $9.4M Corvia put absorb the first $86.2M, so 3x on the $30M new money needs a $546M exit, $435M returns 2.35x, and 3x on the $36.3M B plus B-1 class needs $518M, against a clearing price of $100M for a cleared, waived platform. The 15% bull case's $400-500M exit is 4-5x the clearing price; even $250-350M returns only 1.3-1.9x. The bear is a return of capital: a $50-100M sale covers the $36.3M preference and returns 1.0-1.2x. Weighted 45% base, 40% bear and 15% bull — 0.45 × 1.25x + 0.40 × 1.1x + 0.15 × 2.4x — the expected return is 1.35x over 4.5 years, a 6.9% IRR at $140M, and 2.0x and 16.4% at $70M. [S99, S126, S100]

### Survival is not the same as returns

A 30% revenue miss takes 2029 revenue to $55.0M, worth $70.4M at 2.5x discounted three years — at or below the $76.8M preference stack, so the Series B returns 1.0-1.2x and the common is close to zero. Doubling CAC to $51,200-102,400 makes 402 analyzers cost $20.6-41.2M to place, more than the round, and cuts LTV:CAC to 0.15-0.3x at observed use. A market 50% smaller removes the strategic premium, -20% of exit value. Financing is tighter: $6.9M at $1.15M a month runs out on 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close, and a six-month delay needs $7.0M of bridge plus the first $166,667 Bluestem payment. Diligence: the FDA letter, the IDE basis for 41 paid sites, the CM-1 change-of-control clause, the Corvia put cap, VD-2 on appeal and ten billing sites' panels per day. Abbott holds a waived menu, and a bundled $20-25 cartridge removes the wedge. Deck p.1 carries a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools claiming no verification is needed and a rating is approved — a document-integrity finding, no evidential weight. Every deck-only claim, from the 41 sites to the $2.4M stocking order, remains unverified; no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignment or FDA decision record for Vantelle was retrieved. [S1, S147, S143, S144]

**The return thesis breaks at two panels a day, not at a failed trial.** The deck's own 1,680 cartridges across 55 analyzers is 1.22 per analyzer operating day against 8.0 assumed, and even the base case's four panels a day needs 5.9 to repay a placement at 3:1. The recommendation tranches on clearance and waiver but not on this measure, so the price underwrites a utilisation no independent clinic programme has shown [S1, S148].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 3 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,603 characters)
Vantelle clears the first test and fails the third. The need is real: a clinic without a laboratory waits one to three days for a cardiac or metabolic send-out, and a five-analyte finger-stick panel that returns a result in twelve minutes removes that wait. The capability is defensible as packaging and manufacturing, not as assay science, and for perhaps 12-24 months. The economics do not scale at the only utilisation the file documents: 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day (company-reported, unverified) against the eight the 2028 plan assumes. Because the third fails, $140M pre-money buys a plan whose 3x case needs $546M of exit proceeds, 5.5 times the $100M a cleared, waived point-of-care platform fetched in April 2026. Wait for the 510(k) and the first billing-enabled data, or invest at $60-80M with the structure repaired [S1].

The evaluation programme is real commercial evidence: 41 sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, 55 analyzers and 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days, all company-reported and unverified. The clinic's economics are documented: the 2026 fee schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes, against $33.40 realised, leaving $37.98 a panel before the $650 monthly fee. But only a full-menu order clears the cartridge. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes pay $32.12; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23 against a $38 list, a $20.77 loss. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts Chemistry 16%, taking the five-code panel to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029 and the clinic's contribution to $10.43, when the fee equals 62 panels of margin [S82, S149].

No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge, and that packaging is worth something: Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and the granted on-board-calibrator patent runs to 2040 (company-reported, unverified). The assay evidence is weaker. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, against the IFCC's <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%; the study is 640 venous samples from 128 patients, run by company staff at one site, with six excluded results and no capillary-versus-venous comparison. The five-assay reader patent received a final rejection in 2026-07 and is on appeal, and the freedom-to-operate opinion excludes the troponin chemistry [S68].

The deck's own operating data undo the revenue plan. Fifty-five analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month — 30.5 per analyzer-month, 1.22 a day on the 300-operating-day convention the market model uses — against 8.0 assumed from 2028, a 6.5-fold gap. Three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 per placement, against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site; the model needs 5.9 panels a day at today's cost, 4.2 at the $7.50 target, for a 3:1 LTV:CAC. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle scores below the threshold for a lead at the ask and inside the range for a wait-for-milestone position. The score is not a verdict on the technology: the need and the team sit in the middle of the scale. It is a verdict on evidence — a product short of its own menu, a regulatory path with no waived cardiac precedent, and unit economics that fail at the company's own utilisation. The recommendation is Wait for milestone: no cheque at the ask, a conditional offer at a lower pre-money, and a re-underwrite when clearance, the waiver pre-submission and the first billing cohort report.

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market need and addressable demand | 15% | 6 | Real clinical need and 41 paying evaluation sites; but the $2.4B SAM is 6.5x observed use, and only the 60.3% traditional urgent-care segment can carry the full-menu economics, which supports $222M | S1 (unverified), S79 |
| Product and technical evidence | 20% | 4 | Five-in-one finger-stick packaging is first-of-kind in the US; troponin at 11.8% CV fails the IFCC <10% benchmark, no capillary data, reader patent on final rejection | S68, S1 (unverified) |
| Regulatory pathway and quality system | 20% | 3 | 2026-08-21 information request pending, 139-day FY2024 average total time to decision against a 124-day goal, no troponin-I waiver precedent, ISO 13485 uncertified | S97, S72, S147, S71 |
| Business model and unit economics | 15% | 3 | 1.22 panels per analyzer-day against 8.0 modelled; three-year LTV $15,621 against $25,600-51,200 CAC; 5.9 panels needed for 3:1 | S1 (unverified), S148 |
| Financial plan and capital efficiency | 10% | 3 | 6.0 months of cash at $1.15M a month; $40M needed against a $30M round; $2.4M of FY2026E revenue cannot ship in FY2026 | S1 (unverified) |
| Team and execution | 10% | 5 | Emergency-physician CEO and microfluidics CTO; thin regulatory, quality and finance bench with turnover in 2025-26 | S1 (unverified) |
| Governance and structure | 5% | 4 | 19.96% post-money option overhang, $9.4M Corvia put ahead of the B, part-time interim CFO, independent board seat vacant | S1 (unverified) |
| Valuation and exit | 5% | 2 | $140M ask against a $50-100M methods cluster; $546M needed for 3x against a $100M 2026 clearing price | S1 (unverified), S126 |

The weighted average is 3.9 (0.9 + 0.8 + 0.6 + 0.45 + 0.3 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.1) [S1]. Two dimensions can re-rate the company quickly. A clearance certificate and an accepted waiver pre-submission would lift regulatory from 3 to 6-7; a first billing cohort above 5.9 panels a day would lift unit economics from 3 to 7 and the composite by roughly two points. Conversely, a second information request or a capillary troponin failure takes product and regulatory to 2 and the composite down by about a point and a half. The asymmetry is why price matters more than the score: on company-reported terms (unverified), the probability-weighted return is 1.35x over 4.5 years at the ask and 2.0x at $70M, a 6.9% versus 16.4% IRR. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores 7 at most, and none of these has one that supports more.

### How the recommendation changes under the downside

The base case carries a 45% weight: clearance in H2 2027, a waiver in 2028-29, 2-4 panels a day and a $150-250M sale in 2031 returning 1.0-1.5x. The bear case carries 40%: a second request or a capillary-troponin deficiency, a refused or deferred waiver, and a $50-100M distressed sale in 2028 that still covers the $36.3M senior preference on company-reported terms, unverified, and returns 1.0-1.2x [S126].

### The branches that change the recommendation

The recommendation becomes Pass if the waiver is refused for the cardiac analyte or the pivotal study misses the cutoff, because both remove the chest-pain use case and 50-65% of equity value. It becomes Invest with conditions at a lower pre-money if clearance arrives and the first billing cohort exceeds four panels a day. It becomes Invest now only if the FDA letter proves documentation-only and a billing cohort prints above six panels — neither of which is in the file today [S68].

### Position sizing and what can be lost

Private company sizing: no capital at the ask. At a lower pre-money, split the cheque between close and clearance, with a follow-on reserve sized to the plan's funding gap rather than to the initial cheque. The maximum loss is not the full commitment: a distressed sale still covers the senior preference, and a full loss needs no sale at all or a price below the preference stack after the Bluestem loan and the Corvia put. The terms that make the cheque worth writing are a board seat, pay-to-play, full pro-rata, a utilisation covenant tied to the second tranche and disinterested approval of the Corvia royalty and put.

### Next diligence and conditions

The diligence list decides the re-underwrite: the FDA information request; the pivotal protocol and any capillary-versus-venous data; the Corvia LLC agreement and the change-of-control clause; the Bluestem rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor's purchase, payment and return terms; the first billing sites' panels per day and collected revenue per cartridge; and the quality-system certificate. The conditions for any cheque are a price at or below the agreed cap, the tranche structure, the Series A participation capped, the Corvia put capped or converted, a permanent CFO and an independent director before closing, and the certificate before launch. A clearance slip or a later waiver filing reopens the price, not just the timetable.

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Billing sites run 6+ panels per analyzer-day | 2-4 panels a day in the base case | First 10 billing sites below 3 a day for two quarters | -55% to -70% EV | High | Best evaluation month stays near 41 cartridges | S1 (unverified), S148 |
| 2 | 510(k) clears by Q2 2027 without a second request | H2 2027 in the base case | Second FDA request or a clinical deficiency | -25% to -35% EV per two-quarter slip | High | New bench or clinical requests; clearance past 2027-06-30 | S69, S92 |
| 3 | CLIA waiver including troponin I by mid-2028 | Filed Q3 2027, decided 2028 | FDA declines the cardiac analyte or the filing slips | -40% EV | High | No pre-submission by mid-2027 | S72, S147 |
| 4 | Clinic economics survive the CY2027 Chemistry cut | $71.38 in 2026 falling to $43.83 in 2029 | Final rule keeps the cut; collections under $30 per cartridge | -25% to -35% EV | Medium | Final CY2027 CLFS; fewer than four codes billed | S149, S154 |
| 5 | $30M funds the plan without a down round | $40M needed, $30M raised | Cash trough below zero before FY2029 profit | 23-32% dilution at half price | Medium | Bluestem principal from 2027-04 plus a clearance slip | S1 (unverified) |
:::

::: takeaways
1. Do not lead at $140M: the price is 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M and needs $546M of exit proceeds for 3x, against a $100M clearing price for a cleared, waived platform in April 2026 [S1, S126].
2. The case turns on utilisation, not regulation: 1.22 panels per analyzer-day against 8.0 assumed, and below 5.9 panels the placement never repays its estimated $25,600-51,200 CAC [S1, S148].
3. Keep the option alive at $60-80M: $15M split between close and clearance, the Series A capped at 1.5x and the Corvia put cleaned up turns a 1.35x expected return into 2.0x [S1, S126].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle. Three risks decide the outcome — utilisation, capillary troponin and the CLIA waiver — and the recommendation prices the last two while assuming the first.

### A placement returns value only above five panels a day

The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers; the independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme running point-of-care chemistry and haematology at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months from three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight — the top of the supported range, not its centre — with 40% on the bear and 15% on the bull. The mechanism is the placement: three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site, four panels a day reaches only 1.1-2.3x LTV:CAC against the 3:1 a direct salesforce needs, and the 3:1 arrives at 5.9. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so 402 analyzers would consume $4.0-14.3M of the round — the plan's 300 sites are a marketing cost, not a franchise. [S1, S148]

### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024, against a 124-day goal it missed, and sets a 112-day goal for FY2025; a December 2026 answer plus the 139-day average points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry figure is database total time, not FDA days. The bear case's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request; the base rate alone points to May 2027. A second request pushes the decision into the second half of 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster, on one 180-day goal. I put 45-55% on clearance later than June 2027 and 30% on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a troponin-panel pre-submission answer and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. [S97, S92, S69, S72, S147]

### The pivotal study is the first honest test of the assay

The only clinical evidence is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, with six results excluded for insufficient sample or cartridge error and 96.1% categorical agreement with no direction for the five discordant results. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, so a true value on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of ±23%. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due in Q2 2027, is the first test of the two variables that caused the exclusions. I put 30-40% on it failing to show acceptable agreement at the cutoff and 15-20% on outright failure; failure removes troponin, the chest-pain use case and the $12.47 code, takes 50-65% off equity value and leaves a four-analyte heart-failure product, not the acute-cardiac platform the price assumes. [S1, S68, S70]

### Reimbursement is priced at 2026 rates everywhere in this report

CMS's preliminary calendar-2027 fee schedule lowers 1,171 of 1,528 laboratory codes, with Chemistry 16% lower and cuts phased at no more than 15% a year through 2029. On that path the five-code panel falls from $71.38 to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029, and the clinic's contribution per $33.40 cartridge falls from $37.98 to $10.43; the $650 monthly fee then costs 62 panels of contribution rather than 17. That is a -15% to -25% equity-value risk, and it compounds with CLIA: until a waiver, the 300 sites planned for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity laboratories, not urgent-care clinics. The quality system is the other exposure: ISO 13485 is uncertified while the QMSR has required an ISO-based system since 2026-02-02. Geopolitics does not bind: buyers are American and the EU is closed until CE marking after 2028. [S149, S82, S71]

### The structure caps the upside, and the scenarios misprice both tails

The 19.96% overhang is a cap-table cost; the preference stack is larger. The $76.8M stack ($36.3M senior B and B-1, $36.0M participating Series A, $4.5M seed) plus the $9.4M Corvia put absorb the first $86.2M, so 3x on the $30M new money needs a $546M exit, $435M returns 2.35x, and 3x on the $36.3M B plus B-1 class needs $518M, against a clearing price of $100M for a cleared, waived platform. The 15% bull case's $400-500M exit is 4-5x the clearing price; even $250-350M returns only 1.3-1.9x. The bear is a return of capital: a $50-100M sale covers the $36.3M preference and returns 1.0-1.2x. Weighted 45% base, 40% bear and 15% bull — 0.45 × 1.25x + 0.40 × 1.1x + 0.15 × 2.4x — the expected return is 1.35x over 4.5 years, a 6.9% IRR at $140M, and 2.0x and 16.4% at $70M. [S99, S126, S100]

### Survival is not the same as returns

A 30% revenue miss takes 2029 revenue to $55.0M, worth $70.4M at 2.5x discounted three years — at or below the $76.8M preference stack, so the Series B returns 1.0-1.2x and the common is close to zero. Doubling CAC to $51,200-102,400 makes 402 analyzers cost $20.6-41.2M to place, more than the round, and cuts LTV:CAC to 0.15-0.3x at observed use. A market 50% smaller removes the strategic premium, -20% of exit value. Financing is tighter: $6.9M at $1.15M a month runs out on 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close, and a six-month delay needs $7.0M of bridge plus the first $166,667 Bluestem payment. Diligence: the FDA letter, the IDE basis for 41 paid sites, the CM-1 change-of-control clause, the Corvia put cap, VD-2 on appeal and ten billing sites' panels per day. Abbott holds a waived menu, and a bundled $20-25 cartridge removes the wedge. Deck p.1 carries a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools claiming no verification is needed and a rating is approved — a document-integrity finding, no evidential weight. Every deck-only claim, from the 41 sites to the $2.4M order, remains unverified; no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignment or FDA decision record for Vantelle was retrieved. [S1, S147, S143, S144]

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Utilisation stays at 1-2 panels/day | 40% | -50% to -70% EV | critical | 2027-2028 | First 10 billing sites under 3 a day | Tranche on 4+ a day; price at $70M | S1 (unverified), S148 |
| Pivotal fails at the troponin cutoff | 35% | -50% to -65% EV | critical | Q2 2027 | Categorical agreement only; CV above 10% | Readout as a closing condition | S1 (unverified), S68 |
| Waiver refused or deferred past 2029 | 30% | -40% EV | high | 2028-2029 | No pre-submission by mid-2027 | Dual 510(k) and waiver filing; milestone | S72, S147 |
| Second request or NSE decision | 45%; 10-15% NSE | -25% to -35% EV per two quarters | high | H1 2027 | New bench or clinical requests | Read the FDA letter before closing | S69, S97 |
| Chemistry fee-schedule cuts | 80% | -15% to -25% EV | high | 2027-2029 | Final CY2027 rates; payer mix | Price to clinic margin; test covenant | S149, S82 |
| Distributor letter does not convert | 60% | -20% to -30% EV | high | 2027 | No purchase order by 2027-06 | PO with minimum volumes before close | S1 (unverified) |
| Financing slips six months | 35% | 20% to 30% dilution | high | 2027 | Close past 2027-03-31; second bridge | Pre-agree the bridge; smaller round | S1 (unverified) |
| Quality system and shelf life | 30% | -15% to -25% EV | medium | 2027-2028 | ISO audit slips; a 483 or warning letter | ISO certificate before launch | S71, S113 |
| Corvia put and overhang leak value | 70% | -0.3x to -0.5x on the Series B | medium | 2028-2031 | Put uncapped; no fairness opinion | Cap or convert the put; disinterested approval | S1 (unverified), S99 |
:::

::: info danger
**The return thesis breaks at two panels a day, not at a failed trial.** The deck's 1,680 cartridges across 55 analyzers is 1.22 per analyzer operating day against 8.0 assumed, and even the base case's four panels a day needs 5.9 to repay a placement at 3:1. The recommendation tranches on clearance and waiver but not on this measure, so the price underwrites a utilisation no independent clinic programme has shown [S1, S148].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle. Three risks decide the outcome — utilisation, capillary troponin and the CLIA waiver — and the recommendation prices the last two while assuming the first.

### A placement returns value only above five panels a day

The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers; the independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme running point-of-care chemistry and haematology at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months from three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight — the top of the supported range, not its centre — with 40% on the bear and 15% on the bull. The mechanism is the placement: three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site, four panels a day reaches only 1.1-2.3x LTV:CAC against the 3:1 a direct salesforce needs, and the 3:1 arrives at 5.9. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so 402 analyzers would consume $4.0-14.3M of the round — which means the plan's 300 sites are a marketing cost, not a franchise. [S1, S148]

### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024, against a 124-day goal it missed, and sets a 112-day goal for FY2025; a December 2026 answer plus the 139-day average points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry figure is database total time, not FDA days. The bear case's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request; the base rate alone points to May 2027. A second request pushes the decision into the second half of 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster. I put a 45-55% probability on clearance later than June 2027 and a 30% probability on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a troponin-panel pre-submission answer and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. [S97, S92, S69, S72, S147]

### The pivotal study is the first honest test of the assay

The only clinical evidence is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, with six results excluded for insufficient sample or cartridge error and 96.1% categorical agreement with no direction for the five discordant results. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, so a true value on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of ±23%. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due in Q2 2027, is the first test of the two variables that caused the exclusions. I put a 30-40% probability on it failing to show acceptable agreement at the cutoff and a 15-20% probability of outright failure; failure removes troponin, the chest-pain use case and the $12.47 code, takes 50-65% off equity value and leaves a four-analyte heart-failure product, not the acute-cardiac platform the price assumes. [S1, S68, S70]

### Reimbursement is priced at 2026 rates everywhere in this report

CMS's preliminary calendar-2027 fee schedule lowers 1,171 of 1,528 laboratory codes, with Chemistry 16% lower and cuts phased at no more than 15% a year through 2029. On that path the five-code panel falls from $71.38 to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029, and the clinic's contribution per $33.40 cartridge falls from $37.98 to $10.43; the $650 monthly fee then costs 62 panels of contribution rather than 17. That is a -15% to -25% equity-value risk, and it compounds with CLIA: until a waiver, the 300 sites planned for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity laboratories. The quality system is the other exposure: ISO 13485 is uncertified while the QMSR has required an ISO-based system since 2026-02-02. Geopolitics does not bind: buyers are American and the EU is closed until CE marking after 2028. [S149, S82, S71]

### The structure caps the upside, and the scenarios misprice both tails

The 19.96% overhang is a cap-table cost; the preference stack is larger. The $76.8M stack ($36.3M senior B and B-1, $36.0M participating Series A, $4.5M seed) plus the $9.4M Corvia put absorb the first $86.2M, so 3x on the $30M new money needs a $546M exit, $435M returns 2.35x, and 3x on the $36.3M B plus B-1 class needs $518M, against a clearing price of $100M for a cleared, waived platform. The 15% bull case's $400-500M exit is 4-5x the clearing price; even $250-350M returns only 1.3-1.9x. The bear is a return of capital: a $50-100M sale covers the $36.3M preference and returns 1.0-1.2x. Weighted 45% base, 40% bear and 15% bull — 0.45 × 1.25x + 0.40 × 1.1x + 0.15 × 2.4x — the expected return is 1.35x over 4.5 years, a 6.9% IRR at $140M, and 2.0x and 16.4% at $70M. [S99, S126, S100]

### Survival is not the same as returns

A 30% revenue miss takes 2029 revenue to $55.0M, worth $70.4M at 2.5x discounted three years — at or below the $76.8M preference stack, so the Series B returns 1.0-1.2x and the common is close to zero. Doubling CAC to $51,200-102,400 makes 402 analyzers cost $20.6-41.2M to place, more than the round, and cuts LTV:CAC to 0.15-0.3x at observed use. A market 50% smaller removes the strategic premium, -20% of exit value. Financing is tighter: $6.9M at $1.15M a month runs out on 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close, and a six-month delay needs $7.0M of bridge plus the first $166,667 Bluestem payment. Diligence: the FDA letter, the IDE basis for 41 paid sites, the CM-1 change-of-control clause, the Corvia put cap, VD-2 on appeal and ten billing sites' panels per day. Abbott holds a waived menu, and a bundled $20-25 cartridge removes the wedge. Deck p.1 carries a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools claiming no verification is needed and a rating is approved — a document-integrity finding, no evidential weight. Every deck-only claim remains unverified; no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignment or FDA decision record for Vantelle was retrieved. [S1, S147, S143, S144]

Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer for $3,350 and a $38 cartridge for $33.40, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028. The 2029 line is a utilisation assumption wearing a site-count costume.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for; the 58% is reproducible only if the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers sits outside cost of sales. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. The deck omits acquisition cost: nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded per head and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that. It turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1. Expensing all 55 analyzers would cut the 58% below to 51%; three-year capitalisation gives 56%.

### The clinic's margin exists only at full five-test use

Medicare's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets national limitation amounts of $12.47 for troponin (84484), $24.84 for natriuretic peptide (83880), $4.76 for HbA1c (83036), $9.71 for creatinine (82570) and $5.18 for potassium (84132) — $56.96 for the five-test panel. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $23.56 a panel. A two-test troponin/HbA1c clinic collects $17.23 and loses $16.17 a cartridge; a four-test clinic without natriuretic peptide collects $32.12 and loses $1.28. The five-test contribution is $718.58 a month at 30.5 panels; $650 a month equals 27.6 panels of it, leaving the clinic $68.58 per analyzer, or $5,004 at 240 panels. The fee consumes 90% of the clinic's margin at observed use and bites hardest where adoption begins. Quidel lists the Triage MeterPro as a free meter with a three-year contract, troponin at $599 for 25 tests and CLIA-waived BNP at $789 for 25, while QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and moved $167.3M of instrument inventory into property, plant and equipment in FY2025 alone [S154, S106, S22].
