FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, and about 567 before 2026 if 2026 ran at 1,680. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume and whether any sustained a higher run rate; the same for the first billing-enabled sites; and the panel mix, since troponin and potassium alone collect less than the cartridge.

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales, and expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that; it turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | $0.43M fees; 20,160 cartridges at $33.40/$16.20; analyzer cost excluded | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | 23,952 cartridges at the only disclosed price and cost | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | residual cost; not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | deck p.10; bridge closes only on the 2026-average volume | S1 (unverified) |

### The clinic's margin rests on the one assay that carries 55% of the payment

CMS's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets these national limitation amounts [S154, S160]:

| Test (CPT code) | CY2026 amount | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | S154; S160 |
| Natriuretic peptide (83880) | $39.26 | S154; S160 |
| Haemoglobin A1c (83036) | $9.71 | S154; S160 |
| Creatinine (82570) | $5.18 | S154; S160 |
| Potassium (84132) | $4.76 | S154; S160 |
| Five-code panel | $71.38 | S154; S160 |

Against the $33.40 cartridge a five-code clinic keeps $37.98 a panel and Vantelle takes 47% of the Medicare payment. Natriuretic peptide alone is $39.26, 55% of it: a clinic billing four codes without that assay collects $32.12 and loses $1.28 a cartridge, and troponin plus potassium collects $17.23 and loses $16.17. At the observed 30.5 panels a month the five-code clinic earns $1,158.39 and keeps $508.39 after the $650 fee — the fee equals 17.1 panels — and $8,465.20 at 240 panels, so it is trivial at scale and 56% of the clinic's margin at adoption. The payment is not fixed either: CMS may cut a test by up to 15% a year in 2027-2029, and three such years would take this panel to $43.84 and the clinic's spread to $10.44. The amounts rest on the quarterly CLFS file, which CMS publishes as a data file rather than on its page; the republication reproduces all five.

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 17.1 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage BNP, CLIA-waived, 25 tests | $789 | $31.56 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| FY2025 line | $M | Share | Repeatable? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use cartridges to CROs | 0.8 | 31% | Repeatable, needs no clearance, small market | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development for one partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, about 567 before 2026. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full five-code reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a low-single-digit panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume; the first billing-enabled sites' run rate; and panel mix, since troponin plus potassium collect $17.23 against a $33.40 cartridge.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the five-code clinic keeps $508.39 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $71.38 and the cartridge costs the clinic $33.40, so the $650 fee equals 17.1 panels of a $37.98 margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154, S160].
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 13 by Product Analyst, 8,940 characters)
The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. Its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The package is five analytes from one finger stick, defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve, pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

::: evidence
**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit; Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].
:::

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills (company description, unverified).

| Metric | Vantelle Q5 | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | IFCC high-sensitivity <10%; i-STAT hs-TnI <5.2% whole blood | S1, S68, S70 |
| Shelf life and cost | 9 months claimed on 6 months of data; $16.20 at pilot volume (unverified) | $7.50 at 2 million units | S1 |

### Precision and capillary collection decide the label

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share lands on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. The deck calls it high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff; on this data it is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none. The 96.1% is categorical agreement; the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress. No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck: the four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in Q2 2027 — is the first test of capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and potassium already exist from Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S1, S13, S15, S16, S21, S68, S70, S74].

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | Siemens epoc | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick | 22 µL whole blood within 3 min | Arterial, venous or capillary | S1, S70, S74 |
| Troponin CV at cutoff | 11.8% (unverified) | Below 5.2% | Not applicable | S1, S68, S70 |
| CLIA status | Moderate; waiver planned Q3 2027 | Waived chemistry and blood gas; hs-TnI moderate | Moderate | S1, S72, S104, S133, S145, S146 |

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is 150 FDA days, and an additional-information request can add 180. arguments.markdown:
The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle. Three risks decide the outcome — utilisation, capillary troponin and the CLIA waiver — and the recommendation prices the last two while assuming the first.

### A placement returns value only above five panels a day

The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers; the independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme running point-of-care chemistry and haematology at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months from three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight — the top of the supported range, not its centre — with 40% on the bear and 15% on the bull. The mechanism is the placement: three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site, four panels a day reaches only 1.1-2.3x LTV:CAC against the 3:1 a direct salesforce needs, and the 3:1 arrives at 5.9. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so 402 analyzers would consume $4.0-14.3M of the round — which means the plan's 300 sites are a marketing cost, not a franchise. [S1, S148]

### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024, against a 124-day goal it missed, and sets a 112-day goal for FY2025; a December 2026 answer plus the 139-day average points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry-panel figure is the 510(k) database's total time, not FDA days. The bear case's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request; the base rate alone points to May 2027. A second request pushes the decision into the second half of 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster. Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. ### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales, and expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, about 567 before 2026. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full panel reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a modest panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume; the first billing-enabled sites' run rate; and panel mix, since troponin plus potassium collect $17.23 against a $33.40 cartridge.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the five-code clinic keeps $508.39 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $71.38 and the cartridge costs the clinic $33.40, so the $650 fee equals 17.1 panels of a $37.98 margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154, S160].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales, and expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that; it turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day (300 days) | 1.0 | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year cartridge LTV | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC, cartridges only | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels a day for 3:1, fee included | 5.9 at $16.20; 4.2 at $7.50 | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | $0.43M fees; 20,160 cartridges at $33.40/$16.20; analyzer cost excluded | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | 23,952 cartridges at the only disclosed price and cost | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | residual cost; not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | deck p.10; bridge closes only on the 2026-average volume | S1 (unverified) |

### The clinic's margin rests on the one assay that carries 55% of the payment

CMS's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets these national limitation amounts:

| Test (CPT code) | CY2026 amount | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | S154; S160 |
| Natriuretic peptide (83880) | $39.26 | S154; S160 |
| Haemoglobin A1c (83036) | $9.71 | S154; S160 |
| Creatinine (82570) | $5.18 | S154; S160 |
| Potassium (84132) | $4.76 | S154; S160 |
| Five-code panel | $71.38 | S154; S160 |

Against the $33.40 cartridge a five-code clinic keeps $37.98 a panel and Vantelle takes 47% of the Medicare payment. Natriuretic peptide alone is $39.26, 55% of it: a clinic billing four codes without that assay collects $32.12 and loses $1.28 a cartridge, and troponin plus potassium collects $17.23 and loses $16.17. At the observed 30.5 panels a month the five-code clinic earns $1,158.39 and keeps $508.39 after the $650 fee — the fee equals 17.1 panels — and $8,465.20 at 240 panels: trivial at scale, 56% of the margin at adoption. The payment is not fixed: CMS may cut a test by up to 15% a year in 2027-2029, and three such years would take this panel to $43.84 and the clinic's spread to $10.44 [S154, S160]. CMS publishes the amounts as a data file rather than on its page; the republication reproduces all five.

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 17.1 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage BNP, CLIA-waived, 25 tests | $789 | $31.56 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| FY2025 line | $M | Share | Repeatable? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use cartridges to CROs | 0.8 | 31% | Repeatable, needs no clearance, small market | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development for one partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, about 567 before 2026. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full panel reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a modest panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume; the first billing-enabled sites' run rate; and panel mix, since troponin plus potassium alone do not cover a cartridge.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the five-code clinic keeps $508.39 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $71.38 and the cartridge costs the clinic $33.40, so the $650 fee equals 17.1 panels of a $37.98 margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154, S160].
:::

2. The problem
Urgent-care clinics and rural hospitals without an on-site laboratory send cardiac and metabolic blood tests to reference labs and wait 1-3 days for
results. Patients with chest pain or uncontrolled diabetes are often transferred, or sent home, before results arrive.
-  A transfer for a suspected heart attack that turns out negative costs thousands of dollars and takes a rural ambulance out of service for hours
(company estimate).
-  Benchtop analyzers that could run these tests on site need venous blood, a trained operator and daily quality control, which small clinics can't staff.
-  The clinics we surveyed send out a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels a day (company survey of 52 clinics, 2024).

3. Our product: the Vantelle Q5
-  A handheld, cartridge-based analyzer that runs a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel from a finger-stick sample in 12 minutes.
-  The panel: high-sensitivity troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine (with eGFR) and potassium.
-  One 40-microliter drop of blood. Each cartridge holds all its reagents and an on-board calibrator, so there is no separate calibration step.
-  The analyzer weighs 640 grams, runs on a battery and sends results to the clinic's electronic health record over Wi-Fi (HL7 and FHIR).
-  Razor-and-blade model: instruments placed at or near cost; recurring revenue from single-use cartridges.
-  Cartridges keep for 9 months at room temperature (our stability data so far covers 6 months).

At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and with the Series A's uncapped participating preference the $30M Series B needs $596M of exit proceeds to return 3x and $1.79B to return 10x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, company-reported and unverified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

Company-reported financing terms, unverified:

| Date | Round | Amount | Price/share | Post-money | Investors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75 (implied) | not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.9032 | $92.5M | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.9032 | $104.5M | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Venture term loan | $5.0M | Warrant strike $2.903 | — | Bluestem Venture Lending (400,000 warrants) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes, 8% | $6.0M | $2.4423 on conversion | — | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027-01 (target) | Series B | $30.0M | $3.2564 | $170.0M | Ardent Peak ($5.0M) and Juniper Rock ($3.0M); $22.0M sought | S1 (unverified) |

The company-reported, unverified terms show the seed at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11. The headline pre-money rises 34% from the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but $13.1M of that is the option-pool refresh to 10% of the post-money: existing holders' effective pre-money is $126.9M, a 21% uplift over 2.9 years, or 6.9% a year. Existing shares fall from 100% to 69.7% — 7.7 points of pool refresh, 4.9 points of bridge and 17.6 points of new Series B — taking the founders from 30.8% to 21.5%, the seed from 16.5% to 11.5% and the Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%; granted options, the unallocated pool and warrants total 20.8% of the post-money. Insiders are committing $8.0M of the $30.0M [S1].

The row formula is published here: after the $9.4M Corvia put, the $76.8M preference stack ($30.0M Series B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A, $4.5M seed) is paid once, and the Series A then receives $36.0M plus 23.75% of the value above that stack; the new Series B receives the greater of $30.0M and 17.65% of the same balance:

| $596M | $157.1M | $90.0M | 3.00x | $25.1M | $314.4M | S1 (unverified) |

The mechanism is value transfer: the B-1's 25% discount and the Series A's uncapped participation leave the new B with $64.2M of a $450M bull-case exit (2.14x) while its class receives $82.1M (2.26x); above a $256M exit each dollar above the stack is worth 17.65 cents to the new B, not the 22.6 cents its class ownership implies. On the deck's fully diluted 52.2M shares, the new $30M is flat at 1.00x from a $45.7M exit (the $9.4M Corvia put plus the $36.3M B/B-1 preference) to $256M; 1.21x needs $292M, 2x $426M, 3x $596M and 10x $1.79B. The Series A takes $122.4M at the $450M bull case, 27.2% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership; the earlier $130.8M at $435M applied its participation above its own $36M preference rather than above the full stack and is corrected here. The Corvia 40% minority put, estimated at $9.4M (3% of FY2029 revenue capitalised at 10x, 40% share; $7.5-11.3M at 8-12x), ranks ahead of the Series B [S1].

### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.22 per analyser per operating day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — a 6.5-fold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's revenue, 41-site and 92% reorder claims are company-reported, unverified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met; adding the $5.0M Bluestem principal, which starts at $0.167M a month in 2027-03 and is repaid by 2029-08, leaves a thin buffer. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on clearance), pay-to-play, full pro rata and a Corvia clean-up before closing. At $70M pre-money the new Series B would own 28.9% after the Series A's broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution (the bridge adds 8.1%) and 3x would need $398M; capping the Series A at 1.5x lowers that to about $350M, against $596M at the ask. Waiting is the alternative: the 510(k) response is due in December 2026, clearance is guided for Q1 2027 and the waiver application for Q3 2027, so a 2027 entry pays more but buys retired regulatory risk. The company had $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30, six months at $1.15M a month and the 2027-01-29 target close, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts amortising in 2027-03. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the valuation range: the 2029 plan is unaudited, the grant dates of the 5.2M options are not disclosed and Truvian's valuation is an aggregator estimate [S1, S125].

arguments.markdown:
At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and with the Series A's uncapped participating preference the $30M Series B needs $596M of exit proceeds to return 3x and $1.79B to return 10x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, company-reported and unverified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

Company-reported financing terms, unverified:

| Date | Round | Amount | Price/share | Post-money | Investors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75 (implied) | not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.9032 | $92.5M | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.9032 | $104.5M | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Venture term loan | $5.0M | Warrant strike $2.903 | — | Bluestem Venture Lending (400,000 warrants) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes, 8% | $6.0M | $2.4423 on conversion | — | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027-01 (target) | Series B | $30.0M | $3.2564 | $170.0M | Ardent Peak ($5.0M) and Juniper Rock ($3.0M); $22.0M sought | S1 (unverified) |

The company-reported, unverified terms show the seed at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11. The headline pre-money rises 34% from the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but $13.1M of that is the option-pool refresh to 10% of the post-money: existing holders' effective pre-money is $126.9M, a 21% uplift over 2.9 years, or 6.9% a year. Existing shares fall from 100% to 69.7% — 7.7 points of pool refresh, 4.9 points of bridge and 17.6 points of new Series B — taking the founders from 30.8% to 21.5%, the seed from 16.5% to 11.5% and the Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%; granted options, the unallocated pool and warrants total 20.8% of the post-money. Insiders are committing $8.0M of the $30.0M [S1].

### What the price assumes

Our calculations on company-reported projections, unverified:

| Method | Inputs | Implied pre-money | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2025A revenue | $2.6M × 2.5x | $6.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2026E ex-stocking | $3.5M × 2.5x | $8.8M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2026E ex-stocking at peer median | $3.5M × 5.5x | $19.3M | S1 (unverified), S28 |
| FY2028P revenue, discounted 2 years | $41.0M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25² | $65.6M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P revenue, discounted 3 years | $78.5M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25³ | $100.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P earnings, discounted 3 years | $9.0M × 15x ÷ 1.30³ | $61.4M | S1 (unverified) |
| Capital invested | $40.5M equity + $11.0M debt | $51.5M (ask = 2.7x) | S1 (unverified) |

| Company | EV | EV/Sales, TTM | P/E, TTM | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho | $1.1B | 0.4x | n/m | Closest point-of-care and cardiac comparable | S22, S23 |
| Abbott | $211.7B | 4.7x | 29.7x | i-STAT, i-STAT Alinity, Afinion | S33, S67 |
| Danaher | $184.2B | 7.2x | 38.1x | Cepheid point-of-care molecular | S34, S35 |
| Bio-Rad | $9.5B | 3.7x | 45.3x | Life-science tools | S36, S37 |
| Thermo Fisher | $295.6B | 6.2x | 36.8x | Mesa Biotech point-of-care molecular | S38, S39 |
| Peer median | — | 5.5x | 37.4x | Diversified tools, not pure-play point of care | S28 |

The methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint: the forward-looking methods and the capital-invested floor range from $51.5M to $100.5M, and the $140M ask is 2.7x the $51.5M of capital raised with no clearance and no waiver. The 5.5x peer median is the wrong benchmark: it is set by diversified tools companies whose point-of-care assets sit inside larger franchises, whereas QuidelOrtho, the only pure-play point-of-care cardiac franchise, has de-rated from 2.9x at FY2022 to 1.7x at FY2025 and 0.4x now. A single-product private company with two assays filed should not be underwritten above the best-capitalised public point-of-care franchise in a de-rating market. Werfen, Siemens Healthineers, Roche Diagnostics and Nova Biomedical are not SEC filers or not listed, so their multiples are not disclosed [S1, S22, S28, S67].

### The Series A takes the first $36M and 23.75% above the stack

Our waterfall on the company-reported terms, unverified. The row formula is published here: after the $9.4M Corvia put, the $76.8M preference stack ($30.0M Series B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A, $4.5M seed) is paid once, and the Series A then receives $36.0M plus 23.75% of the value above that stack; the new Series B receives the greater of $30.0M and 17.65% of the same balance:

| Exit value | Series A total | New Series B | Multiple on $30M | B-1 | Common, seed, options, warrants | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | $48.8M | $30.0M | 1.00x | $6.3M | $45.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| $197M | $62.3M | $30.0M | 1.00x | $6.3M | $89.0M | S1 (unverified) |
| $256M | $76.3M | $30.0M | 1.00x | $8.4M | $131.9M | S1 (unverified) |
| $426M | $116.7M | $60.0M | 2.00x | $16.8M | $223.2M | S1 (unverified) |
| $596M | $157.1M | $90.0M | 3.00x | $25.1M | $314.4M | S1 (unverified) |

The mechanism is value transfer: the B-1's 25% discount and the Series A's uncapped participation leave the new B with $64.2M of a $450M bull-case exit (2.14x) while its class receives $82.1M (2.26x); above a $256M exit each dollar above the stack is worth 17.65 cents to the new B, not the 22.6 cents its class ownership implies. On the deck's fully diluted 52.2M shares, the new $30M is flat at 1.00x from a $45.7M exit (the $9.4M Corvia put plus the $36.3M B/B-1 preference) to $256M; 1.21x needs $292M, 2x $426M, 3x $596M and 10x $1.79B. The Series A takes $122.4M at the $450M bull case, 27.2% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership; the earlier $130.8M at $435M applied its participation above its own $36M preference rather than above the full stack and is corrected here. The Corvia 40% minority put, estimated at $9.4M (3% of FY2029 revenue capitalised at 10x, 40% share; $7.5-11.3M at 8-12x), ranks ahead of the Series B [S1].

### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.22 per analyser per operating day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — a 6.5-fold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's revenue, 41-site and 92% reorder claims are company-reported, unverified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met; adding the $5.0M Bluestem principal, which starts at $0.167M a month in 2027-03 and is repaid by 2029-08, leaves a thin buffer. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on clearance), pay-to-play, full pro rata and a Corvia clean-up before closing. At $70M pre-money the new Series B would own 28.9% after the Series A's broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution (the bridge adds 8.1%) and 3x would need $398M; capping the Series A at 1.5x lowers that to about $350M, against $596M at the ask. Waiting is the alternative: the 510(k) response is due in December 2026, clearance is guided for Q1 2027 and the waiver application for Q3 2027, so a 2027 entry pays more but buys retired regulatory risk. The company had $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30, six months at $1.15M a month and the 2027-01-29 target close, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts amortising in 2027-03. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the valuation range: the 2029 plan is unaudited, the grant dates of the 5.2M options are not disclosed and Truvian's valuation is an aggregator estimate [S1, S125].

The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle. Three risks decide the outcome — utilisation, capillary troponin and the CLIA waiver — and the recommendation prices the last two while assuming the first.

### A placement returns value only above five panels a day

The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers; the independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme running point-of-care chemistry and haematology at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months from three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight — the top of the supported range, not its centre — with 40% on the bear and 15% on the bull. The mechanism is the placement: three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site, four panels a day reaches only 1.1-2.3x LTV:CAC against the 3:1 a direct salesforce needs, and the 3:1 arrives at 5.9. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so 402 analyzers would consume $4.0-14.3M of the round — which means the plan's 300 sites are a marketing cost, not a franchise. [S1, S148]

### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024, against a 124-day goal it missed, and sets a 112-day goal for FY2025; a December 2026 answer plus the 139-day average points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry-panel figure is the 510(k) database's total time, not FDA days. The bear case's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request; the base rate alone points to May 2027. A second request pushes the decision into the second half of 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster. I put a 45-55% probability on clearance later than June 2027 and a 30% probability on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a troponin-panel pre-submission answer and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. [S97, S92, S69, S72, S147]

### The pivotal study is the first honest test of the assay

The only clinical evidence is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, with six results excluded for insufficient sample or cartridge error and 96.1% categorical agreement with no direction for the five discordant results. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, so a true value on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of ±23%. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due in Q2 2027, is the first test of the two variables that caused the exclusions. I put a 30-40% probability on it failing to show acceptable agreement at the cutoff and a 15-20% probability of outright failure; failure removes troponin, the chest-pain use case and the $12.47 code, takes 50-65% off equity value and leaves a four-analyte heart-failure product, not the acute-cardiac platform the price assumes. [S1, S68, S70]

### Reimbursement is priced at 2026 rates everywhere in this report

CMS's preliminary calendar-2027 fee schedule lowers 1,171 of 1,528 laboratory codes, with Chemistry 16% lower and cuts phased at no more than 15% a year through 2029. On that path the five-code panel falls from $71.38 to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029, and the clinic's contribution per $33.40 cartridge falls from $37.98 to $10.43; the $650 monthly fee then costs 62 panels of contribution rather than 17. That is a -15% to -25% equity-value risk, and it compounds with CLIA: until a waiver, the 300 sites planned for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity laboratories. The quality system is the other exposure: ISO 13485 is uncertified while the QMSR has required an ISO-based system since 2026-02-02. Geopolitics does not bind: buyers are American and the EU is closed until CE marking after 2028. [S149, S82, S71]

### The structure caps the upside, and the scenarios misprice both tails

The 19.96% overhang is a cap-table cost; the preference stack is larger. The $76.8M stack ($36.3M senior B and B-1, $36.0M participating Series A, $4.5M seed) plus the $9.4M Corvia put absorb the first $86.2M, so 3x on the $30M new money needs a $546M exit, $435M returns 2.35x, and 3x on the $36.3M B plus B-1 class needs $518M, against a clearing price of $100M for a cleared, waived platform. The 15% bull case's $400-500M exit is 4-5x the clearing price; even $250-350M returns only 1.3-1.9x. The bear is a return of capital: a $50-100M sale covers the $36.3M preference and returns 1.0-1.2x. Weighted 45% base, 40% bear and 15% bull — 0.45 × 1.25x + 0.40 × 1.1x + 0.15 × 2.4x — the expected return is 1.35x over 4.5 years, a 6.9% IRR at $140M, and 2.0x and 16.4% at $70M. [S99, S126, S100]

### Survival is not the same as returns

A 30% revenue miss takes 2029 revenue to $55.0M, worth $70.4M at 2.5x discounted three years — at or below the $76.8M preference stack, so the Series B returns 1.0-1.2x and the common is close to zero. Doubling CAC to $51,200-102,400 makes 402 analyzers cost $20.6-41.2M to place, more than the round, and cuts LTV:CAC to 0.15-0.3x at observed use. A market 50% smaller removes the strategic premium, -20% of exit value. Financing is tighter: $6.9M at $1.15M a month runs out on 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close, and a six-month delay needs $7.0M of bridge plus the first $166,667 Bluestem payment. Diligence: the FDA letter, the IDE basis for 41 paid sites, the CM-1 change-of-control clause, the Corvia put cap, VD-2 on appeal and ten billing sites' panels per day. Abbott holds a waived menu, and a bundled $20-25 cartridge removes the wedge. Deck p.1 carries a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools claiming no verification is needed and a rating is approved — a document-integrity finding, no evidential weight. Every deck-only claim remains unverified; no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignment or FDA decision record for Vantelle was retrieved. [S1, S147, S143, S144]

At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and with the Series A's uncapped participating preference the $30M Series B needs $596M of exit proceeds to return 3x and $1.79B to return 10x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, company-reported and unverified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 6 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,938 characters)
Vantelle's product addresses a real gap in clinic care, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts do not yet support a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque. Four of six board seats are filled today; the Series B seat is Meridian's and the independent seat is vacant. Finance has been run by a part-time interim CFO since March 2026; ISO 13485 certification is absent, audit booked Q1 2027; the lead 510(k) has been under an FDA information request since 2026-08-21; and the deck discloses neither the HIPAA business-associate architecture for HL7/FHIR transfer nor the IDE/IRB basis for 41 paid evaluation sites. Geopolitics is not material: US-only revenue. Labour and environmental exposure is not material at 64 employees and a pilot line. Each gap is fixable; together they make the $15M milestone capital, not a Q1 2027 bet. Company figures are unverified. [S1]

### Two founder seats are not the problem; the empty independent seat is

Two founder directors of six is not control. The gap is the vacant independent seat, no disclosed audit committee and a part-time CFO at a company running an FDA submission, waiver study and scale-up. The CFO left in February 2026; the interim has been part-time since March. Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly burn, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts 30 principal payments in March 2027, one month after close. The gap is a pricing issue: the controls are thinner than the $170M valuation implies. Require a mutually agreed independent director, an audit committee with a financial expert, a permanent CFO within six months and monthly reporting on cash, FDA correspondence and quality metrics. These figures are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### The Corvia royalty is small until it meets an exit

The 3% cartridge royalty goes to Corvia, 60% owned by Vantelle, where CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22% — 0.66% of cartridge sales. Every $10M of cartridge revenue carries $300,000 of royalty, $120,000 to the 40% minority and $66,000 to the CTO. The exit is the larger issue: the minority may put its 40% at fair value on an acquisition, $9.4M capitalising 3% of FY2029 plan revenue at 10x. It ranks ahead of the Series B and should reduce the price. Require disinterested approval and a fairness opinion of the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and cap-table disclosure. These terms are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### Quality culture is the open file

ISO 13485 certification is absent and FDA's QMSR has required an ISO 13485-based system since 2026-02-02. The regulatory vice-president who prepared the 510(k) left in September 2025; her successor joined in November 2025, two months before filing. The Q5 sends results to the clinic EHR over Wi-Fi using HL7 and FHIR, making Vantelle a vendor that creates, receives and transmits PHI for a covered entity. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 5 by Lead Analyst, 8,985 characters)
Vantelle clears the first test and fails the third. The need is real: a clinic without a laboratory waits one to three days for a cardiac or metabolic send-out, and a five-analyte finger-stick panel that returns a result in twelve minutes removes that wait. The capability is defensible as packaging and manufacturing, not as assay science, and for perhaps 12-24 months. The economics do not scale at the only documented utilisation: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day (company-reported, unverified) against the eight the 2028 plan assumes. Because the third fails, $140M buys a plan whose 3x case needs $546M of exit proceeds, 5.5 times the $100M a cleared, waived point-of-care platform fetched in April 2026. Wait for the 510(k) and the first billing-enabled data, or invest at $60-80M with the structure repaired [S1].

The evaluation programme is real commercial evidence: 41 sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, 55 analyzers and 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days, all company-reported and unverified. The clinic's economics are documented: the CY2026 fee schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes, against $33.40 realised, leaving $37.98 a panel before the $650 monthly fee. But only a full-menu order clears the cartridge. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes pay $32.12; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23 against a $38 list, a $20.77 loss. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts Chemistry 16%, taking the five-code panel to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029 and the clinic's contribution to $10.43, when the fee equals 62 panels of margin [S154, S149].

No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge: Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and the granted on-board-calibrator patent runs to 2040 (company-reported, unverified). The assay evidence is weaker. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, against the IFCC's <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%; the study is 640 venous samples from 128 patients, run by company staff at one site, with six excluded results and no capillary-versus-venous comparison. The five-assay reader patent received a final rejection in 2026-07 and is on appeal, and the freedom-to-operate opinion excludes the troponin chemistry [S68].

The deck's own operating data undo the revenue plan. Fifty-five analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in the January-September 2026 average (deck p.7; FY2025 volume not disclosed) — 30.5 per analyzer-month, 1.22 a day on 300 operating days — against 8.0 assumed from 2028, a 6.5-fold gap. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month, so the 2026 rate is roughly double, and the step to $3.5M normalised FY2026 revenue reflects a larger installed base, not per-analyzer growth. Three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 per placement, against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site; the model needs 5.9 panels a day at today's cost, 4.2 at the $7.50 target, for a 3:1 LTV:CAC. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so the 300-site plan is a marketing cost, not a franchise. The counter-case is that evaluation analyzers are investigational and results never reach care, so their use is a floor; a billing-enabled clinic has a reason to run more. The first commercial quarter must prove it [S1, S148].

Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint: 2.5x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M is $8.8M; the FY2029 plan at 2.5x discounted three years is $100.5M; capital invested is $51.5M, or 2.7x the ask. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — with the Series A participating at 23.75% above the stack, and the Corvia 40% put adds $9.4M ahead of the B. The new $30M is flat at 1.00x to a $206M exit, needs $376M for 2x, $546M for 3x and $1.74B for 10x. QuidelOrtho paid $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics on 2026-04-20, Roche paid $295M plus up to $55M for LumiraDx, and QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales [S126].

The company, the $140M pre-money and the $8M insider commitment assume a Q1 2027 clearance, a 2027 waiver, eight panels a day and a $2.4B market. Our view differs on the variables that set the level rather than the timing: utilisation and price. The evidence is internal — 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in the January-September 2026 average, a $368M cartridge market at observed use rather than $2.4B, a 139-day FY2024 average to decision against a 124-day goal, and a waiver pathway with no troponin-I precedent. The thesis is consensus on the need and the strategic logic, non-consensus on price. The decision tree has four branches. Invest now at $140M: no, because the expected return is 1.35x over 4.5 years, a 6.9% IRR. Pass: only if the waiver is refused for the cardiac analyte, which would leave a four-analyte heart-failure product and take 50-65% off equity value. Wait for milestone: yes, the default — the December 2026 answer, clearance, a waiver pre-submission accepted and ten billing sites' panels per day would retire the three unknowns. Invest with conditions: at $60-80M pre-money, $15M at close and $15M on clearance, the Series A capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior B, pay-to-play and full pro-rata, the Corvia put capped or converted, and a permanent CFO, independent director and ISO 13485 certificate before closing; at $70M the new money owns 28.9% and 3x needs $348M, or $301M with the Series A capped [S149, S126, S97].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, 7,567 characters)
Vantelle scores below the threshold for a lead at the ask and inside the range for a wait-for-milestone position. The score is not a verdict on the technology: the need and the team sit in the middle of the scale. It is a verdict on evidence — a product short of its own menu, a regulatory path with no waived cardiac precedent, and unit economics that fail at the company's own utilisation. The recommendation is Wait for milestone: no cheque at the ask, a conditional offer at a lower pre-money, and a re-underwrite when clearance, the waiver pre-submission and the first billing cohort report.

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market need and addressable demand | 15% | 6 | Real clinical need and 41 paying evaluation sites; but the $2.4B SAM is 6.5x observed use, and only the 60.3% traditional urgent-care segment can carry the full-menu economics, which supports $222M | S1 (unverified), S79 |
| Product and technical evidence | 20% | 4 | Five-in-one finger-stick packaging is first-of-kind in the US; troponin at 11.8% CV fails the IFCC <10% benchmark, no capillary data, reader patent on final rejection | S68, S1 (unverified) |
| Regulatory pathway and quality system | 20% | 3 | 2026-08-21 information request pending, 139-day FY2024 average total time to decision against a 124-day goal, no troponin-I waiver precedent, ISO 13485 uncertified | S97, S72, S147, S71 |
| Business model and unit economics | 15% | 3 | 1.22 panels per analyzer-day against 8.0 modelled; three-year LTV $15,621 against $25,600-51,200 CAC; 5.9 panels needed for 3:1 | S1 (unverified), S148 |
| Financial plan and capital efficiency | 10% | 3 | 6.0 months of cash at $1.15M a month; $40M needed against a $30M round; $2.4M of FY2026E revenue cannot ship in FY2026 | S1 (unverified) |
| Team and execution | 10% | 5 | Emergency-physician CEO and microfluidics CTO; thin regulatory, quality and finance bench with turnover in 2025-26 | S1 (unverified) |
| Governance and structure | 5% | 4 | 19.96% post-money option overhang, $9.4M Corvia put ahead of the B, part-time interim CFO, independent board seat vacant | S1 (unverified) |
| Valuation and exit | 5% | 2 | $140M ask against a $50-100M methods cluster; $546M needed for 3x against a $100M 2026 clearing price | S1 (unverified), S126 |

The weighted average is 3.9 (0.9 + 0.8 + 0.6 + 0.45 + 0.3 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.1) [S1]. Two dimensions can re-rate the company quickly. A clearance certificate and an accepted waiver pre-submission would lift regulatory from 3 to 6-7; a first billing cohort above 5.9 panels a day would lift unit economics from 3 to 7 and the composite by roughly two points. Conversely, a second information request or a capillary troponin failure takes product and regulatory to 2 and the composite down by about a point and a half. The asymmetry is why price matters more than the score: on company-reported terms (unverified), the probability-weighted return is 1.35x over 4.5 years at the ask and 2.0x at $70M, a 6.9% versus 16.4% IRR. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores 7 at most, and none of these has one that supports more.

### How the recommendation changes under the downside

The base case carries a 45% weight: clearance in H2 2027, a waiver in 2028-29, 2-4 panels a day and a $150-250M sale in 2031 returning 1.0-1.5x. The bear case carries 40%: a second request or a capillary-troponin deficiency, a refused or deferred waiver, and a $50-100M distressed sale in 2028 that still covers the $36.3M senior preference on company-reported terms, unverified, and returns 1.0-1.2x [S126].

### The branches that change the recommendation

The recommendation becomes Pass if the waiver is refused for the cardiac analyte or the pivotal study misses the cutoff, because both remove the chest-pain use case and 50-65% of equity value. It becomes Invest with conditions at a lower pre-money if clearance arrives and the first billing cohort exceeds four panels a day. It becomes Invest now only if the FDA letter proves documentation-only and a billing cohort prints above six panels — neither of which is in the file today [S68].

### Position sizing and what can be lost

Private company sizing: no capital at the ask. At a lower pre-money, split the cheque between close and clearance, with a follow-on reserve sized to the plan's funding gap rather than to the initial cheque. The maximum loss is not the full commitment: a distressed sale still covers the senior preference, and a full loss needs no sale at all or a price below the preference stack after the Bluestem loan and the Corvia put. The terms that make the cheque worth writing are a board seat, pay-to-play, full pro-rata, a utilisation covenant tied to the second tranche and disinterested approval of the Corvia royalty and put.

### Next diligence and conditions

The diligence list decides the re-underwrite: the FDA information request; the pivotal protocol and any capillary-versus-venous data; the Corvia LLC agreement and the change-of-control clause; the Bluestem rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor's purchase, payment and return terms; the first billing sites' panels per day and collected revenue per cartridge; and the quality-system certificate. The conditions for any cheque are a price at or below the agreed cap, the tranche structure, the Series A participation capped, the Corvia put capped or converted, a permanent CFO and an independent director before closing, and the certificate before launch. A clearance slip or a later waiver filing reopens the price, not just the timetable.

The methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint: the forward-looking methods and the capital-invested floor range from $51.5M to $100.5M, and the $140M ask is 2.7x the $51.5M of capital raised with no clearance and no waiver. The 5.5x peer median is the wrong benchmark: it is set by diversified tools companies whose point-of-care assets sit inside larger franchises, whereas QuidelOrtho, the only pure-play point-of-care cardiac franchise, has de-rated from 2.9x at FY2022 to 1.7x at FY2025 and 0.4x now. A single-product private company with two assays filed should not be underwritten above the best-capitalised public point-of-care franchise in a de-rating market. Werfen, Siemens Healthineers, Roche Diagnostics and Nova Biomedical are not SEC filers or not listed, so their multiples are not disclosed [S1, S22, S28, S67].

### The Series A takes the first $36M and 23.75% above the stack

Our waterfall on the company-reported terms, unverified:

| Exit value | Series A total | New Series B | Multiple on $30M | B-1 | Common, seed, options, warrants | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | $48.8M | $30.0M | 1.00x | $6.3M | $45.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| $197M | $62.3M | $30.0M | 1.00x | $6.3M | $89.0M | S1 (unverified) |
| $256M | $76.3M | $30.0M | 1.00x | $8.4M | $131.9M | S1 (unverified) |
| $426M | $116.7M | $60.0M | 2.00x | $16.8M | $223.2M | S1 (unverified) |
| $596M | $157.1M | $90.0M | 3.00x | $25.1M | $314.4M | S1 (unverified) |

The row formula is Series A = $36.0M + 23.75% × (exit − $9.4M Corvia − $76.8M stack), with the new Series B receiving the greater of $30.0M or 17.65% of the same balance. On the company-reported, unverified terms the mechanism is value transfer: the B-1's 25% discount and the Series A's uncapped participation leave the new B with $64.2M of a $450M bull-case exit (2.14x) while its class receives $82.1M (2.26x); above a $256M exit each dollar above the stack is worth 17.65 cents to the new B, not the 22.6 cents its class ownership implies. On the deck's fully diluted 52.2M shares, the new $30M is flat at 1.00x from a $45.7M exit (the $9.4M Corvia put plus the $36.3M B/B-1 preference) to $256M; 1.21x needs $292M, 2x $426M, 3x $596M and 10x $1.79B. The Series A takes $122.4M at the $450M bull case, 27.2% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership; the earlier $130.8M at $435M applied its participation above its own $36M preference rather than above the full stack and is corrected here. The Corvia 40% minority put, estimated at $9.4M (3% of FY2029 revenue capitalised at 10x, 40% share; $7.5-11.3M at 8-12x), ranks ahead of the Series B [S1].

### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.22 per analyser per operating day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — a 6.5-fold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's revenue, 41-site and 92% reorder claims are company-reported, unverified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met; adding the $5.0M Bluestem principal, which starts at $0.167M a month in 2027-03 and is repaid by 2029-08, leaves a thin buffer. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on clearance), pay-to-play, full pro rata and a Corvia clean-up before closing. At $70M pre-money the new Series B would own 28.9% after the Series A's broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution (the bridge adds 8.1%) and 3x would need $398M; capping the Series A at 1.5x lowers that to about $350M, against $596M at the ask. Waiting is the alternative: the 510(k) response is due in December 2026, clearance is guided for Q1 2027 and the waiver application for Q3 2027, so a 2027 entry pays more but buys retired regulatory risk. The company had $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30, six months at $1.15M a month and the 2027-01-29 target close, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts amortising in 2027-03. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the valuation range: the 2029 plan is unaudited, the grant dates of the 5.2M options are not disclosed and Truvian's valuation is an aggregator estimate [S1, S125].
