The realistic buyer set is five point-of-care incumbents, and the most recent cleared-and-waived platform sold for $100M in April 2026; at $140M pre-money the Series B needs $596M of exit proceeds for 3x, a price only a strategic paying for the platform rather than the plan can justify. The asset being bought is not the 64-person team or the evaluation programme but the cartridge IP — the granted on-board-calibrator patent (VD-1) and the exclusively licensed Corvia sealing film (CM-1) — plus the two-assay 510(k), the CLIA-waiver path and 41 evaluation sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico (company-reported, unverified). QuidelOrtho, Abbott, Roche Diagnostics and Werfen all sell point-of-care instruments into US urgent-care or hospital channels, and none sells a five-analyte finger-stick panel run by clinic staff. Abbott's i-STAT and Afinion platforms cover blood gas, chemistries and cardiometabolic tests; QuidelOrtho's Triage and Sofia cover cardiac and rapid immunoassay; Roche bought LumiraDx's multi-assay platform in 2024; Werfen's acute-care line sits beside hemostasis and autoimmunity. Each has a gap Vantelle would fill, but each also has a platform to protect [S1, S22, S67, S91, S119, S126].

### Who buys, for which asset and when

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale (asset) | Timing | Likelihood (our judgement) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | QuidelOrtho | Triage and Sofia installed base in urgent care; bought LEX for $100M in 2026-04 | 2029-2031 | Medium-low | S22, S126 |
| Trade sale | Abbott | i-STAT and Afinion base; needs a staff-run finger-stick cardiac panel | 2029-2031 | Medium | S67 |
| Trade sale | Roche Diagnostics | LumiraDx platform since 2024; primary-care immunoassay menu | 2029-2031 | Low-medium | S91 |
| Trade sale | Werfen | Acute-care and hemostasis channel; paid $2.0B for Immucor in 2023 | 2029-2031 | Low | S119 |
| Trade sale | Thermo Fisher or Hologic | Molecular point-of-care only (Mesa $450M, Mobidiag $795M) | 2029-2031 | Low | S120, S122 |
| IPO | Nasdaq | Needs $100M+ revenue and a waived menu | 2030 or later | Low | S125 |
| Distressed asset sale | Financial or strategic buyer | IP and 510(k) only, no commercial franchise | 2027-2028 if the waiver fails | Medium in the failure case | S117, S126 |

The strongest fit is QuidelOrtho, which owns Triage and Sofia in exactly the urgent-care channel Vantelle targets and paid $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics in April 2026 — but it also carries $1.1B of enterprise value and negative free cash flow, and it has just bought the molecular platform it wanted. Abbott is the largest and most able payer, with i-STAT Alinity and Afinion already placed in clinics, yet that installed base gives it a build-or-buy option that argues for a lower price. Roche and Werfen are European buyers with no US ownership limits in diagnostics, but Roche has owned a LumiraDx platform since 2024 and Werfen's recent acquisitions have been in transfusion and hemostasis. The practical conclusion is a five-buyer, not a competitive, auction. The strategic logic is scale economics: a waived five-analyte cartridge at $38 lets an incumbent serve the 11,400 US urgent-care sites that cannot staff a laboratory, and the clinic bills the payer under existing test codes rather than to Vantelle. The counter-evidence is that Abbott or QuidelOrtho can add a waived cardiac assay to its own installed analyser and reach the same sites without buying Vantelle, and that a pre-clearance asset carries 510(k) and CLIA risk an acquirer can wait out at no cost. That substitution risk, not the buyer count, is the central threat to a $596M exit [S2, S22, S67, S91, S119, S126].

### The precedent record prices a cleared platform well below the ask

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho–LEX Diagnostics | 2026 | $100M cash | not disclosed; platform pre-commercial | S126 |
| Roche–LumiraDx point-of-care platform | 2023-24 | $295M plus up to $55M | ~3.4x annualised H1 2023 revenue of $86.4M | S91, S117 |
| Quidel–Ortho Clinical Diagnostics | 2021-22 | ~$6.0B | ~3.3x 2020 revenue of $1.8B | S121, S123 |
| Werfen–Immucor | 2022-23 | ~$2.0B | not disclosed | S119 |
| Roche–GenMark Diagnostics | 2021 | $1.8B | not disclosed | S118 |
| Hologic–Mobidiag | 2021 | $795M enterprise value | not disclosed | S122 |
| Thermo Fisher–Mesa Biotech | 2021 | $450M plus up to $100M | not disclosed | S120 |
| LumiraDx de-SPAC listing | 2021 | $3.0B valuation, cut from $5.0B | sold for $295M in 2023-24 | S130, S131 |
| Cue Health Chapter 7 | 2024 | zero equity value | after $480M+ raised | S129, S132 |

The 2026 clearing price is $100M for a platform that already had FDA clearance and a CLIA waiver when it was sold; LumiraDx, a commercial multi-assay platform with 30 assays and H1 2023 revenue of $43.2M, sold its point-of-care technology for $295M after its lenders took control. The larger 2021 prices — $450M plus milestones for Mesa, $795M for Mobidiag, $1.8B for GenMark — were set in the COVID-era liquidity window, and the market has since re-rated: QuidelOrtho itself trades at 0.4x EV/Sales, down 50.9% over 12 months. A $596M exit would be 6.0x the LEX price and 2.0x the LumiraDx assets, a 2021-style price in a 2026 market [S117, S118, S120, S121, S122, S123, S126].

### What the company must be worth after preferences and the minority put

| Entry pre-money | New Series B ownership | Exit needed for 3x on $30M | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | 17.6% | $596M | S1 (unverified) |
| $100M | 22.8% | $481M | S1 (unverified) |
| $70M | 28.9% | $398M | S1 (unverified) |
| $50M | 35.5% | $339M | S1 (unverified) |

The thresholds use 17.65% at $140M; B and B-1 together own 22.6%. At $140M the new Series B needs $596M for 3x, $568M for 3x on the $36.28M class (the B-1's 25% discount makes the class cheaper to return than the new money) and $1.79B for 10x; the $596M corrects two earlier figures: $435M credited the B-1 preference to the new $30M, and $546M applied the Series A participation above its own preference and left out the Corvia put. The 40% Corvia minority put, estimated at $9.4M and ranking ahead of the Series B, is deducted before the stack, as is any remaining Bluestem debt (nil by 2029-08, $4-5M in a 2027-28 sale). The company's unverified FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue at 2.5x gives $196M; after the Corvia put, the new Series B returns 1.0x, below the 4.93% yield on the 10-year Treasury on 2026-10-30. Only a 2031 bull case of $150M revenue at 25% EBITDA and 12x EV/EBITDA reaches $450M, and that returns 2.1x, a 16.4% internal rate of return over five years, not the 24.6% a 3x return needs. Entry price is the first lever: at $70M pre-money the Series B owns 28.9% after anti-dilution and 3x needs $398M; capping the Series A at 1.5x lowers that to about $350M. The Series A's participation is the second: it takes $122.4M at the $450M bull case, 27.2% of proceeds, on 23.8% ownership [S1].

### The base rate is poor and the IPO is not a route

LumiraDx listed at a $3B de-SPAC valuation in September 2021 after cutting the deal from $5B, then sold its technology for $295M; Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after raising $480M+; Truvian, the best-capitalised private comparable, raised $294M, cleared 12 analytes by 2026-01-12 and is still private in October 2026, eleven years after founding. An IPO is not a route before 2029-2030: the company has two assays filed, no CLIA waiver and $3.5M of normalised FY2026 revenue (company-reported, unverified), while the 2025 US medtech IPO market absorbed eight deals raising $1.8B in total. The realistic holding period is 4-5 years — 510(k) clearance in Q1 2027, a waiver decision in 2028, commercial scale in 2028-2029 and a sale in 2030-2031 [S124, S125, S127, S129, S130, S131, S132].

### Policy tests and liquidity

No US foreign-ownership limit applies to diagnostics, so Werfen (Spain) or Roche (Switzerland) would face HSR antitrust review and FDA quality-system scrutiny but not CFIUS on national-security grounds; sanctions and export controls do not bind, and the binding constraints are the 510(k) and the CLIA waiver. The Corvia put and the 3% related-party royalty to a company 22%-owned by the CTO are closing frictions an acquirer will price and may require to be cleaned up before signing; the put is a debt-like claim of $9.4M at 10x the FY2029 royalty. Liquidity: a $15M cheque at $140M pre-money buys 8.8% of the company; a 3x return is $45M, which on a $300-500M IPO with a 25-30% float would be 30-60% of the tradable stock, so an IPO exit would require a discounted block trade after the 180-day lock-up. A trade sale pays cash at closing, typically with 10-15% escrow and an earn-out. At $140M the entry is incompatible with the exit evidence; the same company at $60-80M pre-money, with the Series A participation capped and the cheque tranched, is a defensible wait-for-milestone investment [S1, S119, S125].

The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle. Three risks decide the outcome — utilisation, capillary troponin and the CLIA waiver — and the recommendation prices the last two while assuming the first.

### A placement returns value only above five panels a day

The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 per analyzer-month and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers and 610 cartridges, and the one independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme running point-of-care chemistry and haematology at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months from three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case's 50% weight on 2-4 panels per analyzer-day is the top of the supported range, not its centre; a 45% base, 40% bear and 15% bull split prices the benchmark better. The mechanism is the placement: three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site, four panels a day reaches only 1.1-2.3x LTV:CAC against the 3:1 a direct salesforce needs, and the 3:1 arrives at 5.9. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so 402 analyzers would consume $4.0-14.3M of the round before any annuity matures — which means the plan's 300 sites are a marketing cost, not yet a franchise. [S1, S148]

### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 request restarts the 90-day clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027; the file sits in the Chemistry panel, which averages 175 days from acceptance to decision against a 90-day goal, and denials average 337 days. A second request pushes clearance into the second half of 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in the third quarter of 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in the first quarter of 2028 at the earliest and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The dual 510(k)-plus-waiver submission the plan does not use is the faster route on one 180-day goal. I put a 45-55% probability on clearance later than June 2027 and a 30% probability on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a pre-submission answer accepting a troponin panel, and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. [S69, S72, S92, S147]

### The pivotal study is the first honest test of the assay

The only clinical evidence is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, with six results excluded for insufficient sample or cartridge error and 96.1% categorical agreement that does not disclose the direction of the five discordant troponin results. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, so a true value on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of ±23%. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due in the second quarter of 2027, is the first test of the two variables that caused the exclusions. I put 30-40% on it failing to show acceptable agreement at the cutoff and 15-20% on outright failure; failure removes troponin, the chest-pain use case and the $12.47 code, takes 50-65% off equity value and leaves a four-analyte heart-failure product, not the acute-cardiac platform the price assumes. [S1, S68, S70]

### Reimbursement is priced at 2026 rates everywhere in this report

CMS's preliminary calendar-2027 fee schedule lowers 1,171 of 1,528 laboratory codes, with Chemistry — troponin, creatinine, potassium and HbA1c — 16% lower and cuts phased at no more than 15% a year through 2029. On that path the five-code panel falls from $71.38 to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029, and the clinic's contribution per $33.40 cartridge falls from $37.98 to $10.43; the $650 monthly fee then costs 62 panels of contribution rather than 17. That is a demand risk worth -15% to -25% of equity value, and it compounds with CLIA: until a waiver, the 300 sites planned for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics the pitch addresses. The quality system is the other exposure — ISO 13485 uncertified while the QMSR has required an ISO-based system since 2026-02-02 — but geopolitics does not bind: revenue, buyers and comparables are American and the EU is closed until CE marking after 2028. [S149, S82, S71]

### The structure caps the upside, and the scenarios misprice both tails

The 19.96% overhang is a counted cap-table cost; the larger cost is the preference stack. The Series B's $36.3M senior 1x, the Series A's $36.0M participating preference and the $9.4M Corvia put absorb the first $76.8M of exit value, so 3x on $30M needs a $435M exit and 3x on the $36.3M of B plus B-1 needs $518M, against a clearing price of $100M for a cleared, waived platform. The bull case's 20% to a $400-500M exit is 4-4.5x that clearing price; 12-15% to $250-350M is defensible. The bear case errs the other way: with a senior 1x preference a $50-100M distressed sale returns 1.0-1.2x to the Series B, not 0.3-0.8x, which needs an exit below $25M after the $5.0M Bluestem loan and the $9.4M put. The economics do not scale at the only documented utilisation: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day (company-reported, unverified) against the eight the 2028 plan assumes. Because the third fails, $140M buys a plan whose 3x case needs $546M of exit proceeds, 5.5 times the $100M a cleared, waived point-of-care platform fetched in April 2026. Wait for the 510(k) and the first billing-enabled data, or invest at $60-80M with the structure repaired [S1].

The evaluation programme is real commercial evidence: 41 sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, 55 analyzers and 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days, all company-reported and unverified. The clinic's economics are documented: the CY2026 fee schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes, against $33.40 realised, leaving $37.98 a panel before the $650 monthly fee. But only a full-menu order clears the cartridge. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes pay $32.12; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23 against a $38 list, a $20.77 loss. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts Chemistry 16%, taking the five-code panel to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029 and the clinic's contribution to $10.43, when the fee equals 62 panels of margin [S154, S149].

No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge: Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and the granted on-board-calibrator patent runs to 2040 (company-reported, unverified). The assay evidence is weaker. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, against the IFCC's <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%; the study is 640 venous samples from 128 patients, run by company staff at one site, with six excluded results and no capillary-versus-venous comparison. The five-assay reader patent received a final rejection in 2026-07 and is on appeal, and the freedom-to-operate opinion excludes the troponin chemistry [S68].

The deck's own operating data undo the revenue plan. Fifty-five analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in the January-September 2026 average (deck p.7; FY2025 volume not disclosed) — 30.5 per analyzer-month, 1.22 a day on 300 operating days — against 8.0 assumed from 2028, a 6.5-fold gap. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month, so the 2026 rate is roughly double, and the step to $3.5M normalised FY2026 revenue reflects a larger installed base, not per-analyzer growth. Three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 per placement, against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site; the model needs 5.9 panels a day at today's cost, 4.2 at the $7.50 target, for a 3:1 LTV:CAC. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so the 300-site plan is a marketing cost, not a franchise. The counter-case is that evaluation analyzers are investigational and results never reach care, so their use is a floor; a billing-enabled clinic has a reason to run more. The first commercial quarter must prove it [S1, S148].

Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint: 2.5x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M is $8.8M; the FY2029 plan at 2.5x discounted three years is $100.5M; capital invested is $51.5M, or 2.7x the ask. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — with the Series A participating at 23.75% above the stack, and the Corvia 40% put adds $9.4M ahead of the B. The new $30M is flat at 1.00x to a $206M exit, needs $376M for 2x, $546M for 3x and $1.74B for 10x. QuidelOrtho paid $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics on 2026-04-20, Roche paid $295M plus up to $55M for LumiraDx, and QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales [S126].

The company, the $140M pre-money and the $8M insider commitment assume a Q1 2027 clearance, a 2027 waiver, eight panels a day and a $2.4B market. Our view differs on the variables that set the level rather than the timing: utilisation and price. The evidence is internal — 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in the January-September 2026 average, a $368M cartridge market at observed use rather than $2.4B, a 139-day FY2024 average to decision against a 124-day goal, and a waiver pathway with no troponin-I precedent. The thesis is consensus on the need and the strategic logic, non-consensus on price. The decision tree has four branches. Invest now at $140M: no, because the expected return is 1.35x over 4.5 years, a 6.9% IRR. Pass: only if the waiver is refused for the cardiac analyte, which would leave a four-analyte heart-failure product and take 50-65% off equity value. Wait for milestone: yes, the default — the December 2026 answer, clearance, a waiver pre-submission accepted and ten billing sites' panels per day would retire the three unknowns. Meridian should not lead Vantelle's Series B at $140M pre-money. The company has the strongest clinical wedge in the file — a five-analyte finger-stick panel aimed at clinics that cannot staff a laboratory, 41 paid evaluation sites and a 92% reorder rate — and a first-of-kind packaging position that incumbents would pay for. It also has the weakest operating proof: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series and FY2025 volume not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day against the eight its 2028 plan needs; 27,600 cumulative shipments since March 2024 average 890 a month, so the 2026 rate is roughly double the programme average, and on flat per-analyzer use the $0.9M rise to $3.5M normalised FY2026 revenue has to come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue, which the deck does not decompose; troponin runs at 11.8% CV against the IFCC's <10% standard; the 510(k) is under an information request and a CLIA waiver has no cardiac precedent; and $6.9M of cash is six months at the current burn. Evidence confidence is medium on the regulatory calendar and low on the commercial plan, because every operating figure is company-reported and no public record of the company, its 510(k) or its patents exists [S1].

The price is the second problem. Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint against the $140M ask and $170M post-money. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — and the Series A then participates at 23.75% of value above it, so the $30M Series B needs $546M of proceeds for 3x and $376M for 2x, while the April 2026 clearing price for a cleared, waived platform was $100M. The company's own 2029 plan, at 2.5x revenue, is worth $196M and returns the new money 1.0x. Only a strategic premium to $400-500M makes the bull case work, and that is 4-5x the clearing price [S126].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 7 by Valuation Analyst, 8,991 characters)
The realistic buyer set is five point-of-care incumbents, and the most recent cleared-and-waived platform sold for $100M in April 2026; at $140M pre-money the Series B needs $596M of exit proceeds for 3x, a price only a strategic paying for the platform rather than the plan can justify. The asset being bought is not the 64-person team or the evaluation programme but the cartridge IP — the granted on-board-calibrator patent (VD-1) and the exclusively licensed Corvia sealing film (CM-1) — plus the two-assay 510(k), the CLIA-waiver path and 41 evaluation sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico (company-reported, unverified). QuidelOrtho, Abbott, Roche Diagnostics and Werfen all sell point-of-care instruments into US urgent-care or hospital channels, and none sells a five-analyte finger-stick panel run by clinic staff. Abbott's i-STAT and Afinion platforms cover blood gas, chemistries and cardiometabolic tests; QuidelOrtho's Triage and Sofia cover cardiac and rapid immunoassay; Roche bought LumiraDx's multi-assay platform in 2024; Werfen's acute-care line sits beside hemostasis and autoimmunity. Each has a gap Vantelle would fill, but each also has a platform to protect [S1, S22, S67, S91, S119, S126].

### Who buys, for which asset and when

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale (asset) | Timing | Likelihood (our judgement) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | QuidelOrtho | Triage and Sofia installed base in urgent care; bought LEX for $100M in 2026-04 | 2029-2031 | Medium-low | S22, S126 |
| Trade sale | Abbott | i-STAT and Afinion base; needs a staff-run finger-stick cardiac panel | 2029-2031 | Medium | S67 |
| Trade sale | Roche Diagnostics | LumiraDx platform since 2024; primary-care immunoassay menu | 2029-2031 | Low-medium | S91 |
| Trade sale | Werfen | Acute-care and hemostasis channel; paid $2.0B for Immucor in 2023 | 2029-2031 | Low | S119 |
| Trade sale | Thermo Fisher or Hologic | Molecular point-of-care only (Mesa $450M, Mobidiag $795M) | 2029-2031 | Low | S120, S122 |
| IPO | Nasdaq | Needs $100M+ revenue and a waived menu | 2030 or later | Low | S125 |
| Distressed asset sale | Financial or strategic buyer | IP and 510(k) only, no commercial franchise | 2027-2028 if the waiver fails | Medium in the failure case | S117, S126 |

The strongest fit is QuidelOrtho, which owns Triage and Sofia in exactly the urgent-care channel Vantelle targets and paid $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics in April 2026 — but it also carries $1.1B of enterprise value and negative free cash flow, and it has just bought the molecular platform it wanted. Abbott is the largest and most able payer, with i-STAT Alinity and Afinion already placed in clinics, yet that installed base gives it a build-or-buy option that argues for a lower price. Roche and Werfen are European buyers with no US ownership limits in diagnostics, but Roche has owned a LumiraDx platform since 2024 and Werfen's recent acquisitions have been in transfusion and hemostasis. The practical conclusion is a five-buyer, not a competitive, auction. The strategic logic is scale economics: a waived five-analyte cartridge at $38 lets an incumbent serve the 11,400 US urgent-care sites that cannot staff a laboratory, and the clinic bills the payer under existing test codes rather than to Vantelle. The counter-evidence is that Abbott or QuidelOrtho can add a waived cardiac assay to its own installed analyser and reach the same sites without buying Vantelle, and that a pre-clearance asset carries 510(k) and CLIA risk an acquirer can wait out at no cost. That substitution risk, not the buyer count, is the central threat to a $596M exit [S2, S22, S67, S91, S119, S126].

### The precedent record prices a cleared platform well below the ask

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho–LEX Diagnostics | 2026 | $100M cash | not disclosed; platform pre-commercial | S126 |
| Roche–LumiraDx point-of-care platform | 2023-24 | $295M plus up to $55M | ~3.4x annualised H1 2023 revenue of $86.4M | S91, S117 |
| Quidel–Ortho Clinical Diagnostics | 2021-22 | ~$6.0B | ~3.3x 2020 revenue of $1.8B | S121, S123 |
| Werfen–Immucor | 2022-23 | ~$2.0B | not disclosed | S119 |
| Roche–GenMark Diagnostics | 2021 | $1.8B | not disclosed | S118 |
| Hologic–Mobidiag | 2021 | $795M enterprise value | not disclosed | S122 |
| Thermo Fisher–Mesa Biotech | 2021 | $450M plus up to $100M | not disclosed | S120 |
| LumiraDx de-SPAC listing | 2021 | $3.0B valuation, cut from $5.0B | sold for $295M in 2023-24 | S130, S131 |
| Cue Health Chapter 7 | 2024 | zero equity value | after $480M+ raised | S129, S132 |

The 2026 clearing price is $100M for a platform that already had FDA clearance and a CLIA waiver when it was sold; LumiraDx, a commercial multi-assay platform with 30 assays and H1 2023 revenue of $43.2M, sold its point-of-care technology for $295M after its lenders took control. The larger 2021 prices — $450M plus milestones for Mesa, $795M for Mobidiag, $1.8B for GenMark — were set in the COVID-era liquidity window, and the market has since re-rated: QuidelOrtho itself trades at 0.4x EV/Sales, down 50.9% over 12 months. A $596M exit would be 6.0x the LEX price and 2.0x the LumiraDx assets, a 2021-style price in a 2026 market [S117, S118, S120, S121, S122, S123, S126].

### What the company must be worth after preferences and the minority put

| Entry pre-money | New Series B ownership | Exit needed for 3x on $30M | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | 17.6% | $596M | S1 (unverified) |
| $100M | 22.8% | $481M | S1 (unverified) |
| $70M | 28.9% | $398M | S1 (unverified) |
| $50M | 35.5% | $339M | S1 (unverified) |

The thresholds use 17.65% at $140M; B and B-1 together own 22.6%. At $140M the new Series B needs $596M for 3x, $568M for 3x on the $36.28M class (the B-1's 25% discount makes the class cheaper to return than the new money) and $1.79B for 10x; the $596M corrects two earlier figures: $435M credited the B-1 preference to the new $30M, and $546M applied the Series A participation above its own preference and left out the Corvia put. The 40% Corvia minority put, estimated at $9.4M and ranking ahead of the Series B, is deducted before the stack, as is any remaining Bluestem debt (nil by 2029-08, $4-5M in a 2027-28 sale). The company's unverified FY2029 plan of $78.5M revenue at 2.5x gives $196M; after the Corvia put, the new Series B returns 1.0x, below the 4.93% yield on the 10-year Treasury on 2026-10-30. Only a 2031 bull case of $150M revenue at 25% EBITDA and 12x EV/EBITDA reaches $450M, and that returns 2.1x, a 16.4% internal rate of return over five years, not the 24.6% a 3x return needs. Entry price is the first lever: at $70M pre-money the Series B owns 28.9% after anti-dilution and 3x needs $398M; capping the Series A at 1.5x lowers that to about $350M. The Series A's participation is the second: it takes $122.4M at the $450M bull case, 27.2% of proceeds, on 23.8% ownership [S1].

### The base rate is poor and the IPO is not a route

LumiraDx listed at a $3B de-SPAC valuation in September 2021 after cutting the deal from $5B, then sold its technology for $295M; Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after raising $480M+; Truvian, the best-capitalised private comparable, raised $294M, cleared 12 analytes by 2026-01-12 and is still private in October 2026, eleven years after founding. An IPO is not a route before 2029-2030: the company has two assays filed, no CLIA waiver and $3.5M of normalised FY2026 revenue (company-reported, unverified), while the 2025 US medtech IPO market absorbed eight deals raising $1.8B in total. The realistic holding period is 4-5 years — 510(k) clearance in Q1 2027, a waiver decision in 2028, commercial scale in 2028-2029 and a sale in 2030-2031 [S124, S125, S127, S129, S130, S131, S132].

### Policy tests and liquidity

No US foreign-ownership limit applies to diagnostics, so Werfen (Spain) or Roche (Switzerland) would face HSR antitrust review and FDA quality-system scrutiny but not CFIUS on national-security grounds; sanctions and export controls do not bind, and the binding constraints are the 510(k) and the CLIA waiver. The Corvia put and the 3% related-party royalty to a company 22%-owned by the CTO are closing frictions an acquirer will price and may require to be cleaned up before signing; the put is a debt-like claim of $9.4M at 10x the FY2029 royalty. Liquidity: a $15M cheque at $140M pre-money buys 8.8% of the company; a 3x return is $45M, which on a $300-500M IPO with a 25-30% float would be 30-60% of the tradable stock, so an IPO exit would require a discounted block trade after the 180-day lock-up. A trade sale pays cash at closing, typically with 10-15% escrow and an earn-out. At $140M the entry is incompatible with the exit evidence; the same company at $60-80M pre-money, with the Series A participation capped and the cheque tranched, is a defensible wait-for-milestone investment [S1, S119, S125]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 6 by Red Team Analyst, 8,964 characters)
The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle. Three risks decide the outcome — utilisation, capillary troponin and the CLIA waiver — and the recommendation prices the last two while assuming the first.

### A placement returns value only above five panels a day

The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers; the independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme running point-of-care chemistry and haematology at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months from three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight — the top of the supported range, not its centre — with 40% on the bear and 15% on the bull. The mechanism is the placement: three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site, four panels a day reaches only 1.1-2.3x LTV:CAC against the 3:1 a direct salesforce needs, and the 3:1 arrives at 5.9. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so 402 analyzers would consume $4.0-14.3M of the round — which means the plan's 300 sites are a marketing cost, not a franchise. [S1, S148]

### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024, against a 124-day goal it missed, and sets a 112-day goal for FY2025; a December 2026 answer plus the 139-day average points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry-panel figure is the 510(k) database's total time, not FDA days. The bear case's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request; the base rate alone points to May 2027. A second request pushes the decision into the second half of 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster. I put a 45-55% probability on clearance later than June 2027 and a 30% probability on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a troponin-panel pre-submission answer and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. [S97, S92, S69, S72, S147]

### The pivotal study is the first honest test of the assay

The only clinical evidence is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, with six results excluded for insufficient sample or cartridge error and 96.1% categorical agreement with no direction for the five discordant results. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, so a true value on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of ±23%. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due in Q2 2027, is the first test of the two variables that caused the exclusions. I put a 30-40% probability on it failing to show acceptable agreement at the cutoff and a 15-20% probability of outright failure; failure removes troponin, the chest-pain use case and the $12.47 code, takes 50-65% off equity value and leaves a four-analyte heart-failure product, not the acute-cardiac platform the price assumes. [S1, S68, S70]

### Reimbursement is priced at 2026 rates everywhere in this report

CMS's preliminary calendar-2027 fee schedule lowers 1,171 of 1,528 laboratory codes, with Chemistry 16% lower and cuts phased at no more than 15% a year through 2029. On that path the five-code panel falls from $71.38 to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029, and the clinic's contribution per $33.40 cartridge falls from $37.98 to $10.43; the $650 monthly fee then costs 62 panels of contribution rather than 17. That is a -15% to -25% equity-value risk, and it compounds with CLIA: until a waiver, the 300 sites planned for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity laboratories. The quality system is the other exposure: ISO 13485 is uncertified while the QMSR has required an ISO-based system since 2026-02-02. Geopolitics does not bind: buyers are American and the EU is closed until CE marking after 2028. [S149, S82, S71]

### The structure caps the upside, and the scenarios misprice both tails

The 19.96% overhang is a cap-table cost; the preference stack is larger. The $76.8M stack ($36.3M senior B and B-1, $36.0M participating Series A, $4.5M seed) plus the $9.4M Corvia put absorb the first $86.2M, so 3x on the $30M new money needs a $546M exit, $435M returns 2.35x, and 3x on the $36.3M B plus B-1 class needs $518M, against a clearing price of $100M for a cleared, waived platform. The 15% bull case's $400-500M exit is 4-5x the clearing price; even $250-350M returns only 1.3-1.9x. The bear is a return of capital: a $50-100M sale covers the $36.3M preference and returns 1.0-1.2x. Weighted 45% base, 40% bear and 15% bull — 0.45 × 1.25x + 0.40 × 1.1x + 0.15 × 2.4x — the expected return is 1.35x over 4.5 years, a 6.9% IRR at $140M, and 2.0x and 16.4% at $70M. [S99, S126, S100]

### Survival is not the same as returns

A 30% revenue miss takes 2029 revenue to $55.0M, worth $70.4M at 2.5x discounted three years — at or below the $76.8M preference stack, so the Series B returns 1.0-1.2x and the common is close to zero. Doubling CAC to $51,200-102,400 makes 402 analyzers cost $20.6-41.2M to place, more than the round, and cuts LTV:CAC to 0.15-0.3x at observed use. A market 50% smaller removes the strategic premium, -20% of exit value. Financing is tighter: $6.9M at $1.15M a month runs out on 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close, and a six-month delay needs $7.0M of bridge plus the first $166,667 Bluestem payment. Diligence: the FDA letter, the IDE basis for 41 paid sites, the CM-1 change-of-control clause, the Corvia put cap, VD-2 on appeal and ten billing sites' panels per day. Abbott holds a waived menu, and a bundled $20-25 cartridge removes the wedge. Deck p.1 carries a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools claiming no verification is needed and a rating is approved — a document-integrity finding, no evidential weight. Every deck-only claim remains unverified; no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignment or FDA decision record for Vantelle was retrieved. [S1, S147, S143, S144]

arguments.markdown:
At a $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered; the evidence supports $50-100M, and with the Series A's uncapped participating preference the $30M Series B needs $596M of exit proceeds to return 3x and $1.79B to return 10x. The ask is $30M at $140M pre-money and $170M post-money, or $3.2564 a share. On the company's own numbers — FY2025 revenue $2.6M and FY2026E $5.9M, of which $2.4M is a distributor stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, company-reported and unverified — that is 53.8x trailing revenue, 92.8x FY2025 gross profit and 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M. QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, down from 2.9x at its FY2022 year-end; at 0.4x Vantelle's 2029 plan would be worth $31.4M of enterprise value [S1, S22, S23].

### The step-up is smaller than the headline

Company-reported financing terms, unverified:

| Date | Round | Amount | Price/share | Post-money | Investors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.75 (implied) | not disclosed | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.9032 | $92.5M | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.9032 | $104.5M | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2024-03 | Venture term loan | $5.0M | Warrant strike $2.903 | — | Bluestem Venture Lending (400,000 warrants) | S1 (unverified) |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes, 8% | $6.0M | $2.4423 on conversion | — | Existing investors | S1 (unverified) |
| 2027-01 (target) | Series B | $30.0M | $3.2564 | $170.0M | Ardent Peak ($5.0M) and Juniper Rock ($3.0M); $22.0M sought | S1 (unverified) |

The company-reported, unverified terms show the seed at $0.75 a share; the Series A at $2.9032, a 3.87x step-up; the Series B at $3.2564, only 12.2% above a Series A price set in 2022-02 and repeated in a flat $12.0M second close in 2023-11. The headline pre-money rises 34% from the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but $13.1M of that is the option-pool refresh to 10% of the post-money: existing holders' effective pre-money is $126.9M, a 21% uplift over 2.9 years, or 6.9% a year. Existing shares fall from 100% to 69.7% — 7.7 points of pool refresh, 4.9 points of bridge and 17.6 points of new Series B — taking the founders from 30.8% to 21.5%, the seed from 16.5% to 11.5% and the Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%; granted options, the unallocated pool and warrants total 20.8% of the post-money. Insiders are committing $8.0M of the $30.0M [S1].

### What the price assumes

Our calculations on company-reported projections, unverified:

| Method | Inputs | Implied pre-money | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2025A revenue | $2.6M × 2.5x | $6.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2026E ex-stocking | $3.5M × 2.5x | $8.8M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2026E ex-stocking at peer median | $3.5M × 5.5x | $19.3M | S1 (unverified), S28 |
| FY2028P revenue, discounted 2 years | $41.0M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25² | $65.6M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P revenue, discounted 3 years | $78.5M × 2.5x ÷ 1.25³ | $100.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| FY2029P earnings, discounted 3 years | $9.0M × 15x ÷ 1.30³ | $61.4M | S1 (unverified) |
| Capital invested | $40.5M equity + $11.0M debt | $51.5M (ask = 2.7x) | S1 (unverified) |

| Company | EV | EV/Sales, TTM | P/E, TTM | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| QuidelOrtho | $1.1B | 0.4x | n/m | Closest point-of-care and cardiac comparable | S22, S23 |
| Abbott | $211.7B | 4.7x | 29.7x | i-STAT, i-STAT Alinity, Afinion | S33, S67 |
| Danaher | $184.2B | 7.2x | 38.1x | Cepheid point-of-care molecular | S34, S35 |
| Bio-Rad | $9.5B | 3.7x | 45.3x | Life-science tools | S36, S37 |
| Thermo Fisher | $295.6B | 6.2x | 36.8x | Mesa Biotech point-of-care molecular | S38, S39 |
| Peer median | — | 5.5x | 37.4x | Diversified tools, not pure-play point of care | S28 |

The methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint: the forward-looking methods and the capital-invested floor range from $51.5M to $100.5M, and the $140M ask is 2.7x the $51.5M of capital raised with no clearance and no waiver. The 5.5x peer median is the wrong benchmark: it is set by diversified tools companies whose point-of-care assets sit inside larger franchises, whereas QuidelOrtho, the only pure-play point-of-care cardiac franchise, has de-rated from 2.9x at FY2022 to 1.7x at FY2025 and 0.4x now. A single-product private company with two assays filed should not be underwritten above the best-capitalised public point-of-care franchise in a de-rating market. Werfen, Siemens Healthineers, Roche Diagnostics and Nova Biomedical are not SEC filers or not listed, so their multiples are not disclosed [S1, S22, S28, S67].

### The Series A takes $36M plus 23.75% above the stack

Our waterfall on the company-reported terms, unverified:

| Exit value | Series A total | New Series B | Multiple on $30M | B-1 | Common, seed, options, warrants | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $140M | $48.8M | $30.0M | 1.00x | $6.3M | $45.5M | S1 (unverified) |
| $197M | $62.3M | $30.0M | 1.00x | $6.3M | $89.0M | S1 (unverified) |
| $256M | $76.3M | $30.0M | 1.00x | $8.4M | $131.9M | S1 (unverified) |
| $426M | $116.7M | $60.0M | 2.00x | $16.8M | $223.2M | S1 (unverified) |
| $596M | $157.1M | $90.0M | 3.00x | $25.1M | $314.4M | S1 (unverified) |

The row formula is Series A = $36.0M + 23.75% × (exit − $9.4M Corvia − $76.8M stack), with the new Series B receiving the greater of $30.0M or 17.65% of the same balance. On the company-reported, unverified terms the mechanism is value transfer: the B-1's 25% discount and the Series A's uncapped participation leave the new B with $64.2M of a $450M bull-case exit (2.14x) while its class receives $82.1M (2.26x); above a $256M exit each dollar above the stack is worth 17.65 cents to the new B, not the 22.6 cents its class ownership implies. On the deck's fully diluted 52.2M shares, the new $30M is flat at 1.00x from a $45.7M exit (the $9.4M Corvia put plus the $36.3M B/B-1 preference) to $256M; 1.21x needs $292M, 2x $426M, 3x $596M and 10x $1.79B. The Series A takes $122.4M at the $450M bull case, 27.2% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership; the earlier $130.8M at $435M applied its participation above its own $36M preference rather than above the full stack and is corrected here. The Corvia 40% minority put, estimated at $9.4M (3% of FY2029 revenue capitalised at 10x, 40% share; $7.5-11.3M at 8-12x), ranks ahead of the Series B [S1].

### Four findings that change the price

FY2026E is internally inconsistent: $2.7M of revenue in January-September 2026 leaves $3.2M for the fourth quarter, but $2.4M of that is a stocking order that ships only on clearance, which the deck dates to Q1 2027; normalised FY2026 revenue is $3.5M. Utilisation is the larger problem: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers is 1.22 per analyser per operating day, against the eight assumed from 2028 — a 6.5-fold gap on which the $78.5M FY2029 revenue depends. The deck's revenue, 41-site and 92% reorder claims are company-reported, unverified, and the $30M covers the plan's cumulative 2027-2028 net losses of $22.5M only if the plan is met; adding the $5.0M Bluestem principal, which starts at $0.167M a month in 2027-03 and is repaid by 2029-08, leaves a thin buffer. The deck also carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidential weight [S1].

### The price and terms that make the deal work

The deal becomes attractive at $60-80M pre-money, half the ask, with the Series A's participation capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior Series B, the $30M tranched ($15M at close, $15M on clearance), pay-to-play, full pro rata and a Corvia clean-up before closing. At $70M pre-money the new Series B would own 28.9% after the Series A's broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution (the bridge adds 8.1%) and 3x would need $398M; capping the Series A at 1.5x lowers that to about $350M, against $596M at the ask. Waiting is the alternative: the 510(k) response is due in December 2026, clearance is guided for Q1 2027 and the waiver application for Q3 2027, so a 2027 entry pays more but buys retired regulatory risk. The company had $6.9M of cash on 2026-09-30, six months at $1.15M a month and the 2027-01-29 target close, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts amortising in 2027-03. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the valuation range: the 2029 plan is unaudited, the grant dates of the 5.2M options are not disclosed and Truvian's valuation is an aggregator estimate [S1, S125].

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window to 2027-02-17. ### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: the deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month as its "2026 average" across 41 sites and 55 analyzers (p.7) and repeats 41 a site a month for 2026 (p.9). The deck does not state the months covered; with figures as of 2026-09-30 the average cannot cover more than January-September 2026, and neither 2026 unit volume nor FY2025 cartridge units is disclosed, so no growth rate can be computed. On that average, 1,680 cartridges is 41.0 a site a month (1.35 a site a calendar day) and 30.5 an analyzer-month (1.02 a calendar day; 1.22 on 300 operating days) against the 8 a day the model assumes from 2028. At 1.35 a site a day and $31 a cartridge, a site produces $15,275 a year, so $78.5M needs 5,150 sites, not 300; at the model's two analyzers and eight panels, 300 sites produce $44.6M and $78.5M needs 528. The 2028 line needs 2,680 sites at observed use or 276 at full model utilisation, against 300 planned by end-2027. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order that ships on clearance, a late-March 2027 event — 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026; the 61% FY2026E gross margin also sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below cost, so either an undisclosed line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. From $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of Bluestem principal from April 2027: $10.9M remains at end-2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, pointing to an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

Company data, unverified: the distributor letter is the only commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme; it is non-binding, from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner, so it belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridges and contract development are second curves consuming the same engineering team; the Irish entity and CE mark are a distraction.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |

| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second request | Second request in H1 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level; CV below 10% | Categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |

| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount in single digits against 300 sites | S1, unverified |

Counter-evidence deserves weight: the regulatory vice-president has a record of FDA clearances, the evaluation pipeline and reorder rate are unusual for an investigational device, and a documentation-only request could clear faster. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the FDA request asked and what the answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers; and whether the distributor letter carries a minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 13 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,943 characters)
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales, and expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that; it turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

### The clinic's margin rests on the one assay that carries 55% of the payment

CMS's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets these national limitation amounts:

Against the $33.40 cartridge a five-code clinic keeps $37.98 a panel and Vantelle takes 47% of the Medicare payment. Natriuretic peptide alone is $39.26, 55% of it: a clinic billing four codes without that assay collects $32.12 and loses $1.28 a cartridge, and troponin plus potassium collects $17.23 and loses $16.17. At the observed 30.5 panels a month the five-code clinic earns $1,158.39 and keeps $508.39 after the $650 fee — the fee equals 17.1 panels — and $8,465.20 at 240 panels: trivial at scale, 56% of the margin at adoption. The payment is not fixed: CMS may cut a test by up to 15% a year in 2027-2029, and three such years would take this panel to $43.84 and the clinic's spread to $10.44 [S154, S160]. FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, about 567 before 2026. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full panel reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a modest panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume; the first billing-enabled sites' run rate; and panel mix, since troponin plus potassium alone do not cover a cartridge.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 7 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,968 characters)
Vantelle has six months of cash, company-reported and unverified, and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. The $22.5M of 2027-2028 net losses plus launch capex and working capital exceed the $32.3M left at close, so the plan needs $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. It starts at $6.9M on 2026-09-30 and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months — left at the 2027-01-29 close. The burn is understated: $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M is the P&L loss with no capex or working capital in it.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue — 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each, twice the 300 sites targeted for end-2027. The cost target fails the same test. Two million cartridges a year is what buys the $7.50 cost; at the 1.2 panels a day the 41 evaluation sites actually ran, an analyzer consumes about 360 cartridges a year, so that volume needs 5,500 analyzers, and the 402 analyzers behind the 300-site plan produce 147,000 cartridges, 7% of it, where the only disclosed cost is $16.20 and the margin 48%, not 76%. Capital efficiency is poor: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, dated Q1 2027, under a non-binding LOI. At $33.40 a cartridge it is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M; with $2.7M booked in nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's use of funds has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and debt service after 2027-03 is $210,000 a month, 18% of burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting at 75% of the $3.2564 round price into 2,571,392 shares, 4.9% of the post-round count [S1, S22].

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's $12.0M outflow takes it to negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit and the shortfall is $8-10M. The base keeps clearance in Q1 2027, consistent with the one review-time series in the FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report: average total time to decision (FDA days plus company time) was 127 days for the FY2023 receipt cohort and 139 days for FY2024, the last closed cohort; 112 days is the FY2025 goal, not an outcome, and FY2025 is open. Its file is slower already: the 2026-08-21 additional-information request stops the clock, the company plans to answer in December 2026 within the 180-day limit to 2027-02-17, and the response resumes the 90-day FDA clock. That leaves a first-cycle decision in Q1 2027; the stress adds a second information request and a full 90-day cycle, moving clearance to Q3 2027, the CLIA waiver to 2028 and utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M: a two-quarter slip moves the shortfall from $8-10M to $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M post-round count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S97, S140].

These are capital-intensive instrument economics: growth is bought with placed hardware and funded receivables, so the faster Vantelle sells, the more cash it burns before the cartridge annuity arrives. The variable that moves the outcome is panels per analyzer-day, not sites, price or the clearance date: clearance moves the clock, utilisation sets the level. The counter-case is discretionary burn: cutting cost and slowing the site ramp would close most of the gap, and a distributor that finances inventory would remove much of the working-capital need, so the shortfall is about this plan, not survival. Size the round larger or tranche it on clearance and utilisation, and price for a further financing before breakeven. Diligence: the Bluestem rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor's payment, return and pricing terms; and the Tempe line's cost and yield at launch volumes. Confidence is high on the arithmetic, which reconciles to the deck, and medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates with no auditor, quarterly statements or covenant disclosure.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 13 by Market Analyst, 8,995 characters)
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites delivered in the 2026 year to date, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the cartridge volume behind it are company-provided, unaudited and not independently confirmed [S1, S67].

The site count is the only input that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% hospital-owned or affiliated and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 in September 2024. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of that range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base near 2,400. The volume is dated precisely: deck p.7 heads its column "Cartridges a month, 2026 average", and with all figures as of 2026-09-30 that is a 2026 year-to-date average, not an FY2025 average; FY2025 monthly volume is not disclosed. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, so 1,680 is roughly double the program-to-date rate. Across 55 analyzers it is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days, or 1.35 per site-day; the model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap. That gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at $31 realised, almost exactly the model's eight and six times the observed rate. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M; it has 41. Its 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used [S79, S80, S78, S1].

| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. A $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17%-83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M figure is still 60% of the smallest estimate. Abbott's global Point of Care line generated $606M in FY2025, four times the claimed US SAM [S93, S94, S96, S67].

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. CMS's CY2026 national limitation amounts pay $71.38 for all five codes; without the natriuretic peptide the other four cap at $32.12, below the $38 list and the $33.40 realised price. HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collect $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; troponin plus potassium collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation supports $222M, not $368M [S154, S79, S1].

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico hold 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived laboratories. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 faces FDA's 150-day decision goal from filing and a 180-day window to answer an information request, so no waiver before 2028 is the realistic case; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base. The first 510(k), filed 2026-05-18, drew an additional-information request on 2026-08-21 with a response planned for December 2026; FDA's own series reports average total time to decision of 127 days in FY2023 and 139 days in FY2024 against goals of 128 and 124, with FY2025 pending at 2025-09-30, so Q1 2027 clearance is plausible but company-provided. Ownership consolidation compounds the friction: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024. The market systems are US; exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents; the EU is blocked until CE marking after 2028 [S81, S72, S97, S95, S1].

The commercial path is unproven at each step, on company-provided and unverified evidence. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation program two and a half years later; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. The deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, installed EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price evidence. What would settle it: signed contracts with start dates, the first ten sites' CLIA certificates and EHR go-live dates, and collected revenue per cartridge by payer [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more. Medicare is the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until then, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price.

Dr. Albescu's founder-market fit is specific: an emergency physician who practised from 2011 to 2017 and then spent a year as medical director at a diagnostics company has lived the 1-3 day reference-lab wait the Q5 is designed to remove, and the 41-site evaluation program shows she can sell a pilot into clinics. But 8.6 years as CEO have not produced a clearance, a CLIA waiver or a launch, and no prior P&L, FDA submission or distribution build is publicly disclosed; the CV itself is unverified. Dr. Lindqvist supplies the technical depth — a 2012 bioengineering PhD, four years in microfluidics at Pellucid, then Corvia and the CM-1 patent — but he is a single point of failure: inventor of the licensed sealing patent, owner of 22% of the licensor and recipient of 0.66% of cartridge sales through it. [S99]

The regulatory function is the thinnest part of the executive bench. Grace Oyelaran joined in 2025-11 and is credited with 14 510(k) clearances across 2009-2025 at Meridale Medical, a claim public records cannot check because the FDA database lists applicants, not individuals. She owns three parallel workstreams: the troponin I and HbA1c file and its additional-information response, the ISO 13485 audit booked for Q1 2027 (not yet certified), and the CLIA-waiver application planned for Q3 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report gives one 510(k) series, total time to decision: 127 days in FY2023 against a 128-day goal and 139 days in FY2024 against a 124-day goal (missed); the FY2025 goal is 112 days and that cohort was still pending at 2025-09-30. The 90-day clock is FDA days and stops while an additional-information request is open, so a December 2026 answer plus 90 FDA days is late March 2027 at the earliest, while the FY2024 total-time average of 139 days points to mid-May 2027; the 175-day Chemistry-panel figure used elsewhere in this report is a 510(k)-database average, not FDA's. QuidelOrtho describes CLIA-waiver requirements as "onerous", so a Q1 2027 clearance after a 2026-12 response and a Q3 2027 waiver are plausible only if the first AI is the last one. [S97, S92, S22]

The commercial bench is sized for a pilot, not a launch. Luis Arrellano's 17 years at Tavora Health Systems map onto Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, but 9 sales and support staff cover 41 sites; 300 sites would put 33 on each person, with only a non-binding distributor LOI as bridge. QuidelOrtho carries more than 2,500 sales, service and marketing employees. Manufacturing is thin at the top: 18 staff run the Tempe pilot line, no VP Manufacturing or VP Quality is named, ISO 13485 certification is ahead, and the 9-month shelf life rests on 6 months of data. Cue Health's 2024 warning letter found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes and a lot-release AQL that could allow a failure rate above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, putting its 9-month stability claim at issue after clearance, not before it. [S99, S22]

The finance and control gap is the easiest to fix and the most revealing. Darnell Whitcombe has been interim CFO on a part-time basis since 2026-03, after the prior CFO left in 2026-02, and the deck discloses no prior operating CFO role or fundraise for him; a $30M round, a $5.0M amortising loan and a $2.4M stocking order on a non-binding LOI are represented by a fractional adviser, unverified. Six months of cash makes the hire urgent. What public records confirm is narrow: the company name returns no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignee or FDA decision record, and near matches — Vanta Diagnostics and Vantelle Health Group, LLC, filed in California on 2026-09-09 — are different entities. Reference checks are therefore the only verification available: Meridale Medical for the 14 clearances and the 2025-09 departure; Tavora Health Systems for Arrellano's quota; Quillon Diagnostics for Albescu; Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock for board behaviour; Southwest Clinical Supply on whether the LOI names sites. [S99]

The team is a clinical-insight team that has not yet become a regulatory-and-commercial execution team. Who invents is clear — the CTO and the CM-1 patent; who sells is clear — the VP Commercial and the evaluation base; who raises is the CEO. The missing hires are a full-time CFO, VP Manufacturing and Operations, VP Quality, a clinical-affairs lead for the pivotal study, a payer lead and an EU PRRC for Ireland. The lead check should be conditioned on the CFO and Quality hires, verified clearance history and an independent director before money moves.

The need is real: a clinic without a laboratory waits one to three days for a cardiac or metabolic send-out, and a five-analyte finger-stick panel that returns a result in twelve minutes removes that wait. The capability is defensible as packaging and manufacturing, not as assay science, and for perhaps 12-24 months. The economics do not scale at the only documented utilisation: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day (company-reported, unverified) against the eight the 2028 plan assumes. Because the third fails, $140M buys a plan whose 3x case needs $596M of exit proceeds, 6.0 times the $100M a cleared, waived point-of-care platform fetched in April 2026. Wait for the 510(k) and the first billing-enabled data, or invest at $60-80M with the structure repaired [S1].

The evaluation programme is real commercial evidence: 41 sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, 55 analyzers and 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days, all company-reported and unverified. The clinic's economics are documented: the CY2026 fee schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes, against $33.40 realised, leaving $37.98 a panel before the $650 monthly fee. But only a full-menu order clears the cartridge. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes pay $32.12; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23 against a $38 list, a $20.77 loss. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts Chemistry 16%, taking the five-code panel to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029 and the clinic's contribution to $10.43, when the fee equals 62 panels of margin [S154, S149].

No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge: Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and the granted on-board-calibrator patent runs to 2040 (company-reported, unverified). The assay evidence is weaker. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, against the IFCC's <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%; the study is 640 venous samples from 128 patients, run by company staff at one site, with six excluded results and no capillary-versus-venous comparison. Meridian should not lead Vantelle's Series B at $140M pre-money. The company has the strongest clinical wedge in the file — a five-analyte finger-stick panel aimed at clinics that cannot staff a laboratory, 41 paid evaluation sites and a 92% reorder rate — and a first-of-kind packaging position that incumbents would pay for. It also has the weakest operating proof: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series and FY2025 volume not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day against the eight its 2028 plan needs; 27,600 cumulative shipments since March 2024 average 890 a month, so the 2026 rate is roughly double the programme average, and on flat per-analyzer use the $0.9M rise to $3.5M normalised FY2026 revenue has to come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue, which the deck does not decompose; troponin runs at 11.8% CV against the IFCC's <10% standard; the 510(k) is under an information request and a CLIA waiver has no cardiac precedent; and $6.9M of cash is six months at the current burn. Evidence confidence is medium on the regulatory calendar and low on the commercial plan, because every operating figure is company-reported and no public record of the company, its 510(k) or its patents exists [S1].

The price is the second problem. Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint against the $140M ask and $170M post-money. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — and the Series A then participates at 23.75% of value above it, so the $30M Series B needs $596M of proceeds for 3x and $426M for 2x, while the April 2026 clearing price for a cleared, waived platform was $100M. The consensus — the company plan, the $8M insider commitment, a Q1 2027 clearance and a 2027 waiver — is not the report's view. We differ on utilisation and price, not on the need: a first billing cohort above six panels a day and a waiver path accepted by FDA would re-rate the asset, while a second information request, a capillary troponin failure or a refused cardiac waiver would take most of the equity value. If Meridian wants exposure before the proofs arrive, the only defensible structure is a lower pre-money, a tranched cheque, a capped Series A participation and a capped or converted Corvia put [S72].

Three risks decide the outcome: utilisation staying near the evaluation rate, the capillary troponin study failing at the cutoff, and a waiver refused or deferred for the cardiac analyte. Vantelle scores below the threshold for a lead at the ask and inside the range for a wait-for-milestone position. The score is not a verdict on the technology: the need and the team sit in the middle of the scale. It is a verdict on evidence — a product short of its own menu, a regulatory path with no waived cardiac precedent, and unit economics that fail at the company's own utilisation. The recommendation is Wait for milestone: no cheque at the ask, a conditional offer at a lower pre-money, and a re-underwrite when clearance, the waiver pre-submission and the first billing cohort report.
