arguments.markdown:
Vantelle clears the first test and fails the third. The need is real: a clinic without a laboratory waits one to three days for a send-out, and a five-analyte finger-stick panel that returns a result in twelve minutes removes that wait. The capability is defensible as packaging and manufacturing, not as assay science, and for perhaps 12-24 months. The economics do not scale at the only documented utilisation: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day (company-reported, unverified) against the eight the 2028 plan assumes. Because the third fails, $140M buys a plan whose 3x case needs $596M of exit proceeds, 6.0 times the $100M a cleared, waived point-of-care platform fetched in April 2026. Wait for the 510(k) and the first billing-enabled data, or invest at $60-80M with the structure repaired [S1].

The evaluation programme is real commercial evidence: 41 sites in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, 55 analyzers and 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days, company-reported and unverified. Clinic economics: the CY2026 fee schedule pays $71.38 for the five codes, against $33.40 realised, leaving $37.98 a panel before the $650 monthly fee. But only a full-menu order clears the cartridge. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes pay $32.12; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23 against a $38 list, a $20.77 loss. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule proposes a 16% Chemistry cut, capped at 15% a year, taking the panel to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029; the clinic keeps $10.43 [S154, S149].

No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge: Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per test group, and the granted on-board-calibrator patent runs to 2040 (company-reported, unverified). The assay evidence is weaker. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, against the IFCC's <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%; the study is 640 venous samples from 128 patients, run by company staff at one site, with six excluded results and no capillary-versus-venous comparison. The five-assay reader patent was finally rejected in 2026-07 and is on appeal; the freedom-to-operate opinion excludes the troponin chemistry [S68].

The deck's own operating data undo the revenue plan. Fifty-five analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in the January-September 2026 average (deck p.7; FY2025 volume not disclosed) — 30.5 per analyzer-month, 1.22 a day on 300 operating days — against 8.0 assumed from 2028, a 6.5-fold gap. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month, so the 2026 rate is roughly double, and the step to $3.5M normalised FY2026 revenue reflects a larger installed base. The financial section's FY2025 split of 20,160 evaluation and 23,952 research-use cartridges is a reconstruction from that average, not a disclosed series; 44,112 FY2025 cartridges cannot coexist with 27,600 shipped to date, so the 1.22 rate and the FY2025 margin bridge carry low confidence until a shipment ledger arrives. Three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 per placement, against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site; the model needs 5.9 panels a day at today's cost, 4.2 at the $7.50 target, for a 3:1 LTV:CAC. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so the 300-site plan is a marketing cost, not a franchise. The counter-case is that evaluation analyzers are investigational and results never reach care, so their use is a floor; a billing-enabled clinic has a reason to run more. The first commercial quarter must prove it [S1, S148].

Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint: 2.5x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M is $8.8M; the FY2029 plan at 2.5x discounted three years is $100.5M; capital invested is $51.5M, or 2.7x the ask. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — with the Series A participating at 23.75% above the stack, and the Corvia 40% put adds $9.4M ahead of the B. The new $30M is flat at 1.00x to a $256M exit, needs $426M for 2x, $596M for 3x and $1.79B for 10x. The base case consumes $55-70M before breakeven, not the $30M raised. QuidelOrtho paid $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics on 2026-04-20, Roche paid $295M plus up to $55M for LumiraDx, and QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales [S126].

The company, the $140M pre-money and the $8M insider commitment assume a Q1 2027 clearance, a 2027 waiver, eight panels a day and a $2.4B market. Our view differs on the variables that set the level rather than the timing: utilisation and price. The evidence is internal — 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in the January-September 2026 average, a $368M cartridge market at observed use rather than $2.4B, a 139-day FY2024 average to decision against a 124-day goal, and a waiver pathway with no troponin-I precedent. The thesis is consensus on the need and the strategic logic, non-consensus on price. The decision tree has four branches. Invest now at $140M: no, because the weighted return is 1.17x over 4.5 years, a 3.6% IRR. Pass: only if the waiver is refused for the cardiac analyte, which would leave a four-analyte heart-failure product and take 50-65% off value. Wait for milestone: yes, the default — the December 2026 answer, clearance, a waiver pre-submission accepted and ten billing sites' panels per day would retire the three unknowns. Invest with conditions: at $60-80M pre-money with Meridian's $15M split $7.5M at close and $7.5M on clearance, the Series A capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior B, pay-to-play and pro-rata, the Corvia put capped or converted, and a permanent CFO, independent director and ISO 13485 certificate before closing; at $70M the new money owns 28.9% and 3x needs $398M, or $350M with the Series A capped, lifting the weighted return to 1.40x [S149, S126, S97].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 15% | Q1 2027 clearance; dual 510(k) and waiver accepted; billing sites run 6-8 panels a day; cartridge cost reaches $10 by 2028 | $78.5M of 2029 revenue; $400-500M sale in 2030-31; 2.1x on the $30M at $450M (16.4% IRR) | First billing sites above 6 panels a day; no second FDA request | S1 (unverified), S67, S72 |
| Base | 45% | Clearance in H2 2027 after one more cycle; waiver in 2028-29; 2-4 panels a day; cartridge cost near $12 | 2029 revenue of $25-35M; $150-250M sale in 2031 after a $20-30M inside round; 1.0x on the Series B | Clearance slips past June 2027; waiver filed after Q1 2028 | S1 (unverified), S92, S148 |
| Bear | 40% | Second information request or capillary troponin deficiency; waiver refused or deferred past 2029; utilisation near one panel a day | $50-100M distressed sale in 2028; $36.3M senior preference covered; Series B 1.0x, common near zero | Second FDA request; no waiver pre-submission by mid-2027 | S1 (unverified), S68, S147, S153 |

| Cue Health Chapter 7 | Cautionary | 2021-2024 | $480M+ raised and a cleared product ended in liquidation after a warning letter on unauthorised changes and lot-release failures | S129, S132, S153, S113 |
| QuidelOrtho buys LEX Diagnostics | Pricing | 2026 | $100M cash for a platform already cleared and waived is the current clearing price for the asset Vantelle will hold in 2028 | S126 |
| Truvian Health | Cautionary | 2015-2026 | An estimated $208-294M raised and a CBC cleared only in January 2026, eleven years after founding | S152, S125 |

arguments.markdown:
Meridian should not lead Vantelle's Series B at $140M pre-money. The company has the strongest clinical wedge in the file — a five-analyte finger-stick panel aimed at clinics that cannot staff a laboratory, 41 paid evaluation sites and a 92% reorder rate — and a first-of-kind packaging position that incumbents would pay for. It also has the weakest operating proof: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series and FY2025 volume not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day against the eight its 2028 plan needs; 27,600 cumulative shipments since March 2024 average 890 a month, so the 2026 rate is roughly double the programme average, and on flat per-analyzer use the $0.9M rise to $3.5M normalised FY2026 revenue has to come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue, which the deck does not decompose; the financial section's FY2025 split of 20,160 evaluation and 23,952 research-use cartridges is a reconstruction from that 2026 average, and 44,112 FY2025 cartridges cannot coexist with 27,600 shipped to date, so the 1.22 rate and the FY2025 margin bridge carry low confidence until a shipment ledger arrives; troponin runs at 11.8% CV against the IFCC's <10% standard; the 510(k) is under an information request and a CLIA waiver has no cardiac precedent; and $6.9M of cash is six months at the current burn. Evidence confidence is medium on the regulatory calendar and low on the commercial plan, because every operating figure is company-reported and no public record of the company, its 510(k) or its patents exists [S1].

The price is the second problem. Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint against the $140M ask and $170M post-money. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — and the Series A then participates at 23.75% of value above it, so the $30M Series B needs $596M of proceeds for 3x and $426M for 2x, while the April 2026 clearing price for a cleared, waived platform was $100M. The company's own 2029 plan, at 2.5x revenue, is worth $196M and returns the new money 1.0x. Only a strategic premium to $400-500M makes the bull case work, and that is 4-5x the clearing price [S126].

The consensus — the company plan, the $8M insider commitment, a Q1 2027 clearance and a 2027 waiver — is not the report's view. We differ on utilisation and price, not on the need: a first billing cohort above six panels a day and a waiver path accepted by FDA would re-rate the asset, while a second information request, a capillary troponin failure or a refused cardiac waiver would take most of the equity value. If Meridian wants exposure before the proofs arrive, the only defensible structure is a lower pre-money, a tranched cheque, a capped Series A participation and a capped or converted Corvia put [S72].

Three risks decide the outcome: utilisation staying near the evaluation rate, the capillary troponin study failing at the cutoff, and a waiver refused or deferred for the cardiac analyte. Each has an early warning in the sensitivity analysis and none is priced at the ask. The immediate financial risk is six months of cash against a close that still has to be signed, and a base case that consumes $55-70M, not $30M, before breakeven.

Before any cheque, Meridian's diligence list should obtain the FDA letter and the pivotal protocol, the Corvia LLC agreement and its change-of-control clause, the Bluestem rate and covenants, the distributor's purchase terms, and the first billing cohort's panels per day and collected revenue per cartridge. Those items, not another meeting with management, decide whether the price is defensible or zero.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 13 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,943 characters)
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); it is not a single month, the monthly series is not disclosed, and 41 sites is the count at that date [S1]. Across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028.

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales, and expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line that has never run above 2,000 units a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit, $15,621, does not repay that; it turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day (300 days) | 1.0 | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year cartridge LTV | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC, cartridges only | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels a day for 3:1, fee included | 5.9 at $16.20; 4.2 at $7.50 | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | $0.43M fees; 20,160 cartridges at $33.40/$16.20; analyzer cost excluded | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | 23,952 cartridges at the only disclosed price and cost | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | residual cost; not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | deck p.10; bridge closes only on the 2026-average volume | S1 (unverified) |

### The clinic's margin rests on the one assay that carries 55% of the payment

CMS's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule sets these national limitation amounts:

| Test (CPT code) | CY2026 amount | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | S154; S160 |
| Natriuretic peptide (83880) | $39.26 | S154; S160 |
| Haemoglobin A1c (83036) | $9.71 | S154; S160 |
| Creatinine (82570) | $5.18 | S154; S160 |
| Potassium (84132) | $4.76 | S154; S160 |
| Five-code panel | $71.38 | S154; S160 |

Against the $33.40 cartridge a five-code clinic keeps $37.98 a panel and Vantelle takes 47% of the Medicare payment. Natriuretic peptide alone is $39.26, 55% of it: a clinic billing four codes without that assay collects $32.12 and loses $1.28 a cartridge, and troponin plus potassium collects $17.23 and loses $16.17. At the observed 30.5 panels a month the five-code clinic earns $1,158.39 and keeps $508.39 after the $650 fee — the fee equals 17.1 panels — and $8,465.20 at 240 panels: trivial at scale, 56% of the margin at adoption. The payment is not fixed: CMS may cut a test by up to 15% a year in 2027-2029, and three such years would take this panel to $43.84 and the clinic's spread to $10.44 [S154, S160]. CMS publishes the amounts as a data file rather than on its page; the republication reproduces all five.

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 17.1 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage BNP, CLIA-waived, 25 tests | $789 | $31.56 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### Three businesses are wearing one revenue line

| FY2025 line | $M | Share | Repeatable? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation program: fees and cartridges | 1.1 | 42% | Recurring while the program runs; ends at clearance | S1 (unverified) |
| Research-use cartridges to CROs | 0.8 | 31% | Repeatable, needs no clearance, small market | S1 (unverified) |
| Contract development for one partner | 0.7 | 27% | One-off, single customer | S1 (unverified) |
| Mesa Verde: largest customer, 12 of 41 sites | 0.385 | 15% | 18 of 55 analyzers; 610 of 1,680 cartridges | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Total | 2.6 | 100% | — | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The evaluation line equals 12 months of the 2026 average — $0.43M of fees plus $0.67M of cartridges — which is why it has been read as an FY2025 figure; 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month, about 567 before 2026. The deck gives no FY2025 volume. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4. On flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year at 240 a month — 57 times today's 20,160 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The counter-evidence is structural: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full panel reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a modest panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume; the first billing-enabled sites' run rate; and panel mix, since troponin plus potassium alone do not cover a cartridge.

**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the five-code clinic keeps $508.39 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $71.38 and the cartridge costs the clinic $33.40, so the $650 fee equals 17.1 panels of a $37.98 margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154, S160].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 7 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,968 characters)
Vantelle has six months of cash, company-reported and unverified, and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. The $22.5M of 2027-2028 net losses plus launch capex and working capital exceed the $32.3M left at close, so the plan needs $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. It starts at $6.9M on 2026-09-30 and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months — left at the 2027-01-29 close. The burn is understated: $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M is the P&L loss with no capex or working capital in it.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue — 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each, twice the 300 sites targeted for end-2027. The cost target fails the same test. Two million cartridges a year is what buys the $7.50 cost; at the 1.2 panels a day the 41 evaluation sites actually ran, an analyzer consumes about 360 cartridges a year, so that volume needs 5,500 analyzers, and the 402 analyzers behind the 300-site plan produce 147,000 cartridges, 7% of it, where the only disclosed cost is $16.20 and the margin 48%, not 76%. Capital efficiency is poor: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

| Line item, $M | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | FY2029P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 1.1 | 2.6 | 5.9 | 16.8 | 41.0 | 78.5 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue growth | — | 136% | 127% | 185% | 144% | 91% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Gross margin | 49% | 58% | 61% | 63% | 67% | 71% | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit | 0.5 | 1.5 | 3.6 | 10.6 | 27.5 | 55.7 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Net loss | (9.8) | (12.4) | (14.0) | (16.5) | (6.0) | 9.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Implied operating cost | 10.3 | 13.9 | 17.6 | 27.1 | 33.5 | 46.7 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Revenue excluding the stocking order | — | — | 3.5 | — | — | — | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash at year end | 21.0 | 11.3 | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | S1 (unverified) |

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, dated Q1 2027, under a non-binding LOI. At $33.40 a cartridge it is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M; with $2.7M booked in nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's use of funds has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and debt service after 2027-03 is $210,000 a month, 18% of burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting at 75% of the $3.2564 round price into 2,571,392 shares, 4.9% of the post-round count [S1, S22].

| Metric | FY2025 | FY2026E | Benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Net margin | (477%) | (237%) | QuidelOrtho (41.5%) | S1 (unverified), S22 |
| Burn multiple | 8.3x | 4.2x, or 15.6x ex-stocking order | Series B median 1.4x | S1 (unverified), S134 |
| ROE and ROIC | not meaningful | not meaningful | Accumulated deficit above $36.2M against $40.5M of equity raised | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Receivable days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 55.7 days | S22 |
| Inventory days | not disclosed | not disclosed | QuidelOrtho 145 days | S22 |

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's $12.0M outflow takes it to negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit and the shortfall is $8-10M. The base keeps clearance in Q1 2027, consistent with the one review-time series in the FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report: average total time to decision (FDA days plus company time) was 127 days for the FY2023 receipt cohort and 139 days for FY2024, the last closed cohort; 112 days is the FY2025 goal, not an outcome, and FY2025 is open. Its file is slower already: the 2026-08-21 additional-information request stops the clock, the company plans to answer in December 2026 within the 180-day limit to 2027-02-17, and the response resumes the 90-day FDA clock. That leaves a first-cycle decision in Q1 2027; the stress adds a second information request and a full 90-day cycle, moving clearance to Q3 2027, the CLIA waiver to 2028 and utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M: a two-quarter slip moves the shortfall from $8-10M to $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M post-round count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S97, S140].

| Item | Base | Stress | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) clearance | Q1 2027 (first AI cycle) | Q3 2027 (second AI cycle) | S1 (unverified), S97, S140 |
| CLIA waiver | applied Q3 2027 | 2028 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day, 2028 | 8.0 | 4.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Revenue, FY2027 / 2028 / 2029 | 16.8 / 41.0 / 78.5 | 5.0 / 14.0 / 32.0 | S1 (unverified); analyst estimate |
| Cumulative net loss, 2027-2029 | (13.5) | (55.3) | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Cash trough | (4.7) in 2028 | below (25) in 2029 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Additional capital needed, $M | 8-10 | 25-40 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Dilution at half the Series B price | none | 23-32% | S1 (unverified); calculated |

These are capital-intensive instrument economics: growth is bought with placed hardware and funded receivables, so the faster Vantelle sells, the more cash it burns before the cartridge annuity arrives. The variable that moves the outcome is panels per analyzer-day, not sites, price or the clearance date: clearance moves the clock, utilisation sets the level. The counter-case is discretionary burn: cutting cost and slowing the site ramp would close most of the gap, and a distributor that finances inventory would remove much of the working-capital need, so the shortfall is about this plan, not survival. Size the round larger or tranche it on clearance and utilisation, and price for a further financing before breakeven. Diligence: the Bluestem rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor's payment, return and pricing terms; and the Tempe line's cost and yield at launch volumes. Confidence is high on the arithmetic, which reconciles to the deck, and medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates with no auditor, quarterly statements or covenant disclosure.

::: info danger
**The largest single line of FY2026 revenue cannot be delivered in FY2026 and has no evidence of pull-through.**

Company-reported and unverified: $2.4M of the $5.9M projection is a stocking order from a distributor under a non-binding letter of intent; it ships only on 510(k) clearance, dated Q1 2027, and equals 71,856 cartridges, 3.6 years of current volume, on six months of stability data against a nine-month claim [S1].
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 6 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,938 characters)
Vantelle's product addresses a real gap in clinic care, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts do not yet support a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque. Four of six board seats are filled today; the Series B seat is Meridian's and the independent seat is vacant. Finance has been run by a part-time interim CFO since March 2026; ISO 13485 certification is absent, audit booked Q1 2027; the lead 510(k) has been under an FDA information request since 2026-08-21; and the deck discloses neither the HIPAA business-associate architecture for HL7/FHIR transfer nor the IDE/IRB basis for 41 paid evaluation sites. Geopolitics is not material: US-only revenue. Labour and environmental exposure is not material at 64 employees and a pilot line. Each gap is fixable; together they make the $15M milestone capital, not a Q1 2027 bet. Company figures are unverified. [S1]

### Two founder seats are not the problem; the empty independent seat is

Two founder directors of six is not control. The gap is the vacant independent seat, no disclosed audit committee and a part-time CFO at a company running an FDA submission, waiver study and scale-up. The CFO left in February 2026; the interim has been part-time since March. Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly burn, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts 30 principal payments in March 2027, one month after close. The gap is a pricing issue: the controls are thinner than the $170M valuation implies. Require a mutually agreed independent director, an audit committee with a financial expert, a permanent CFO within six months and monthly reporting on cash, FDA correspondence and quality metrics. These figures are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### The Corvia royalty is small until it meets an exit

The 3% cartridge royalty goes to Corvia, 60% owned by Vantelle, where CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22% — 0.66% of cartridge sales. Every $10M of cartridge revenue carries $300,000 of royalty, $120,000 to the 40% minority and $66,000 to the CTO. The exit is the larger issue: the minority may put its 40% at fair value on an acquisition, $9.4M capitalising 3% of FY2029 plan revenue at 10x. It ranks ahead of the Series B and should reduce the price. Require disinterested approval and a fairness opinion of the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and cap-table disclosure. These terms are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### Quality culture is the open file

ISO 13485 certification is absent and FDA's QMSR has required an ISO 13485-based system since 2026-02-02. The regulatory vice-president who prepared the 510(k) left in September 2025; her successor joined in November 2025, two months before filing. The 2026-08-21 request's content is undisclosed, so the deficiency could be labelling, the 640-sample study or the quality system. FDA's 2024-05-09 warning letter to Cue Health cited unauthorised device changes and lot-release failures, and ordered a stop-sale. A warning letter before clearance would delay launch, complicate the waiver and give 41 clinic customers pause. [S1, S71, S113]

### Patient data has no visible contract

The Q5 sends results to the clinic EHR over Wi-Fi using HL7 and FHIR, making Vantelle a vendor that creates, receives and transmits PHI for a covered entity. Under HHS rules that requires a BAA with each clinic, equivalent terms with subcontractors, Security Rule safeguards and breach reporting; the business associate is directly liable. The deck discloses no BAA count, SOC 2 or HITRUST report, named privacy officer, encryption or incident-response terms, or cyber insurance. Silence is not proof, but it is material non-disclosure at 41 PHI sites. Executed BAAs, a current security report and a named security owner should be closing conditions. [S1, S135]

### The evaluation programme is the largest unexamined exposure

Forty-one sites and 55 analyzers have run devices labelled "investigational use only" in a paid programme since March 2024, at $650 a month plus $38 cartridges costing $16.20. The company says results are not used for care, but the programme is the source of the $1.1M evaluation revenue. Meridian should not lead at $140M pre-money on this record: wait for clearance, ISO certification and a permanent CFO, or lead a smaller, tranched $15M at a lower pre-money with an independent director, disinterested approval of the Corvia terms, BAA conditions and a separate waiver milestone. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 13 by Market Analyst, 8,995 characters)
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites delivered in the 2026 year to date, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, a seventh of the claim and roughly 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the cartridge volume behind it are company-provided, unaudited and not independently confirmed [S1, S67].

The site count is the only input that survives independent checks, and it is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% hospital-owned or affiliated and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 in September 2024. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of that range, and 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible against a rural base near 2,400. The volume is dated precisely: deck p.7 heads its column "Cartridges a month, 2026 average", and with all figures as of 2026-09-30 that is a 2026 year-to-date average, not an FY2025 average; FY2025 monthly volume is not disclosed. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, so 1,680 is roughly double the program-to-date rate. Across 55 analyzers it is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days, or 1.35 per site-day; the model assumes 8.0, a 6.5x gap. That gap does not stay inside the market-size line: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites with two analyzers each implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at $31 realised, almost exactly the model's eight and six times the observed rate. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach the same $41.0M; it has 41. Its 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used [S79, S80, S78, S1].

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% to 2034), a fivefold spread that shows how definition-dependent the category is. A $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17%-83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US; the $368M figure is still 60% of the smallest estimate. Abbott's global Point of Care line generated $606M in FY2025, four times the claimed US SAM [S93, S94, S96, S67].

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. CMS's CY2026 national limitation amounts pay $71.38 for all five codes; without the natriuretic peptide the other four cap at $32.12, below the $38 list and the $33.40 realised price. HbA1c, creatinine and potassium collect $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; troponin plus potassium collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer fees, $718.58 before staff and billing cost. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 generic clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation supports $222M, not $368M [S154, S79, S1].

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| All five codes | — | $71.38 | S154 |
| Four codes excluding 83880 | — | $32.12 | S154 |
| Troponin plus potassium | — | $17.23 | S154 |

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a certificate of waiver, while only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico hold 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived laboratories. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 faces FDA's 150-day decision goal from filing and a 180-day window to answer an information request, so no waiver before 2028 is the realistic case; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base. The first 510(k), filed 2026-05-18, drew an additional-information request on 2026-08-21 with a response planned for December 2026; FDA's own series reports average total time to decision of 127 days in FY2023 and 139 days in FY2024 against goals of 128 and 124, with FY2025 pending at 2025-09-30, so Q1 2027 clearance is plausible but company-provided. Ownership consolidation compounds the friction: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy demand is small: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act had 32 conversions in 14 states as of October 2024. The market systems are US; exit buyers are US and European diagnostics incumbents; the EU is blocked until CE marking after 2028 [S81, S72, S97, S95, S1].

The commercial path is unproven at each step, on company-provided and unverified evidence. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation program two and a half years later; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. The deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, installed EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price evidence. What would settle it: signed contracts with start dates, the first ten sites' CLIA certificates and EHR go-live dates, and collected revenue per cartridge by payer [S1].

The strongest counter-evidence is structural: evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more. Medicare is the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, in the commercial reading medium. The diligence that would settle it is narrow: ordered tests and collected revenue per cartridge in the first billing-enabled sites; payer mix and write-off rate across the evaluation base; and whether any site sustained a materially higher run rate in any month. Until then, the section underwrites the US cartridge market well below the company's estimate, and the difference belongs in the price.

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: TX, AZ, NM | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA labs (2026) | US POC 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only | Moderate-complexity certificate and staffed QC until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital labs | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of US | $2.89B-$14.0B US POC market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR | Blocked until a 2028 waiver; 300 sites by end-2027 via non-binding LOI, as moderate-complexity customers | CLIA; payer coverage | Abbott, Siemens, Roche, Radiometer, Quest | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15, no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens | S1 (unverified) |

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in the 2026 year-to-date average month across 55 analyzers, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge. Source: S1 and S154.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 10 by Market Analyst, 8,993 characters)
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim and Boditech sells a six-test fingertip immunoassay menu. The advantage lasts until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships and cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is the incumbent owning the buyer's analyser slot [S1, S67, S104, S157].

A three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options. Direct: Abbott's i-STAT 1, a waived handheld that added hs-troponin I in January 2025; Siemens epoc, QuidelOrtho's Triage cardiac panel, Roche's cobas h 232 and Radiometer's AQT90 FLEX. Adjacent: Boditech's AFIAS-6 (six immunoassays including troponin I, NT-proBNP and HbA1c from fingertip blood), Truvian's TruVerus (12 cleared tests, no cardiac marker) and Babson's BetterWay (retail-pharmacy collection routed to a central lab). Substitute: Quest Diagnostics, the reference laboratory, no capital and a one-to-three-day turnaround. Status quo: transfer the chest-pain patient or call later. No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge, the gap the company sells into [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109, S157, S127, S158, S156, S65].

| Competitor | Product and status | Menu | Price | Scale and distribution | Advantage / gap vs Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1, Alinity; hs-TnI 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11; waived manual; CG8+ capillary 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c or NT-proBNP | Not disclosed | POC line $606M FY2025; hospital and laboratory channel; installed base not disclosed | Waived slot and capillary claim; one cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro | Waived cardiac panel; EDTA blood | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin | $599 per 25 tests, $23.96 a test | $2.73B FY2025; urgent-care base | Lowest cost per test; no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Siemens/Radiometer/Roche | epoc; AQT90 FLEX; cobas h 232 | Marketed; venous or moderate-complexity | Blood gas; troponin and NT-proBNP separately | Not disclosed | Hospital emergency and laboratory base | Laboratory-quality assays; benchtop, trained staff | S107, S109, S111 |
| Boditech | AFIAS-6 | 510(k) cleared; CLIA waiver not stated | Troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c; six tests a run; fingertip C-tip | Not disclosed | Hospitals, emergency rooms and clinics; US distribution not disclosed | Menu breadth and Asian cost base; no creatinine or potassium, no US waiver | S157 |
| Truvian | TruVerus | 510(k) K251058 and nine analytes 2026-01-12; waiver not stated | 12 tests including creatinine, glucose and lipids; no troponin, natriuretic peptide or HbA1c | Not disclosed | Benchtop; waitlist, distribution not disclosed | Multimodal whole blood; no cardiac menu or waiver | S127 |
| Babson | BetterWay | 510(k) for a collection component; not a clinic analyser; no waiver claimed | Retail-pharmacy finger-stick collection with central-lab testing | Not disclosed | 20+ Austin pharmacies and a national retailer | Removes the venous draw; still a one-to-three-day turnaround | S158, S156 |
| Waived readers | Roche cobas b 101; Nova StatSensor | Near-patient capillary; single-analyte waiver categories | HbA1c, lipids and CRP; creatinine and eGFR | Reader under $1,000 (company claim) | Pharmacy and medical distributors | Low cost; one analyte, no cardiac panel | S73, S77, S90, S1 |

Abbott decides the price. It publishes a waived-test manual for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026. Its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's $2.6M of FY2025 revenue is a 0.1% share of QuidelOrtho's $2.73B in FY2025. Analyser, cartridge, installed-base and per-test prices are undisclosed. When an incumbent matches the finger-stick offer, Vantelle's economics invert: the Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites received theirs free, so every placement loses money before a price war; the cartridge earns 51% margin at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, 100 times current volume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20-$25 with a free analyser takes the account against $38 plus $650 a month; Vantelle's cartridge margin falls to 19-35% on today's cost and it has no second product. Boditech's AFIAS-6 shows the menu is assemblable: six immunoassays, including troponin I and NT-proBNP, from a fingertip [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67, S1, S157].

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core would be a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and Vantelle has not applied for, plus the granted VD-1 cartridge patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, assemblable from parts incumbents already sell. Sight Diagnostics' OLO finger-stick CBC was cleared in 2021 as moderately complex. LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M at closing after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024 [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1].

The funnel is unproven. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation program two years later; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. The company-provided, unverified deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, completed EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price evidence. What would settle it: signed contracts, the first sites' CLIA certificates and EHR go-live dates, and collected revenue per cartridge by payer [S1].

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, and Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per group. That is an opening of a year or two, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; that Vantelle keeps a premium beyond the plan period is low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the evaluation sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived and accepts capillary blood; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design.

| Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Vantelle share | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Five-analyte finger-stick cardiac and metabolic panel for clinics without a laboratory | Abbott (waived i-STAT, capillary claim) | Siemens Healthineers (epoc) and Roche (cobas h 232) | QuidelOrtho Triage and Radiometer AQT90 FLEX | Boditech AFIAS-6, Truvian TruVerus and a combined cartridge from any incumbent | 0.3% share, on $1.1M of 2025 evaluation revenue against a $368M cartridge market at observed utilisation | S104, S107, S111, S108, S109, S157, S127, S1 |

::: evidence
**The buyer's default alternative is a waived Abbott handheld, not a reference lab.**
Abbott cleared hs-troponin for the i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and the Alinity in June 2026, publishes a waived-test manual for the i-STAT 1, and cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. No US competitor retrieved sells a waived five-analyte finger-stick panel; Boditech's AFIAS-6 comes closest with three of the five analytes. Source: S67, S6, S104, S105, S157, S1.
:::

Vantelle Diagnostics: Series B investor presentation
Confidential: prepared for Meridian Capital Ventures. Do not distribute.
October 2026. Figures are as of September 30, 2026 unless a slide says otherwise. Company data, estimates and projections are marked as such.
1. Vantelle Diagnostics at a glance

-  Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc.: a Delaware corporation headquartered in Albuquerque, New Mexico, founded in March 2018, with cartridge production in

2. The problem
Urgent-care clinics and rural hospitals without an on-site laboratory send cardiac and metabolic blood tests to reference labs and wait 1-3 days for
results. Patients with chest pain or uncontrolled diabetes are often transferred, or sent home, before results arrive.
-  A transfer for a suspected heart attack that turns out negative costs thousands of dollars and takes a rural ambulance out of service for hours
(company estimate).
-  Benchtop analyzers that could run these tests on site need venous blood, a trained operator and daily quality control, which small clinics can't staff.
-  The clinics we surveyed send out a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels a day (company survey of 52 clinics, 2024).
Vantelle Diagnostics: Series B investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 2 of 15

3. Our product: the Vantelle Q5
-  A handheld, cartridge-based analyzer that runs a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel from a finger-stick sample in 12 minutes.
-  The panel: high-sensitivity troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine (with eGFR) and potassium.
-  One 40-microliter drop of blood. Each cartridge holds all its reagents and an on-board calibrator, so there is no separate calibration step.
-  The analyzer weighs 640 grams, runs on a battery and sends results to the clinic's electronic health record over Wi-Fi (HL7 and FHIR).
-  Razor-and-blade model: instruments placed at or near cost; recurring revenue from single-use cartridges.
-  Cartridges keep for 9 months at room temperature (our stability data so far covers 6 months).

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 9 by Lead Analyst, 8,998 characters)
Vantelle clears the first test and fails the third. The need is real: a clinic without a laboratory waits one to three days for a send-out, and a five-analyte finger-stick panel returns a result in twelve minutes. The capability is defensible as packaging and manufacturing, not assay science, for 12-24 months. The economics do not scale at the only documented utilisation: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day (company-reported, unverified) against the eight the 2028 plan assumes. Because the third fails, $140M buys a plan whose 3x case needs $596M, 6.0 times the $100M a cleared, waived platform fetched in April 2026. Wait for the 510(k) and the first billing-enabled data, or invest at $60-80M with the structure repaired [S1].

The evaluation programme is evidence: 41 sites, 55 analyzers and 34 of 37 reordering within 90 days, company-reported and unverified. Clinic economics: the CY2026 fee schedule pays $71.38 for five codes against $33.40 realised, leaving $37.98 a panel before the $650 monthly fee. Without the natriuretic peptide the other four codes pay $32.12; a troponin-plus-potassium run collects $17.23 against a $38 list, a $20.77 loss. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule proposes a 16% Chemistry cut, capped at 15% a year, taking the panel to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029; the clinic keeps $10.43 [S154, S149].

No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge: Abbott's i-STAT needs a cartridge per test group, and the granted on-board-calibrator patent runs to 2040 (company-reported, unverified). The assay evidence is weaker. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, against the IFCC's <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%; the study is 640 venous samples from 128 patients, run by company staff at one site, with six excluded results and no capillary-versus-venous comparison. The five-assay reader patent was finally rejected in 2026-07 and is on appeal; the freedom-to-operate opinion excludes the troponin chemistry [S68].

The deck's own operating data undo the revenue plan. Fifty-five analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges in the January-September 2026 average (deck p.7; FY2025 volume not disclosed) — 30.5 per analyzer-month, 1.22 a day — against 8.0 assumed from 2028, a 6.5-fold gap. Cumulative shipments of 27,600 since March 2024 average 890 a month, so the 2026 rate is double, and the step to $3.5M normalised FY2026 revenue reflects a larger installed base. The financial section's FY2025 split — 20,160 evaluation and 23,952 research-use cartridges — is a reconstruction from that average, not disclosed; 44,112 FY2025 cartridges cannot coexist with 27,600 shipped to date, so the 1.22 rate and the FY2025 margin bridge carry low confidence until a shipment ledger arrives. Three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 per placement against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site; 5.9 panels a day at today's cost, 4.2 at the $7.50 target, are needed for a 3:1 LTV:CAC. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579. The counter-case is that evaluation analyzers are investigational and results never reach care, so their use is a floor; a billing-enabled clinic has a reason to run more. The first commercial quarter must prove it [S1, S148].

Five methods cluster at $50-100M, midpoint $76M: 2.5x normalised FY2026 revenue of $3.5M is $8.8M; the FY2029 plan at 2.5x discounted three years is $100.5M; capital invested is $51.5M, 2.7x the ask. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — with the Series A participating at 23.75% above the stack, and the Corvia 40% put adds $9.4M ahead of the B. The new $30M is flat at 1.00x to a $256M exit, needs $426M for 2x, $596M for 3x and $1.79B for 10x. The base case consumes $55-70M before breakeven, not the $30M raised. QuidelOrtho paid $100M for LEX Diagnostics on 2026-04-20 and Roche $295M for LumiraDx; QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales [S126].

The company, the $140M pre-money and the $8M insider commitment assume a Q1 2027 clearance, a 2027 waiver, eight panels a day and a $2.4B market. Our view differs on the variables that set the level rather than the timing: utilisation and price. The evidence is internal — 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in the January-September 2026 average, a $368M cartridge market at observed use rather than $2.4B, a 139-day FY2024 average to decision against a 124-day goal, and a waiver pathway with no troponin-I precedent. The thesis is consensus on the need and the strategic logic, non-consensus on price. The decision tree has four branches. Invest now at $140M: no, because the weighted return is 1.17x over 4.5 years, a 3.6% IRR. Pass: only if the waiver is refused for the cardiac analyte, leaving a four-analyte product and 50-65% of value gone. Wait for milestone: yes, the default — the December 2026 answer, clearance, an accepted waiver pre-submission and ten billing sites' panels per day would retire the unknowns. Invest with conditions: at $60-80M pre-money with $15M split $7.5M at close and $7.5M on clearance, the Series A capped at 1.5x, a 1x non-participating senior B, pay-to-play and pro-rata, the Corvia put capped or converted, and a permanent CFO, independent director and ISO 13485 certificate before closing; at $70M the new money owns 28.9% and 3x needs $398M, or $350M with the Series A capped, lifting the weighted return to 1.40x [S149, S126, S97].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 11 by Red Team Analyst, 8,971 characters)
The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle and the risk-free rate. Three risks decide the outcome — utilisation, capillary troponin and the CLIA waiver — and the recommendation prices the last two while assuming the first.

### A placement returns value only above five panels a day

The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers; the independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months across three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight — the top of the supported range, not its centre — with 40% bear and 15% bull. The mechanism is the placement: three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site, four panels a day reaches only 1.1-2.3x LTV:CAC against the 3:1 a direct salesforce needs; 3:1 arrives at 5.9. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so 402 analyzers would consume $4.0-14.3M of the round — which means the plan's 300 sites are a marketing cost, not a franchise. [S1, S148]

### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024, against a 124-day goal it missed, and sets a 112-day goal for FY2025; a December 2026 answer plus the 139-day average points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry figure is database total time, not FDA days. The bear case's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request; the base rate alone points to May 2027. A second request pushes the decision into the second half of 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster. I put a 45-55% probability on clearance later than June 2027 and a 30% probability on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a troponin-panel pre-submission answer and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. [S97, S92, S69, S72, S147]

### The pivotal study is the first honest test of the assay

The only clinical evidence is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, with six results excluded for insufficient sample or cartridge error and 96.1% categorical agreement with no direction for the five discordant results. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, so a true value on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of ±23%. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due in Q2 2027, is the first test of the two variables that caused the exclusions. I put a 30-40% probability on it failing to show acceptable agreement at the cutoff and a 15-20% probability of outright failure; failure removes troponin, the chest-pain use case and the $12.47 code, takes 50-65% off equity value and leaves a four-analyte heart-failure product, not the acute-cardiac platform the price assumes. [S1, S68, S70]

### Reimbursement is priced at 2026 rates everywhere in this report

CMS's preliminary calendar-2027 fee schedule lowers 1,171 of 1,528 laboratory codes, Chemistry 16% lower, phased at no more than 15% a year through 2029. On that path the five-code panel falls from $71.38 to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029, and the clinic's contribution per $33.40 cartridge falls from $37.98 to $10.43; the $650 monthly fee then costs 62 panels of contribution rather than 17. That is a -15% to -25% equity-value risk, and it compounds with CLIA: until a waiver, the 300 sites planned for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity laboratories. The quality system is the other exposure: ISO 13485 is uncertified while the QMSR has required an ISO-based system since 2026-02-02. Geopolitics does not bind: buyers are American and the EU is closed until CE marking after 2028. [S149, S154, S155, S71]

### The structure caps the upside, and the scenarios misprice both tails

The 19.96% overhang costs equity; the preference stack is larger. Corvia's $9.4M put comes off first and the $76.8M stack ($36.3M senior B and B-1, $36.0M participating Series A, $4.5M seed) follows, so the new $30M is flat at 1.00x from a $45.7M exit to $256M and needs $426M for 2x and $596M for 3x; 3x on the $36.28M B-plus-B-1 class needs $568M, against a $100M clearing price for a cleared, waived platform. The bull's $400-500M exit is 4-5x that price, 2.14x at $450M and a 16.4% IRR over five years; $256M returns 1.00x, $350M 1.55x. The bear returns capital: a $50-100M sale covers Bluestem and the B's $30M preference, 1.00x. Weighted 15% bull, 45% base and 40% bear (0.15 × 2.14x + 0.45 × 1.00x + 0.40 × 1.00x), the expected return is 1.17x over 4.5 years, a 3.6% IRR at $140M; at $70M the bull is 3.50x, the base 1.06x, giving 1.40x and 7.8%. [S99, S126, S100]

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified, and at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. arguments.title: Getein 1100 Immunofluorescence Quantitative Analyzer — product page
arguments.claims: Getein 1100 immunofluorescence analyzer: 50+ test items including cTnI, TnT, BNP, NT-proBNP, HbA1c and renal markers; capillary whole blood accepted; 3-15 minutes per test; 2.0 kg; certificates listed are CE, ISO and NMPA only, with no FDA clearance claimed; LIS/HIS connectivity.
arguments.claims_weakened: Shows a finger-stick cardiac-metabolic menu exists at low cost outside the US, but without FDA clearance or a CLIA waiver it cannot compete for US clinic budgets in the plan period.

arguments.title: Wondfo Finecare FIA Meters — immunofluorescence point-of-care platform
arguments.claims: Wondfo's Finecare fluorescence immunoassay platform: 50+ reagents and seven meters covering cardiac, inflammation, kidney, diabetes (HbA1c) and other markers; the company says its Finecare meter installed base is the largest in China; no US regulatory status stated on the page.
arguments.claims_weakened: Confirms a low-cost Asian finger-stick immunoassay menu exists, but the page makes no FDA or CLIA-waiver claim; FDA's 510(k) database returns only Wondfo lateral-flow antigen, pregnancy and drug tests.

arguments.title: Snibe MAGLUMI M Series — fully automated CLIA analyzers
arguments.claims: Snibe's MAGLUMI M series are fully automated chemiluminescence immunoassay analyzers for small to large laboratories, up to 180 tests/hour; MAGLUMI 2000 described as the first Chinese CLIA analyzer to receive FDA clearance; product line sits in central laboratories, not clinics.
arguments.claims_weakened: Snibe holds US clearances (S171-S175) but for laboratory immunoassay analyzers, not a clinic point-of-care device and not a waived test.

arguments.markdown:
The investment case breaks on utilisation, not regulation. At the rate Vantelle's own evaluation sites run the panel, every placement destroys value and the ask buys an expected return below the venture hurdle and the risk-free rate. Three risks decide the outcome — utilisation, capillary troponin and the CLIA waiver — and the recommendation prices the last two while assuming the first.

### A placement returns value only above five panels a day

The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers and 1.22 per analyzer operating day against the 8.0 the 2028 model assumes. One customer holds 18 analyzers; the independent comparator is unkind: an academic urgent-care programme at two clinics logged 100,000 results in 38 months across three panel types, 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day. The base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight — the top of the supported range, not its centre — with 40% bear and 15% bull. The mechanism is the placement: three years of cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost is $15,621 against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win a site, four panels a day reaches only 1.1-2.3x LTV:CAC against the 3:1 a direct salesforce needs; 3:1 arrives at 5.9. At observed use each placement destroys $9,979-35,579, so 402 analyzers would consume $4.0-14.3M of the round — making the plan's 300 sites a marketing cost, not a franchise. [S1, S148]

### The regulatory clock is a sequence problem, not a date problem

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024 against a 124-day goal, with a 112-day goal for FY2025; a December 2026 answer plus 139 days points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry figure is database total time, not FDA days. The bear's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request. A second request pushes the decision into H2 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster. I put a 45-55% probability on clearance later than June 2027 and a 30% probability on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a troponin-panel pre-submission answer and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. [S97, S92, S69, S72, S147]

### The pivotal study is the first honest test of the assay

The only clinical evidence is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, with six results excluded for insufficient sample or cartridge error and 96.1% categorical agreement with no direction for the five discordant results. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, so a true value on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of ±23%. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due Q2 2027, is the first test of the two variables behind the exclusions. I put a 30-40% probability on it failing to show acceptable agreement at the cutoff and a 15-20% probability of outright failure; failure removes troponin, the chest-pain use case and the $12.47 code, takes 50-65% off equity value and leaves a four-analyte heart-failure product, not the acute-cardiac platform the price assumes. [S1, S68, S70]

### Reimbursement is priced at 2026 rates everywhere in this report

CMS's CY2026 CLFS data file (26CLABQ4, the Q4 release updated October 2026) sets 84484 at $12.47, 83880 at $39.26, 83036 at $9.71, 82570 at $5.18 and 84132 at $4.76 — $71.38 for the five-code panel; CMS governs where third-party republications differ. The preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts 1,171 of 1,528 codes, Chemistry 16%, capped at 15% a year through 2029. At that ceiling the panel falls to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.84 in 2029, and clinic contribution per $33.40 cartridge falls $37.98 to $10.44; the $650 fee then costs 62 panels rather than 17. That is a -15% to -25% equity-value risk, and it compounds with CLIA: until a waiver, the 300 sites planned for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity laboratories. ISO 13485 is uncertified while the QMSR has required an ISO-based system since 2026-02-02. Geopolitics does not bind: buyers are American and the EU is closed until CE marking after 2028. [S149, S154, S155, S179, S71]

### The structure caps the upside, and the scenarios misprice both tails

The 19.96% overhang costs equity; the stack costs more. Corvia's $9.4M put comes off first and the $76.8M stack ($36.3M senior B and B-1, $36.0M participating Series A, $4.5M seed) follows, so the new $30M is flat at 1.00x from a $45.7M exit to $256M and needs $426M for 2x and $596M for 3x; 3x on the $36.28M B-plus-B-1 class needs $568M, against a $100M clearing price for a cleared, waived platform. The bull's $400-500M exit is 4-5x that price, 2.14x at $450M and a 16.4% IRR over five years; $256M returns 1.00x, $350M 1.55x. The bear returns capital: a $50-100M sale covers Bluestem and the B's $30M preference, 1.00x. Weighted 15% bull, 45% base and 40% bear (0.15 × 2.14x + 0.45 × 1.00x + 0.40 × 1.00x), the expected return is 1.17x over 4.5 years, a 3.6% IRR at $140M; at $70M the bull is 3.50x, the base 1.06x, giving 1.40x and 7.8%. [S99, S126, S100]

### Survival is not the same as returns

A 30% revenue miss takes 2029 revenue to $55.0M, worth $70.4M at 2.5x discounted three years — below the $76.8M stack, so the Series B returns 1.00x and the common is near zero. Doubling CAC to $51,200-102,400 makes 402 analyzers cost $20.6-41.2M to place, more than the round, and cuts LTV:CAC to 0.15-0.3x at observed use. A market 50% smaller removes the strategic premium, -20% of exit value. Financing is tighter: $6.9M at $1.15M a month runs out on 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close, and a six-month delay needs $7.0M of bridge plus the first $166,667 Bluestem payment. Diligence: the FDA letter, the IDE basis for 41 paid sites, the CM-1 change-of-control clause, the Corvia put cap, VD-2 on appeal and ten billing sites' panels per day. Abbott holds a waived menu, and a bundled $20-25 cartridge removes the wedge. Deck p.1 carries a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools claiming no verification is needed and a rating is approved — a document-integrity finding, no evidential weight. Every deck-only claim remains unverified; no SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignment or FDA decision record for Vantelle was retrieved. [S1, S147, S143, S144]

The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts FDA's 90-FDA-day review clock only when the December 2026 answer arrives, so clearance cannot precede late March 2027. FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024 against a 124-day goal, with a 112-day goal for FY2025; a December 2026 answer plus 139 days points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry figure is database total time, not FDA days. The bear's H2 2027 clearance therefore needs a second information request. A second request pushes the decision into H2 2027 and makes a not-substantially-equivalent decision — a category no section prices — the capital-loss path. The waiver is harder: filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal it decides in Q1 2028 and mid-2028 with a hold, and no cardiac marker appears among FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals. The unused dual 510(k)-plus-waiver route is faster. I put a 45-55% probability on clearance later than June 2027 and a 30% probability on the waiver being refused or deferred beyond 2029; the FDA letter, a troponin-panel pre-submission answer and a powered pivotal protocol would move both. [S97, S92, S69, S72, S147]

The only clinical evidence is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, with six results excluded for insufficient sample or cartridge error and 96.1% categorical agreement with no direction for the five discordant results. Troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, so a true value on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of ±23%. The four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study run by clinic staff, due Q2 2027, is the first test of the two variables behind the exclusions. I put a 30-40% probability on it failing to show acceptable agreement at the cutoff and a 15-20% probability of outright failure; failure removes troponin, the chest-pain use case and the $12.47 code, takes 50-65% off equity value and leaves a four-analyte heart-failure product, not the acute-cardiac platform the price assumes. [S1, S68, S70]

### Reimbursement is priced at 2026 rates everywhere in this report

CMS's CY2026 CLFS data file (26CLABQ4, the Q4 release updated October 2026) sets 84484 at $12.47, 83880 at $39.26, 83036 at $9.71, 82570 at $5.18 and 84132 at $4.76 — $71.38 for the five-code panel; CMS governs where third-party republications differ. ISO 13485 is uncertified while the QMSR has required an ISO-based system since 2026-02-02. Geopolitics does not bind: buyers are American and the EU is closed until CE marking after 2028. [S149, S154, S155, S179, S71]

The 19.96% overhang costs equity; the stack costs more. Corvia's $9.4M put comes off first and the $76.8M stack ($36.3M senior B and B-1, $36.0M participating Series A, $4.5M seed) follows, so the new $30M is flat at 1.00x from a $45.7M exit to $256M and needs $426M for 2x and $596M for 3x; 3x on the $36.28M B-plus-B-1 class needs $568M, against a $100M clearing price for a cleared, waived platform. A 30% revenue miss takes 2029 revenue to $55.0M, worth $70.4M at 2.5x discounted three years — below the $76.8M stack, so the Series B returns 1.00x and the common is near zero. Doubling CAC to $51,200-102,400 makes 402 analyzers cost $20.6-41.2M to place, more than the round, and cuts LTV:CAC to 0.15-0.3x at observed use. Financing is tighter: $6.9M at $1.15M a month runs out on 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close, and a six-month delay needs $7.0M of bridge plus the first $166,667 Bluestem payment.
