arguments.markdown:
The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites delivered in the 2026 year to date, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, 15% of the claim and 60.7% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care revenue line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the volume behind it are company-provided, unaudited and not independently confirmed [S1, S67].

The site count survives independent checks and is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% hospital-owned or affiliated and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 in September 2024. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the range; 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible. Volume is where the file breaks. Deck p.7 heads its column "Cartridges a month, 2026 average": 1,680 across 41 sites and 55 analyzers, 41 a site on p.9, with figures as of 2026-09-30, a 2026 year-to-date average; FY2025 monthly volume is not disclosed. The same page states 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024, 890 a month over 31 months. Any FY2025 line split is a reconstruction from the 2026 average and cannot coexist with that cumulative total: 20,160 evaluation plus 23,952 research-use would total 44,112, and 20,160 plus the 15,120 implied by nine months at 1,680 already exceeds 27,600. A residual of 12,480 over the 22 pre-2026 months, 567 a month, follows only if 1,680 held every 2026 month; it is an inference, not a disclosure, and conflicts with the FY2025 line build. Across 55 analyzers, 1,680 is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days, or 1.35 per site-day against the model's 8.0, a 6.5x gap that carries low confidence until a shipment ledger arrives. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach $41.0M; it has 41. Its 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used [S79, S80, S78, S1].

| Input or output | Deck build-up | Observed utilisation, two analyzers | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sites | 13,200 | 13,200 | S1 (unverified) |
| Analyzers per site | 2 | 2 | S1 (unverified) |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 8.0 | 1.22 | S1 (unverified) |
| Operating days | 300 | 300 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge price | $38 | $38 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge market | $2.41B | $0.37B | Calculated from S1 (unverified) |

The top-down check does not rescue the figure. Total US point-of-care diagnostics was $2.89B in 2025 on Polaris Market Research's estimate (7.8% CAGR to 2034), $6.4B on MarketsandMarkets' (9.2% to 2031) and $14.0B on IMARC's (6.43% to 2034), a fivefold spread showing how definition-dependent the category is. A $2.4B SAM for one five-analyte panel would be 17%-83% of every point-of-care test sold in the US. The $368M figure at observed utilisation is 12.7% of the smallest published US point-of-care estimate and 60.7% of Abbott's $606M global point-of-care revenue, which is a revenue line, not a market estimate [S93, S94, S96, S67].

The budget owner is the clinic operator, not the clinician, and at Medicare rates the cartridge pays only when the natriuretic peptide is ordered. CMS's CY2026 national limitation amounts pay $71.38 for all five codes; without 83880 the other four cap at $32.12, below the $38 list and the $33.40 realised price. The three metabolic codes collect $19.65, an $18.35 loss per cartridge; troponin plus potassium collects $17.23, a $20.77 loss. At 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $1,558 of cartridges and $650 per analyzer, so the observed 1.34-analyzer site nets about $496 and a two-analyzer site $69 before staff and billing. The $2.4B build therefore needs not 13,200 clinics but the subset ordering a natriuretic peptide in chest-pain and heart-failure workups, chiefly rural emergency departments and traditional urgent care: if the 31.5% of centres the Urgent Care Association classes as limited-scope cannot run that workup, only the 60.3% traditional segment qualifies, and observed utilisation supports $222M, not $368M [S154, S79, S1].

| CPT | Descriptor | CY2026 national limitation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 84484 | Troponin, quantitative | $12.47 | S154 |
| 83880 | Natriuretic peptide | $39.26 | S154 |
| 83036 | Hemoglobin A1c | $9.71 | S154 |
| 82570 | Creatinine | $5.18 | S154 |
| 84132 | Potassium | $4.76 | S154 |
| All five codes | — | $71.38 | S154 |
| Four codes excluding 83880 | — | $32.12 | S154 |
| Troponin plus potassium | — | $17.23 | S154 |

Reimbursement is not the binding constraint; CLIA is. Of 301,284 registered laboratories in September 2026, 233,448 held a waiver certificate; only 15,214 compliance and 15,542 accreditation laboratories could run a moderate-complexity test; Texas, Arizona and New Mexico hold 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived laboratories. A waiver application planned for Q3 2027 faces FDA's 150-day decision goal from filing, 90 days of substantive interaction, and 180 days to answer an information request, so no waiver before 2028 is the realistic case; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, not the urgent-care base. The first 510(k), filed 2026-05-18, drew an information request on 2026-08-21, answer planned for December 2026; FDA's average total time to decision was 127 days in FY2023 and 139 in FY2024 against goals of 128 and 124, so Q1 2027 clearance is plausible but company-provided. Ownership consolidation compounds the friction: 39% of urgent-care centres are hospital-affiliated and their first call is the health system's own laboratory. Policy support is thin: the Rural Emergency Hospital designation, created by the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act, had 32 conversions in 14 states by October 2024 [S81, S72, S97, S95, S1].

The commercial path is unproven on company-provided, unverified evidence. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation programme; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. The deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price. Evaluation devices cannot be used for patient care, so the observed rate is a floor and a billing-enabled site could run several times more. Medicare is the lowest payer, and commercial or cash prices could make a two-test run viable. Confidence in the arithmetic is high, in the 1.22 rate low until a shipment ledger arrives, and in the commercial reading medium. The diligence is narrow: signed contracts with start dates, the first ten sites' CLIA certificates and EHR go-live dates, ordered tests and collections per cartridge, and payer mix. The gap between $2.4B and $368M is the difference between a category bet and site-by-site sales execution; for the investor, that means underwriting $222M-$368M of US cartridge revenue, not $2.4B, and the difference belongs in the price [S1].

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Southwest: TX, AZ, NM | 41 evaluation sites; 4,296 moderate-complexity and 31,720 waived CLIA labs (2026) | US POC 6.4%-9.2% | Entered, evaluation only | Moderate-complexity certificate and staffed QC until a waiver; state scope of practice | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, hospital labs | S1 (unverified), S81 |
| Rest of US | $2.89B-$14.0B US POC market (2025) | 6.4%-9.2% CAGR | Blocked until a 2028 waiver; 300 sites by end-2027 via non-binding LOI | CLIA; payer coverage | Abbott, Siemens, Roche, Radiometer, Quest | S93, S94, S96, S65 |
| EU/EEA | Not sized; CE marking not before 2028 | n/a | Blocked: Irish entity formed 2025-01-15, no staff | CE marking, local reimbursement | Roche, Radiometer, Siemens | S1 (unverified) |

::: evidence
**Company evaluation data contradicts the company's own market estimate.**
The 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges in the 2026 year-to-date average across 55 analyzers, 1.22 per analyzer per operating day; the model's eight a day is unverified, and at eight a day 13,200 sites and $38 produce $2.41B. At 1.22 a day the same sites and price produce $368M, and the 2026 schedule pays $32.12 at most for the four codes other than the natriuretic peptide, less than the $38 cartridge. The rate is low confidence until a shipment ledger reconciles 27,600 cumulative shipments with the 2026 average. Source: S1 and S154.
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's product addresses a real gap in clinic care, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts do not yet support a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque. Four of six board seats are filled; the Series B seat is Meridian's, the independent seat vacant. Finance has been run by a part-time interim CFO since March 2026; ISO 13485 certification is absent, audit booked Q1 2027; the lead 510(k) has been under an FDA information request since 2026-08-21; and the deck discloses neither the HIPAA business-associate architecture for HL7/FHIR transfer nor the IDE/IRB basis for 41 paid sites. Geopolitics, labour and environment are not material: US-only revenue, 64 employees, a pilot line. Each gap is fixable; together they make the $15M milestone capital, not a Q1 2027 bet. Company figures are unverified. [S1]

### Two founder seats are not the problem; the empty independent seat is

Two founder directors of six is not control. The gap is the vacant independent seat, no disclosed audit committee and a part-time CFO at a company running an FDA submission, waiver study and scale-up. The CFO left in February 2026; the interim has been part-time since March. Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly burn, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan starts 30 principal payments in March 2027, one month after close. The gap is a pricing issue: the controls are thinner than the $170M valuation implies. Require a mutually agreed independent director, an audit committee with a financial expert, a permanent CFO within six months and monthly reporting on cash, FDA correspondence and quality metrics. These figures are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### The Corvia royalty is small until it meets an exit

The 3% cartridge royalty goes to Corvia, 60% owned by Vantelle, where CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist holds 22% — 0.66% of cartridge sales. Every $10M of cartridge revenue carries $300,000 of royalty, $120,000 to the 40% minority and $66,000 to the CTO. The exit is the larger issue: the minority may put its 40% at fair value on an acquisition, $9.4M capitalising 3% of FY2029 plan revenue at 10x. It ranks ahead of the Series B and should reduce the price. Require disinterested approval and a fairness opinion of the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and cap-table disclosure. These terms are company-provided and unverified. [S1]

### Quality culture is the open file

ISO 13485 certification is absent and FDA's QMSR has required an ISO 13485-based system since 2026-02-02. The regulatory vice-president who prepared the 510(k) left in September 2025; her successor joined in November 2025, two months before filing. The 2026-08-21 request's content is undisclosed, so the deficiency could be labelling, the 640-sample study or the quality system. FDA's 2024-05-09 warning letter to Cue Health cited unauthorised device changes and lot-release failures, and ordered a stop-sale. A warning letter before clearance would delay launch, complicate the waiver and give 41 clinic customers pause. [S1, S71, S113]

### Patient data has no visible contract

The Q5 sends results to the clinic EHR over Wi-Fi using HL7 and FHIR, making Vantelle a vendor that creates, receives and transmits PHI for a covered entity. Under HHS rules that requires a BAA with each clinic, equivalent terms with subcontractors, Security Rule safeguards and breach reporting; the business associate is directly liable. The deck discloses no BAA count, SOC 2 or HITRUST report, named privacy officer, encryption or incident-response terms, or cyber insurance. Silence is not proof, but it is material non-disclosure at 41 PHI sites. Executed BAAs, a current security report and a named security owner should be closing conditions. [S1, S135]

### The evaluation programme is the largest unexamined exposure

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the January-September 2026 average (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028 [S1].

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales; expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line running 1,680 a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit less the $2,190 subsidy, $15,621, does not repay that; it turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

| Line | 2026 actual | 2028 model | 2029 target | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 1.0 (1.22 on 300 days) | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year cartridge LTV less subsidy | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC, cartridges only | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### FY2025 revenue is three businesses, and its volume is not disclosed

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | S1 (unverified) |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The volumes in the table are reconstructions at the only disclosed prices, not disclosures: at $33.40 and $16.20, $1.10M of evaluation revenue implies about 20,160 cartridges only if the $650 fee were charged on all 55 analyzers for twelve months ($0.43M, an upper bound), and the 58% is the deck's total, so the line costs are allocations and the bridge does not close by line. The reconstruction cannot be squared with the deck's own shipment total: 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, and at the January-September 2026 average of 1,680 a month, nine months consume 15,120, leaving 12,480 — 567 a month — for the 22 months to December 2025. A FY2025 of 20,160 evaluation plus 23,952 research-use cartridges, 44,112 in all, exceeds the entire 27,600; either the cumulative counts only part of the business, or the revenue mix is misstated, or the evaluation line carries revenue beyond fees and cartridges. The 1.22 panels a day is a January-September 2026 figure only, and utilisation carries low confidence until a monthly shipment ledger arrives. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4; on flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### The clinic's margin rests on the one assay that carries 55% of the payment

CMS's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule amounts, from the 26CLABQ4 data file:

| Test (CPT code) | CY2026 amount | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | S154; S179 |
| Natriuretic peptide (83880) | $39.26 | S154; S179 |
| Haemoglobin A1c (83036) | $9.71 | S154; S179 |
| Creatinine (82570) | $5.18 | S154; S179 |
| Potassium (84132) | $4.76 | S154; S179 |
| Five-code panel | $71.38 | S154; S179 |

Against the $33.40 cartridge a five-code clinic keeps $37.98 a panel and Vantelle takes 47% of the Medicare payment. Natriuretic peptide alone is $39.26, 55% of it: a clinic billing four codes without that assay collects $32.12 and loses $1.28 a cartridge, and troponin plus potassium collects $17.23 and loses $16.17. At 30.5 panels a month the five-code clinic earns $1,158.39 and keeps $508.39 after the $650 fee — the fee equals 17.1 panels — and $8,465.20 at 240 panels: trivial at scale, 56% of the margin at adoption. CMS may cut a test by up to 15% a year in 2027-2029, and three such years would take this panel to $43.84 and the clinic's spread to $10.44 [S154, S179].

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 17.1 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified) |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified. The 37 are the sites in the programme at least 90 days; the other four are too new to qualify. The deck does not say whether the three later reordered or left. No site can become a paying commercial customer before clearance, so no lost-deal evidence exists yet; the first will come from the 300-site distributor pipeline. At 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle sells a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the January-September 2026 average (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028 [S1].

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales; expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line running 1,680 a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit less the $2,190 subsidy, $15,621, does not repay that; it turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

| Line | 2026 actual | 2028 model | 2029 target | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 1.0 (1.22 on 300 days) | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year cartridge LTV less subsidy | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC, cartridges only | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### FY2025 revenue is three businesses, and its volume is not disclosed

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | S1 (unverified) |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The volumes in the table are reconstructions at the only disclosed prices, not disclosures: at $33.40 and $16.20, $1.10M of evaluation revenue implies about 20,160 cartridges only if the $650 fee were charged on all 55 analyzers for twelve months ($0.43M, an upper bound), and the 58% is the deck's total, so line costs are allocations and the bridge does not close by line. The reconstruction cannot be squared with the deck's own shipment total: 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, and at the January-September 2026 average of 1,680 a month, nine months consume 15,120, leaving 12,480 — 567 a month — for the 22 months to December 2025. A FY2025 of 20,160 evaluation plus 23,952 research-use cartridges, 44,112 in all, exceeds the entire 27,600; either the cumulative counts only part of the business, or the revenue mix is misstated, or the evaluation line carries revenue beyond fees and cartridges. The 1.22 panels a day is a January-September 2026 figure only, and utilisation carries low confidence until a monthly shipment ledger arrives. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4; on flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### The clinic's margin rests on the one assay that carries 55% of the payment

CMS's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule amounts, from the 26CLABQ4 data file:

| Test (CPT code) | CY2026 amount | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | S154; S179 |
| Natriuretic peptide (83880) | $39.26 | S154; S179 |
| Haemoglobin A1c (83036) | $9.71 | S154; S179 |
| Creatinine (82570) | $5.18 | S154; S179 |
| Potassium (84132) | $4.76 | S154; S179 |
| Five-code panel | $71.38 | S154; S179 |

Against the $33.40 cartridge a five-code clinic keeps $37.98 a panel and Vantelle takes 47% of the Medicare payment. Natriuretic peptide alone is $39.26, 55% of it: a clinic billing four codes without that assay collects $32.12 and loses $1.28 a cartridge, and troponin plus potassium collects $17.23 and loses $16.17. At 30.5 panels a month the five-code clinic earns $1,158.39 and keeps $508.39 after the $650 fee — the fee equals 17.1 panels — and $8,465.20 at 240 panels: trivial at scale, 56% of the margin at adoption. CMS may cut a test by up to 15% a year in 2027-2029, and three such years would take this panel to $43.84 and the clinic's spread to $10.44 [S154, S179].

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 17.1 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified) |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified. The 37 are the sites in the programme at least 90 days; the other four are too new to qualify. The deck does not say whether the three later reordered or left. No site can become a paying commercial customer before clearance, so no lost-deal evidence exists yet; the first will come from the 300-site distributor pipeline. At 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. A clinic that collects the full panel reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a modest panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Capital should be underwritten against panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and the monthly fee tested against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume; the first billing-enabled sites' run rate; and panel mix, since troponin plus potassium alone do not cover a cartridge.

**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the five-code clinic keeps $508.39 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the January-September 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $71.38 and the cartridge costs the clinic $33.40, so the $650 fee equals 17.1 panels of a $37.98 margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154]. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes and no calibration is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim and Boditech sells a six-test fingertip immunoassay menu. The advantage lasts until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships and cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of Vantelle's $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is the incumbent owning the buyer's analyzer slot [S1, S67, S104, S157].

A three-to-five-site urgent-care operator faces four options: direct (Abbott i-STAT 1, Siemens epoc, QuidelOrtho Triage, Roche cobas h 232, Radiometer AQT90 FLEX), adjacent (Boditech AFIAS-6, Truvian TruVerus, Babson BetterWay), substitute (Quest reference laboratory) and status quo (transfer the chest-pain patient or call later). No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109, S157, S127, S158, S156, S65].

| Competitor | Product and status | Menu | Price | Scale and distribution | Advantage / gap vs Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1, Alinity; hs-TnI 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11; waived manual; CG8+ capillary 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c or NT-proBNP | Not disclosed | POC line $606M FY2025; hospital and lab channel; installed base not disclosed | Waived slot and capillary claim; one cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro; waived cardiac panel; EDTA blood | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin | $599 per 25 tests, $23.96 a test | $2.73B FY2025; urgent-care base | Lowest cost per test; no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Siemens/Radiometer/Roche | epoc; AQT90 FLEX; cobas h 232; marketed | Blood gas; troponin and NT-proBNP separately | Not disclosed | Hospital emergency and laboratory base | Laboratory-quality assays; benchtop, trained staff | S107, S109, S111 |
| Boditech | AFIAS-6; 510(k) cleared; waiver not stated | Troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c; six tests a run; fingertip C-tip | Not disclosed | Hospitals, emergency rooms and clinics; US distribution not disclosed | Menu breadth and Asian cost base; no creatinine or potassium, no US waiver | S157 |
| Truvian | TruVerus; 510(k) K251058 and nine analytes 2026-01-12; waiver not stated | 12 tests including creatinine and lipids; no troponin, natriuretic peptide or HbA1c | Not disclosed | Benchtop; waitlist, distribution not disclosed | Multimodal whole blood; no cardiac menu or waiver | S127 |
| Babson | BetterWay; 510(k) for a collection component; not a clinic analyzer; no waiver claimed | Retail-pharmacy finger-stick collection with central-lab testing | Not disclosed | 20+ Austin pharmacies and a national retailer | Removes the venous draw; still a one-to-three-day turnaround | S158, S156 |
| Waived readers | Roche cobas b 101; Nova StatSensor; single-analyte waiver categories | HbA1c, lipids and CRP; creatinine and eGFR | Reader under $1,000 (company claim) | Pharmacy and medical distributors | Low cost; one analyte, no cardiac panel | S73, S77, S90, S1 |

Abbott decides the price. It publishes a waived-test manual for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's $2.6M of FY2025 revenue is 0.1% of QuidelOrtho's $2.73B. Analyzer, cartridge, installed-base and per-test prices are undisclosed. A price match inverts the economics: the Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of evaluation sites got theirs free, so every placement loses money; the cartridge earns 51% at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, 100 times current volume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20-$25 with a free analyzer takes the account against $38 plus $650 a month; Vantelle's margin falls to 19%-35% and it has no second product [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67, S1].

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a wide copyable shell. The durable core is a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and Vantelle has not applied for, plus the granted VD-1 patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, assemblable from parts incumbents already sell: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. Three Asian suppliers show how easily the menu is assembled, but none can sell it in the US yet. Getein's 1100 runs 50+ immunoassays including cTnI, NT-proBNP, HbA1c and renal markers from capillary blood, with CE, ISO and NMPA certificates but no FDA clearance. Wondfo's Finecare covers cardiac, kidney and HbA1c markers and claims China's largest installed base, but its US clearances are lateral-flow antigen, pregnancy and drug tests, not the analyzer. Snibe's MAGLUMI is a 180-test/hour central-laboratory analyzer with US clearances, not a clinic device. With no US clearance or waiver, a Chinese entrant needs a 510(k), a waiver and a distribution build: a 2029-2031 revenue threat and a financing risk for the next round, not a 2027 selling objection [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1, S177, S178, S176, S161, S171].

The funnel is unproven. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation programme; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. Reorders are 34 of the 37 sites in the programme at least 90 days (92%); the deck does not say why three did not reorder — they remain in the 41-site base and the 1,680 average — and the four outside the denominator joined in the last 90 days. No lost deal exists yet because no site can convert before clearance; the first lost-deal evidence will come from the 300-site distributor pipeline. The deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price. What would settle it: signed contracts, CLIA certificates, EHR go-live dates and collections per cartridge [S1].

The counter-evidence matters: no US competitor sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, and Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per group. That is an opening of a year or two, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; that Vantelle keeps a premium beyond the plan period is low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the evaluation sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived for capillary blood; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design [S1].

| Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Vantelle share | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Five-analyte finger-stick cardiac and metabolic panel for clinics without a lab | Abbott (waived i-STAT, capillary claim) | Siemens Healthineers (epoc) and Roche (cobas h 232) | QuidelOrtho Triage and Radiometer AQT90 FLEX | Boditech AFIAS-6, Truvian TruVerus and a combined cartridge from any incumbent | 0.3% on $1.1M FY2025 evaluation revenue against $368M at observed utilisation | S104, S107, S111, S108, S109, S157, S127, S1 |

::: evidence
**The buyer's default alternative is a waived Abbott handheld, not a reference lab.**
Abbott cleared hs-troponin for the i-STAT 1 in January 2025 and the Alinity in June 2026, publishes a waived-test manual, and cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. No US competitor retrieved sells a waived five-analyte finger-stick panel; Boditech's AFIAS-6 comes closest with three of the five analytes. Source: S67, S6, S104, S105, S157, S1.
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes; 12-minute run with on-board calibration; $2,900 analyzer versus $15,000-$40,000 benchtops; 34 of 37 eligible sites reordered; granted US cartridge patent VD-1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Weaknesses | Cartridge cost $16.20 against $7.50 at two million units; analyzer below cost and 60% given free; three of five assays uncleared; no CLIA waiver; 41 sites and $2.6M revenue | S1 (unverified) |
| Opportunities | No US product combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge; 233,448 waived and 30,756 moderate-complexity labs post-waiver; 32 Rural Emergency Hospitals | S81, S79, S95 |
| Threats | Abbott holds the waived slot, capillary claim and hs-troponin menu; Boditech sells six fingertip immunoassays; Truvian cleared for 12 tests; no waiver before 2028; LumiraDx and Cue Health failed or were sold | S67, S104, S105, S157, S127, S65, S72, S112, S110 |
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's revenue model: a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and the model only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the January-September 2026 average (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028 [S1].

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales; expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line running 1,680 a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit less the $2,190 subsidy, $15,621, does not repay that; it turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 1.0 (1.22 on 300 days) | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year cartridge LTV less subsidy | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC, cartridges only | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### FY2025 revenue is three businesses, and its volume is not disclosed

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Research-use | 0.80 | 0.39 | 51% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Contract development | 0.70 | 0.38 | 46% | S1 (unverified) |
| Total | 2.60 | 1.09 | 58% | S1 (unverified) |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. The volumes in the table are reconstructions at the only disclosed prices, not disclosures: at $33.40 and $16.20, $1.10M of evaluation revenue implies about 20,160 cartridges only if the $650 fee were charged on all 55 analyzers for twelve months ($0.43M, an upper bound), and the 58% is the deck's total, so line costs are allocations and the bridge does not close by line. The reconstruction cannot be squared with the deck's own shipment total: 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months, and at the January-September 2026 average of 1,680 a month, nine months consume 15,120, leaving 12,480 — 567 a month — for the 22 months to December 2025. A FY2025 of 20,160 evaluation plus 23,952 research-use cartridges, 44,112 in all, exceeds the entire 27,600; either the cumulative counts only part of the business, or the revenue mix is misstated, or the evaluation line carries revenue beyond fees and cartridges. The 1.22 panels a day is a January-September 2026 figure only, and utilisation carries low confidence until a monthly shipment ledger arrives. Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4; on flat per-analyzer use, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue. With the largest customer at 15% and the development partner at 27%, the top two relationships are 42% [S1].

### The clinic's margin rests on the one assay that carries 55% of the payment

CMS's CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule national limitation amounts:

| Test (CPT code) | CY2026 amount | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Troponin, quantitative (84484) | $12.47 | S154; S179 |
| Natriuretic peptide (83880) | $39.26 | S154; S179 |
| Haemoglobin A1c (83036) | $9.71 | S154; S179 |
| Creatinine (82570) | $5.18 | S154; S179 |
| Potassium (84132) | $4.76 | S154; S179 |
| Five-code panel | $71.38 | S154; S179 |

Against the $33.40 cartridge a five-code clinic keeps $37.98 a panel and Vantelle takes 47% of the Medicare payment. Natriuretic peptide alone is $39.26, 55% of it: a clinic billing four codes without that assay collects $32.12 and loses $1.28 a cartridge, and troponin plus potassium collects $17.23 and loses $16.17. At 30.5 panels a month the five-code clinic earns $1,158.39 and keeps $508.39 after the $650 fee — the fee equals 17.1 panels — and $8,465.20 at 240 panels: trivial at scale, 56% of the margin at adoption. CMS may cut a test by up to 15% a year in 2027-2029, and three such years would take this panel to $43.84 and the clinic's spread to $10.44 [S154, S179].

| Product or fee | Price | Per test or analyte | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Q5 cartridge, five assays | $38.00 list; $33.40 realised | $7.60 per analyte at list | S1 (unverified) |
| Vantelle evaluation fee | $650 per analyzer-month | 17.1 panels of clinic margin at observed use | S1 (unverified) |
| Quidel Triage Troponin, 25 tests | $599 | $23.96 | S106 |
| Quidel Triage MeterPro | Free with three-year contract | — | S106 |

### 92% reorder is engagement, not demand

Thirty-four of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, company-reported and unverified. The 37 are the sites in the programme at least 90 days; the other four are too new to qualify. The deck does not say whether the three later reordered or left. No site can become a paying commercial customer before clearance, so no lost-deal evidence exists yet; the first will come from the 300-site distributor pipeline. At 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is one month of consumption: the metric shows repeat use at a price already accepted, not commercial demand. Per site the run rate is 1.35 panels a day against a median of 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out daily at the 52 clinics Vantelle surveyed — 10% capture. The plan needs two analyzers at eight panels each, 16 a site, 114% of that median: the model assumes the panel replaces the entire send-out, not the urgent slice. Reaching 300 sites by end-2027 means 259 net adds in twelve months, 21.6 a month against 1.3 a month averaged since March 2024, 402 analyzers and about 1.16M cartridges a year — 57 times the January-September 2026 average of 1,680 — from an 18-person pilot line [S1].

The counter-evidence: evaluation analyzers are investigational, results never reach patient care, and no site has a billing reason to run more. A clinic that collects the full panel reimbursement has an incentive no evaluation site has, and the survey's latent send-out volume makes a modest panel count credible; the plan's is not, until a billing-enabled site demonstrates it. Underwrite panels per analyzer-day, with the site count a milestone, and test the monthly fee against a free-instrument, minimum-volume alternative. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the interpretation: evaluation data cannot distinguish a floor from a ceiling. Three diligence items: the best evaluation site's monthly volume; the first billing-enabled sites' run rate; and panel mix, since troponin plus potassium alone do not cover a cartridge.

::: evidence
**A placement runs one panel a day, not eight; at CMS's CY2026 rates the five-code clinic keeps $508.39 a month.**
55 analyzers consumed 1,680 cartridges a month, the January-September 2026 average, company-reported and unverified — 30.5 per analyzer-month against 240; the five-code panel pays $71.38 and the cartridge costs the clinic $33.40, so the $650 fee equals 17.1 panels of a $37.98 margin and a placement's $15,621 three-year gross profit does not repay an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win it [S1, S154]. The FY2025 line volumes do not reconcile with 27,600 cumulative shipments, so the 58% margin and the 1.22 rate carry low confidence until the shipment ledger arrives.
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim and Boditech sells a six-test fingertip immunoassay menu. The advantage lasts until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships and cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of $16.20. The most dangerous competitor is the incumbent owning the buyer's analyzer slot [S1, S67, S104, S157].

A three-to-five-site urgent-care operator has four options: direct (Abbott i-STAT 1, Siemens epoc, QuidelOrtho Triage, Roche cobas h 232, Radiometer AQT90 FLEX), adjacent (Boditech AFIAS-6, Truvian TruVerus, Babson BetterWay), substitute (Quest reference laboratory) and status quo (transfer the chest-pain patient or call later). No US product retrieved combines the five analytes in one finger-stick cartridge [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109, S157, S127, S158, S156, S65].

| Competitor | Product and status | Menu | Price | Scale and distribution | Advantage / gap vs Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro; waived cardiac panel; EDTA blood | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin | $599 per 25 tests, $23.96 a test | $2.73B FY2025; urgent-care base | Lowest cost per test; no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Siemens/Radiometer/Roche | epoc; AQT90 FLEX; cobas h 232; marketed | Blood gas; troponin and NT-proBNP separately | Not disclosed | Hospital emergency and laboratory base | Laboratory-quality assays; benchtop, trained staff | S107, S109, S111 |
| Boditech | AFIAS-6; 510(k) cleared; waiver not stated | Troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c; six tests a run; fingertip C-tip | Not disclosed | Hospitals, emergency rooms and clinics; US distribution not disclosed | Menu breadth and Asian cost base; no creatinine or potassium, no US waiver | S157 |

Abbott decides the price. It publishes a waived-test manual for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Vantelle's $2.6M of FY2025 revenue is 0.1% of QuidelOrtho's $2.73B. A price match inverts the economics: the Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of sites got theirs free, so every placement loses money; the cartridge earns 51% at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, 100 times current volume. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20-$25 with a free analyzer takes the account against $38 plus $650 a month; Vantelle's margin falls to 19%-35% and it has no second product [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67, S1].

The wedge has a narrow durable core and a copyable shell. The durable core is a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and Vantelle has not applied for, plus the granted VD-1 patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, assemblable from parts incumbents already sell: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M after failing to scale alone, and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. Three Asian suppliers show how easily the menu is assembled, but none can sell in the US yet. Getein's 1100 runs 50+ immunoassays including cTnI, NT-proBNP, HbA1c and renal markers from capillary blood, with CE, ISO and NMPA certificates but no FDA clearance. Wondfo's Finecare covers cardiac, kidney and HbA1c markers and claims China's largest installed base, but its US clearances are lateral-flow antigen, pregnancy and drug tests, not the analyzer. Snibe's MAGLUMI is a 180-test/hour central-laboratory analyzer with US clearances, not a clinic device. With no US clearance or waiver, a Chinese entrant needs a 510(k), a waiver and a distribution build: a 2029-2031 revenue threat and a financing risk for the next round, not a 2027 selling objection [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1, S177, S178, S176, S161, S171].

The funnel is unproven. The first evaluation site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid evaluation programme; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. Reorders are 34 of 37 sites in the programme at least 90 days (92%); the deck does not say why three did not reorder — they remain in the 41-site base and the 1,680 average — and the four outside the denominator joined in the last 90 days. No lost deal exists yet because no site can convert before clearance; the first lost-deal evidence will come from the 300-site distributor pipeline. The deck discloses no evaluation-to-paid conversion, sales-cycle length, site CLIA certificate type, EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price. That is an opening of a year or two, not a moat, because every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; that Vantelle keeps a premium beyond the plan period, low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote the evaluation sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived for capillary blood; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design [S1].

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's revenue model: a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 consumable cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and it only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the January-September 2026 average (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028 [S1].

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales; expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line running 1,680 a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit less the $2,190 subsidy, $15,621, does not repay that; it turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cartridges per analyzer-month | 30.5 | 200 | 200 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Panels per analyzer-day | 1.0 (1.22 on 300 days) | 8.0 | 8.0 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| Three-year cartridge LTV less subsidy | $15,621 | $140,658 | $160,314 | S1 (unverified); calculated |
| LTV:CAC, cartridges only | 0.3-0.6x | 2.7-5.5x | 3.1-6.3x | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### FY2025 revenue is three businesses, and its volume is not disclosed

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | S1 (unverified); calculated |

FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, company-reported and unverified, is $1.1M evaluation, $0.8M research-use and $0.7M development. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's wedge is real but shallow. One finger stick, one cartridge, five analytes in 12 minutes is a workflow no US competitor offers today, but Abbott already sells the same buyer a waived handheld with a capillary claim and Boditech sells a six-test fingertip immunoassay menu. The advantage lasts until a combined finger-stick cardiac-metabolic cartridge ships and cannot survive a matched price from a competitor whose cartridge cost is a fraction of $16.20. The most dangerous competitor owns the buyer's analyzer slot [S1, S67, S104, S157].

A three-to-five-site urgent-care operator has four options: direct (Abbott i-STAT 1, Siemens epoc, QuidelOrtho Triage, Roche cobas h 232, Radiometer AQT90 FLEX), adjacent (Boditech AFIAS-6, Truvian TruVerus, Babson BetterWay), substitute (Quest reference laboratory) and status quo (transfer the chest-pain patient or call later). No US product retrieved combines all five [S104, S6, S107, S108, S111, S109, S157, S127, S158, S156, S65].

| Competitor | Product and status | Menu | Price | Scale and distribution | Advantage / gap vs Vantelle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1, Alinity; hs-TnI 2025-01-03 and 2026-06-11; waived manual; CG8+ capillary 2023 | Troponin, creatinine, potassium, glucose, blood gas; no HbA1c or NT-proBNP | Not disclosed | POC line $606M FY2025; hospital and lab channel; installed base not disclosed | Waived slot and capillary claim; one cartridge per test group | S6, S2, S104, S105, S67 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro; waived cardiac panel; EDTA blood | Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin | $599 per 25 tests, $23.96 a test | $2.73B FY2025; urgent-care base | Lowest cost per test; no metabolic menu | S106, S108, S22 |
| Siemens/Radiometer/Roche | epoc; AQT90 FLEX; cobas h 232; marketed | Blood gas; troponin and NT-proBNP separately | Not disclosed | Hospital emergency and laboratory base | Laboratory-quality assays; benchtop, trained staff | S107, S109, S111 |
| Boditech | AFIAS-6; 510(k) cleared; waiver not stated | Troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c; six tests a run; fingertip C-tip | Not disclosed | Hospitals, emergency rooms and clinics; US distribution not disclosed | Menu breadth and Asian cost base; no creatinine or potassium, no US waiver | S157 |
| Truvian | TruVerus; 510(k) K251058 and nine analytes 2026-01-12; waiver not stated | 12 tests including creatinine and lipids; no troponin, natriuretic peptide or HbA1c | Not disclosed | Benchtop; waitlist, distribution not disclosed | Multimodal whole blood; no cardiac menu or waiver | S127 |
| Babson | BetterWay; 510(k) for a collection component; not a clinic analyzer; no waiver claimed | Retail-pharmacy finger-stick collection, central-lab testing | Not disclosed | 20+ Austin pharmacies and a national retailer | Removes the venous draw; still a one-to-three-day turnaround | S158, S156 |
| Waived readers | Roche cobas b 101; Nova StatSensor; single-analyte waiver categories | HbA1c, lipids and CRP; creatinine and eGFR | Reader under $1,000 (company claim) | Pharmacy and medical distributors | Low cost; one analyte, no cardiac panel | S73, S77, S90, S1 |

Abbott decides the price. It publishes a waived-test manual for non-laboratory staff, cleared CG8+ for capillary whole blood in 2023, and extended hs-troponin to the Alinity in June 2026; its Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025. Its $1.1M FY2025 evaluation revenue is a 0.3% share of the $368M observed-utilisation market; total revenue is 0.1% of QuidelOrtho's $2.73B. A price match inverts the economics: the Q5 lists at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost and 60% of sites got theirs free, so every placement loses money; the cartridge earns 51% at $33.40 realised and $16.20 cost, and the $7.50 target needs two million cartridges a year, 100 times current. An incumbent bundling a five-analyte finger-stick cartridge at $20-$25 with a free analyzer takes the account against $38 plus $650 a month; Vantelle's margin falls to 19%-35% and it has no second product [S6, S2, S104, S105, S67, S1].

The wedge has a narrow durable core and copyable shell. The durable core is a CLIA waiver for a five-analyte panel, which no competitor holds and Vantelle has not applied for, plus the granted VD-1 patent. The copyable shell is the sample type, run time and menu, assemblable from parts incumbents already sell: LumiraDx sold to Roche in July 2024 for $353.5M after failing to scale; Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down in May 2024. Three Asian suppliers show how easily the menu is assembled, but none can sell in the US. Getein's 1100 runs 50+ immunoassays including cTnI, NT-proBNP, HbA1c and renal markers from capillary blood, with CE, ISO and NMPA certificates but no FDA clearance. Wondfo's Finecare covers cardiac, kidney and HbA1c markers and claims China's largest installed base, but its US clearances are lateral-flow antigen, pregnancy and drug tests, not the analyzer. Snibe's MAGLUMI is a 180-test/hour central-laboratory analyzer with US clearances, not a clinic device. With no US clearance or waiver, a Chinese entrant needs a 510(k), a waiver and a distribution build: a 2029-2031 revenue threat and a financing risk for the next round, not a 2027 selling objection [S112, S91, S116, S110, S1, S177, S178, S176, S161, S171].

The funnel is unproven on company-provided, unverified data. The first site joined in March 2024 and all 41 remain in a paid programme; no site can convert before clearance, and the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 rest on a non-binding distributor letter of intent. Reorders are 34 of 37 sites in the programme at least 90 days (92%); the deck does not say why three did not reorder — they remain in the 41-site base and the 1,680 average — and the four outside the denominator joined in the last 90 days. No lost deal exists yet because no site can convert before clearance; the first lost-deal evidence will come from the 300-site distributor pipeline. The deck discloses no conversion rate, sales-cycle length, CLIA certificate type, EHR interface or payer enrolment; the $650 monthly fee is the only site-level price. What would settle it: signed contracts, CLIA certificates, EHR go-live dates and collections per cartridge [S1].

The counter-evidence is partially verified: no US competitor's published record sells the exact five-analyte finger-stick combination, and Abbott's i-STAT needs a separate cartridge per group. That is an opening of a year or two, not a moat: every component exists separately and the incumbent owns the account, the waiver and the distribution. Confidence that Abbott is the price-setter is high; that Vantelle keeps a premium beyond the plan period, low. Diligence would settle it: what Abbott and QuidelOrtho quote sites; whether Abbott's hs-troponin cartridge is waived for capillary blood; and whether VD-1 covers a five-analyte cartridge or only the capillary-fill design [S1].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 7 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,968 characters)
Vantelle has six months of cash, company-reported and unverified, and a $30M round that funds its own plan only into 2028. The $22.5M of 2027-2028 net losses plus launch capex and working capital exceed the $32.3M left at close, so the plan needs $40M to reach its 2029 profit year and $55-70M if clearance slips two quarters and utilisation halves. It starts at $6.9M on 2026-09-30 and $1.15M a month [S1]: 6.0 months, exhaustion around 2027-03-30, and $2.3M — 2.0 months — left at the 2027-01-29 close. The burn is understated: $13.8M a year against an FY2026E net loss of $14.0M is the P&L loss with no capex or working capital in it.

### The operating leverage is real and rests on one variable

Implied operating cost — gross profit minus net loss — rises from $10.3M in FY2024 to $17.6M in FY2026E and $46.7M in FY2029P while revenue rises 13.3x, and that gap is the investment case. It also sets the target: at the 2029 margin of 71%, breakeven needs $65.8M of revenue — 884 analyzers running 2,400 panels a year at $31, or 660 sites at 1.34 analyzers each, twice the 300 sites targeted for end-2027. The cost target fails the same test. Two million cartridges a year is what buys the $7.50 cost; at the 1.2 panels a day the 41 evaluation sites actually ran, an analyzer consumes about 360 cartridges a year, so that volume needs 5,500 analyzers, and the 402 analyzers behind the 300-site plan produce 147,000 cartridges, 7% of it, where the only disclosed cost is $16.20 and the margin 48%, not 76%. Capital efficiency is poor: the burn multiple is 8.3x in FY2025, 4.2x in FY2026E, 15.6x excluding the stocking order and 1.5x in FY2027P, against a Series B median near 1.4x [S1, S22, S134]. Revenue per dollar of capital raised is $0.05 in FY2025 on $51.5M, and $0.21 in FY2027P on $81.5M including the round — $4.85 of capital per dollar of 2027 revenue.

### Forty-one per cent of 2026 revenue cannot be delivered in 2026

Company-reported FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order from Southwest Clinical Supply that ships only on 510(k) clearance, dated Q1 2027, under a non-binding LOI. At $33.40 a cartridge it is 71,856 cartridges — 3.6 years of today's 20,160 annual volume — for a product with six months of stability data behind a nine-month claim. Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M; with $2.7M booked in nine months the fourth quarter is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average, so the base business is not growing into the year-end. Gross margin makes the same point: 61% in FY2026E is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts toward a distributor, and a 30% wholesale discount would take the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M [S1].

### Working capital is the missing line in the use of funds

The launch consumes cash before it produces it, and the deck's use of funds has no working-capital line. At peer working-capital intensity — QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025 — 2028 revenue of $41.0M and COGS of $13.5M imply $6.3M of receivables and $2.2-5.4M of inventory at 60-145 days, so $8-12M of working capital against near zero today. The debt compounds the timing: the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with the rate and covenants not disclosed — at 10-12% interest is $42,000-50,000 a month, and debt service after 2027-03 is $210,000 a month, 18% of burn. The $6.0M of bridge notes at 8% cost $40,000 a month and become $6.28M at close, converting at 75% of the $3.2564 round price into 2,571,392 shares, 4.9% of the post-round count [S1, S22].

### The round does not cover the plan, and the stress case needs a second one

In the base case, $32.3M at close less 2027 outflows of $25.0M (the $16.5M loss, $6.0M of capex, $3.0M of working capital and $1.5M of principal, net of $2.0M of depreciation) leaves $7.3M, and 2028's $12.0M outflow takes it to negative $4.7M: the trough arrives before the 2029 profit and the shortfall is $8-10M. The base keeps clearance in Q1 2027, consistent with the one review-time series in the FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report: average total time to decision (FDA days plus company time) was 127 days for the FY2023 receipt cohort and 139 days for FY2024, the last closed cohort; 112 days is the FY2025 goal, not an outcome, and FY2025 is open. Its file is slower already: the 2026-08-21 additional-information request stops the clock, the company plans to answer in December 2026 within the 180-day limit to 2027-02-17, and the response resumes the 90-day FDA clock. That leaves a first-cycle decision in Q1 2027; the stress adds a second information request and a full 90-day cycle, moving clearance to Q3 2027, the CLIA waiver to 2028 and utilisation to 4 panels a day. Revenue becomes $5.0M, $14.0M and $32.0M instead of $16.8M, $41.0M and $78.5M; the three-year loss is $55.3M even with cost 11-23% below plan, and with $8M of capex, $4M of working capital and $5M of principal the gap is $25-40M: a two-quarter slip moves the shortfall from $8-10M to $25-40M. A $25-40M raise at half the Series B price is 15.3-24.6M new shares, 23-32% dilution on today's 52.2M post-round count, before any pay-to-play or anti-dilution adjustment [S1, S97, S140].

Diligence: the Bluestem rate, covenants and minimum-cash test; the distributor's payment, return and pricing terms; and the Tempe line's cost and yield at launch volumes. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 9 by Product Analyst, 8,991 characters)
The plan does not survive its own regulatory sequence. A late-December 2026 answer to the FDA's August 2026 request restarts a 90-FDA-day clock, putting the first clearance at late March 2027 at the earliest and mid-May 2027 at the FY2024 average total time to decision, against a company plan of Q1 2027; a waiver filed in Q3 2027 cannot be granted before 2028 under FDA's 150-FDA-day goal; and at the 1.35 cartridges a site a day the evaluation sites run, $78.5M of 2029 revenue needs 5,150 sites, not 300. Each step is defensible; the chain is not [S1, S69, S72, S97].

### The regulatory chain sets the calendar, not the sales plan

The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18 for troponin I and HbA1c only. FDA asked for additional information on 2026-08-21, and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, within the 180-day window to 2027-02-17. The review clock resumes on receipt, and FDA's goal is 90 FDA days; a late-December answer therefore puts the floor in late March 2027, and the FY2024 average total time to decision of 139 days points to mid-May 2027 if this file behaves like the average. Those are calendar days; the MDUFA series is 127 days in FY2023 against a 128-day goal, met, and 139 days in FY2024 against a 124-day goal, missed, with the FY2025 cohort incomplete at 2025-09-30. The 175-day Chemistry-panel and 337-day denial figures used elsewhere are third-party total-time averages, not FDA's series [S92, S97].

The second submission covers three assays whose pivotal data are not expected until Q2 2027, so a Q2 2027 filing is impossible; a Q3 2027 filing plus 90 FDA days gives a Q4 2027 decision and the FY2024 average points to Q1 2028. The five-assay menu is at best a Q4 2027 product, not the Q2 2027 the plan assumes [S1, S97].

| Milestone | Target date | Status as of 2026-10-31 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Answer to FDA request | 2026-12 (company) | Received 2026-08-21; unanswered; deadline 2027-02-17 | Documentation gap or new data | S1, S69 |
| First 510(k) clearance | Late March 2027 (90-day goal); mid-May 2027 (FY2024 average) | Filed 2026-05-18; clock restarts on answer | Two-assay clearance only | S1, S69, S97 |
| Pivotal results, 4 sites, 1,150 patients | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | Capillary equivalence; intended-user performance | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k): NT-proBNP, creatinine, potassium | Q3 2027 filing; Q4 2027-Q1 2028 decision | Needs pivotal results due Q2 2027 | Five-assay menu | S1, S97 |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 (company); first two assays | Not filed; needs cleared application, flex and user studies | Waived status for two assays | S1, S72 |
| CLIA waiver decision | Q1 2028 at 150 FDA days; mid-2028 with a hold; five-assay waiver 2028-2029 | No company date | Whether 2028 revenue is reachable | S72, S97 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites, investigational use | Demand beyond evaluation | S1, unverified |

### The waiver is sequenced last and gates the customer set

The CLIA waiver is the most valuable asset and the one scheduled latest. A submission references an already cleared application and must carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is a decision within 150 FDA days. A Q3 2027 filing therefore decides in Q1 2028, and an information request adds up to 180 days, so mid-2028 is realistic. A five-assay waiver cannot be filed until the second 510(k) clears, which puts its decision in 2028 at the earliest and 2029 if the second file slips. Until then the panel is moderate complexity: only a CLIA-certified laboratory with qualified staff may run it, and a Certificate of Waiver site cannot. The 300 sites planned for end-2027 are hospital and reference laboratories, not the urgent-care clinics in the market model [S72, S81, S87, S90].

### The revenue line needs a utilisation step-change that has not been observed

Company data, unverified: the deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month as its "2026 average" across 41 sites and 55 analyzers (p.7) and repeats 41 a site a month for 2026 (p.9). The deck does not state the months covered; with figures as of 2026-09-30 the average cannot cover more than January-September 2026, and neither 2026 unit volume nor FY2025 cartridge units is disclosed, so no growth rate can be computed. On that average, 1,680 cartridges is 41.0 a site a month (1.35 a site a calendar day) and 30.5 an analyzer-month (1.02 a calendar day; 1.22 on 300 operating days) against the 8 a day the model assumes from 2028. At 1.35 a site a day and $31 a cartridge, a site produces $15,275 a year, so $78.5M needs 5,150 sites, not 300; at the model's two analyzers and eight panels, 300 sites produce $44.6M and $78.5M needs 528. The 2028 line needs 2,680 sites at observed use or 276 at full model utilisation, against 300 planned by end-2027. FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order that ships on clearance, a late-March 2027 event — 41% of 2026 revenue that cannot be recognised in 2026; the 61% FY2026E gross margin also sits above the 51% cartridge margin while the analyzer sells below cost, so either an undisclosed line carries the blend or the projection is optimistic [S1].

### What the $30M buys

The split is $10.5M for FDA clearance, $12.0M for cartridge scale-up and $7.5M for launch. From $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 plus $30M, subtract planned net losses of $16.5M in 2027 and $6.0M in 2028 and $3.5M of Bluestem principal from April 2027: $10.9M remains at end-2028 before capital expenditure and the inventory for a 2-million-cartridge year. A one-year waiver slip adds a year of losses without waived revenue and consumes that cushion, pointing to an inside or down round in 2028, not the 2029 profit the deck projects [S1, S72].

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Regional distributor, 300 sites, $2.4M opening stocking order | Not dated (letter of intent) | Non-binding | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics (60% owned) | Exclusive license to the CM-1 sealing patent, 3% royalty on cartridge sales | Patent 2021-01; stake acquired 2021-04 | Active; the CTO holds 22% of Corvia | S1, unverified |
| Ardent Peak Ventures, Juniper Rock Capital | $5.0M and $3.0M of the Series B | October 2026 commitment | Committed; round open | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan, interest-only to 2027-03 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-04 | S1, unverified |
| Corvia related-party terms | 3% royalty on cartridge net sales; the CTO owns 22% of Corvia | — | Related-party cost in gross margin | S1, unverified |

Company data, unverified: the distributor letter is the only commercial commitment outside the evaluation programme; it is non-binding, from a regional supplier with no obligation to stock. The Corvia license is a permanent royalty on the product that must carry the company, paid to an entity in which the chief technology officer is an owner, so it belongs in the gross-margin model. Research-use cartridges and contract development are second curves consuming the same engineering team; the Irish entity and CE mark are a distraction.

### What must be true in twelve months

| Test | Signpost it is happening | Signpost it is not | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 510(k) cleared | Decision without a second request | Second request in H1 2027 | S1, S69 |
| Capillary equivalence | Slope, bias and total error at each decision level; CV below 10% | Categorical agreement only | S1, S68 |
| Waiver on the critical path | Pre-submission for flex and user studies, or a dual filing | Standalone waiver after clearance | S1, S72 |
| Manufacturing ready | ISO 13485 certificate; automation ordered | Audit slipped; no automation by mid-2027 | S1, S71 |
| Commercial demand | Letter converted to a purchase order; cartridges per site per day rising | Sales headcount in single digits against 300 sites | S1, unverified |

Counter-evidence deserves weight: the regulatory vice-president has a record of FDA clearances, the evaluation pipeline and reorder rate are unusual for an investigational device, and a documentation-only request could clear faster. No single milestone is implausible; three sit on the same critical path with no float, and the round assumes all three land on schedule.

Diligence questions: what the FDA request asked and what the answer adds; whether the company will convert to a dual submission with the waiver; what utilisation the evaluation sites reached at maturity and what the sales model assumes per cleared assay; what capital expenditure and working capital the scale-up budget covers; and whether the distributor letter carries a minimum purchase obligation. Confidence in the sequencing is high because it rests on FDA's published clocks and the company's own dates; the revenue arithmetic is high-confidence, but the utilisation forecast is unverifiable until commercial sites run the panel."}],"isError":false}

arguments.markdown:
The revenue model is a $2,900 analyzer that costs $3,350 to build and a $38 consumable cartridge it realises $33.40 on, and it only clears its own costs at four to six panels per analyzer per day — four to six times what its 55 evaluation analyzers run. That gap decides whether the $78.5M of 2029 revenue exists. Figures are company-reported and unverified. The only dated volume is 1,680 cartridges a month, the January-September 2026 average (p.7, headed "2026 average"; figures as of 2026-09-30); across 55 analyzers that is 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day (1.22 on 300 operating days), against 8.0 in 2028 [S1].

### The razor loses money twice before the blade earns anything

Each placement is subsidised twice, company-reported and unverified. Build cost is $3,350 against a $2,900 list, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so an average placement realises $1,160 against $3,350 of cost — a $2,190 cash subsidy. The deck does not say how the analyzer is accounted for: the 58% margin needs the $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers outside cost of sales; expensing it gives 51%, three-year capitalisation 56%. The cartridge earns $17.20 at $33.40 against $16.20 cost, a 51.5% gross margin, less a 3% royalty to Corvia Microfluidics, the 60%-owned affiliate whose 22% minority holder is the chief technology officer; that royalty is $1.00 a cartridge today and $2.35M a year at the 2029 plan — a related-party claim. $7.50 at two million cartridges is a 54% cut from $16.20 on a line running 1,680 a month — a redesign, not a learning curve. Nine sales and support staff placed 55 analyzers in 31 months; at $120,000-240,000 fully loaded and half charged to placements, CAC is $25,600-51,200 [S1]. Three years of cartridge gross profit less the $2,190 subsidy, $15,621, does not repay that; it turns positive at 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target, where a three-year LTV:CAC reaches 3:1.

| Realised cartridge price | $33.40 | $31.00 | $31.00 | S1 (unverified) |
| Cartridge cost | $16.20 | $10.23 | $7.50 | S1 (unverified) |
| Annual cartridge gross profit per analyzer | $5,937 | $47,616 | $54,168 | S1 (unverified); calculated |

### FY2025 revenue is three businesses, and its volume is not disclosed

| FY2025 line | Revenue $M | Cost $M | Gross margin | Source |

| Evaluation: fees and cartridges | 1.10 | 0.33 | 70% | S1 (unverified); calculated |
