rows.finding: Vantelle reports troponin I imprecision of 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, while the IFCC definition of a high-sensitivity assay requires total imprecision below 10% CV there; Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified at <5.2% CV in whole blood at its 13-28 ng/L cut-offs.
rows.mechanism: A CV above 10% at the decision limit means repeated measurements of a true value at the cutoff scatter across it, so the assay cannot support the high-sensitivity label or the 0/1-hour chest-pain algorithms built on it, and clinicians will re-test or send to a lab.
rows.benchmark: IFCC high-sensitivity criteria (<10% CV at the 99th percentile and measurable above LoD in >=50% of healthy adults); Abbott ARCHITECT/Alinity hs-TnI at 2.0-5.0% CV; i-STAT hs-TnI <5.2% whole blood.
rows.weakens: The company's 96.1% categorical agreement and 92% cartridge reorder rate suggest the panel is usable in practice even if it is not high-sensitivity by IFCC criteria.
rows.implication: Price the word high-sensitivity out of the thesis and require a repeat precision study at the cutoff before paying a technology premium; treat the assay as a conventional cTnI at best.
rows.confidence: high - two independent sources (company deck and IFCC criteria via Abbott) plus a cleared predicate's published specification.
rows.follow_up: What is the assay's 99th-percentile value, limit of detection and share of healthy adults measurable above LoD, and what CV does the pivotal study show at each cutoff?

rows.finding: The 640-sample, 128-patient study was venous blood run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site between September and December 2025; six results were excluded and agreement is a two-bucket normal/abnormal match, not a method comparison.
rows.mechanism: Categorical agreement hides direction and magnitude of error at the cut-off; without slope, intercept, bias and total error across the measuring interval, the data cannot show that the device measures the same quantity as the laboratory, which is what a Class II cardiac assay submission has to demonstrate.
rows.benchmark: FDA-cleared POC hs-troponin summaries report multi-day precision, LoB/LoD/LoQ, linearity, interference and method comparison against a laboratory method; the capsule study reports only percent agreement.
rows.weakens: A 128-patient study is enough to generate a plausible signal and the pivotal study (about 1,150 patients, four sites, finger-stick, clinic staff) is designed to answer the question properly.
rows.implication: Add a condition: clearance must rest on the pivotal study's analytical equivalence data, not on the internal agreement study; a 510(k) built on the latter alone would likely draw another additional-information request.
rows.confidence: high - the study design is stated in the deck and the deficiency is visible against how cleared predicates were evaluated.
rows.follow_up: Will the pivotal study report Passing-Bablok slope, intercept, bias and total error at the clinical cut-offs, and will the raw data be available in the FDA decision summary?

rows.finding: No capillary-versus-venous equivalence data exists in the deck; the only published capillary high-sensitivity troponin verification located is a 2026 study in an African population, and the haemolysis-sensitive potassium assay has a documented pseudohyperkalaemia failure mode in whole-blood analysis.
rows.mechanism: A finger stick produces interstitial-fluid-contaminated, often haemolysed capillary blood; potassium is the analyte most sensitive to haemolysis, so a 40 microlitre sample that is partly haemolysed biases potassium upward and can trigger false hyperkalaemia alerts.
rows.benchmark: Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI accepts whole blood without anticoagulant only if tested within three minutes; Siemens epoc accepts capillary whole blood for creatinine and potassium but is a moderate-complexity system; the capillary hs-troponin literature is only now being published.
rows.weakens: The pivotal study uses finger-stick samples run by clinic staff, so it is the right design; if it succeeds, the gap closes.
rows.implication: Make capillary-venous equivalence for all five analytes, with a haemolysis index, the single most important diligence item before the Series B closes.
rows.confidence: medium-high - the absence of data is certain from the deck; the size of the haemolysis bias for this cartridge is not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Does the cartridge measure a haemolysis index and reject or flag samples, and what share of finger sticks in the pivotal study were haemolysed?

rows.finding: Every constituent assay already exists at the point of care: finger-stick creatinine (Nova StatSensor), capillary HbA1c (Roche cobas b 101), capillary whole-blood creatinine and potassium (Siemens epoc), and whole-blood hs-troponin (Abbott i-STAT, cleared 2025-01-03).
rows.mechanism: The defensible novelty is integration, not any single measurement: one 40 microlitre cartridge, five analytes, on-board calibration and a 12-minute turnaround. That is an engineering and workflow advantage that incumbents can copy assay by assay, and Abbott already owns the cardiac call point.
rows.benchmark: Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI: 22 microlitres, about 15 minutes, LoD 1.61 ng/L, CV <5.2%; Quidel TriageTrue hs-TnI is not sold in the US, which narrows the US field but does not empty it.
rows.weakens: No competitor offers all five analytes on one finger-stick cartridge, which is the workflow problem the company is actually solving.
rows.implication: Value the company as a workflow integrator with manufacturing upside, not as the owner of a unique biomarker; check what stops Abbott from adding HbA1c or Siemens from adding troponin.
rows.confidence: high - cleared clearances and product pages for four incumbents.
rows.follow_up: Which of the five assays carries the 510(k) and which are considered modifications, and what is the predicate for each?

rows.finding: Cartridge cost is $16.20 today on an 18-person pilot line, with a target of $10 at 1 million units and $7.50 at 2 million; the claimed 9-month shelf life rests on 6 months of stability data.
rows.mechanism: Going from roughly 20,000 cartridges a year to 2 million is a hundredfold volume step that requires automated assembly, in-line metering and quality control; the 54% cost reduction is a learning-curve promise whose timing depends on capital the plan does not itemise, and a shelf-life claim beyond the data creates expiry and field-failure risk.
rows.benchmark: Learning-curve arithmetic: 16.20 to 7.50 is a 54% reduction over about seven doublings, roughly consistent with 10-15% cost decline per doubling, but only if yield and automation arrive on schedule.
rows.weakens: The pilot line already ships 27,600 cartridges since March 2024 and 1,680 a month, so the process is real and not a slide.
rows.implication: Hold the cost curve as an assumption, not a fact; a scale-up that stalls at $12-13 destroys the 2029 gross margin and forces another round.
rows.confidence: medium - costs are company figures; no third-party validation of yield or line speed.
rows.follow_up: What are current line yield, cycle time and the capex and timeline to reach 1 million and 2 million units, and what real-time stability data supports 9 months?

rows.finding: IP is one granted family (US, March 2023), one reader family under final rejection since July 2026 with an appeal under consideration, two unpublished families, and a licensed sealing patent owned by 60%-held Corvia on a 3% royalty; the 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion excluded the troponin chemistry.
rows.mechanism: The troponin chemistry - the assay that anchors the cardiac use case - has no opined freedom to operate, while the reader claims are contested; a competitor can attack either the chemistry or the reader and the royalty leaks 3% of cartridge sales to a related party.
rows.benchmark: A defensible IVD position normally needs a granted claim that reads on the cartridge or the detection method plus an FTO opinion covering the lead assay; here the granted claim covers the cartridge and the FTO opinion stops short of the chemistry.
rows.weakens: The cartridge architecture is granted and the sealing IP is exclusively licensed, so the manufacturing design has some cover.
rows.implication: Commission an FTO opinion on the troponin chemistry and a validity assessment of the reader appeal before closing; if the appeal fails, the moat narrows to the cartridge and the cost curve.
rows.confidence: medium - patent facts come only from the deck; no public patent record was retrievable for the company in this run.
rows.follow_up: What are the granted claim numbers and their scope, who owns the troponin chemistry rights, and what does the appeal record say about the examiner's grounds?

rows.finding: The base rate for cartridge-based point-of-care platforms is poor: LumiraDx's platform was sold to Roche after administration in 2023-2024, Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after the FDA revoked its authorization, and Truvian Health needed more than $150 million to approach a first FDA submission.
rows.mechanism: These platforms fail on regulatory and quality execution and on cash consumed before scale, not on demand; Vantelle's plan front-loads manufacturing scale and a 300-site launch before a waiver or a five-assay clearance exists.
rows.benchmark: LumiraDx (administration 2023-12-29, sale closed 2024-07-29), Cue Health (Chapter 7, 2024-05-28), Truvian (>$150M raised, submission targeted 2024-2025).
rows.weakens: Cue and LumiraDx were largely COVID-demand stories; Vantelle's cardiac and metabolic use case is less cyclical.
rows.implication: Demand a staged capital plan tied to the waiver and the pivotal data rather than a single $30M cheque that funds scale before the evidence exists.
rows.confidence: high - primary filings and announcements for each analog.
rows.follow_up: What does the company's quality system look like today, and has any third party audited the Tempe line?

plan.decision_question: Is the five-analyte finger-stick panel technically proven and defensible, or is the evidence a venous-blood feasibility study run by the company's own staff?

plan.why_different: Goes below the product description to assay-level and manufacturing-level proof: what is analytically demonstrated, under what specimen and operator conditions, and what a funded competitor would need to replicate.
plan.mechanism: Imprecision at the decision limit drives misclassification of chest-pain patients and forfeits the high-sensitivity label; cartridge yield and real-time stability drive gross margin and field reliability; patent scope decides whether the cost curve can be defended or is free to copy.

rows.finding: Vantelle's troponin I runs at 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, above the IFCC <10% high-sensitivity definition and more than twice Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI (<5.2% CV whole blood, 1.61 ng/L LoD).
rows.mechanism: A high-sensitivity troponin is defined by imprecision at the decision limit; at 11.8% CV a true value on the cutoff spreads roughly +/-23% at 95%, so results cross the line and rule-out pathways built on hs-TnI cannot be replicated.
rows.benchmark: IFCC/AACC <10% CV at the 99th percentile; Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI below 5.2% CV.
rows.weakens: Company may be measuring CV at a different level or with a different sample matrix; neither the cutoff value nor the LoD is disclosed, so the comparison is to a claim, not a verified dataset.
rows.implication: Price the assay as conventional cTnI, not hs-TnI; require the cutoff, LoD and precision profile before the round closes.
rows.confidence: high on the gap, medium on magnitude because the dataset is company-reported and partial.
rows.follow_up: What is the 99th-percentile value, the LoD and the full precision profile at each decision level?

rows.finding: The 640-sample, 128-patient method comparison is venous blood, run by company staff, at a single urgent-care site; it reports 96.1% categorical agreement (123/128) with six exclusions for insufficient sample or cartridge error, and no capillary data.
rows.mechanism: Categorical agreement hides direction and magnitude of error; a false negative on troponin is the error that matters. The exclusions and the venous, staff-run design remove exactly the variables (capillary collection, untrained operators, short fills) that a 510(k) specimen comparison and CLIA flex studies test.
rows.benchmark: Class II cardiac assay submissions require multi-level precision, LoB/LoD/LoQ, linearity, haemolysis interference, specimen comparison and method comparison with slope, bias and total error.
rows.weakens: Categorical agreement of 96.1% is respectable for a first feasibility set; the 95% interval (93-99%) does not exclude acceptable performance, and the pivotal study is designed to answer the gap.
rows.implication: Treat the pivotal capillary study, not the existing dataset, as the binary risk; the section's confidence cannot rise until it reports.
rows.confidence: high - the design limitations are stated in the company's own materials.
rows.follow_up: What were the six excluded results, and what were the five discordant troponin results and their direction?

rows.finding: A CLIA Waiver by Application must reference an already cleared or approved application and include flex studies plus a clinical study in the hands of intended users at intended-use sites; FDA's goal is a substantive interaction at 90 days and a MDUFA decision at 150 FDA days (180 for a dual 510(k)+CW), and an additional-information request adds up to 180 days.
rows.mechanism: The waiver is a second validation exercise with its own evidence standard, not paperwork appended to a clearance; it cannot start until the 510(k) is cleared, so a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028.
rows.benchmark: Company plan: waiver application Q3 2027.
rows.weakens: A dual submission filed with the second 510(k) would collapse both clocks into one 180-day goal and could decide in late 2027; the company has not said it will use that pathway.
rows.implication: Model waived-site revenue from 2028, not 2027; ask whether the company will convert to a dual submission.
rows.confidence: high - published FDA review goals.
rows.follow_up: Will Vantelle file the waiver as a dual submission with the second 510(k), and has it pre-submitted the flex and user-study protocols?

rows.finding: No point-of-care troponin system reviewed carries waived status: Abbott's i-STAT publishes a separate waived-test manual for chemistry and blood-gas cartridges, its hs-TnI cartridge launched 2025-01-03 as a moderate-complexity test, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for i-STAT cTnI on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is listed moderate (its Cardio3 panel is not sold in the U.S.).
rows.mechanism: Waived cardiac testing has no established precedent to copy; a five-analyte waived panel would need its own user study and flex data, and the closest analog proves the opposite - the market leader sells troponin as moderate complexity.
rows.benchmark: Abbott i-STAT waived chemistry/blood-gas menu; Quidel Triage MeterPro troponin moderate complexity.
rows.weakens: Abbott's waived menu changes with new clearances, and the PulseAid list is a secondary rendering of the FDA CLIA database; a future waiver by a competitor would not help Vantelle but would prove feasibility.
rows.implication: The waiver is the highest-risk, least-precedented regulatory step and the gate to the urgent-care customer set; the plan must fund a waiver study it has not described.
rows.confidence: high on Abbott and CMS documents; medium on completeness of the troponin list.
rows.follow_up: Which intended users and sites will run the waiver study, and what flex studies are planned for haemolysis and short fills?

rows.finding: The cartridge costs $16.20 at pilot volume against $10 at 1 million units and $7.50 at 2 million, on an 18-person pilot line with six months of stability data against a nine-month claimed shelf life.
rows.mechanism: The margin case depends on yield and line speed that only volume production proves; stability is the gating variable for a distributed, inventory-held consumable, and a six-month dataset cannot support a nine-month claim to a reviewer.
rows.benchmark: Peer point-of-care consumables are sold at $10-20 with validated shelf lives of 12 months or more; the company's own cost targets.
rows.weakens: If the device is manufactured at low volume for evaluation only, unit cost is not yet meaningful; automation could deliver the curve faster than a linear read-across suggests.
rows.implication: Treat the scale-up budget ($12.0M of the $30M) as the real test; a yield or stability miss converts the gross-margin story into a working-capital problem.
rows.confidence: medium - company data, no independent manufacturing evidence.
rows.follow_up: What is line yield at the pilot line, what cycle time is assumed at 1 million units, and what stability data exist at 6, 9 and 12 months?

rows.finding: One patent family is granted (2023-03), the five-assay reader application received a final rejection in 2026-07 with an appeal under consideration, two families are unpublished, and the licensed Corvia sealing patent is the only opined freedom to operate - the opinion excludes the troponin chemistry.
rows.mechanism: Without an opined route on the lead assay, the company's defensibility rests on trade secrets and manufacturing know-how, which are weaker against a funded competitor and do not stop a design-around.
rows.benchmark: Typical point-of-care cartridge portfolios hold 5-15 granted families; a single granted family plus one licensed patent is thin for a platform claim.
rows.weakens: Pending and unpublished applications may mature into granted claims; the rejection is appealable and the company says it is contesting it.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite an IP moat on the troponin assay; require the file wrappers and the FTO opinion's scope before closing.
rows.confidence: medium - no public patent record was retrievable, so all patent facts are unverified company statements.
rows.follow_up: Can the company produce the file wrappers and the FTO opinion, and what claims survive the reader rejection?

rows.benchmark: Abbott's global Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025 [S67]; $2.4B would be 4x that, $368M about 60% of it.

plan.decision_question: Is the $2.4B US serviceable market real, and how much is reachable within five years at the utilization the company's own evaluation sites deliver?
plan.thesis_sentence: The $2.4B US serviceable market is an arithmetic artefact of an unproven utilization assumption: at the 1.2 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites actually run, the same 13,200 sites and $38 price support about $368M of annual cartridge revenue, roughly a seventh of the claim and about 60% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care line, so the need is real but the number the $140M pre-money rests on is not.
plan.why_different: Only this section rebuilds the market from independent site counts, CLIA certificate data and CMS reimbursement rather than from the company model, and it separates the size of the opportunity from the price the buyer can actually collect.
plan.mechanism: Market size = sites x analyzers per site x panels per analyzer-day x operating days x price. Revenue arrives per analyte ordered and paid, while cartridge cost is fixed per run, so two inputs carry nearly all the error: panels per analyzer-day and the number of analytes actually ordered on each run.
plan.comparison_set: Abbott's global Point of Care line ($606M FY2025, 10-K); three independent US point-of-care diagnostics estimates ($2.89B, $6.4B, $14.0B for 2025); 2026 Medicare CLFS rates for the five analytes; CLIA certificate mix (233,448 waiver vs 30,756 moderate-complexity laboratories).
plan.counter_evidence: The 41 evaluation sites run investigational devices whose results cannot be used for patient care, so 1.2 panels per analyzer-day is a floor rather than a commercial run-rate; the company's 52-clinic survey reports a median of 14 send-outs a day, which if true would support several times the observed utilization.
plan.visual: Market size table comparing the deck build-up, observed-utilization, one-analyzer and half-model scenarios, plus the regional market table with CLIA facility counts for Texas, Arizona and New Mexico.
plan.prohibited: huge market; large addressable market; strong demand; clear business model; fierce competition; well positioned; risks are manageable; vague counts such as about 5 or many clinics; any sentence describing how the section is written

Its own 41 evaluation sites ran 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers in 2026: 30.5 per analyzer-month, 1.22 per operating day at 300 days. The same site base and price at 1.22 produce $368M.
rows.mechanism: Cartridge revenue scales linearly with panels per analyzer-day, so a 6.5x utilisation gap cuts the market by 6.5x; the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites and two analyzers implies 7.35 panels per analyzer-day at $31, close to the model's eight and six times the observed rate.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's global Point of Care line sold $606M in FY2025; the claimed $2.4B US SAM is four times that, and the observed-utilisation $368M is 60% of it.
rows.weakens: Evaluation analyzers are labelled investigational use only and cannot be used for patient care, so 1.22 a day is a floor; billing-enabled sites could run more. The 41 sites are also a selected, early-adopter base.
rows.implication: Underwrite the US cartridge opportunity at $368M or less and price the round on that, not on $2.4B.

rows.finding: 2026 Medicare CLFS pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine and $4.76 for potassium: $71.38 for all five, $61.67 for troponin plus NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, and $51.73 for troponin plus NT-proBNP. The other four codes without the natriuretic peptide cap at $32.12, below the $38 list and the $33.40 average realised price; an HbA1c-creatinine-potassium metabolic run pays $19.65 and a troponin-potassium run $17.23.
rows.mechanism: The clinic's revenue per cartridge is the sum of the fee-schedule rates of the assays actually ordered, so the natriuretic peptide carries 55% of a full-menu collection; without it the cartridge is a loss at Medicare rates regardless of how many of the other four are ordered.
rows.benchmark: Cartridge at $38 list and $33.40 realised in 2026, plus a $650 monthly analyzer fee: at 41 cartridges a month the full panel collects $2,926.58 against $2,208 of cartridge and analyzer cost, $718.58 of gross margin before staff and billing.

rows.implication: No waiver decision before Q1 2028 and mid-2028 realistic; the 300 sites targeted for end-2027 must be moderate-complexity hospital or reference laboratories, and 2027 revenue cannot come from waived urgent care.

rows.confidence: High on the counts; medium on the traditional/limited split as a proxy for chest-pain capability.
rows.follow_up: What is the company's site mix by ownership and scope, and how many evaluation sites are hospital-affiliated?

rows.mechanism: The certificate, not the sales force, sets the addressable site count: a Certificate of Waiver site cannot legally run a moderate-complexity cardiac panel, and a waiver cannot be granted until the device is cleared and the user studies are reviewed.

rows.benchmark: The deck's own market sizing assumes 8 panels a day per analyzer; evaluation sites average 1.35 cartridges a day per site (41 a month across 41 sites).

rows.confidence: high - arithmetic on disclosed figures.

Separately, FY2026E gross margin of 61% sits above the 51% cartridge margin while instruments sell below cost.
rows.mechanism: A stocking order tied to a clearance date after the fiscal year end inflates the current year and flatters the growth rate into 2027; a blended margin above the mix's best component signals either an undisclosed high-margin line or an error.
rows.benchmark: A blended 61% gross margin is below the 51% cartridge margin only if other revenue carries near-zero cost.
rows.weakens: The order could ship in December 2026 if clearance arrives early, but the company's own clearance estimate is Q1 2027.
rows.implication: Treat FY2026E as a 2027 number and haircut the 2026 revenue and margin; the plan's first projection line fails a basic timing test.

rows.implication: Discount the distributor pipeline to zero until a purchase order exists, and model the Corvia royalty as a permanent 3% cost of goods.

rows.benchmark: Triage's $23.96 a test against Vantelle's $38 a cartridge, a 59% premium that only five ordered analytes justify.
rows.weakens: Triage needs EDTA whole blood or plasma, so it cannot be run from a finger stick in a clinic without a phlebotomist and does not substitute for Vantelle at the labour-poor site.
rows.implication: Model $25-$30 realized per cartridge for the first commercial years, not $38; a $30 price on a $16.20 cost leaves 46% gross margin, not the 51% the deck shows.

rows.follow_up: What price and menu did Southwest Clinical Supply commit to in its non-binding letter of intent for 300 sites?

rows.source_type: primary company release, independent deal note, independent media
rows.finding: Roche closed its purchase of LumiraDx's point-of-care platform on 2024-07-29 [S91] for an aggregate $353.5M at closing after a $295M upfront payment [S116], and Cue Health, once valued at $2.3B, shut down and laid off all staff in May 2024 [S110].
rows.mechanism: Finger-stick point-of-care platforms need menu breadth, placement volume and reimbursement at once; missing one is fatal regardless of assay quality, and the platform is worth more inside an incumbent's menu than standalone.
rows.benchmark: LumiraDx sold for about $354M after raising far more; Vantelle's $140M pre-money is 40% of that price with no clearance and no waiver.
rows.weakens: Both failures were tied to COVID-19 demand collapse, while a cardiac and metabolic panel addresses recurring non-pandemic use, so the base rate overstates the risk.
rows.implication: Price the round against a $350M platform exit, not against a $2.4B market; at $140M pre-money the entry multiple leaves little room for a waiver delay.

rows.follow_up: Which strategic acquirer would pay for a single-panel platform with 300 sites, and at what multiple of cartridge revenue?

rows.benchmark: Each competitor covers two to three of the five analytes; none covers all five from one finger stick in the US.
rows.weakens: Regulatory integration of five assays into one cartridge with one sample and one calibration is harder than the component list suggests, and Vantelle's VD-1 cartridge patent is granted in the US.
rows.implication: The gap Vantelle targets is a packaging gap, not an unmet clinical need; it is closeable by any of four incumbents within one product cycle.
rows.confidence: High on the source documents, medium on the negative claim because the FDA waived-analyte database did not render.
rows.follow_up: Is Abbott's hs-TnI cartridge CLIA-waived, and is capillary blood an accepted sample type for it?

rows.finding: Quest Diagnostics earned $11.04B in FY2025 at a 33.2% gross margin [S65]; QuidelOrtho earned $2.73B in FY2025 across four business units and names Abbott, Danaher, Roche and Siemens Healthineers among its principal competitors [S22].
rows.mechanism: The substitute is a national network with payer contracts and a one-to-three-day service; the clinic bears no capital, so point-of-care wins only where turnaround time has clinical value or the patient will not return.
rows.benchmark: Reference labs at roughly 18x Abbott's point-of-care line, with no instrument cost to the clinic.
rows.weakens: Turnaround time is decisive for suspected myocardial infarction and heart failure, and a rural emergency department cannot send a chest-pain patient home for a result in three days.
rows.implication: The beachhead is time-critical cardiac testing at sites far from a laboratory, not routine metabolic screening, which the reference labs already deliver at a lower cost per test.
rows.confidence: High.
rows.follow_up: What share of the 41 sites' runs were cardiac (time-critical) versus metabolic (routine)?

rows.finding: Four entities: Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. (Delaware, formed 2018-03-12) is the Series B issuer, holds patent families VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC (Arizona, formed 2022-05-09) runs the Tempe pilot line with 18 staff and leases the plant; Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited (Ireland, formed 2025-01-15) has no staff; Corvia Microfluidics LLC (Texas, formed 2016-02-01; 60% acquired 2021-04 for stock) holds the CM-1 sealing patent licensed exclusively to Vantelle.
rows.mechanism: The parent holds the IP and the FDA registration, so a new investor in the parent owns the regulatory dossier and the patents; the Arizona LLC ring-fences the plant lease and employment liabilities; the Irish entity ring-fences future EU product-liability exposure but has no PRRC or staff, so it cannot yet act as an IVDR legal manufacturer.
rows.benchmark: Standard single-US-issuer structure, no VIE and no offshore holding chain. Corvia is a 60%-owned consolidated subsidiary with a 40% noncontrolling interest, which is unusual for a core patent.
rows.weakens: The deck does not state whether the Corvia licence survives a change of control, whether the 40% put is capped, or whether the Irish entity has signed intercompany or transfer-pricing agreements; any of these can move value or liability outside the entity being priced.
rows.implication: Investable at the parent level, but the $15M should be conditioned on the Corvia operating agreement, licence and put terms and on confirmation that no IP is pledged to the lender.
rows.confidence: medium - entity roles come from the deck only; no state registry or Form D record located to confirm formation dates.
rows.follow_up: Obtain the Corvia LLC agreement, the CM-1 exclusive licence with change-of-control and termination terms, the Arizona lease, and the Irish entity's constitutional documents.

rows.finding: The $140M pre-money is stated on 42,991,881 fully diluted shares, not the 36,400,000 'shares today' the deck displays: the difference is the bridge conversion (2,571,392 Series B-1 shares at $2.4423, being 75% of the $3.2564 price, for $6.28M of principal plus 8% interest) and 4,020,489 new option-pool shares. On that basis the CEO holds 14.89% pre-money and the CTO 11.17%, not the 17.6% and 13.2% shown in the 'today' column.
rows.mechanism: The pre-money column includes securities that do not yet exist as issued shares, so a reader comparing the two deck columns overstates founder ownership by roughly 2.7 points; the price itself is internally consistent ($140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564; 52,204,508 x $3.2564 = $170.0M post-money).
rows.benchmark: Cooley Q2 2025: 98% of venture rounds use a 1x preference and 95% non-participating; Osler 2025: 20.4% of rounds give new investors a senior preference. Vantelle's bridge discount and pool top-up are conventional; its Series A participation is not.
rows.weakens: The arithmetic is internally consistent and the deck discloses the bridge conversion and pool increase in footnotes, so this is a presentation-basis issue rather than a misstatement.
rows.implication: Price the deal off the 42,991,881-share pre-money; the $15M lead buys 4,606,314 shares, or 8.82% of the 52,204,508 post-money, not 15/170 of a notional clean cap table.
rows.confidence: high - all figures derive from deck shares and prices and reproduce exactly.
rows.follow_up: Confirm the bridge note principal, accrued interest to close and any warrants issued to bridge holders, none of which the deck discloses.

rows.finding: Post-money the option overhang is 19.96%: 5,200,000 granted options (9.96%) plus 5,220,489 unallocated pool shares (10.00%), against a typical Series B total pool of 10-15% of fully diluted equity. The 10% unallocated pool is created inside the $140M pre-money, so existing holders bear it; it is worth $17.0M at $3.2564 and is 12.1% of the stated pre-money.
rows.mechanism: A pool shuffle moves value from existing holders to future employees and, because it is counted in the pre-money share count, it lowers the effective operating-business valuation the new investor is paying: excluding the 4,020,489 new pool shares, the pre-money is $126.9M, not $140M.
rows.benchmark: terms.law stage benchmarks: 10-12% at seed, 15-20% at Series A, 10-15% at Series B and later, measured as total pool. Vantelle's combined 19.96% is above the Series B range.
rows.weakens: A 10% unallocated pool ahead of a 300-site launch and a CFO/quality hiring wave is defensible on hiring grounds; the issue is that the deck presents 10% as the pool while the granted options make the true overhang double that.
rows.implication: Treat $126.9M as the operating pre-money and require a hiring plan that ties the 5.22M unallocated shares to named roles, or the company will return for another pool refresh within 12 months.
rows.confidence: high for the arithmetic; medium for the benchmark.
rows.follow_up: Obtain the 2026 equity incentive plan, the strike prices of the 5.2M granted options and the vesting/acceleration terms for the founders and the CTO.

rows.finding: The preference stack absorbs the first $76.8M of exit value before common: Series B/B-1 $36.28M (1x, senior, non-participating), Series A $36.0M (1x, participating), Seed $4.5M (1x, non-participating). At a $100M exit the founders receive about $7.6M (7.6% of proceeds); at $170M (the round's own post-money) about $29.9M (17.6%); at $250M about $46.0M (18.4%).
rows.mechanism: The Series A's participation takes 23.75% of residual proceeds after its preference, so founder proceeds plateau near 18-20% of exit value well above the round price; the new Series B returns 1.0x at a $170M exit and needs roughly a $357M exit for 2x.
rows.benchmark: Only about 5% of 2025 venture deals (Cooley Q2 2025) use participating preferred; Vantelle's Series A is one of them, and the new Series B ranks senior to it in 20.4%-of-deals territory (Osler 2025).
rows.weakens: At high exits the participation matters less and the structure converges with a standard stack; the Series A's $36M preference is modest relative to a $500M exit.
rows.implication: The $15M lead check is a 1.0x instrument at the round price and a ~1.6x instrument at a $300M exit; the underwriting case must rest on an exit well above $350M, or the Series A participation should be bought out or capped as a condition.
rows.confidence: medium - the waterfall is an analyst calculation from deck share counts and preference terms, ignoring option exercise proceeds and any senior fees.
rows.follow_up: Confirm whether the Series A participation is capped, whether the Series B is pari passu with or senior to the Series A in a deemed liquidation, and whether any investor holds a redemption right.

rows.finding: The core cartridge-sealing patent CM-1 is owned by Corvia, 40% of which is held by Corvia's founders including CTO Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist with 22%; Vantelle pays Corvia a 3% royalty on cartridge net sales, so the CTO personally receives 0.66% of cartridge sales (about $0.52M on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M). Corvia's minority may put its 40% to Vantelle at fair market value, worth roughly $9.4M on the FY2029 royalty stream at a 10x multiple.
rows.mechanism: Cash leaves the consolidated group to the 40% minority and to the CTO personally, and the put converts a future royalty into a cash obligation at the moment of an exit when fair value is highest; the acquirer of Vantelle would also need the licence to survive the change of control.
rows.benchmark: No third-party valuation or arm's-length benchmarking of the 3% royalty is disclosed; a related-party licence to a company 22%-owned by the CTO is a governance flag, not a market benchmark.
rows.weakens: Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, so the net cost to the group is 1.2% of cartridge sales; the 2021 acquisition was priced in stock, and the put gives the minority an exit rather than a perpetual claim.
rows.implication: Capitalise roughly $9-10M of leakage at plan and require a Corvia buyout, a royalty cap or a right to acquire the 40% at a pre-agreed formula before the Series B closes; also obtain a patent-assignment or licence-survival opinion.
rows.confidence: medium - royalty and ownership are disclosed; the value of the put is an analyst estimate with no disclosed formula.
rows.follow_up: Who are the other Corvia minority holders and what are their put terms, exercise windows and valuation mechanics? Does the CM-1 licence terminate on a Vantelle change of control?

rows.finding: The board after closing is 6 seats: 2 common (Dr. Wren Albescu, Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist), 1 Seed (Owen Pakula, Juniper Rock Capital), 1 Series A (Celeste Moreau, Ardent Peak Ventures), 1 Series B (Meridian, if it leads) and 1 independent seat that is vacant. No founder super-voting shares are disclosed; founders hold 21.45% of post-money economics.
rows.mechanism: The founders cannot control the board alone, which is the main structural difference from Theranos, where Holmes held super-majority Class B voting control and the SEC settlement stripped it; but an unfilled independent seat and undisclosed protective provisions leave the related-party royalty, new debt and a sale without a documented independent check.
rows.benchmark: Theranos (SEC 2018-41): founder voting control and a board without independent verification; the SEC remedy required Holmes to convert super-voting shares and return 18.9M shares. Vantelle's 2-of-6 founder seats are materially stronger governance than that base case.
rows.weakens: The deck does not disclose the voting agreement, protective provisions, or who designates the independent seat, so the board may be more investor-controlled or more founder-controlled than the seat count implies.
rows.implication: Make the independent director a closing condition and require audit-committee and related-party approval of the Corvia royalty and any new debt; the $15M lead should not close with a vacant independent seat.
rows.confidence: high for composition; low for protective provisions, which are not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Obtain the voting agreement, investors' rights agreement, ROFR/co-sale agreement and charter protective provisions; confirm the independent director nomination right.

rows.finding: Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to about 2027-03-31, while the target close is 2027-01-29; the $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only only until 2027-03, then amortises over 30 months at about $0.167M of principal a month. The FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance (40.7% of the year).
rows.mechanism: A closing slip of more than two months pushes the company into a bridge or a down round at the same moment debt amortisation begins, which strengthens the incoming investor's hand but also raises the risk that the company is financed by insiders at a higher preference ahead of the new money.
rows.benchmark: A Series B close normally funds 12-18 months of operations; 6.0 months pre-close and roughly 24-30 months post-close at the current burn leaves little room for a second FDA cycle or a CLIA-waiver delay.
rows.weakens: The company could cut burn, and existing investors have already shown willingness to bridge ($6.0M in 2026-06); the $2.4M order is contracted by a non-binding LOI, so it is not certain revenue.
rows.implication: Set the closing date and a minimum cash covenant; require lender consent and evidence that the term loan is not secured by IP before funding, and stress the plan for a Q3 2027 rather than Q1 2027 clearance.
rows.confidence: high for the burn arithmetic; medium for the loan terms, which are not disclosed beyond the amortisation schedule.
rows.follow_up: What is the interest rate, covenant package and collateral for the Bluestem loan? Are there UCC filings over patents or receivables? What is the liquidation preference of any bridge needed if the round slips?

rows.finding: No public record of the issuer was located on 2026-10-31: zero results for the company name in SEC EDGAR/Form D searches, Delaware and New Mexico searches, USPTO assignee searches, FDA 510(k) searches and news searches. Searches for the CEO return Vanta Diagnostics (a different company, CEO Christopher Howlett, ~39 employees) and Vantelle Health Group, LLC (California LLC B20260410893, filed 2026-09-09, healthcare administrative support, Upland CA), neither of which is the Delaware issuer in the deck.
rows.mechanism: A 2018 Delaware C-corporation that has raised at least $46.5M across seed, Series A and bridge and filed a 510(k) should leave a Form D, state annual-report and patent-assignee trail; its absence means every entity fact, ownership percentage and IP claim rests on company-provided material and cannot be checked before signing.
rows.benchmark: Cue Health and Theranos show that private diagnostics companies do leave public regulatory, court and press records; silence of this kind is a verification gap, not proof of wrongdoing.
rows.weakens: A private company can legitimately have a thin web footprint, and pending 510(k)s are not in the FDA's public database, so absence is not evidence that the filing does not exist. Name collisions also make negative search results unreliable.
rows.implication: Do not fund before obtaining the Delaware good-standing certificate, the complete Form D history, the Arizona and Texas registry records and the USPTO assignment records; treat every deck CV and entity date as unverified until then.
rows.confidence: medium - absence of evidence after six independent searches, not evidence of absence.
rows.follow_up: File a user data request for Delaware good standing, Form D filings, Arizona/Texas registry records and USPTO assignments; run a trademark search on 'Vantelle' against the California entity.

plan.decision_question: Is the legal and capital structure clean, fully disclosed and stable enough to underwrite a $15M lead check at a $140M pre-money?
plan.thesis_sentence: The structure is investable but not yet underwritable: one Delaware issuer cleanly holds the patents and the FDA submission, while a 40%-owned Texas affiliate holds the core sealing patent under an undisclosed licence and put, the CTO personally shares in its 3% royalty, and a 19.96% post-money option overhang leaves the $140M pre-money worth about $126.9M on the operating business.
plan.why_different: This section establishes who the issuer is, which entity holds the IP and the regulatory liability, and how exit proceeds and control rights divide; the technology, market and financial sections price the product and the plan, not the legal and capital plumbing.
plan.mechanism: Cash-flow and control rights: the preference stack, the related-party royalty and put, the pool shuffle and board composition determine who receives exit value and who can approve related-party deals and new debt.
plan.comparison_set: Cooley Q2 2025 (98% 1x, 95% non-participating), Osler 2025 (20.4% senior preference), terms.law pool benchmarks (10-15% Series B), Theranos SEC 2018-41 (founder voting control), Cue Health (quality failure after clearance), postmoneyvaluation Series B median ($200M post-money, 16.3% new money).
plan.counter_evidence: The cap-table arithmetic is internally consistent and the deck discloses the bridge and pool footnotes; there is no founder super-voting; founders hold only 2 of 6 board seats; Vantelle keeps 60% of the Corvia royalty; and the Corvia put is at fair market value, which may be a fair price rather than a leak.
plan.visual: Legal entity table plus the rebuilt cap table and a preference waterfall at $100M/$170M/$250M exits, with the KPI strip and timeline.
plan.prohibited: clean cap table, market-standard terms, founder-controlled, no red flags, standard structure, well positioned, strong governance

rows.finding: The fully diluted pre-money is 42,991,881 shares and the post-money 52,204,508 at $3.2564; $140.0M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564 and 52,204,508 x $3.2564 = $170.0M.
rows.mechanism: The bridge converts at a 75% discount and the pool top-up is carved out of the pre-money, so both dilute existing holders before Meridian's shares are issued.
rows.benchmark: Deck's pre-conversion share count of about 36.4M; the $3.2564 price and $170.0M post-money check only on 42,991,881 pre-money shares.
rows.weakens: No public filing corroborates any share count or the bridge terms.
rows.implication: Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% post-money; the bridge conversion and pool top-up must be conditions precedent, not assumptions.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; ownership percentages rest on unverified deck share counts.
rows.follow_up: Will the company provide the signed cap table and all bridge and seed side letters?

rows.finding: The Series A is a 1x participating preference: $36.0M back plus 23.75% of the residual; Cooley's Q2 2026 survey shows 96.4% of deals non-participating and 95.8% at 1x.
rows.mechanism: Participation lets the Series A take its preference and share the residual, stacking ahead of common and ahead of the founders' 14.89% pre-money stake.
rows.benchmark: Cooley Q2 2026: 96.4% of 166 financings had non-participating preferred, so participating structures are ~3.6% of deals.
rows.weakens: Cooley's percentage mixes stages and sectors; it establishes that participation is unusual, not that this term is unfair.
rows.implication: Model exits on the participating structure, not a simple 1x; the Series A takes value from the common at every exit above $36M.
rows.confidence: high on the Cooley benchmark; medium on the Vantelle terms because they are company-provided.
rows.follow_up: Does the Series A certificate of incorporation cap or convert the participation, and what protective provisions attach?

rows.finding: Granted plus unallocated options are 19.96% of post-money: 5,200,000 granted plus 5,220,489 unallocated; the top-up adds 4,020,489 shares, 7.7 points and $13.1M at $3.2564.
rows.mechanism: A pool created inside the pre-money dilutes existing holders, not the new money; granted options plus unallocated pool determine the true overhang.
rows.benchmark: The 10% post-money pool this round itself creates; no primary NVCA or Cooley survey Series B option-pool median could be retrieved.
rows.weakens: The 10% pool is itself the round's term, so it is not an independent benchmark.
rows.implication: Score the overhang warn rather than critical because the 10-15% comparison rests on secondary blogs; negotiate the pool top-up as a closing condition.
rows.confidence: medium — overhang figure company-provided; the absence of a primary benchmark is stated as a limitation.
rows.follow_up: What is the grant-by-grant option schedule, and will the pool top-up be post-money rather than pre-money?

rows.finding: Vantelle owns 60% of Corvia Microfluidics, which owns the CM-1 sealing patent and licenses it exclusively at a 3% royalty; the CTO owns 22% of Corvia and receives 0.66% of cartridge sales, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M.
rows.mechanism: A minority put at fair market value converts a perpetual royalty into a lump-sum exit liability; the CTO's dual role makes the royalty a related-party transfer.
rows.benchmark: 10x FY2029 royalty as an illustrative put value; no fairness opinion or LLC agreement disclosed.
rows.weakens: The put may be capped, may lapse on a sale, or may be priced below 10x; none of that is disclosed.
rows.implication: Treat the put as a $9.4M claim on exit proceeds and require a disinterested approval of the royalty and any change-of-control waiver.
rows.confidence: medium — inputs unverified, arithmetic clear.
rows.follow_up: What are the Corvia LLC agreement's put and change-of-control terms, and who holds the other 18% of the 40% minority?

rows.finding: The $140.0M pre-money is below the Q2 2026 Cooley Series B median of $185.2M, yet the deck's own FY2026E revenue of $5.9M puts the price at 23.7x revenue.
rows.mechanism: Median pre-money reflects companies with more revenue and later milestones; the sticker discount can coexist with a rich revenue multiple.
rows.benchmark: Cooley Q2 2026 median Series B pre-money $185.2M; Vantelle's $140.0M is 24% below, but on FY2026E revenue of $5.9M it is 23.7x.
rows.weakens: The Cooley median covers all sectors and stages within Series B and is not risk-adjusted.
rows.implication: A below-median sticker is not a discount; underwrite the price on the company's revenue and the preference stack, not the median.
rows.confidence: medium — valuation figures company-provided; the benchmark is primary survey data but not like-for-like.
rows.follow_up: What revenue and gross margin do the Series B comparables carry at closing?

rows.finding: Searches on 2026-10-31 found no SEC Form D, Delaware or Arizona registry record, USPTO assignee record, FDA decision or news for Vantelle Diagnostics.
rows.mechanism: Without a public record, every entity date, ownership percentage and IP claim in this section rests on company-provided material.
rows.benchmark: Zero hits is the expected result for a private company that has not filed a Form D, but the absence also means no independent confirmation of entity dates or IP ownership.
rows.weakens: A private company can be legitimately absent from all of these databases, especially before a priced round.
rows.implication: Make registry good standing, the Corvia LLC agreement and the CM-1 licence chain closing conditions.
rows.confidence: high that the public record is silent; not evidence that the deck is wrong.
rows.follow_up: Will the company provide certified Delaware and Arizona good-standing certificates and the USPTO assignment for CM-1?

plan.why_different: This section establishes entity identity, IP ownership, cap table, preferences and control; the financial, valuation and risk sections take the share count and preference stack as inputs.
plan.mechanism: The Series A's 1x participating preference and the senior Series B absorb the first $76.8M of exit value; the 10% pool top-up dilutes existing holders inside the pre-money; the Corvia 40% minority converts a 3% royalty into a put liability at exit.
plan.comparison_set: Cooley Q2 2026 median Series B pre-money $185.2M and 96.4% non-participating preferred; Theranos as the founder-control governance failure; the $170.0M post-money against the valuation section's $70M recommended price.
plan.counter_evidence: The Delaware issuer holds the patents and the FDA file, there is no VIE or dual-class structure, and $140M pre-money is 24% below Cooley's Q2 2026 Series B median; the Corvia put and the Series A participation are the structural costs that survive those points.

team.author: Company Analyst
queries: "Vantelle Diagnostics" leadership / chief executive officer: no public source names any Vantelle executive; results are Vanta Diagnostics (different company) and Vantelle Health Group LLC (CA, filed 2026-09-09)
"Vantelle Diagnostics" site:linkedin.com: only an auto-generated jobs page, no company or executive profile
"Vantelle Diagnostics" news / Albuquerque: zero results
QuidelOrtho FY2025 10-K Item 1: commercial headcount, ISO 13485 sites, CLIA-waiver burden
FDA warning letter Cue Health CMS# 675673 (2024-05-09): change control, lot release AQL and 9-month stability failure
Roche cobas liat 510(k) plus CLIA waiver for multiplex STI panels (2025-01-22): precedent for a multi-analyte waived panel
FDA FY2025 MDUFA report and Ova Solutions 510(k) review-time analysis: 112-139 day total time to decision
SEC press release 2018-41: Theranos founder control and governance failure

rows.finding: Dr. Wren Albescu has been CEO and a director since founding on 2018-03-12: MD in 2008, emergency physician at St. Brennan Regional Medical Center in Tucson 2011-2017, then medical director at Quillon Diagnostics 2017-2018. She has run the company for 8.6 years but has no disclosed prior P&L, regulatory filing or commercial launch experience.
rows.mechanism: An emergency physician who lived the 1-3 day lab turnaround understands the buyer and the workflow, which explains the 41-site evaluation program; the same background does not supply the FDA negotiation, quality-system or 300-site distribution experience that the next 18 months require.
rows.benchmark: Cue Health reached a $3B IPO and more than $480M raised before its quality failure and Chapter 7; Theranos raised over $700M on a founder with no diagnostics operating experience. Clinical insight alone is not a base rate for regulatory or commercial success.
rows.weakens: Her 2017-2018 medical-director role at a diagnostics company is one year of industry experience, and the deck gives no clearance, launch or revenue result attributable to her.
rows.implication: The clinical insight behind the 12-minute clinic workflow is credible and specific; the unproven part is regulatory and commercial scaling, which is what the $30M is for. Condition the round on a regulatory and commercial leadership layer around her.
rows.confidence: medium - dates come from the deck only; no public source confirms any role.
rows.follow_up: Reference-check two former Quillon colleagues and the lead Series A partner on her handling of the 2026 FDA additional-information request and the CFO departure.

rows.finding: Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist, CTO and director, holds a PhD in bioengineering (2012), was a senior microfluidics scientist at Pellucid Biosystems 2012-2016, founded Corvia Microfluidics in 2016-02, and is the inventor behind the CM-1 sealing patent that Vantelle licenses exclusively. Vantelle bought 60% of Corvia for stock in 2021-04; he retains 22% of Corvia and therefore 0.66% of Vantelle's cartridge net sales, on top of 4.8M Vantelle common shares (9.19% post-money).
rows.mechanism: The company's core manufacturing IP sits in an entity he co-owns, so his departure or a dispute over the licence impairs both product supply and the patent position; his royalty aligns him with cartridge volume but not with exit value per share.
rows.benchmark: No arm's-length benchmark is disclosed for the 3% royalty; the conflict is structural rather than comparable.
rows.weakens: The 2021 stock acquisition and continued role suggest alignment, and 60% of the royalty returns to Vantelle, so the net leakage is smaller than the headline 3%.
rows.implication: He is both the technical key person and a related-party counterparty; the round should require key-person insurance, a stay agreement and a Corvia simplification before closing.
rows.confidence: medium - patents and ownership are deck facts; inventorship and the licence terms are not publicly confirmed.
rows.follow_up: Is the CM-1 licence assignable on a Vantelle change of control? What are the other Corvia holders' put terms, and will the CTO exchange his Corvia interest for Vantelle equity?

rows.finding: Grace Oyelaran, RAC, VP Regulatory and Quality since 2025-11, holds an MS in regulatory science (2008) and spent 2009-2025 at Meridale Medical, rising from regulatory affairs manager to director; the deck credits her with leading 14 FDA 510(k) clearances. She joined 2025-11; the 510(k) was filed 2026-05-18 and the FDA's additional-information request arrived 2026-08-21, with the company planning to respond in 2026-12.
rows.mechanism: A single regulatory leader with no disclosed deputy is a key-person and throughput constraint at exactly the point where the FDA clock, the quality audit and the waiver study overlap; the 14-clearance claim is the credential the whole regulatory plan rests on, and it is the one claim the deck does not evidence.
rows.benchmark: Individual clearance counts are not published in the FDA 510(k) database, which lists applicants, not responsible individuals; the FDA's own 510(k) total time to decision averaged 139 days in FY2024 and 112 days in FY2025.
rows.weakens: Her 16-year tenure at one IVD employer and the RAC credential are appropriate, and the predecessor's September 2025 departure was covered by a November 2025 successor within two months.
rows.implication: The hire is well matched on paper, but she is one person owning 510(k) strategy, the AI response, ISO 13485 certification (audit booked Q1 2027, not yet certified), the 2027 CLIA-waiver application and EU IVDR readiness; that is four regulatory workstreams on one desk.
rows.confidence: medium - employment dates are deck facts; the 14-clearance claim is unverified and cannot be checked without employer confirmation or a list of submission numbers.
rows.follow_up: Ask for a list of the 14 submission numbers and their decisions, and reference-check her directly at Meridale Medical; ask who drafted the 2026-05-18 submission and who owns the AI response.

rows.finding: Luis Arrellano, VP Commercial since 2024-01, holds a BA in communications (2003) and spent 2006-2023 at Tavora Health Systems as a sales representative then regional vice president for the Southwest. Vantelle's 9 sales and support staff cover 41 evaluation sites (one per 4.6 sites) and its only route to 300 sites is a non-binding letter of intent with Southwest Clinical Supply and a $2.4M opening stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance.
rows.mechanism: Site coverage per commercial head falls from 4.6 to 33 sites at the 300-site target, a 7.2x increase in load, while the product is still investigational; the channel depends on one regional distributor with a non-binding LOI.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho employs more than 2,500 people in sales, service and marketing across more than 140 countries and about 1,200 service employees; Vantelle has 9 sales and support staff for 41 sites.
rows.weakens: Seventeen years of Southwest health-system sales is a direct match to the three current states, and a distributor model can scale sites without proportional headcount if the distributor performs.
rows.implication: The commercial plan is a distributor LOI, not a built channel; budget 6-8 commercial hires and a payer/health-economics lead before a 300-site launch, and do not underwrite the $2.4M stocking order as revenue until clearance.
rows.confidence: high for the headcount arithmetic from the deck; medium for the productivity inference.
rows.follow_up: Reference-check the Southwest Clinical Supply relationship and the two named evaluation customers; ask for the 300-site pipeline by name, contract status and expected cartridges per site.

rows.finding: Darnell Whitcombe, CPA, has been interim CFO on a part-time basis since 2026-03, after the prior CFO left in 2026-02; he holds a BS in accounting (1999) and has been a partner at Whitcombe Advisory, a fractional-finance firm, since 2014. The deck gives no prior operating CFO role, no fundraise history and no equity grant for him.
rows.mechanism: The raise, the burn model ($1.15M a month), the $5.0M loan covenants and the revenue recognition of a $2.4M stocking order all need an owner with full-time command of the numbers; a fractional adviser is a stopgap, not a control.
rows.benchmark: A company raising $30M from an institutional lead would normally have a full-time CFO or VP Finance; Vantelle has a part-time adviser whose firm's other clients and fee arrangement are not disclosed.
rows.weakens: The interim appointment is disclosed, the CPA credential is real and a fractional CFO is common at this stage; the risk is timing, not competence.
rows.implication: A part-time CFO during a $30M institutional raise and a 6-month cash runway is a control gap; make a full-time CFO or a named VP Finance a closing condition and require audited or reviewed FY2026 accounts.
rows.confidence: high for the dates and part-time status; medium for the control conclusion.
rows.follow_up: Who signs the Series B financial representations? Is the interim CFO engaged through a related party? Will a full-time CFO be hired before or after closing, and who prepared the FY2026E and the 2029 plan?

rows.finding: No public source located on 2026-10-31 names any of the five executives in a Vantelle role: searches on the company name return a generated jobs page, a similarly named Vanta Diagnostics (CEO Christopher Howlett, about 39 employees) and Vantelle Health Group, LLC (California, filed 2026-09-09), neither of which is the issuer. Every CV date, degree and achievement in the deck is therefore company-provided and unverified.
rows.mechanism: The underwriting case rests on claims that cannot be checked from public records - a 14-clearance regulatory career, a medical-director stint and a 17-year sales career - so a false or inflated claim would surface only in diligence, after pricing.
rows.benchmark: A 64-person FDA-regulated company with 41 evaluation sites should have a LinkedIn company page, executive profiles, trade-press coverage or FDA database entries; none was located.
rows.weakens: The company may deliberately keep a low profile, and the name collisions make negative search results unreliable; the absence is a diligence gap rather than a contradiction.
rows.implication: Price the team on verified execution, not on CVs: require written references from two former employers or investors per executive and a background check before the $15M is released.
rows.confidence: medium - six independent searches found nothing, but absence of indexing is not absence of the people.
rows.follow_up: Run reference checks with Meridale Medical, Tavora Health Systems, Quillon Diagnostics and Whitcombe Advisory; verify degrees with the institutions; run a litigation and liens search on each director.

rows.finding: The team's manufacturing and quality bench is thin relative to its claims: 18 manufacturing staff on a pilot line, no named VP Manufacturing or VP Quality, ISO 13485 certification not yet obtained, and a 9-month cartridge shelf-life claim supported by 6 months of data. Cue Health's 2024 FDA warning letter found unauthorised reagent and firmware changes (change order CP-4166) and a lot-release AQL that could allow a failure rate above the claimed 99.1% negative percent agreement, with the device's 9-month stability specifically at issue.
rows.mechanism: Scaling from pilot volumes to a 300-site launch multiplies lot-release and change-control exposure at exactly the stage when the quality system is still uncertified; Cue Health shows that a cleared, capitalised cartridge franchise can be destroyed by manufacturing discipline rather than by the clinical data.
rows.benchmark: Cue Health had EUA authorisation and a large capital base and still failed on change control and lot release; QuidelOrtho's manufacturing sites are ISO 13485:2016 certified, while Vantelle's ISO 13485 audit is booked for Q1 2027 and not yet passed.
rows.weakens: Vantelle's product is a Class II 510(k) device rather than an EUA product, and its 18-person manufacturing team is materially larger than a pure pilot line would need; the Cue failure is a warning, not a prediction.
rows.implication: Make ISO 13485 certification and the appointment of a VP Quality/Operations pre-conditions to scaling cartridge volume beyond the pilot line; the $30M use of funds allocates 40% to manufacturing, so this is the largest single execution risk.
rows.confidence: high for the Cue findings; medium for the inference to Vantelle.
rows.follow_up: Who owns change control and lot release today? What is the AQL on the cartridge line, and what stability data support 9 months at room temperature?

plan.decision_question: Can this team take a Class II IVD through 510(k) clearance, a CLIA waiver and a 300-site launch?
plan.thesis_sentence: The founders have the right clinical insight and the CTO has the right technical pedigree, but the team as disclosed has never taken a cartridge product through a CLIA waiver and a 300-site launch, and the two functions that decide whether it does - regulatory/quality and finance - rest on one 11-month hire and a part-time interim CFO, so the round should be conditioned on senior hires and verified clearance history rather than priced on the founders' credentials.
plan.why_different: The technology and market sections judge the product and the opportunity; this section judges the people against the specific regulatory and commercial milestones, separates invention from regulatory execution, sales execution and financial control, and states what public records do and do not confirm.
plan.mechanism: Execution capacity: who owns the FDA and quality relationship, whether the quality system is mature before cartridge volumes rise, how many sites each commercial person can carry, and whether a full-time CFO controls the raise and the burn determine whether $30M converts into a cleared, waived, launched product or into another Cue Health.
plan.comparison_set: QuidelOrtho FY2025 10-K (2,500+ commercial staff, 1,200 service employees, ISO 13485-certified manufacturing, CLIA waiver 'onerous'), Roche cobas liat 510(k) plus CLIA waiver for multiplex panels (2025-01-22), Cue Health FDA warning letter 2024-05-09 and Chapter 7 (2024-05-28), Theranos SEC 2018-41, FDA 510(k) total time to decision 112-139 days (FY2024-FY2025).
plan.counter_evidence: The CEO's emergency-medicine career (2011-2017) is directly relevant to the 12-minute clinic workflow; the CTO's PhD and 2012-2016 microfluidics work led to the patent that the product depends on; the VP Regulatory has 16 years at one IVD employer plus a RAC credential; the VP Commercial's 17 years in Southwest health-system sales matches the current Texas/Arizona/New Mexico footprint; 22 R&D staff is substantial for a 64-person company; and the regulatory vacancy was filled in two months.
plan.visual: Education and career tables for the five disclosed executives, a team assessment matrix across technical depth, regulatory execution, commercial scaling, fundraising, key-person dependency and retention risk, and an evidence component on the single strongest capability signal.
plan.prohibited: strong team, experienced management, proven track record, world-class, seasoned executives, deep bench

queries: FDA FY2025 MDUFA performance report 510(k) total time to decision FY2023 FY2024 days
510(k) total time to decision 139 days FY2024 124-day goal 127 days FY2023
510(k) review time Chemistry panel 175 days database
Vantelle Diagnostics founder Wren Albescu Tomasz Lindqvist Grace Oyelaran public record

rows.finding: FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report gives the 510(k) average total time to decision as 127 days in FY2023 against a 128-day goal (met) and 139 days in FY2024 against a 124-day goal (missed); the FY2025 goal is 112 days and the FY2025 cohort was still pending at 2025-09-30.
rows.mechanism: Total time to decision includes applicant hold time; an additional-information request stops the 90-day FDA clock, so a December 2026 answer plus 90 FDA days is the floor, not the expected case.
rows.benchmark: The company's Q1 2027 target assumes FDA days only; the FY2024 total-time average implies mid-May 2027 from a December 2026 answer.
rows.weakens: The 510(k) database series (146 days for 2025 clearances; 175 days for the Chemistry panel) is longer, and a second request pushes the decision past mid-2027.
rows.implication: Underwrite a mid-May 2027 clearance base case, not late March 2027; any milestone or tranche tied to Q1 2027 should slip a quarter.
rows.confidence: high — FDA primary report, single series; the exact FY2025 preliminary average is not yet published.
rows.follow_up: What did the 2026-08-21 additional-information request ask, and does the December 2026 answer add bench or clinical data?

rows.finding: The 175-day Chemistry-panel review figure used in this report comes from the 510(k) database (S92), not from FDA's MDUFA report; FDA's own FY2024 510(k) average total time to decision is 139 days.
rows.mechanism: Database averages are computed from cleared submissions and include panel and cohort effects; they are not the MDUFA goal series.
rows.benchmark: FDA FY2024 average total time to decision 139 days vs database 146 days for 2025 clearances and 175 days for Chemistry.
rows.weakens: Using two series in one report overstates precision; the Chemistry panel is a narrower, slower cohort.
rows.implication: Cite the 175-day figure as a database average when discussing the Chemistry panel, and keep the FDA series for the clearance-date judgement.
rows.confidence: high — both sources identified.
rows.follow_up: Which review panel will FDA assign the troponin I and HbA1c file to, and does the panel average match the database?

rows.finding: Grace Oyelaran is credited with 14 510(k) clearances across 2009-2025 at Meridale Medical; neither the FDA database nor any public record names individual reviewers, so the claim cannot be verified.
rows.mechanism: Regulatory execution depends on the VP's personal FDA relationships and on a quality team; the deck discloses neither the clearances' product codes nor the quality headcount.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho and Abbott staff regulatory affairs in dozens; Vantelle has 9 clinical and regulatory staff in total.
rows.weakens: A single recent hire (2025-11) owns four workstreams: the pending 510(k), ISO 13485, the CLIA waiver and IVDR.
rows.implication: Make reference checks with Meridale Medical and a direct review of the 510(k) letter a closing condition.
rows.confidence: low — company-provided only, no public confirmation.
rows.follow_up: Can Meridale Medical confirm the 14 clearances, and can the company produce the FDA correspondence for each?

rows.finding: The commercial bench is 9 sales and support staff for 41 evaluation sites; a 300-site launch implies 33 sites per person, bridged only by a non-binding distributor letter of intent.
rows.mechanism: Direct placement of instruments into clinics is a feet-on-the-street model; each analyzer needs installation, training and reagent replenishment.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho carries more than 2,500 sales, service and marketing employees.
rows.weakens: The 41-site evaluation program shows the CEO can open clinics, and a distributor could carry the long tail.
rows.implication: A 300-site plan needs a distributor with minimum purchase obligations or a sales build the round does not fund.
rows.confidence: medium — company figures unverified; peer count from QuidelOrtho 10-K.
rows.follow_up: Does the Southwest Clinical Supply LOI name sites, minimum volumes or a date?

rows.finding: The two founders combine an emergency-medicine clinical background (Albescu, MD 2008, practising 2011-2017) with a microfluidics PhD and CM-1 patent (Lindqvist, PhD 2012), but neither has public record of a prior FDA clearance, CLIA-waived launch or exit.
rows.mechanism: Founder-market fit is real at the clinical-insight and cartridge-design layer; the missing layer is regulatory-and-commercial scale execution.
rows.benchmark: Theranos and Cue Health had technically credentialed founders and failed on quality and regulatory execution; Truvian took until 2026 to clear a CBC panel.
rows.weakens: No public source locates either founder in a Vantelle role or verifies the prior employers and dates.
rows.implication: Fund the team only with a full-time CFO, a VP Quality and an independent director added before or at close.
rows.confidence: medium — chronology internally consistent but company-provided.
rows.follow_up: Reference checks: Quillon Diagnostics and St. Brennan for Albescu; Pellucid Biosystems for Lindqvist; Ardent Peak and Juniper Rock for board behaviour.

plan.decision_question: Can this team take a Class II IVD through 510(k) clearance, a CLIA waiver and a 300-site launch?
plan.thesis_sentence: The founders have the right clinical insight and the CTO the right technical pedigree, but the team as disclosed has not taken a cartridge product through a CLIA waiver and a 300-site launch, and the two functions that decide whether it does — regulatory/quality and finance — rest on one 11-month hire and a part-time interim CFO.
plan.why_different: This section judges the people and the bench; it verifies each CV chronology and tests regulatory, commercial and finance depth against the launch plan, leaving product, market and valuation to other sections.
plan.mechanism: FDA total time to decision (not FDA days) sets the clearance date; regulatory and quality headcount, not R&D, determines whether a 510(k) and CLIA waiver survive review; sales headcount per site determines whether a 300-site plan is executable.
plan.comparison_set: QuidelOrtho's 2,500 sales/service staff, Cue Health's quality-system failure and Truvian's 2026 clearances as the peer and cautionary base rate.
plan.counter_evidence: The 41-site paid evaluation program and the CTO's CM-1 patent are real execution evidence; a documentation-only additional-information request would keep a Q1 2027 clearance alive.
plan.visual: The evidence component and the team assessment matrix.
plan.prohibited: strong team, experienced team, world-class, proven, huge market, about/many/various counts
