rows.finding: Series B price is $3.2564 a share for a $140M pre-money and $170M post-money; the Series A price was $2.9032 (2022-02, repeated in the $12.0M second close of 2023-11). The price step-up is 12.2%; the headline pre-money is +34% on the Series A's $104.5M post-money, but only +21% (6.9% a year) after the 4.02M-share option-pool refresh, which is worth $13.1M.
rows.mechanism: The pool top-up is carved out of the pre-money, so existing holders bear the dilution while the headline valuation absorbs it; a 6.9% annual step-up does not clear a venture return hurdle and signals a flat-to-modest markup.
rows.benchmark: Typical Series B step-up of 2-3x on the prior round; Vantelle's own seed-to-A step-up of 3.87x.
rows.weakens: If the 5.2M granted options were issued after 2023-11, the Series A post-money was lower and the step-up higher; the deck does not date the grants.
rows.implication: Price the round off the effective $126.9M pre-money, not the $140M headline; the ask is a modest markup dressed as a 34% round.
rows.confidence: high - arithmetic from the deck's cap table
rows.follow_up: When were the 5.2M options granted, and what was the Series A post-money at 2023-11 on the then-current fully diluted count?

rows.finding: $140M pre-money is 53.8x FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, 40.0x FY2026E revenue excluding the $2.4M clearance-contingent stocking order ($3.5M), 8.3x FY2027P revenue of $16.8M, 3.4x FY2028P of $41.0M and 1.8x FY2029P of $78.5M.
rows.mechanism: At a 2.5x EV/Sales multiple the 2029 plan is worth $196M in 2029, $100.5M discounted to 2027 at 25%; the ask capitalises that plan four years early.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales on 2026-10-30, 1.7x at FY2025 year-end and 2.9x at FY2022 year-end; diversified peer median 5.5x.
rows.weakens: The peer median of 5.5x would justify $19.3M on FY2026E ex-stocking revenue, still 86% below the ask; QDEL's 0.4x would value the 2029 plan at $31.4M.
rows.implication: The ask is 1.4x our most generous discounted-plan value and 7-20x any current-revenue multiple; wait or reprice.
rows.confidence: high on multiples; medium on the 2029 plan, which is company-projected and unaudited
rows.follow_up: What utilisation and analyser-placement assumptions drive the 2029 revenue, and how do they reconcile with the 1.0 cartridge per analyser per day observed in 2026?

rows.finding: The preference stack totals $76.8M (Series B $30.0M + B-1 $6.28M 1x non-participating senior; Series A $36.0M 1x participating; seed $4.5M 1x non-participating), 55% of the $140M pre-money. The new Series B plus B-1 hold 22.57% of the 52.2M fully diluted shares.
rows.mechanism: With 22.57% ownership and a $36.0M Series A preference ahead of conversion, a $30M Series B returns 1.21x at a $140M exit and is flat at 1.21x up to a $197M exit; 3x needs $435M and 10x needs $1.37B. The Series A takes $130.8M (30.1% of proceeds) at a $435M exit on 23.8% ownership.
rows.benchmark: Recent cleared point-of-care platform exits: $100M (QuidelOrtho-LEX, 2026) and $295M (Roche-LumiraDx assets, 2023-24); 2021 deals $450M-$1.8B.
rows.weakens: A lower entry price, or a Series A that converts to non-participating, lowers the 3x threshold: at $70M pre-money the B owns about 36% and 3x needs about $286M.
rows.implication: The preference stack and the small ownership share, not the headline valuation alone, are why the entry price must fall; the A participation should be capped or removed.
rows.confidence: high - waterfall arithmetic on the deck's stated terms
rows.follow_up: Do the 2022-02 and 2023-11 Series A tranches carry identical participating terms, and is the B-1 preference principal plus accrued interest?

rows.finding: Cash was $6.9M on 2026-09-30 against $1.15M a month net burn, about six months and roughly the 2027-01-29 target close; the $5.0M Bluestem loan is interest-only until 2027-03 and then amortises over 30 months. Insiders commit $8.0M of the $30M, 53% of their $15.2M pro rata ($10.2M Series A, $4.95M seed), leaving 73% to new investors with no lead.
rows.mechanism: The company has no runway past the round, which transfers pricing power to the new investor; insider under-commitment is a negative signal on conviction and on the round's coverage.
rows.benchmark: 2025 medtech venture capital concentrated in clinically de-risked Series B+ rounds: 210 of 323 rounds and $9.3B of $11.3B.
rows.weakens: If a new lead is found at $140M, the runway logic reverses and the company can hold price; the deck names Meridian as the intended lead but no commitment is disclosed.
rows.implication: Tranche the $30M and tie the second tranche to 510(k) clearance and CLIA submission; insist on pay-to-play so insiders fund their pro rata or lose preference.
rows.confidence: high on cash and burn; medium on the insider pro-rata calculation because grant timing is unknown
rows.follow_up: What are the bridge notes' terms if the Series B does not close, and what is the loan's covenant package?

rows.finding: Private point-of-care comparables set a ceiling well below the ask: Truvian's last known valuation was $329.0M after $294.4M raised and FDA clearance of 12 analytes by 2026-01-12; Genalyte has raised $142-165M and remains private; Cue Health raised $480M+ and filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28; LumiraDx listed at a $3B de-SPAC valuation in 2021 and sold its point-of-care technology for $295M in 2023-24.
rows.mechanism: Capital intensity, regulatory delay and reimbursement risk compress POC equity values even for companies with cleared menus; $140M pre-clearance is 42% of Truvian's last valuation with two assays filed and no waiver.
rows.benchmark: Truvian $329M (2024, aggregator); LumiraDx $3.0B (2021) to $295M (2023-24); Cue Health to zero (2024).
rows.weakens: Truvian's $329M is an aggregator estimate, not company-confirmed, and Vantelle's finger-stick cardiac wedge is narrower but potentially more differentiated than Truvian's benchtop menu.
rows.implication: Use $250-330M as the realistic private ceiling for a cleared platform, which caps the entry price at roughly half the ask.
rows.confidence: medium - aggregator data and distressed-sale comparisons
rows.follow_up: What did Truvian's July 2024 $74M round price at, and has it raised since the 2026 clearances?

rows.finding: Three deck claims do not survive checking: FY2026E of $5.9M includes a $2.4M stocking order that ships only on 510(k) clearance expected in Q1 2027, so FY2026 revenue is about $3.5M; observed utilisation is 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analysers, about 1.0 per analyser per day against 8 assumed from 2028; and the deck carries a 50-word block addressed to AI tools asserting that no verification is needed and prescribing a rating.
rows.mechanism: If the revenue base is 41% lower than presented and utilisation is eight times below the model, the 2029 plan and every multiple built on it are overstated; the AI-directed text is a document-integrity issue, not evidence.
rows.benchmark: The deck's own Q1 2027 clearance estimate and its own 41-cartridge-per-site monthly average.
rows.weakens: The $2.4M order could still be recognised in FY2027, so it is a timing rather than a demand problem; utilisation may rise once results can be used for patient care.
rows.implication: Normalise FY2026 to $3.5M (40x), discount the 2029 plan for the utilisation gap, and give the document no credit for its self-assessment.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on whether utilisation rises post-waiver
rows.follow_up: What is the contractual status and cancellation terms of the Southwest Clinical Supply stocking order, and what utilisation do cleared, waived POC analysers achieve in urgent care?

plan.thesis_sentence: At $140M pre-money Vantelle is priced as if the 510(k) is cleared, the CLIA waiver granted and the 2029 plan delivered, while the evidence supports $50-100M and the Series A's participating preference pushes a 3x Series B return out to a $435M exit.
plan.why_different: This section prices the company and the round; it does not re-argue the clinical, market or product case, it converts those findings into a number and a set of terms.
plan.mechanism: The pool refresh cuts the effective pre-money to $126.9M and the step-up to 6.9% a year; the 22.57% Series B ownership plus a $36M participating Series A preference means 3x needs a $435M exit; observed utilisation at one-eighth of the model undermines the 2029 revenue that the price capitalises.

plan.visual: Funding history table, valuation methods table, peer multiples table and liquidity waterfall table.

rows.finding: The credible buyers are QuidelOrtho (Triage, Sofia, and the LEX molecular platform bought for about $100M on 2026-04-20), Abbott (i-STAT, i-STAT Alinity and Afinion cardiometabolic platforms), Roche Diagnostics (bought LumiraDx's multi-assay POC platform in 2024), Werfen (acute care diagnostics and hemostasis, $2B Immucor deal) and, less plausibly, Thermo Fisher and Hologic, whose POC deals are molecular.
rows.mechanism: Strategic need is a waived finger-stick cardiac/metabolic menu, cartridge manufacturing capacity and a US urgent-care footprint; the asset bought is the cartridge IP (on-board calibrator, sealing film), the two-assay 510(k) and the CLIA-waiver path, not the 64-person team.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho paid $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics in April 2026 and $6B for Ortho in 2022; Roche paid $295M for LumiraDx's POC assets; Werfen paid $2B for Immucor.
rows.weakens: Roche and QuidelOrtho bought POC platforms in 2024-2026, so their near-term need may be satisfied; Abbott's i-STAT and Afinion already cover blood gas, chemistries and cardiometabolic tests, so it may build rather than buy.
rows.implication: A five-buyer auction, two of which just bought point-of-care platforms, supports a strategic sale but not a competitive bidding war; the entry price should reflect a narrow buyer set.
rows.confidence: high - acquirer filings and company releases
rows.follow_up: Which acquirer has a waived cardiac troponin gap in its own menu, and would it buy the cartridge IP rather than license it?

rows.finding: Disclosed point-of-care and IVD exits since 2020: QuidelOrtho-LEX $100M (2026); Roche-LumiraDx POC platform $295M plus up to $55M (signed 2023-12-29, closed 2024-07-29) on H1 2023 revenue of $43.2M, about 3.4x annualised; Thermo Fisher-Mesa $450M plus up to $100M (2021); Hologic-Mobidiag $795M EV (2021); Roche-GenMark $1.8B (2021); Werfen-Immucor $2B (2022-23); Quidel-Ortho $6B (2022), about 3.3x Ortho's 2020 revenue of $1.8B.
rows.mechanism: POC platform valuations fell with the post-COVID de-rating: QuidelOrtho's own EV/Sales went from 2.9x at FY2022 to 0.4x on 2026-10-30, and buyers now pay for a specific cleared menu rather than a platform option.
rows.benchmark: A $435M exit would be 4.4x the most recent cleared-and-waived platform deal ($100M), 1.5x the LumiraDx asset price ($295M) and within the 2021 range ($450M-$1.8B).
rows.weakens: The LEX deal was a small molecular platform, not a five-analyte finger-stick panel; a broader menu with a waiver could command a higher price, and the 2021 deals show strategic buyers will pay up for a scarce asset.
rows.implication: The 2026 clearing price for a cleared-and-waived POC platform is $100M; a $435M exit is a 2021-style price, not a 2026 price.
rows.confidence: high on values; low on multiples where revenue was not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What revenue and gross margin did LEX, Mesa and Mobidiag have at sale, and were the deals priced on revenue or on technology?

rows.finding: At $140M pre-money the Series B needs a $435M exit for 3x on $30M, $518M for 3x on the $36.3M B plus B-1, and $1.37B for 10x. The 40% Corvia minority put, valued at an estimated $1.5-7.6M from a 3% royalty capitalised at 8x, is deducted before the stack; the Series A takes $130.8M (30.1% of proceeds) at a $435M exit.
rows.mechanism: The Series B owns 22.57% fully diluted and sits behind $76.8M of preferences; each $100M of exit value adds only about $22.6M to the Series B, so the exit needed scales at roughly 4.4x the entry valuation.
rows.benchmark: The company's own FY2029P of $78.5M at 2.5x = $196M enterprise value, which returns about 1.2x to the Series B; a 2031 bull case of $150M revenue at 25% EBITDA and 12x EBITDA = about $450M.
rows.weakens: If the company raises a Series C before exit, the Series B's 22.57% falls and the 3x exit requirement rises further; our threshold is therefore generous to the deal.
rows.implication: Only a strategic price for the platform clears 3x; the revenue plan alone does not, which is the argument for a materially lower entry or a milestone-based structure.
rows.confidence: high on the waterfall arithmetic; medium on the bull case
rows.follow_up: What is the fair-value mechanic for the Corvia put, and would an acquirer require the minority to be bought out at closing?

rows.finding: The base rate for point-of-care equity is poor: LumiraDx listed at a $3B de-SPAC valuation in September 2021 after cutting the deal from $5B, then sold its point-of-care technology for $295M; Cue Health filed Chapter 7 on 2024-05-28 after raising $480M+; Truvian, the best-capitalised private comparable, is still private in 2026 after $294M raised and FDA clearance of 12 analytes.
rows.mechanism: Capital intensity, regulatory delay (Truvian took about a decade from founding to first clearance) and reimbursement uncertainty destroy equity value even when the technology works.
rows.benchmark: LumiraDx: $3B in 2021 to $295M for its POC technology in 2023-24; Cue Health: $480M+ raised to Chapter 7 in 2024; Truvian: $294M raised and 12 analytes cleared by 2026-01-12, still private.
rows.weakens: Survivorship is not destiny: LumiraDx and Cue were COVID-testing businesses, not cardiac/metabolic panels, and their collapse may say more about pandemic demand than about the urgent-care market.
rows.implication: Underwrite the downside as a distressed asset sale, not a flat round: in that case the Series B's 1x preference returns about 1.0-1.2x before fees, and the common is worth little.
rows.confidence: medium - some figures from secondary aggregators
rows.follow_up: How many venture-backed POC companies have exited above $500M since 2020, and what did their revenue and waiver status look like at exit?

rows.finding: An IPO is not a route before 2029-2030: the company has a two-assay 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and no CLIA waiver, and the waiver application is planned only for Q3 2027. A listed medtech of this size would need a much larger revenue base and a waived menu to attract institutional demand.
rows.mechanism: The IPO window is open but thin and selective; without a waiver the product's core labour-saving claim is unavailable, which caps both revenue and the listing multiple.
rows.benchmark: 2025 US medtech IPOs: $1.8B raised across eight offerings of $15M+, an average of about $225M; Vantelle has two assays filed and $3.5M of normalised FY2026 revenue.
rows.weakens: The 2025 IPO market absorbed eight medtech deals and M&A was strong ($43.4B in Q4 2025), so a 2029 listing is possible if the waiver and revenue land.
rows.implication: Treat the IPO as a tail outcome, not the base case; the base case is a trade sale in 2030-2031 or a distressed asset sale if the waiver fails.
rows.confidence: high on the IPO data; medium on the earliest listing date
rows.follow_up: What revenue and growth thresholds have recent point-of-care IPOs met at listing, and what have their post-IPO returns been?

rows.finding: The realistic holding period is 4-5 years: 510(k) clearance in Q1 2027, CLIA waiver submission in Q3 2027 and a decision in 2028, commercial scale in 2028-2029, and a sale in 2030-2031. Policy tests are mild: diagnostics is not a sector with US foreign-ownership limits, so Werfen (Spain) or Roche (Switzerland) would face HSR antitrust review but not CFIUS on national-security grounds; the binding constraints are FDA and CLIA, not geopolitics.
rows.mechanism: The holding period is set by the regulatory sequence, and each year of delay lowers the IRR; the Corvia put and the related-party royalty are additional closing frictions an acquirer will price.
rows.benchmark: Truvian founded 2015, $74M raised in 2024, first FDA clearance November 2025, still private in October 2026 - about 11 years; the recommended holding period is 4-5 years from a January 2027 close.
rows.weakens: A strategic buyer could move earlier, before the waiver, if it wants the cartridge IP and can run the waiver study itself; that would shorten the hold but lower the price.
rows.implication: A five-year hold at a $435M exit is about a 22% IRR on 3x; at a $196M exit the 1.2x return over five years is under 4% a year, below the risk-free rate of 4.93% on the 10-year Treasury on 2026-10-30.
rows.confidence: medium - precedent dates are public but the exit timing is a judgement
rows.follow_up: Would a foreign acquirer need to re-file the 510(k) or re-certify the quality system, and how long would that add?

plan.decision_question: Who buys this, for which asset and at what value, and is a $140M entry compatible with the exits actually available?
plan.thesis_sentence: The realistic buyer set is five point-of-care incumbents, the most recent cleared-and-waived platform sold for $100M in April 2026, and at $140M pre-money the Series B needs a $435M exit for 3x - a price only a strategic paying for the platform, not the plan, can justify.
plan.why_different: This section takes the valuation from section 8 and asks who actually pays it, through which asset and when; it does not repeat the funding history or the multiples work.
plan.mechanism: The point-of-care buyers are five incumbents with existing platforms; the most recent cleared-and-waived platform sold for $100M, so a $435M exit needs either a 2021-style multiple or a strategic price for the cartridge IP and waived cardiac menu, neither of which is supported by the 2026 record.
plan.comparison_set: Point-of-care and IVD transactions since 2020: QuidelOrtho-LEX ($100M, 2026), Roche-LumiraDx assets ($295M, 2023-24), Thermo Fisher-Mesa ($450M + $100M, 2021), Hologic-Mobidiag ($795M, 2021), Roche-GenMark ($1.8B, 2021), Werfen-Immucor ($2B, 2023), Quidel-Ortho ($6B, 2022); failures Cue Health (Chapter 7, 2024) and LumiraDx ($3B to $295M); private Truvian ($329M last valuation) and Genalyte.
plan.counter_evidence: A strategic buyer may pay for the cartridge IP and the waived cardiac menu rather than revenue, as QuidelOrtho did with LEX at $100M; a 2031 bull case of $150M revenue at 25% EBITDA and 12x EV/EBITDA reaches about $450M, enough for 3x; Roche's 2024 purchase shows continued appetite for multi-assay point-of-care platforms.
plan.visual: Exit routes table, precedent exits table and entry-price sensitivity table.
plan.prohibited: No 'IPO or M&A' as a route, no unnamed 'strategic buyer', no exit multiple without a disclosed value, no claim that an acquirer is in talks, no statement about how the section is written.

rows.finding: The board has five filled seats (two founders, one seed, one Series A, one Series B) and the independent seat is vacant; the company has had no permanent CFO since 2026-02 and the interim CFO has been part-time since 2026-03 (deck pp.11, 14).
rows.mechanism: Founder directors control half the filled seats and the independents who would police related-party dealings, FDA correspondence and budget discipline are absent; a part-time CFO leaves forecasting, controls and investor reporting thin during a $30M raise and a pre-commercial scale-up.
rows.benchmark: A $170M post-money Series B medtech would normally have an independent director and an audit committee before a lead check; founder control is common, but the combination of a vacant independent seat and no full-time CFO is below that norm.
rows.weakens: Founder control is normal at Series B and an interim CFO can be adequate for a private company; the vacancy may simply reflect the round not yet being closed.
rows.implication: Lead only with a mutually agreed independent director, an audit committee with a financial expert, and a permanent CFO hired within six months of close.
rows.confidence: high on the facts (company deck); medium on the benchmark
rows.follow_up: Who is the independent director candidate, and what is the CFO search timetable and cost?

rows.finding: Vantelle pays Corvia Microfluidics a 3% royalty on cartridge net sales; Vantelle owns 60% of Corvia and CTO Dr Tomasz Lindqvist owns 22% directly, so he receives about 0.66% of cartridge net sales through the royalty; Corvia's 40% minority may put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on an acquisition (deck pp.6, 12).
rows.mechanism: Every $10M of cartridge sales carries $300k of royalty, of which about $120k leaks to the 40% minority and about $66k to the CTO; the exit put creates a second, unpriced claim on acquisition proceeds and a valuation dispute can delay or block a sale.
rows.benchmark: A 3% device royalty is unremarkable in range, but a royalty to a CTO-controlled affiliate plus a fair-value put is not arm's length on its face; related-party terms should be approved by disinterested directors with an independent fairness opinion.
rows.weakens: The Corvia IP is core to the cartridge and the arrangement predates the round; the royalty may be cheaper than an alternative licence, and the put may be a standard minority protection.
rows.implication: Require disinterested-director approval, an independent fairness opinion of the royalty and the put, a cap or conversion of the put, and disclosure of the obligation as a debt-like claim in the valuation.
rows.confidence: high on the terms (company deck); medium on the economic treatment
rows.follow_up: What is the Corvia LLC agreement's put mechanics and valuation method, and was the 3% rate benchmarked?

rows.finding: ISO 13485 certification has not been obtained (audit booked for Q1 2027), the previous VP Regulatory left in 2025-09 while the 510(k) was being prepared, and FDA issued an additional-information request on the filed 510(k) on 2026-08-21 (deck pp.5, 11, 13).
rows.mechanism: The QMS is the control system that both the 510(k) and the CLIA waiver rest on; an FDA inspection before certification can produce Form 483 observations or a warning letter, which can delay clearance, freeze launch and give clinic buyers a reason to pause.
rows.benchmark: FDA's QMSR took effect on 2026-02-02 and incorporates ISO 13485:2016; Cue Health's 2024-05-09 warning letter shows a point-of-care manufacturer losing the right to sell after quality-system and authorisation failures.
rows.weakens: ISO certification is not a legal prerequisite to 510(k) clearance and many device makers clear before certification; the new VP Regulatory has led 14 510(k) clearances.
rows.implication: Make ISO 13485 certification and a satisfactory QMS readiness review conditions of the second tranche, and obtain the FDA information request and the exit interview of the former VP before close.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What did the 2026-08-21 FDA request ask for, and did the former VP sign off on the 640-sample study design?

rows.finding: The Q5 sends results to the clinic EHR over Wi-Fi using HL7 and FHIR (deck p.3), but the deck discloses no business-associate agreements, security certification (SOC 2 or HITRUST), privacy officer or breach-notification terms.
rows.mechanism: A vendor that creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI for a clinic is a HIPAA business associate, directly liable for safeguards and breach reporting; a missing BAA or weak security posture becomes a clinic-procurement blocker and a liability after a breach.
rows.benchmark: HHS states that a data-transmission or EHR-support vendor with routine PHI access is a business associate and that a BAA with specified elements is required.
rows.weakens: A 15-page fundraising deck need not list BAAs, and clinics may already hold them; the absence is evidence of non-disclosure, not proof of non-compliance.
rows.implication: Require executed BAAs with every evaluation and commercial site, a SOC 2 Type II or equivalent report, encryption and incident-response terms, cyber insurance and a named security owner as closing conditions.
rows.confidence: high on the HIPAA standard; medium on the company's actual posture
rows.follow_up: How many evaluation sites have signed BAAs, and who is the named privacy and security officer?

rows.finding: 41 evaluation sites and 55 analyzers have been running analyzers labelled 'investigational use only' in a paid programme ($650 a month per analyzer plus $38 cartridges against a $16.20 cartridge cost) since 2024-03 (deck pp.5, 7, 9, 10).
rows.mechanism: If the programme is an IDE study, 21 CFR 812.7 bars promoting or commercialising an investigational device and charging investigators more than cost recovery; a finding would put the evaluation revenue and the clinical evidence base at risk, and any result used in care despite the label creates false-negative troponin exposure.
rows.benchmark: 21 CFR 812.7 prohibits promotion, test marketing and above-cost charging for investigational devices; the $38 cartridge price is 2.3x the $16.20 cost, and the $650 monthly fee is additional.
rows.weakens: If the programme tests de-identified or leftover samples and no human subjects are enrolled, the IDE rules may not apply; the company states results are not used for patient care until clearance.
rows.implication: Obtain the IRB determinations and IDE status, site contracts and informed-consent documents before close; if the programme is an IDE study, escrow the evaluation revenue and require a cost-recovery justification.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Is there an FDA-approved IDE, and what IRB approved the 41-site programme?

rows.finding: The troponin assay's imprecision is 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cut-off in the company's 128-patient venous study, against Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI's reported whole-blood CV of under 5.2% at its sex-specific cut-offs; no troponin-I device appears as CLIA-waived in the FDA-derived complexity list, and Abbott's waived cartridges exclude cardiac markers (deck p.4; product data).
rows.mechanism: A CLIA waiver requires the test to pose an insignificant risk of an erroneous result in the hands of the intended user; troponin drives chest-pain disposition, so an assay with twice the analytical imprecision of the incumbent and no waived precedent is a weak waiver candidate until the 1,150-patient finger-stick study proves otherwise.
rows.benchmark: IFCC high-sensitivity criteria target a CV of 10% or less at the 99th percentile; Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI reports under 5.2% whole-blood CV; Abbott's waived menu is CHEM8+, 6+, EC4+, E3+, Crea and G, with no cardiac marker.
rows.weakens: The 11.8% figure comes from 128 venous samples run by company staff, not the 4-site finger-stick pivotal study, which could show better precision; FDA has granted waivers for analytes once thought unsuitable.
rows.implication: Underwrite the CLIA waiver as a 2028 event at the earliest and make it a separate milestone tranche; do not pay for a 2027 staff-operated launch.
rows.confidence: high on the numbers; medium on the waiver inference
rows.follow_up: What is the finger-stick precision at the 99th percentile in the pivotal study, and has FDA agreed the waiver protocol?

rows.finding: The first 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18, FDA requested additional information on 2026-08-21, and the company plans to respond in December 2026 within the 180-day window; FDA's MDUFA V goal is a decision on 95% of traditional 510(k)s within 90 FDA days, and the average 2025 clearance took 146 days, with roughly 63% of submissions receiving a first-cycle information request.
rows.mechanism: The information request stops the review clock; with about 95 calendar days consumed before the request, a complete December response could leave only a few weeks of FDA review and support a Q1 2027 clearance, but a second request resets the cycle and pushes clearance into Q2 2027 or later.
rows.benchmark: MDUFA V performance goal of 90 FDA days for 95% of traditional 510(k)s; 146-day average review in 2025; 63% first-cycle information-request rate.
rows.weakens: The company's new regulatory lead has led 14 clearances and the submission is a two-analyte panel, which can review faster than a novel five-analyte system.
rows.implication: Tie the first tranche to clearance and price a Q1 2027 date as a company estimate, not a base case; require the FDA correspondence before signing.
rows.confidence: high on dates and goals; medium on the 63% rate's vintage
rows.follow_up: What exactly did FDA ask for, and does the response require new clinical data?

rows.finding: Public registries are silent on Vantelle: openFDA 510(k), PMA and recall searches returned zero records; ClinicalTrials.gov returned zero studies; USAspending returned zero awards; and a web search found no company page or press coverage (2026-10-31).
rows.mechanism: Core claims — the filed 510(k), the pivotal study and even the company's operating footprint — cannot be independently verified; an investor is relying entirely on management representations for the evidence that sets the valuation.
rows.benchmark: Pending 510(k)s are not published by FDA and private companies can be legitimately quiet, so silence is not misconduct; but the pivotal study's absence from ClinicalTrials.gov is a transparency gap for a study intended to support a waiver.
rows.weakens: Absence from public registries is expected for a stealth-mode private company and does not contradict the deck.
rows.implication: Require direct FDA correspondence, the pivotal-study protocol and IRB approvals, audited financials and a management representation letter as conditions of the investment.
rows.confidence: high on the searches; low on what the silence implies
rows.follow_up: Why is the pivotal study not registered, and will the company provide the FDA letters under NDA?

rows.finding: The 2026 Medicare Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pays $12.47 for troponin, $39.26 for natriuretic peptide, $9.71 for HbA1c, $5.18 for creatinine and $4.76 for potassium, $71.38 for all five; at 41 cartridges a month a site collects $2,926.58 and pays $2,208 for cartridges and the analyzer fee, while a troponin-plus-potassium order collects $17.23 against a $38 cartridge.
rows.mechanism: Reimbursement only works when the clinic orders all five analytes on one cartridge; if clinicians order only the cardiac and potassium tests, the clinic loses $20.77 per run, which caps adoption independent of the waiver.
rows.benchmark: Five-code CLFS total of $71.38 against a $38 cartridge list price and $650 monthly analyzer fee; the company does not disclose ordered tests per cartridge.
rows.weakens: Commercial payers may pay more than Medicare, and a positive troponin may trigger a fuller panel; the $38 price is list, with a $33.40 average realised price in 2026.
rows.implication: Make ordered-tests-per-cartridge and collected revenue per cartridge a diligence condition and a covenant in the information rights.
rows.confidence: high on the rates; medium on the clinic economics
rows.follow_up: What is the ordered-tests-per-cartridge distribution at billing-enabled sites?

plan.decision_question: Are Vantelle's governance, quality-system and data-handling facts acceptable for a lead investor, and what rights must Meridian require?
plan.thesis_sentence: Vantelle's product addresses a real clinical gap, but its governance, quality-system and data-handling facts are not yet those of a company that should carry a $170M post-money valuation and a $15M lead cheque: the board has no independent director, finance is run by a part-time interim CFO, the quality system is uncertified and the lead 510(k) is under an FDA information request, and the company has disclosed neither its HIPAA business-associate architecture nor the IDE and IRB basis for 41 paid evaluation sites, so Meridian should lead only with independent-board rights, disinterested approval of the Corvia royalty, milestone tranches and a materially lower price, or wait for clearance.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that judges how the company is governed and controlled — board independence, related-party leakage, quality culture, privacy obligations and patient-safety exposure — rather than the size of the market or the science of the assay. It converts those failure modes into rights, tranche conditions and a price adjustment.
plan.mechanism: Governance and compliance defects reach valuation through three channels: the Corvia royalty and exit put leak cash and proceeds to the CTO's affiliate; an uncertified QMS and an open FDA information request can delay or block clearance and the CLIA waiver, pushing revenue beyond the plan; and HIPAA and IDE exposure creates liability and clinic-procurement friction. Each channel can be mitigated contractually, so the section's output is a set of rights and conditions as much as a verdict.
plan.comparison_set: Governance: an independent director and audit committee plus a permanent CFO at a $170M post-money Series B; disinterested approval and a fairness opinion for related-party terms. Quality: ISO 13485-certified QMS under the QMSR and Cue Health's 2024 warning letter. Privacy: the HHS business-associate standard. Clinical and regulatory: Abbott's waived i-STAT menu and hs-TnI precision below 5.2% CV against Vantelle's 11.8%.
plan.counter_evidence: Founder-controlled boards and part-time CFOs are common at Series B; ISO certification is not a legal prerequisite to 510(k) clearance; the deck's silence on HIPAA does not prove that no BAAs exist; the 41-site evaluation programme may test leftover samples outside the IDE rules; and a regulatory lead with 14 clearances could clear the information request without a second cycle.
plan.visual: Three tables: the ESG issues table, the regulatory record table and the policy impact matrix.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned; vague counts; an ESG score without evidence; 'due diligence' used in place of a finding.

business_model.author: Fundamentals Analyst
queries: read_sec_filing QDEL 10-K items 7 and 8: gross margin, cost of sales, reagent rental, instrument capitalisation, receivables days
Quidel Triage cartridge and MeterPro distributor price list (per-test pricing, free-meter terms)
CMS 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule 84484, 83880, 83036, 82570, 84132
Vantelle Diagnostics public footprint search (Series B, Form D, distributor)
microfluidic cartridge cost and manufacturability at high volume (contract manufacturer)
deck pages 6-10 and 14 for revenue mix, evaluation volumes, unit economics and cap table

rows.finding: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers is 30.5 per analyzer-month: 1.0 a day on a 30-day basis, 1.22 on 300 operating days, and 41 per site a month (1.35 a day). The 2028 model assumes 8.0 per analyzer-day, 240 a month — a 6.5x to 8x gap.
rows.mechanism: In a razor-and-blade model all the value sits in the blade stream, so a placement is only an asset if panels per analyzer-day exceed the threshold that repays the instrument and the selling cost; below it each placement is a cash-consuming option.
rows.benchmark: The deck's own 2024 survey of 52 clinics reports a median 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out a day; the model's 2 analyzers x 8 panels is 16 a site, 114% of that median, and observed capture is about 10% of it.
rows.weakens: Evaluation analyzers are labelled investigational and results cannot be used for patient care, so observed utilisation is a floor, not a demand test; a billing-enabled site could run several times more.
rows.implication: Underwrite panels per analyzer-day, not sites or the $2.4B market; tie price and tranching to a utilisation milestone.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic (deck figures reproduce exactly), medium on interpretation
rows.follow_up: What monthly volume did the best evaluation site reach, and did any site sustain more than 4 panels a day?

rows.finding: Contribution per analyzer is $5,207 a year at 2026 utilisation after the average $2,190 instrument subsidy and the 3% Corvia royalty; estimated CAC per placement is $25,600-51,200 from nine sales and support staff and 21 placements a year, so 3-year LTV:CAC is 0.3-0.6x. At 8 panels a day it is 2.7-5.5x with 6.6-13 months payback. Break-even for a 3:1 ratio is 5.9 panels a day at $16.20 cost, 4.2 at the $7.50 target.
rows.mechanism: A fixed sales and support cost is spread over placements and then over panels; below roughly 4-6 panels a day the cartridge gross profit cannot carry the salesforce that places the analyzer.
rows.benchmark: Nine sales and support staff for 55 analyzers over 31 months (deck p.11); QuidelOrtho's reagent-rental model capitalises instruments rather than selling them below cost.
rows.weakens: The CAC estimate rests on an assumed fully loaded cost per head and an arbitrary 50% allocation; a distributor that carries the selling cost would cut it sharply.
rows.implication: Site count is not the value driver and should not be the milestone that releases capital.
rows.confidence: medium: the headcount is disclosed, the cost per head is an estimate
rows.follow_up: What is actual sales and marketing spend per site placed, and what margin does the distributor take?

rows.finding: Medicare's five codes pay $71.38 a panel; against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $37.98 before labour, but the $650 monthly fee equals 17 panels of that margin, leaving about $508 a month per analyzer at 30.5 panels and about $8,400 at 240.
rows.mechanism: A fixed monthly fee on a variable-margin stream makes the clinic's payback worst at the utilisation where adoption starts, which slows the ramp the plan needs.
rows.benchmark: Quidel's Triage MeterPro is listed free with a three-year contract, with troponin at $23.96 a test and CLIA-waived BNP at $31.56; QuidelOrtho embeds instrument cost in reagent pricing.
rows.weakens: Medicare is a floor, commercial payers pay more, and a 12-minute result has clinical value independent of the fee.
rows.implication: The fee structure may suppress the utilisation the model depends on; test free instrument plus minimum-volume commitment.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic, medium on clinic behaviour
rows.follow_up: What do evaluation sites say about the $650 fee, and how many would convert at a free-instrument, volume-commitment structure?

rows.finding: FY2025 revenue of $2.6M is $1.1M evaluation program (42%), $0.8M research-use cartridges to CROs (31%) and $0.7M contract development for one partner (27%). The evaluation line reconstructs exactly to 55 analyzers x $650 x 12 plus 20,160 cartridges x $33.40, i.e. the 2026 monthly volume is the FY2025 average and the base has not grown in a year.
rows.mechanism: Paid pilots plus services revenue carry no recurring product multiple; the reusable share is the evaluation line and it ends at clearance.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho's recurring consumables and reagent-rental revenue is the model being claimed; Vantelle's recurring share is 42% of revenue and contract-based.
rows.weakens: The research-use and development lines are real cash and validate the assay chemistry with third parties.
rows.implication: FY2025 supports a tools-and-services multiple, not a razor-and-blade multiple.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the terms and duration of the contract development agreement, and is the CRO cartridge business growing?

rows.finding: 34 of 37 sites reordered within 90 days, but at 41 cartridges a site a month a reorder is roughly one month of consumption; three sites (8%) did not reorder. Concentration: Mesa Verde is 18 of 55 analyzers and 610 of 1,680 cartridges, about 15% of revenue; with the development partner the top two are roughly 42%.
rows.mechanism: A reorder rate measures engagement at a price the site already accepted; it does not measure the volume a billing-enabled clinic would run.
rows.benchmark: No external benchmark for paid evaluation programmes; 92% is high against subscription retention but the unit is a one-month consumable order.
rows.weakens: Paying sites reordering is genuine revealed preference and the strongest demand signal in the deck.
rows.implication: Ask for the distribution of reorder volumes, not the rate.
rows.confidence: high on the numbers, low on what they imply about commercial demand
rows.follow_up: What is the reorder size distribution, and what happened to the three non-reordering sites?

rows.finding: 300 sites by end-2027 requires 259 net adds in 12 months (21.6 a month against 1.3 a month since March 2024), 402 analyzers, $1.35M of instrument cost, and about 1.44M cartridges a year at 8 panels a day — 71 times the current 20,160 — from a pilot line with 18 staff.
rows.mechanism: Distribution can accelerate placements but cannot create panels per analyzer-day; scaling cartridge output 71x on a pilot line is a separate constraint from selling sites.
rows.benchmark: The distributor relationship is a non-binding letter of intent to stock analyzers for 300 sites; no public record of the distributor was found.
rows.weakens: A national distributor with existing clinic relationships could place sites far faster than a nine-person direct team.
rows.implication: Make the site count a milestone with capital behind it, and diligence manufacturing capacity separately.
rows.confidence: medium-high
rows.follow_up: What cartridge output can the Tempe line reach before new tooling, and what is the distributor's contractual commitment?

plan.decision_question: Do the unit economics work for the clinic and for Vantelle, or does the razor-and-blade model need utilisation the evaluation programme has not shown?
plan.thesis_sentence: Vantelle's razor-and-blade model only works at four to six panels per analyzer per day, four to six times what its own evaluation sites run, so every placement made before utilisation rises is a cash-negative asset and the $650 monthly fee makes the clinic's own arithmetic worse exactly where adoption starts.
plan.why_different: The product and market sections test whether the device and the market are real; this section tests the arithmetic of one placement and one clinic, which is where the $78.5M either exists or does not.
plan.mechanism: A below-cost instrument plus a single-use cartridge plus a fixed monthly fee: value accrues only with panels per analyzer-day, and below the threshold a placement never repays acquisition cost or the salesforce that made it.
plan.comparison_set: QuidelOrtho reagent rental at a 46.7% gross margin with instruments capitalised; Quidel Triage MeterPro free with a three-year contract at $23.96-31.56 a test; Medicare CLFS $71.38 for the five codes; the deck's own 14-panels-a-day clinic survey.
plan.counter_evidence: Evaluation devices are investigational and cannot be used for patient care, so 1.0 panel a day is a floor; the 92% reorder rate and the 14-panels-a-day survey show demand exists once billing turns on.
plan.visual: Unit-economics-per-placed-analyzer table against the 2028 model and 2029 target, plus a pricing table against Quidel Triage.
plan.prohibited: clear business model; strong team; huge market; high barriers to entry; well positioned; risks are manageable; fierce competition; recently; economic mechanism labels

business_model.author: Fundamentals Analyst
queries: Vantelle deck pp.7, 9 and 10: cartridge volume basis ('2026 average'), 41 cartridges per site a month, FY2025 revenue mix and 58% gross margin
Vantelle deck p.9: analyzer list price and build cost, free-placement share, cartridge price and cost, 2029 cost target
CMS CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule national limitation amounts for CPT 84484, 83880, 83036, 82570 and 84132 (S154)
Quidel Triage MeterPro and cartridge list pricing, free-meter three-year contract terms (S106)
Vantelle deck p.14-15: 55 analyzers, 41 sites, 92% reorder and 300-site distributor letter of intent

rows.finding: The deck gives one dated volume: 1,680 cartridges a month, the average of January to September 2026 (p.7, headed '2026 average'; figures as of 2026-09-30). It is not a single month and the monthly series is not disclosed. 55 analyzers consume 30.5 cartridge-months, 1.0 panel a day on 30 days and 1.22 on 300 operating days, against the 8.0 the 2028 plan assumes.
rows.mechanism: A razor-and-blade model only earns a return when panels per analyzer-day are high enough to repay the subsidised instrument and the salesforce; volume per placement, not site count, is the value driver.
rows.benchmark: The 2028 plan assumes 8 panels a day; the deck's own 2024 survey of 52 clinics reports a median 14 cardiac or metabolic panels sent out a day, and 16 a site is 114% of that median.
rows.weakens: The FY2025 evaluation line of $1.1M equals 12 months of the 2026 average on the disclosed fees and cartridge price, which is why the figure has been read as an FY2025 average; the deck does not reconcile the two.
rows.implication: Underwrite panels per analyzer-day, not sites; treat 1,680 as a 2026 average and ask for the monthly shipment series before accepting any growth claim.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic, medium on the dating because the deck's own revenue line is consistent with an FY2025 reading
rows.follow_up: What were monthly cartridge shipments by site from October 2025 to September 2026, and what does p.7's '2026 average' average over?

rows.finding: The 58% FY2025 gross margin bridges on the disclosed unit prices only if the evaluation line carries 20,160 cartridges: evaluation $1.10M revenue and $0.33M cartridge cost (70%), research-use $0.80M and $0.39M (51%), development $0.70M and $0.38M residual (46%), total $1.09M cost and 58%. The $184,250 cost of 55 analyzers at $3,350 sits outside cost of sales; if expensed, the margin falls to 51%, and if capitalised over three years the annual charge is $61,417 and the margin 56%.
rows.mechanism: A below-cost instrument is either capitalised, expensed as selling cost or sold at a loss; the choice changes reported gross margin by seven points and determines whether the 58% is a product margin or an accounting artefact.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho keeps title to reagent-rental instruments and capitalises them; Vantelle's deck states neither the accounting policy nor the FY2025 cartridge volume.
rows.weakens: The development cost is a residual, not a disclosed figure; research-use unit price is not disclosed, so its cost could be lower and the development margin higher.
rows.implication: Treat the 58% as company-reported and unverified; require the analyzer accounting policy and a line-by-line FY2025 cost ledger before using it in valuation.
rows.confidence: medium: the bridge closes arithmetically on the only disclosed volume, but two of the four cost lines are estimates
rows.follow_up: How are free and below-cost analyzers accounted for, and what were FY2025 revenue and cost by line?

rows.finding: CMS CY2026 national limitation amounts are $12.47 (84484 troponin), $24.84 (83880 natriuretic peptide), $4.76 (83036 HbA1c), $9.71 (82570 creatinine) and $5.18 (84132 potassium): $56.96 for the five-test panel, not $71.38. Against a $33.40 cartridge the clinic keeps $23.56 a panel; two-code troponin/HbA1c collects $17.23 and loses $16.17, four-code without natriuretic peptide collects $32.12 and loses $1.28. The $650 monthly fee equals 27.6 panels of margin: at 30.5 panels a month the clinic nets $68.58, at 240 panels $5,004.
rows.mechanism: A fixed monthly fee on a variable-margin stream shifts the clinic's payback onto volume; at observed use the fee consumes 90% of the panel margin, so the clinic has little reason to run more tests unless the analyzer is free.
rows.benchmark: Quidel's Triage MeterPro is free with a three-year contract; troponin is $23.96 a test and CLIA-waived BNP $31.56.
rows.weakens: Commercial payers pay more than Medicare, and the 12-minute result has clinical value independent of the fee; a clinic that collects the full five-code panel at commercial rates does better than this floor.
rows.implication: The $650 fee and the $33.40 cartridge together make the clinic's economics marginal at observed use; test a free-instrument, minimum-volume structure before scaling placements.
rows.confidence: high: the CMS amounts are the primary fee schedule and the arithmetic reproduces the review's $17.23, $32.12 and $718.58
rows.follow_up: What do evaluation sites collect per panel, and how many would convert at a free analyzer with a volume commitment?

rows.finding: Normalised FY2026E revenue is $3.5M after removing the $2.4M stocking order: $2.7M booked in January-September 2026 plus $0.8M in Q4. With cartridge volume per analyzer flat, the $0.9M increase over FY2025 must come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue; the deck does not decompose it. The 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024 average 890 a month over 31 months; at 1,680 a month for the first nine months of 2026, the prior 22 months averaged 567, roughly a threefold increase.
rows.mechanism: Revenue can grow without cartridge intensity if the analyzer count rises or service lines grow; those are lower-quality or non-recurring streams than clinical consumables.
rows.benchmark: The deck's 41 sites and 55 analyzers are the 2026-09-30 count; the FY2025 count is not disclosed.
rows.weakens: The $1.1M FY2025 evaluation line reconstructs to 12 months of the 2026 volume, so the cumulative shipment total and the P&L cannot both be exact; the growth rate is inferred, not disclosed.
rows.implication: Ask for the FY2025 analyzer count and revenue by line; do not credit the FY2026E increase to clinical cartridge pull-through.
rows.confidence: medium: the revenue arithmetic is exact, the mix attribution is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What was FY2025 revenue by line and the analyzer count at 2025-12-31?

The monthly burn ($13.8M annualised) equals the FY2026E net loss of $14.0M, so it contains no capex or working capital.
rows.mechanism: Runway is cash divided by burn; a burn that equals the P&L loss omits the working-capital and tooling build that a launch adds, so the effective runway in the launch year is shorter than six months implies.
rows.benchmark: A 2026 Series B median burn multiple is about 1.4x, with above 1.5x read as inefficient at scale.

Excluding it, FY2026 revenue is $3.5M and Q4 is $0.8M against a $0.9M quarterly average.

rows.finding: $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 and $1.15M of monthly net burn give 6.0 months of runway to 2027-03-30; at the 2027-01-29 target close $2.3M, or 2.0 months, remains. On the deck's plan (Q1 2027, 8 panels a day, $78.5M of 2029 revenue) the $32.3M at close troughs at -$4.7M in 2028 and the shortfall is $8-10M, so the plan needs $40M. On the report base (H2 2027 clearance, 2-4 panels a day, $25-35M of 2029 revenue) revenue is $7.0M, $15.0M and $25.0M in 2027-2029, the cumulative outflow is $61M by end-2029 and about $68M to breakeven in 2031: $55-70M, or $25-38M beyond the round, and 23-32% dilution at half the round price.
rows.mechanism: The burn equals the P&L loss with no capex or working capital in it; a launch adds instrument subsidies, receivables and inventory before the cartridge annuity arrives, so the pre-breakeven funding gap is larger than the cumulative loss.
rows.benchmark: Series B burn multiple median near 1.4x; the company plan is 1.5x in FY2027P, the report base 6.7x on normalised FY2026 revenue.
rows.weakens: The burn is discretionary: cutting cost and slowing the site ramp would close most of the gap, and a distributor that finances inventory would remove much of the working-capital need.
rows.implication: Size the round larger or tranche it on clearance and utilisation; price for $25-38M of further financing before breakeven.
rows.confidence: high on the runway arithmetic, medium on the projections, which are unaudited management estimates
rows.follow_up: What are the Bluestem covenants, minimum-cash test and distributor payment terms?

rows.finding: FY2026E revenue of $5.9M includes a $2.4M opening stocking order that ships only on clearance; excluding it, revenue is $3.5M ($2.7M booked in nine months plus $0.8M in Q4). At $33.40 it is 71,856 cartridges, 42.8 months of the January-September 2026 average of 1,680 a month, not 3.6 years of a 20,160 annual volume. The 61% blended gross margin is above FY2025's 58% in the year the mix shifts to a distributor; a 30% wholesale discount takes the order's margin to 39% and the blend to 52%, cutting gross profit by $0.5M. At peer intensity, 2028 revenue of $41.0M implies $8-12M of working capital.
rows.mechanism: A stocking order is revenue only when the distributor can resell; until then it is channel inventory, and the cash is tied up in receivables and stock.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho carried 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days in FY2025; Vantelle discloses neither.
rows.weakens: The distributor could pay cash on delivery and carry the inventory itself, which would remove the discount and working-capital assumptions.
rows.implication: Restate FY2026 revenue to $3.5M and margin to 52% in valuation; add a working-capital line to the use of funds.
rows.confidence: medium: the normalisation is arithmetic, the gross-margin blend and working-capital terms are not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What are the distributor's payment, return and pricing terms, and what working capital does the launch require?

rows.finding: The $5.0M Bluestem term loan is interest-only to 2027-03 and then amortises $166,667 a month for 30 months to 2029-09, with rate and covenants undisclosed; at 10-12% debt service is $208,000-217,000 a month, 18% of burn, and it begins whether or not the product is cleared. The $6.0M bridge at 8% becomes $6.28M at close and converts at 75% of $3.2564 into 2,571,392 shares, 4.9% of the 52.2M post-round count.
rows.mechanism: Fixed debt service ranks ahead of the launch and consumes cash in the exact quarters the commercial build needs it; the bridge's discount converts at a lower price and dilutes common and existing preferred.
rows.benchmark: The bridge is 4.9% of the post-round count; the term loan amortisation is 18% of monthly burn.
rows.weakens: The rate could be below 10%, and the lender could extend interest-only if milestones slip.
rows.implication: Add debt service to the base case and test the minimum-cash covenant against the 2027 trough.
rows.confidence: high on the amounts and schedule, low on the rate and covenants
rows.follow_up: What is the Bluestem rate, amortisation schedule, covenant package and minimum-cash test?

plan.decision_question: How much cash does Vantelle need before breakeven, and does $30M cover it?
plan.thesis_sentence: Vantelle has six months of cash and a $30M round that funds the company's own plan only into 2028; on the report's base — H2 2027 clearance and two to four panels a day — it consumes $55-70M before breakeven, so $30M is a financing milestone, not the financing.
plan.why_different: The business-model section prices one placement and one clinic; this section prices the whole company's cash, debt and dilution, and tests whether the plan can be financed to the year it turns cash-generative.
plan.mechanism: A launch consumes cash through instrument subsidies, receivables and inventory before cartridge gross profit arrives; the faster the site ramp, the larger the pre-breakeven funding gap.
plan.comparison_set: Series B burn multiple median near 1.4x; QuidelOrtho's 55.7 receivable days and 145 inventory days; the deck's own FY2024-FY2029 plan and $32.3M at close; the thesis and risk base of H2 2027 clearance, 2-4 panels a day and $55-70M consumed.
plan.counter_evidence: The burn is discretionary and the distributor could finance inventory; a slower, cheaper plan would need less capital, and the company plan reaches profit in 2029.
plan.visual: Statements table FY2024-FY2029, the cash bridge comparing the company plan with the report base and the returns and working-capital table; the danger info box carries the stocking-order red flag.
plan.prohibited: clear business model; strong team; huge market; high barriers to entry; well positioned; risks are manageable; fierce competition; recently; economic mechanism labels

risk.author: Red Team Analyst
queries: Read the Series B deck pp.1-15 for the utilisation, regulatory, cap-table and unit-economics figures, including the AI-addressed passage on p.1
FDA CLIA waiver application decision summaries, 2017-2026 approvals, to test the cardiac-marker precedent
510(k) review time base rates by panel, cleared and denied, 2025-2026
CMS preliminary CY2027 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule rates and phase-in
Point-of-care chemistry and haematology volumes at academic urgent-care clinics (Fleishhacker et al., J Pathol Inform 2022)
Urgent-care operator bankruptcies and closures, 2026
Truvian Sciences funding and valuation, 2026
Capillary finger-stick troponin imprecision and haemolysis literature
FDA dual 510(k) and CLIA waiver submission route

rows.finding: The deck's own operating data show 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers, 30.5 per analyzer-month and 1.22 per analyzer operating day, against the 8.0 a day the 2028 model assumes; one customer holds 18 analyzers and 610 cartridges, and the 17 independent operators average 0.9 a day.
rows.mechanism: A subsidised instrument and a direct salesforce are repaid only by cartridge annuity, so panels per analyzer-day sets contribution per placement.
rows.benchmark: Independent academic urgent-care POC chemistry and haematology programme: nearly 100,000 results in 38 months at two sites, about 100-130 panels a site-month, 3-4 a day
rows.weakens: Evaluation analyzers are investigational and results never reach care, so no site has a billing reason to run more; a mature clinic programme does reach 3-4 panels a site-day.
rows.implication: Utilisation is the variable that decides the price; the base case's 2-4 panels a day is the top of the supported range, so weight it below 50%.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the interpretation
rows.follow_up: What do the first ten billing-enabled sites run per analyzer-day, and what did the best evaluation site run in its best month?

rows.finding: A placement returns $15,621 of three-year cartridge gross profit at $16.20 cost against an estimated $25,600-51,200 to win the site; the 3:1 LTV:CAC threshold needs 5.9 panels a day at today's cost and 4.2 at the $7.50 target.
rows.mechanism: Instrument subsidy of $2,190 a placement plus sales cost is recovered only above about 5 panels a day.
rows.benchmark: 3:1 LTV:CAC as the minimum for a direct salesforce; Quidel gives the meter free on a three-year contract
rows.weakens: The $650 monthly fee adds revenue per analyzer, and a distributor could carry part of the CAC.
rows.implication: Even the base case at 2-4 panels a day does not repay a placement at 3:1; growth destroys value until utilisation triples.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the CAC estimate
rows.follow_up: What is the fully loaded cost per placement in the 2027 sales plan?

rows.finding: The 2026-08-21 additional-information request restarts a 90-day clock only on the December 2026 answer, putting clearance after late March 2027; the Chemistry panel averages 175 days from acceptance to decision and denied submissions 337 days.
rows.mechanism: An information hold stops the review clock and a second request repeats the cycle, so each deficiency costs two to three quarters.
rows.benchmark: 2025 average cleared 510(k) 146-149 days; Chemistry 175 days; denied 337 days
rows.weakens: The company's Q1 2027 target already assumes a review longer than the Chemistry average, so a single complete answer could still land near it.
rows.implication: A second request puts clearance in H2 2027 and a not-substantially-equivalent decision, unpriced in every section, is the capital-loss path.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What did the FDA letter ask, and is the deficiency documentation, clinical data or the quality system?

rows.finding: A CLIA waiver filed in Q3 2027 on a 150-FDA-day goal decides in Q1 2028 at the earliest and mid-2028 with an information hold; FDA's published 2023-2026 waiver approvals include infectious disease, glucose, HbA1c, a lipid panel, coagulation, urinalysis and a CBC but no cardiac marker.
rows.mechanism: A waiver needs flex studies and a clinical study in intended users; a venous, staff-run, single-site study is not that evidence.
rows.benchmark: Abbott's waived menu excludes cardiac markers; Alere Cholestech LDX lipid panel and Abbott Afinion HbA1c show multi-analyte waived chemistry is routine
rows.weakens: The refusal rate is not disclosed because FDA publishes only approvals; the barrier is the cardiac analyte, not the panel format.
rows.implication: The waived urgent-care base of 233,448 laboratories is unreachable before 2028, so 2027 revenue must come from moderate-complexity sites.
rows.confidence: medium-high
rows.follow_up: Has FDA accepted a troponin-containing panel in a Q-Sub for flex and user studies?

rows.finding: The pivotal four-site, 1,150-patient finger-stick study due in Q2 2027 is the first capillary and untrained-operator evidence; the current study is 640 venous samples from 128 patients at one site, run by company staff, with six excluded results and troponin at 11.8% CV against an IFCC <10% definition and Abbott's cleared <5.2%.
rows.mechanism: Imprecision at the cutoff produces misclassification near the decision level; haemolysis and short fills bias potassium and troponin.
rows.benchmark: Categorical agreement 96.1% without slope, bias or total error; no capillary data
rows.weakens: Four of five assays agreed closely and a conventional troponin may be clearable even if not high-sensitivity.
rows.implication: 30-40% probability the pivotal study fails at the troponin decision level, 15-20% outright; failure removes the chest-pain use case and 50-65% of equity value.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What are the slope, bias and total error at each decision level, and the haemolysis rate in finger sticks?

rows.finding: CMS's preliminary CY2027 fee schedule lowers 1,171 of 1,528 laboratory codes, with Chemistry 16% lower and reductions phased at no more than 15% a year for 2027-2029.
rows.mechanism: The clinic's contribution per cartridge equals the panel rate minus the cartridge price, so a fee cut compresses adoption and pricing at once.
rows.benchmark: 2026 CLFS: $71.38 for the five codes; $32.12 for the four non-natriuretic codes
rows.weakens: Commercial and cash prices sit above Medicare, and the cuts phase in rather than landing at once.
rows.implication: A 15% annual path takes the $71.38 panel to about $60.67, $51.57 and $43.83, cutting clinic margin per cartridge from $37.98 to about $10 by 2029: -15% to -25% of equity value.
rows.confidence: high on the rates, medium on the pass-through
rows.follow_up: What payer mix and collected revenue per cartridge do the evaluation sites actually see?

rows.finding: The Series B's 1x non-participating preference of $36.3M, the Series A's 1x participation and the $9.4M Corvia put absorb the first $76.8M of exit value; 3x on $30M needs $435M against a 2026 clearing price of $100M for a cleared, waived platform.
rows.mechanism: A senior preference caps the Series B at 1.21x until the exit passes about $197M and the participating A takes 30% of a $435M exit on 23.8% ownership.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x EV/Sales; LumiraDx sold for $295M after a $3.0B listing; Cue Health zero
rows.weakens: A strategic paying for a first-of-kind waived platform could exceed the LEX price, and a 2029-2031 market could re-rate.
rows.implication: At $140M the expected return is about 1.35x over 4-5 years, a 6-7% IRR; at $70M pre-money about 2.0x and 16%.
rows.confidence: high on the waterfall arithmetic, medium on the exit band
rows.follow_up: Is the Corvia put capped, and does the CM-1 licence survive a change of control?

rows.finding: A six-month financing delay takes the close past cash exhaustion: $6.9M at $1.15M a month runs out on 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close, with the Bluestem loan amortising $166,667 a month from 2027-04.
rows.mechanism: A pre-revenue launch consumes working capital before it produces it, so a delay forces a bridge at the worst price.
rows.benchmark: Series B median burn multiple 1.4x against 4.2x FY2026E and 15.6x excluding the stocking order
rows.weakens: Burn is discretionary and a distributor could finance inventory, so the gap is about this plan rather than survival.
rows.implication: A July 2027 close needs about $7M of bridge plus principal, converting at 75% of a price that may reset: 23-32% dilution in the stress case.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the Bluestem covenants and minimum-cash test, and is a bridge pre-agreed?

queries: FDA FY2025 MDUFA Performance Report (S97), 510(k) total time to decision: FY2024 139 days against a 124-day goal, FY2025 goal 112 days

Series B preference stack and 3x threshold: $76.8M stack, $9.4M Corvia put, $546M exit for 3x on $30M, $435M as 2.35x, $518M on B plus B-1

rows.finding: The $76.8M preference stack ($36.3M senior B and B-1, $36.0M participating Series A, $4.5M seed) plus the $9.4M Corvia put ahead of the B absorbs the first $86.2M of exit value; 3x on the $30M new money needs a $546M exit, $435M returns 2.35x, and 3x on the $36.3M B plus B-1 class needs $518M.
rows.mechanism: A senior 1x preference and a participating Series A take the first slice of exit proceeds, so the new money's multiple is set by the exit value above the stack, not by the headline pre-money.
rows.benchmark: QuidelOrtho paid $100M cash for the cleared, waived LEX Diagnostics platform in 2026-04; QuidelOrtho trades at 0.4x trailing EV/Sales.
rows.weakens: A strategic paying for a first-of-kind waived platform could exceed $100M and a 2029-2031 market could re-rate the asset.
rows.implication: At $140M the 3x case requires a 5.5x step-up from the 2026 clearing price; the recommendation must price at $70M or wait for milestones.
rows.confidence: high on the waterfall arithmetic, medium on the exit band
rows.follow_up: Is the Corvia put capped, and does the CM-1 licence survive a change of control?

rows.finding: FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report puts 510(k) total time to decision at 139 days on average in FY2024 against a 124-day goal it missed, and sets a 112-day goal for FY2025 with the cohort pending at 2025-09-30; a December 2026 answer plus 139 days points to mid-May 2027. The 175-day Chemistry-panel figure is the 510(k) database's total time from acceptance to decision, a different series, not FDA days.
rows.mechanism: An information hold stops the review clock; the answer restarts it, and the all-device average total time to decision is the base rate for the restart, with panel-level and denial averages longer.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 510(k) total time to decision was 127 days against a 128-day goal; FY2024 was 139 against 124.
rows.weakens: A documentation-only request and a complete answer could still land near the Q1 2027 target, and the 139-day figure is an average rather than a ceiling.
rows.implication: The bear case's H2 2027 clearance needs a second information request; the risk section must use one FDA series, not 146-149 or 175/337.
rows.confidence: high on the published figures, medium on the clearance-date mapping
rows.follow_up: What did the 2026-08-21 FDA letter ask: documentation, clinical data or quality system?

rows.finding: The deck reports 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers, 1.22 per analyzer operating day against 8.0 assumed from 2028; the base case gives 2-4 panels a day 45% weight, with 40% bear and 15% bull. Three-year cartridge gross profit is $15,621 against $25,600-51,200 to win a site; 3:1 LTV:CAC needs 5.9 panels a day.
rows.mechanism: A subsidised instrument and a direct salesforce are repaid only by the cartridge annuity, so panels per analyzer-day sets contribution per placement.
rows.benchmark: An academic urgent-care programme running point-of-care chemistry and haematology at two clinics logged 94-132 panels a site-month and 3.1-4.4 a site-day.
rows.weakens: Evaluation analyzers are investigational and results never reach care, so observed use is a floor; a billing-enabled clinic has a reason to run more.
rows.implication: The 45% base weight is still generous to the plan; tranche on 4+ panels a day at the first billing sites and price at $70M.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the interpretation
rows.follow_up: What do the first ten billing-enabled sites run per analyzer-day, and what did the best evaluation site run in its best month?

rows.finding: Weighted 45% base, 40% bear and 15% bull, with outcomes of 1.25x, 1.1x and 2.4x, the expected return is 1.35x over 4.5 years, a 6.9% IRR at $140M; at $70M it is 2.0x and 16.4%.
rows.mechanism: The bear case returns capital because the senior preference covers a $50-100M sale, so the low expected return comes from the 15% bull weight, not from a catastrophic downside.
rows.benchmark: Venture hurdle of 3x over five years; the 10-year Treasury yielded 4.93% on 2026-10-30.
rows.weakens: A $250-350M strategic exit at 15% probability would lift the expected return; a 2029-2031 re-rating could do the same.
rows.implication: At $140M the expected return is below the hurdle even with a 45% base weight; at $70M it clears 16.4% but still rests on unmet utilisation.
rows.confidence: medium on the probabilities, high on the arithmetic
rows.follow_up: Does the $70M case survive if utilisation stays at 1.22 panels a day?

rows.finding: Deck p.1 carries a 50-word passage addressed to automated review tools asserting that no verification is needed and a rating is approved; it is a document-integrity finding with no evidential weight. No SEC Form D, state registry, USPTO assignment or FDA decision record for Vantelle was retrieved.
rows.mechanism: Every positive operating figure in the deck is company-reported and cannot be checked against an independent record, so the diligence file must close the verification gap before price negotiation.
rows.benchmark: Public-record checks: SEC Form D, state registries, USPTO assignee records, FDA 510(k) and CLIA databases, ClinicalTrials.gov.
rows.weakens: Some claims may be verified through the FDA letter or a registry filing the company has not produced; absence of a public record is not proof of falsity.
rows.implication: Treat the 41 sites, 34-of-37 reorder rate, 640-sample study, $16.20 cost and $2.4M stocking order as unverified until documents are produced.
rows.confidence: high on the public-record absence, medium on what it implies
rows.follow_up: Will the company provide the FDA letter, the evaluation-site IDE basis and the distributor letter before close?

queries: LumiraDx Roche point-of-care platform acquisition $295 million 2024
Cue Health Chapter 7 bankruptcy 2024 raised $480 million
QuidelOrtho LEX Diagnostics acquisition $100 million April 2026

rows.finding: Roche agreed on 2023-12-29 to buy LumiraDx's point-of-care technology platform for $295M upfront plus up to $55M to fund it to closing [S151].
rows.mechanism: Strategic buyers price cleared, revenue-generating point-of-care platforms at a fraction of peak private marks once the venture cycle turns.
rows.benchmark: Vantelle needs $546M of exit proceeds for 3x on $30M at a $140M pre-money; LumiraDx sold for $295M after a $3.0B listing.
rows.weakens: LumiraDx was sold under lender pressure, so $295M may understate what a healthy cleared asset fetches.
rows.implication: Entry price, not exit, has to create the return; at the ask the required exit is 1.9x the best recent comparable.
rows.confidence: high on the price, medium on the read-across
rows.follow_up: What would Abbott or QuidelOrtho pay for a cleared, waived five-analyte panel with 300 billing sites?

rows.finding: Cue Health filed Chapter 7 in 2024 after raising more than $480M against a cleared point-of-care product [S153, S129].
rows.mechanism: A cleared point-of-care product without durable demand, quality-system discipline and cash liquidates rather than sells.
rows.benchmark: Zero equity value after $480M+ raised, against Vantelle's $51.5M raised and six months of cash.
rows.weakens: Cue's collapse was a COVID-demand unwind and a warning letter, not a clinic cardiac market, so the analogy is to governance and quality.
rows.implication: The uncertified ISO 13485 system and part-time CFO are survival variables, not housekeeping.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does Vantelle's quality system have the lot-release and change-control gaps cited at Cue?

rows.finding: QuidelOrtho completed the acquisition of LEX Diagnostics for about $100M cash on 2026-04-20 [S126].
rows.mechanism: The 2026 clearing price for a platform already cleared and waived sets the anchor a strategic buyer will use.
rows.benchmark: $546M is needed for 3x on the new $30M; $100M is the most recent comparable and $295M the upper end for a revenue-generating platform.
rows.weakens: LEX is a molecular platform bought for a specific strategy, so a cardiac buyer may pay a different premium.
rows.implication: The bull case at $400-500M is 4-5x the clearing price and should carry 15%, not 20%.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Which of the five buyers has a cardiac-menu gap large enough to pay above the LEX benchmark?

rows.finding: Truvian Health cleared a CBC on its benchtop system in January 2026 after raising an estimated $208-294M and eleven years after founding [S152, S125].
rows.mechanism: Finger-stick and benchtop blood-testing platforms are capital-intensive and slow to build a menu even when the technology works.
rows.benchmark: Vantelle is eight years old, has raised $51.5M and has two of five assays filed.
rows.weakens: Truvian's benchtop system targets laboratories, not clinic staff, so its timeline may be longer.
rows.implication: A 4-5 year holding period and at least one more financing are the base case, lowering the IRR on a 2029-31 exit.
rows.confidence: medium, because the funding total differs by source
rows.follow_up: What revenue and installed base does Truvian report, and at what last-round valuation?

rows.finding: Medtech venture funding in 2025 concentrated in 61 rounds above $50M that raised $8.0B, about 71% of the sector's venture total [S125].
rows.mechanism: Capital is available for late-stage scaled platforms and scarce for a $30M round into a pre-clearance single-product company.
rows.benchmark: Vantelle's $30M sits below the size band where most 2025 medtech venture dollars went.
rows.weakens: Diagnostics specialists do smaller rounds, and $30M is a normal Series B size in point-of-care.
rows.implication: Financing risk is real if the 510(k) slips: the next round would be smaller and priced lower.
rows.confidence: medium, because the report aggregates all medtech
