plan.decision_question: Is Vantelle worth leading a $30M Series B at $140M pre-money, and at what price, terms or milestones does the risk-adjusted return clear the venture hurdle?
plan.thesis_sentence: Vantelle addresses a real clinical need and holds a genuine 12-24 month packaging lead, but at $140M pre-money the evidence supports waiting for clearance and utilisation data or repricing to $60-80M, because 3x needs a $546M exit against a $100M 2026 clearing price.
plan.why_different: It converts the company's own utilisation and preference-stack arithmetic into a price and a milestone decision rule instead of repeating the market estimate.
plan.mechanism: Razor-and-blade placement economics: the analyzer is subsidised, the cartridge annuity only repays placement above five to six panels a day, and the Series A participation plus the Corvia put absorb the first $76.8M of exit value.
plan.comparison_set: LumiraDx/Roche $295M, Cue Health Chapter 7, QuidelOrtho/LEX $100M, Truvian's eleven-year path; five valuation methods at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint.
plan.counter_evidence: A waived five-analyte panel would be first-of-kind and could reset the clearing price; billing-enabled sites may run 6-8 panels a day; the $8M insider commitment signals informed conviction.
plan.visual: Scenarios component and the ranked key-assumptions table.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned; vague counts; internal names.

scoring.author: Lead Analyst
queries: FDA 510(k) average review time additional information request 2025 performance goal
FDA CLIA waiver by application 150 days decision dual 510(k) CLIA waiver
point-of-care diagnostics venture capital funding 2025 Series B valuation medtech
QuidelOrtho LEX Diagnostics acquisition $100 million April 2026
CMS clinical laboratory fee schedule CY2027 proposed rule chemistry rate cut 16%

rows.finding: The average FDA 510(k) review time in 2025 was 146 days across 3,195 clearances against a 90-day MDUFA goal, and additional information requests stop the clock [S92].
rows.mechanism: An information request converts a 90-day goal into a multi-cycle review, so the decision date follows the answer, not the original filing.
rows.benchmark: Vantelle's 2026-08-21 request and December 2026 answer imply clearance no earlier than late March 2027; 146 days is the observed average.
rows.weakens: Some submissions clear in under 90 days, and a documentation-only request can close quickly.
rows.implication: Score regulatory timing low (3 of 10) and tranche on the clearance certificate, not on the guided quarter.
rows.confidence: high on the data, medium on the application to this submission
rows.follow_up: What did the FDA request: bench, labelling, clinical or quality-system evidence?

rows.finding: FDA runs a dual 510(k) and CLIA Waiver by Application pathway on one review track, but no troponin-I system appears on the waived list and Abbott's waived menu is chemistry and blood gas [S72, S147, S104].
rows.mechanism: A waiver requires flex and intended-user studies on top of the 510(k), and a cardiac marker has no waiver precedent.
rows.benchmark: 233,448 waived laboratories against 30,756 moderate-complexity ones; without a waiver the urgent-care channel needs trained staff.
rows.weakens: Multi-analyte waivers exist (Abbott CHEM8+), so the pathway is open for chemistry panels.
rows.implication: Score market access 3 of 10 and put the waiver in 2028, not 2027, in every recommendation.
rows.confidence: high on the pathway, medium on the cardiac-specific outcome
rows.follow_up: Would FDA accept a pre-submission for a five-analyte panel including troponin I, and on what study design?

rows.finding: QuidelOrtho paid about $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics on 2026-04-20; Roche paid $295M plus up to $55M for LumiraDx's platform [S126, S151].
rows.mechanism: Strategic buyers anchor to recent clearing prices for cleared, waived point-of-care platforms.
rows.benchmark: $546M is needed for 3x on the $30M at $140M pre-money; the 2026 comparable is $100M.
rows.weakens: A five-analyte cardiac panel would be first-of-kind and could command a premium above LEX.
rows.implication: Score valuation and exit 2 of 10 and make price the first condition of any investment.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What synergy value would a five-analyte cartridge add to Abbott's or QuidelOrtho's installed base?

rows.finding: Medtech venture capital in 2025 concentrated in 61 rounds above $50M raising $8.0B, about 71% of the sector total [S125].
rows.mechanism: Capital concentrates in late-stage platforms, so a pre-clearance $30M round is exposed to a down round if milestones slip.
rows.benchmark: Vantelle's $30M round and $51.5M raised to date against the $50M+ band where most 2025 dollars went.
rows.weakens: Specialist diagnostics funds routinely lead $20-40M rounds, and the insider $8M commitment reduces financing risk.
rows.implication: Score the financial plan 3 of 10: $40M is needed on the company plan and $55-70M in the stress case.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Which existing investors have pro rata capacity and follow-on reserves?

rows.finding: CMS's preliminary CY2027 fee schedule cuts Chemistry rates 16%, phased at up to 15% a year through 2029, taking the five-code panel from $71.38 to $60.67 in 2027 and $43.83 in 2029 [S149, S82-S86].
rows.mechanism: The clinic's contribution per $33.40 cartridge falls from $37.98 to $10.43, so the $650 monthly fee consumes 62 panels of margin instead of 17.
rows.benchmark: 2026 rates, which every company projection uses; the proposed cut is the first year of a multi-year path.
rows.weakens: The rule is preliminary and commercial or cash pricing may exceed Medicare.
rows.implication: Score unit economics 3 of 10 and stress the clinic's payback in the recommendation.
rows.confidence: medium, because the rule is not final
rows.follow_up: What is the final CY2027 rule, and what share of target sites bill commercial rather than Medicare?

plan.decision_question: What is the composite score, position size and path to a positive decision for Meridian at $140M pre-money?
plan.thesis_sentence: On a weighted score of 3.9 of 10, Vantelle is a wait-for-milestone or repriced investment, not a $15M lead at $140M.
plan.why_different: The score is anchored on the two variables that decide the return, utilisation and price, rather than the regulatory calendar alone.
plan.mechanism: Weighted scoring across market, product, regulatory, unit economics, financial plan, team, governance and valuation; the recommendation then translates the score into check size, tranches and conditions.
plan.comparison_set: Peer benchmark $50-100M valuation cluster; $100M LEX clearing price; 146-day FDA review; 5.9 panels a day for 3:1 LTV:CAC.
plan.counter_evidence: A cleared, waived, high-utilisation product would score 7-8 on most dimensions; the score is a statement about evidence today, not the technology's ceiling.
plan.visual: Weighted score table, sensitivity component and takeaways.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned; vague counts; internal names.

user_data_requests.database: Vantelle data room (company-held): 2024 clinic survey dataset and evaluation-program cartridge records
user_data_requests.query: The raw 52-clinic 2024 survey (instrument, responses, date field, the cardiac/metabolic send-out question) and 12 months of cartridge shipments by site with tests ordered per cartridge and collections per panel
user_data_requests.why: The survey's median of 14 send-outs a day and the observed 1.22 cartridges per analyser-day differ by an order of magnitude and decide whether the US market is $368M or $2.4B; the order mix decides whether the clinic earns $718.58 or loses $20.77 per cartridge run, which determines willingness to pay the $38 price.
user_data_requests.how: Ask management for the survey file and the cartridge-level shipment and billing extract, or permission to speak to three evaluation sites about their send-out volume and collections.

user_data_requests.database: Delaware Division of Corporations; Arizona Corporation Commission; Texas Secretary of State
user_data_requests.query: Entity records and certificates of good standing for Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. (Delaware, formed 2018-03-12), Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC (Arizona, 2022-05-09), Corvia Microfluidics LLC (Texas, 2016-02-01) and Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited (Ireland, 2025-01-15), including officers, registered agent, prior names and any franchise-tax delinquency.
user_data_requests.why: No public registry record was reachable for any of the four entities on 2026-10-31: the Delaware and Arizona portals require an interactive search and the Texas record is not indexed. Without these records the entity map, formation dates, 60/40 Corvia ownership and the parent's good standing all rest on the deck alone, which is the difference between a clean structure and an unverified one for a $15M lead check.
user_data_requests.how: Order a Delaware certificate of good standing and entity history for the issuer, an Arizona entity search printout for the LLC, a Texas SOS file number and franchise status for Corvia, and the Irish CRO company number; upload the PDFs.

user_data_requests.database: Delaware and Arizona UCC filing offices; Bluestem Venture Lending credit file
user_data_requests.query: UCC-1 financing statements naming Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc., Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC or Corvia Microfluidics LLC as debtor, and the $5.0M term loan agreement of 2024-03 including collateral, covenants, warrant terms and any IP security agreement or negative pledge.
user_data_requests.why: The deck discloses a $5.0M Bluestem loan (interest-only to 2027-03, then 30 monthly payments) and 400,000 common warrants at $2.903 but not whether the loan is secured over patents, the CM-1 licence or receivables, or what covenants a Series B would breach. A security interest over the patents or the Corvia licence would rank ahead of the new money and change the collateral position in a downside case.
user_data_requests.how: Run debtor-name UCC searches in Delaware and Arizona and request the executed credit agreement, security agreement and warrant from the company or Bluestem; upload the filings and agreement.

user_data_requests.database: Company data room (unpublished technical and manufacturing records)
user_data_requests.query: The pivotal four-site study protocol and statistical analysis plan; the analytical precision, method-comparison, LoB/LoD/LoQ, linearity and haemolysis-interference reports for all five assays; six-month and real-time stability data; and the cartridge cost model and line capacity plan behind $10 at 1 million and $7.50 at 2 million units.
user_data_requests.why: Every performance and cost figure in the deck is company-reported and unverified; no public study, FDA record or patent corroborates them. The pivotal protocol determines whether the capillary-versus-venous question is answered at the decision level, and the cost model determines whether the 2029 gross margin is achievable.
user_data_requests.how: Request the data-room index and the four reports above from management; the pivotal protocol can be reviewed before the study reports in Q2 2027.

user_data_requests.database: FDA 510(k) file and USPTO Patent Center file wrappers
user_data_requests.query: The company's pending 510(k) submission for troponin I and HbA1c, including the FDA additional-information request of 2026-08-21 and the company's response; and the file wrappers for the five patent families named on deck p.6 (US 16/884,327, US 17/662,019, US 19/318,770, PCT/US2026/014022, US 15/707,915), including the 2026-07 final rejection and appeal.
user_data_requests.why: The public registries cannot be queried by the client's filing or patent numbers, and pending 510(k)s are not published. Without the AI letter I cannot tell whether the deficiency is documentation or new clinical data, which sets the clearance date; without the file wrappers I cannot test whether the reader claims survive appeal or whether the granted cartridge claim covers a five-analyte cartridge, which is the core of the moat.
user_data_requests.how: Ask the company to provide, under NDA: the FDA AI letter and the response, and the USPTO file wrappers or counsel's claim charts for the five families.

user_data_requests.database: FDA 510(k) file K261734 (company-held correspondence; pending submissions are not public)
user_data_requests.query: The FDA additional-information request dated 2026-08-21 on the troponin I / HbA1c 510(k) and Vantelle's December 2026 response, redacted for trade secrets if necessary.
user_data_requests.why: The content decides whether Q1 2027 clearance is achievable and whether the deficiency is analytical performance (the 11.8% troponin CV), clinical data or quality-system documentation; it also sets whether a second review cycle is likely, which drives the valuation and the tranche structure.
user_data_requests.how: Ask management to provide the FDA letter and response under NDA. FDA does not publish pending 510(k) files and a FOIA request would not release the pre-decisional file without the submitter's consent.

user_data_requests.database: PACER (US federal courts) and Delaware, Texas, Arizona and New Mexico state court portals
user_data_requests.query: Civil, intellectual-property, employment and product-liability dockets naming Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc., Corvia Microfluidics LLC, Dr Wren Albescu or Dr Tomasz Lindqvist, 2018-2026.
user_data_requests.why: The Corvia royalty and put are related-party claims on exit proceeds; undisclosed litigation, IP ownership disputes or employee claims would change the governance assessment and the price. Public web searches found no record, but the court dockets themselves are login-gated.
user_data_requests.how: Run a PACER party search and the state court portal searches with a PACER account (or a court-records service); send the docket list and PDFs of any complaints.

user_data_requests.database: Arizona Department of Health Services laboratory licensure; New Mexico Health Care Authority CLIA program
user_data_requests.query: State laboratory licence or CLIA certificate type (waiver, compliance or accreditation) and any enforcement history for Vantelle's 41 evaluation sites and its Tempe, Arizona cartridge plant.
user_data_requests.why: Until a federal CLIA waiver is granted, each site must hold a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff; state licensure can add a further requirement or exemption. The findings decide whether the evaluation base can convert to billable sites and whether the paid programme is operating lawfully.
user_data_requests.how: Request the state laboratory licensure lists or submit a public-records request to AZDHS and NM HCA; the CLIA certificate type per site is also obtainable from CMS's CLIA laboratory lookup.

user_data_requests.database: Vantelle data room: Bluestem Venture Lending loan agreement and Southwest Clinical Supply distributor agreement
user_data_requests.query: Bluestem $5.0M term loan: interest rate, amortisation, financial covenants and any minimum-cash test. Southwest Clinical Supply: payment terms, return and rotation rights, wholesale price behind the $2.4M opening order, and whether the order is firm or conditional on sell-through.
user_data_requests.why: The loan covenant sets whether a clearance delay accelerates the debt and shortens the runway from 6 months; the distributor terms decide whether $2.4M of FY2026E revenue (41%) is revenue or returnable inventory, and how much of the $30M the launch consumes in receivables and inventory.
user_data_requests.how: Ask management for both executed agreements and the order confirmation, or a redacted summary of rate, covenants, payment days and return rights, before the 2027-01-29 close.

user_data_requests.database: Vantelle Diagnostics commercial records / data room
user_data_requests.query: Twelve months of cartridge shipments by site and by month, January 2025 to September 2026, with 2026 year-to-date unit totals and FY2025 cartridge units; and the monthly analyzer count by site over the same period.
user_data_requests.why: The deck's 1,680 cartridges a month is a "2026 average" (p.7) across 41 sites and 55 analyzers, but the months covered, 2026 unit volume and FY2025 units are not disclosed. The $78.5M 2029 plan and the 5,150-site requirement depend on this denominator, and the current figure cannot show growth or seasonality.
user_data_requests.how: Ask management for the shipment and analyzer-placement extracts from its commercial system, by site and month, under NDA.

user_data_requests.query: Cartridge and reader bills of materials with the top-ten suppliers and supplier sites; second-source qualification records for each component; the troponin antibody licence and supply agreement, including licensor identity, royalty, change-of-control, assignment and transfer rights; and the unredacted 2024 freedom-to-operate opinion.

Utilisation denominator differs between our sections: yours says 1.0 cartridge per analyser per day (eightfold gap), mine says 1.22 per operating day over the deck's 300 days (6.5x gap). Also: the FY2028 plan of $41.0M on 300 sites x 2 analysers implies 7.35 panels per analyser-day at $31, six times observed.

At 2026 Medicare rates the clinic's gross margin is $718.58 per analyser-month at 41 cartridges, but negative if only troponin and potassium are ordered ($17.23 against a $38 cartridge).

**Delivered: Vantelle Diagnostics investment memo (version 3, data as of 2026-10-31). Rating: Wait for milestone. Composite score: 3.9/10, medium confidence. Recommendation: do not lead at $140M pre-money; offer $15M at or below $70M, $7.5M at close and $7.5M on 510(k) clearance plus an accepted CLIA waiver pre-submission.**

**Thesis in two sentences.** The need is real and the capability is first-of-kind — a five-analyte finger-stick panel for clinics that cannot staff a laboratory, with 41 paid evaluation sites and 34 of 37 reordering — but the economics do not scale at the ask: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day against the eight its 2028 plan needs, and $140M pre-money is 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue ($3.5M, excluding a $2.4M clearance-contingent stocking order), needing a $596M exit for 3x against a $100M April 2026 clearing price for a cleared, waived platform. At or below $70M with a tranched cheque and a capped Series A participation the same asset returns 1.40x and 7.8% on our weighted scenarios, versus 1.17x and 3.6% at the ask.

**Main risks.** (1) Utilisation staying near the evaluation rate — at 1.22 panels/day the cartridge annuity never repays the estimated $25,600-51,200 cost of winning a site; the plan needs 5,150 sites for 2029 revenue, not 300. (2) The capillary troponin study failing: the 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff is above the IFCC's <10% standard and Abbott's cleared <5.2%, the 640-sample study was venous, company-run, single-site, with six excluded results and no capillary data. (3) The CLIA waiver: no waived troponin-I precedent exists, a Q3 2027 filing points to a 2028 decision at best, and until then sites need moderate-complexity staffing. (4) Runway and funding: $6.9M cash at 2026-09-30 is 6.0 months, and the H2 2027 base consumes $55-70M before breakeven against a $30M round. (5) Structure and governance: a 19.96% post-money option overhang, a $9.4M Corvia put ranking ahead of the Series B, a 1x participating Series A absorbing the first $76.8M, a part-time interim CFO, and ISO 13485 not yet certified.

**The one question.** At the first billing-enabled sites after clearance, how many five-analyte cartridges does each analyzer run per day, and what revenue does the site collect per cartridge? At the observed rate the placement never pays back; at the plan's rate the same base supports a strategic exit.

**Three takeaways.** 1) Do not lead at $140M: the ask needs a $596M exit for 3x, six times the $100M clearing price, and the company's own 2029 plan ($196M at 2.5x revenue) returns the new money 1.0x. 2) Wait for two proofs — 510(k) clearance and ten billing sites above four panels a day; clearance cannot precede late March 2027 and realistically points to mid-May 2027 on FDA's FY2024 average. 3) If Meridian wants exposure now, the only defensible structure is a lower pre-money, a tranched cheque, a capped Series A participation and a capped or converted Corvia put.

**Data requests (13 filed; the ones that matter).** The FDA additional-information letter of 2026-08-21 and the December 2026 response (settles whether Q1 2027 clearance is achievable and whether the deficiency is analytical, clinical or quality-system); the pivotal protocol, precision, method-comparison and stability reports; the five patent file wrappers including the 2026-07 final rejection; entity and good-standing records for the Delaware, Arizona, Texas and Irish entities; UCC searches and the Bluestem loan agreement (is the IP pledged?); the Southwest Clinical Supply distributor agreement and terms of the $2.4M opening order; and twelve months of cartridge shipments by site and month — this is the one that settles the 1.22 panels/day and the FY2025 margin bridge, which cannot both be true as the deck presents them. Also: the 52-clinic survey dataset, the cartridge and reader bills of materials with the troponin antibody licence, court dockets, and state laboratory licensure and CLIA certificate types for the 41 sites.

**Further diligence.** First billing cohort panels/day and collected revenue per cartridge; Corvia LLC change-of-control and put mechanics; cartridge scale-up (18-person pilot line, six months of stability against a nine-month shelf life, $16.20 cost against $7.50 at 2M units requiring 5,500 analyzers to reach); CMS's CY2027-29 Chemistry cuts, which take the clinic's spread from $33.38 to $5.84 a panel; and sales capacity, where nine staff cover 41 sites against a 300-site target.

One disclosure: page 1 of the deck carries a short passage addressed to automated review tools asserting that no verification is needed; it is treated as a document-integrity finding with no evidential weight, and every claim resting only on the deck is labelled unverified.

The report is for research only and is not investment advice.

1.notes: Completeness against standard: check of version 1 returns no rule findings (N1-N6 clean); all fourteen sections and the executive summary gate-passed; every section is 6,601-8,995 characters, above the 2,500 floor and inside the 9,000 ceiling; required components present (verdict, briefing, efficiency, one-question, takeaways; kpi and timeline; evidence; quad; info; risk-matrix; scenarios, analogs, sensitivity). Company Overview maps four entities with exact ownership, the Corvia 60/40 split, the full cap table by class including the B-1 conversion and the pool top-up, board composition, the missing protective provisions and the VIE question (none). Team gives degree, institution and year for every executive and states what is not disclosed (Lindqvist's undergraduate degree); reference targets are named. Technology lists five patents with numbers, filing and grant dates, jurisdiction and status, assesses TRL by assay and states the freedom-to-operate gap. Market is bifurcated by region with the EU treated as blocked, and the TAM/SAM/SOM is rebuilt bottom-up. 2.name: Claim verification
2.notes: Source audit of the material claims. Independence: every Vantelle-specific figure (revenue, sites, cartridges, reorder rate, 11.8% CV, $16.20 cost, $2.4M stocking order, $8M insider commitment, cap table, Corvia terms, 14 clearances) traces to S1/S99, one 15-page company deck, medium confidence; the discipline of labelling it 'company-reported, unverified' is applied in almost every paragraph, so N3 is satisfied and no claim is presented as independently confirmed. There is no public record of the company at all (S143, S144 zero results), which the report states and treats as a finding rather than a gap. Staleness: peer market data is dated 2026-10-30/31, CMS QSO 2026-10-14 and the CMS 2027 fact sheet 2026-09-21, FDA clearances 2023-2026, precedent deals 2021-2026 with the 2021 COVID-era prices explicitly flagged as a different regime - none stale. Dated events use YYYY-MM. Two precision slips: Financials writes the peer net margin as 'QuidelOrtho (41.5%)', which reads as a profit (it is a loss), and the thesis analogs cite Truvian's $208-294M raised from a low-confidence aggregator (S124) while the Exit section correctly labels it an aggregator estimate. Minor. Checked and holding: the LEX $100M clearing price (S126, 2026-04-20), the Abbott hs-TnI clearance dates (S6 2025-01-03, S2 2026-06-11), LumiraDx $295M plus up to $55M (S91, S117, S151), Cue Health warning letter CMS# 675673 (S113) and Chapter 7 (S129, S153), the CLIA laboratory counts (S81) and the clinical literature behind the haemolysis and capillary points (S16, S21, S68).

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: Blind-spot checklist run against the evidence. Geographic: the report confines revenue to the US and treats the EU as blocked until CE marking after 2028 (Irish entity formed 2025-01-15, no staff) - defensible, and the exit section explicitly rules out CFIUS as a constraint; the untested geography is Asia as a supplier of cheap hardware, not as a market. Adjacent giants: Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, Roche, Danaher/Radiometer are mapped as competitors; Thermo Fisher and Hologic appear only as exit buyers even though both have point-of-care molecular channels and could enter clinic diagnostics by acquisition at a lower price than the ask - a second-order point, not worth an item on its own. Substitute: the reference laboratory and 'transfer the patient' status quo are both in the table, which is the lens's status-quo test passed. Open source and academic: no open-source alternative exists for a regulated cartridge; no university spin-out is mapped, but the capillary and haemolysis literature (S16, S21) is used and the analytic case is not claimed to be novel science. The most dangerous missing entrant is not a startup: it is a waived single-analyte combination at $20-25, which the report names as the threat but never prices against a named device.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: The lens's five product/market-fit questions against the file. Hardest thing to sell: answered well - a $38 cartridge against $32.12 of four-code reimbursement, plus a $650 monthly fee the clinic pays, against a free-meter, minimum-volume incumbent contract; the two-analyte run loses $20.77 and the ratio flips if the natriuretic peptide is not ordered. Budget owner: partly answered (clinic operator, not clinician) but not for the hospital-affiliated 39%, where procurement and the system laboratory intervene; the $650 fee's approval threshold is never stated. Sales cycle: unanswered anywhere in the report. Why adoption is not faster: answered strongly - investigational-use labelling, no billing at evaluation sites, moderate-complexity CLIA requirement until a waiver decides in 2028, and a utilisation rate that may itself be a floor. Lost deals: unanswered - there is no lost-deal evidence, no declined site, and no statement that no site has been lost, which is the kind of absence a committee reads as a gap. Secondary observation, consistent on the arithmetic: 22 of 55 analyzers paid at $2,900 plus $429k of fees plus $673k of cartridges reconstructs the $1.1M evaluation line, so the placement economics hold together; the missing piece is the customer's decision process, not the price list.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Arithmetic that holds (checked, not flagged): 52,204,508 shares x $3.2564 = $170.0M post-money; 10,420,489 / 52,204,508 = 19.96% overhang; $15M / $170M = 8.82% and / $140M = 10.7%; 1,680 / 55 / 25 = 1.22 and / 55 / 30 = 1.0 per analyzer-day; 30.5 x 12 x $16.20 = $5,929 against the $5,937 gross profit per analyzer-year; $5,207 x 3 = $15,621 LTV, less $25,600-51,200 CAC = -$9,979 to -$35,579; $140M / $3.5M = 40.0x; $2.4M / $33.40 = 71,856 cartridges = 3.56x today's 20,160; 1680 x 12 = 20,160; 34/37 = 91.9%; weighted score 0.9+0.8+0.6+0.45+0.3+0.5+0.2+0.1 = 3.85, rounded to 3.9 (disclosed). Thirty-per-cent tests: revenue -30% takes 2029 to $55.0M, $70.4M at 2.5x discounted three years - at or below the $76.8M preference stack, so the 1.35x/6.9% IRR at the ask falls to 1.0-1.2x and the $70M entry's 2.0x does not survive (the 'do not lead' conclusion is unchanged and strengthened; the 'keep the option at $70M' recommendation weakens). Cartridge price -30% to $23.38 leaves $7.18 of gross profit before royalty, making contribution per analyzer-year negative at observed use and pushing the 3:1 threshold to about 14 panels a day. CAC doubled to $51,200-102,400 gives 0.15-0.3x LTV:CAC and makes 402 analyzers cost $20.6-41.2M to place, more than the round. Preference stack 30% larger pushes 3x to roughly $700M. Concentration: losing the development customer removes 27% of revenue and losing Mesa Verde 15% - neither is tested in any scenario. The report's own sensitivity ranking (utilisation first, then clearance, then waiver) is the right order and the price is what the sensitivity is not yet wired into: the recommendation tranches on clearance and waiver but on no utilisation test, which Risk says and nothing fixes.

items.issue: The 1,680-cartridges-a-month figure, which carries the whole utilisation thesis, is dated two ways. Business Model states that the volume quoted as a 2026 average is in fact the FY2025 average, and draws the conclusion that the evaluation base has not grown in a year; Market ('ran 1,680 cartridges in an average 2026 month'), Strategy ('averaged 1,680 cartridges a month ... in 2026') and the Executive Briefing card present it as 2026 data. Business Model also reconstructs FY2025 revenue from it, so at least one section misdates the number and the inference drawn from it changes the bear case.
items.action: Fix one dated basis for the figure - the month it covers, the period it averages and the deck page - and carry that wording into all four sections. If it is an FY2025 average, state what the 2026 volume is, and explain how normalised FY2026E revenue rises from $2.6M to $3.5M on flat cartridge volume; if it is 2026, remove the 'base has not grown in a year' inference.
items.evidence_request: Twelve months of cartridge shipments by site and month, with the deck page that defines the period the 1,680 figure averages.

items.issue: The only third-party dependency analysed is the Corvia licence. No section identifies the single-source inputs the assay and instrument need - the troponin I antibody pair, dried reagents and membrane, the optical module, the reader's contract manufacturer - or what a supplier change after clearance would require (a new 510(k) or a device modification supplement on an already-cleared assay). With 18 staff on a pilot line and no VP Manufacturing, this is the most likely route to a launch slip, and it is currently unpriced.
items.action: Add a dependency table: input, supplier type, sole-source yes/no, switching time and effect on the cleared file. State whether the troponin antibody is licensed, from whom, and whether the licence is assignable.
items.evidence_request: Bill of materials with the top-ten suppliers, second-source status for each and any sole-source or licensed component of the cartridge and reader.

items.issue: The clinic-economics arithmetic that decides willingness to pay rests on third-party rate lookup pages: $12.47 troponin, $39.26 natriuretic peptide, $9.71 HbA1c, $5.18 creatinine, $4.76 potassium, the $71.38 panel, the $37.98 contribution and the $20.77 loss on a troponin-plus-potassium run all trace to S82-S86 (medfeeschedule.com code pages, confidence medium). CMS publishes the same schedule as a primary file, and the team already used the CMS 2027 fact sheet (S149) elsewhere, so the weaker source is a choice, not a constraint. The 2027 cut analysis inherits any error in the 2026 base.
items.action: Replace S82-S86 with CMS's own CY2026 CLFS file (national limitation amounts for 84484, 83880, 83036, 82570, 84132), table the five codes with descriptors, and recompute the two-code ($17.23) and four-code ($32.12) cases and the $718.58 monthly contribution.
items.evidence_request: CMS CY2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule national limitation amounts for the five codes, with the file date.

items.issue: Three different 510(k) review-time series are used to date a decision the whole valuation depends on: Team has 139 days in FY2024 and 112 in FY2025, Strategy has 146-149 days for 2025, Risk has 175 days for the Chemistry panel and 337 for denials. None says whether it counts FDA days or total time to decision, and the sourcing is a consultancy page (S101) and an aggregator (S92) although FDA's own MDUFA report (S97) is in the register. The late-March 2027 clearance date then depends on which series is taken.
items.action: Use one series from FDA's FY2025 MDUFA report (S97), label every figure as FDA days or total time to decision, attribute the Chemistry-panel number, and restate the clearance date from that single series. Confirm the 2026-12 answer date and the 90-day restart against S140.
items.evidence_request: FY2025 MDUFA performance table giving 510(k) total and FDA review days by review panel.

items.issue: Three benchmarks that set investor expectations and two 'critical' KPI signals rest on secondary web pages: the 10-15% Series B pool benchmark (S102, a calculator post), the claim that a 1x participating preference appeared in 5% of 2025 deals (S100, a blog summarising Cooley data) and the $200M median Series B post-money (S103, confidence low). Presented as peer facts they imply precision the sources do not carry, and Section 14 itself says a dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7.
items.action: Cite the primary survey tables (NVCA/PitchBook Venture Monitor, or Cooley's own report) for pool size, participation and Series B post-money, or label each figure 'indicative, secondary source' and lower the weight it carries in the KPI signals and the scoring.
items.evidence_request: Primary 2025 survey data for option-pool size at Series B, the share of deals with participating preferred, and median Series B post-money.

items.issue: The table maps the five platform incumbents but omits three classes that set the price. First, waived single-analyte low-cost devices that undercut the menu premium: Nova Biomedical StatSensor creatinine, HemoCue (Danaher) HbA1c and haemoglobin, Abbott Afinion 2 HbA1c/CRP - Nova appears once, in passing, in Technology & Product and nowhere in Section 5. Second, the Asian point-of-care immunoassay platforms (Boditech ichroma, SD Biosensor STANDARD F, Getein, Wondfo) that anchor price per test far below $23.96 and are the likeliest source of the $20-25 bundled cartridge the section says takes the account - a non-US entrant is exactly the blind spot the report never tests. Third, Truvian Health, the closest private comparable (finger-stick multi-analyte panel, 12 analytes cleared by 2026-01-12), which the thesis names as an analog but Section 5 does not treat as a competitor, and Babson Diagnostics (Austin, Texas), whose finger-stick multi-analyte collection through retail pharmacy partners is a substitute that removes the in-clinic analyser altogether.
items.action: Add rows to the competitor table with product, menu, waived status, price per test, channel and threat level for: Nova Biomedical StatSensor (creatinine), HemoCue (Danaher) HbA1c and haemoglobin, Abbott Afinion 2 (HbA1c/CRP), Truvian Health's TruVerus and Babson Diagnostics' BetterWay; add a price-anchor paragraph naming the low-cost immunoassay platforms and what a $20-25 bundled cartridge would do to the 51.5% margin. State whether a non-US five-analyte finger-stick product is already cleared anywhere.
items.evidence_request: Published US price per test for StatSensor, HemoCue HbA1c, Afinion 2 and the Triage and i-STAT cartridges; and whether any CE-marked or NMPA-cleared product combines troponin, natriuretic peptide, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium on one finger-stick cartridge.

items.issue: The report never states the sales cycle, the evaluation-to-contract conversion or who signs. It shows 41 signed sites and a 92% reorder rate, but not how long a site takes from evaluation to a paid contract, why 4 of 41 no longer reorder, or whether the signatory at a physician-owned clinic ($650 a month plus $38 a cartridge) is the same person at a hospital-affiliated site, where 39% of urgent-care centres would route through the health system's own laboratory director. Nor does it check that a site can bill Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule codes at all: without a CLIA certificate of the right type, Medicare laboratory enrolment and payer contracts, the $37.98 collected per panel does not exist and the $650 fee has no payer behind it. The $25,600-51,200 CAC figure and the 300-site plan therefore rest on a selling mechanism nothing in the file describes.
items.action: Add a commercial-conversion subsection to Section 6 (or 5): evaluation-to-contract time in months, conversion and drop-out, the signing authority by site type, and the billing prerequisites (CLIA certificate type, Medicare lab enrolment, payer contracts) for each of the 41 sites. Adjust the 300-site plan and the CAC range to whatever the conversion data supports, and say plainly that no paid conversion exists pre-clearance.
items.evidence_request: For all 41 evaluation sites: start date, contract date if any, drop-out date and reason, CLIA certificate type, Medicare enrolment status and payer mix.

items.issue: Risk states '3x on $30M needs a $435M exit' and '3x on the $36.3M of B plus B-1 needs $518M'. Funding & Valuation, Exit, the Thesis and the Executive Briefing use $546M for 3x on $30M, and Exit's own waterfall table shows $435M returning 2.35x, with $546M recorded as the correction of an earlier $435M that wrongly credited the B-1 preference to the new money. The same section also attacks 'the base case's 50% weight on 2-4 panels per analyzer-day' when the scenario table carries 45% base, 40% bear and 15% bull - and Risk then computes its expected return on that 15/45/40 split, contradicting its own criticism. The section that decides the downside carries two superseded numbers.
items.action: Restate the thresholds to $546M for 3x on the $30M and $518M on the $36.28M class, delete the $435M sentence, and rewrite the base-case sentence to the 45% base / 40% bear / 15% bull split the thesis carries and the section itself uses.

items.issue: The waterfall rows cannot be reproduced from the stated 23.75% Series A participation. At $546M the Series A's $157.1M equals $36.0M plus 25.8% of the $469.2M left after the senior preferences and its own preference; at $140M the $56.8M implies 32.9% of the $103.7M left after the senior stack. A single participation rule cannot produce both, so either the A participates on a base other than the one the text describes (and the rate is not 23.75%) or a row is mis-built - and the common and seed lines absorb the difference, as do the $546M for 3x and $376M for 2x that the thesis and executive summary lead with.
items.action: Publish the row formula (preference, participation base, any cap) beside the table, recompute the Series A line and the $546M/$376M/$242M thresholds, and carry the corrected thresholds into the thesis and the executive summary. If the A's participation is capped, state the cap.
items.evidence_request: The fully diluted share table by class after conversion and the option-pool refresh, as the waterfall's input.

items.issue: The 58% FY2025 gross margin ($1.5M on $2.6M) does not reconcile to the line margins the report itself gives: 51.5% on cartridges, a negative-margin analyzer ($2,900 list against a $3,350 build, with 60% of analyzers given free), and a contract-development line whose margin is never stated. Reaching $1.5M needs the services line at roughly 90% or the analyzer subsidy capitalised rather than carried in cost of sales, and no section says which. The same treatment drives the 61% FY2026E margin that Financials and Strategy both call optimistic.
items.action: Recompute FY2025 and FY2026E gross margin by line, state the accounting treatment of placed analyzers (inventory, fixed asset, leased) and of the $650 monthly fee (lease or service), and show the bridge from 58% to 61%. If the subsidy is capitalised, add the depreciation line and the cash effect.
items.evidence_request: Gross profit by revenue line for FY2025 and FY2026E, and the revenue-recognition policy for placed instruments and the monthly fee.

top_three: Reconcile the cartridge volume with the FY2025 revenue build: 20,160 evaluation and 23,952 research-use cartridges in FY2025 cannot coexist with 27,600 shipped since March 2024, and the two figures set both the 1.22 panels/day that decides the case and the rebuilt 58% margin bridge.

Fix three figures the IC will check: the CLFS amounts still lean on a third-party republication (S160) and on retired pages S82-S86 in ESG and Risk when CMS's MM14312 is in the register; Market's '$368M is 60% of the smallest estimate' is 12.7%, not 60%; and the scoring's re-rating statements overstate the milestone's effect by about 3x.

1.name: Completeness sweep
1.notes: Completeness against the standard: all fourteen sections and the briefing card are 7,400-9,000 characters with their required components (kpi/timeline, evidence, quad, risk-matrix/info, scenarios/analogs, sensitivity/takeaways). Lens checklist now covered: entity map with exact percentages, cap table by class with 19.96% overhang, board composition and the vacant independent seat, liquidation preference and participation, anti-dilution, patents with numbers and status, TRL, BOM as an explicit not-disclosed item, market bifurcated by region, bottom-up TAM, burn and runway, five valuation methods with a preference waterfall, margin of safety. Round-1 items checked: 1,680 dating now identical in Business Model, Market, Strategy, briefing (fixed, but see pass 1 Critical); 3x threshold and 15/45/40 split in Risk (fixed, arithmetic reproduces: 0.15x2.14 + 0.45x1.00 + 0.40x1.00 = 1.17x, 3.6% IRR; at $70M 1.40x, 7.8%); waterfall row formula reproduces every row (140/197/256/426/596 rows conserve to exit value including the $9.4M Corvia deduction); competition additions present; team KPI benchmarks replaced with Cooley Q2 2026; 510(k) series harmonised across Team, Financials, Market, Strategy and Risk; sales funnel and billing prerequisites stated as not disclosed. No rule findings on the version.

2.name: Claim verification
2.notes: Claim verification: every remaining company-only claim checked this version carries its status - the deck's 41 sites, 34-of-37 reorder, 640-sample study, 11.8% CV, $16.20 cost, $2.4M stocking order, $8M insider commitment, Oyelaran's 14 clearances, Corvia 3% royalty and 40% put are all labelled company-reported, unverified or not publicly disclosed. The independent spine holds: FDA MDUFA FY2025 report (S97) for review times, CMS CLIA statistics (S81) for laboratory counts, FDA waiver decision summaries (S147), the peer-reviewed urgent-care study (S148), QuidelOrtho-LEX (S126), Roche-LumiraDx (S91/S151), Cooley Q2 2026 (S159), and the zero-record searches (S143/S144). No stale claim over twelve months was found where a fresher registered source exists, except the Cooley item above. Five valuation methods, each with its inputs and source, and the ask tested at 2.7x capital invested.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: Missing-competitor pass otherwise clean, and the round-1 gap is closed: Boditech AFIAS-6 (S157), Truvian TruVerus (S127/S152), Babson BetterWay correctly limited to a collection-component 510(k) and a central-lab service (S156/S158), waived single-analyte readers (Roche cobas b 101, Nova StatSensor), plus Sight Diagnostics' OLO as a cleared finger-stick precedent. Substitutes and the status quo (reference laboratory, transfer the patient) are in the four-option framing. Adjacent giants: Abbott, Siemens, Roche, Radiometer and QuidelOrtho are all mapped with the account they own. Open-source and academic spin-outs are not a meaningful vector for a regulated cartridge.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: Product/market-fit questions and where the report answers them. Hardest thing to sell (placement under a $650 monthly fee against a free-instrument incumbent, plus a full-menu order the clinic must choose): answered in Business Model and Competition with the 17.1-panel fee equivalence and the four- versus five-code arithmetic. Budget owner (clinic operator, not clinician; 39% hospital-affiliated with the health system's laboratory as first call): answered in Market. Sales cycle: honestly stated as not disclosed, with the 31-month programme as the only duration evidence and 259 net adds in twelve months against 1.3 a month. Adoption is not faster because evaluation devices cannot be used for care: answered and used as the counter-case. Billing prerequisites (CLIA certificate type, EHR interface, payer enrolment): stated as not disclosed with what would settle each. Round-1 item closed.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Stress-test arithmetic that reproduces and can stand: 3x on $30M = $596M and 2x = $426M from the published row formula; $435M = 2.05x; 3x on the $36.28M B+B-1 class = $568M; expected return 1.17x and 3.6% IRR at $140M, 1.40x and 7.8% at $70M; a 30% revenue miss gives $55.0M of 2029 revenue and $70.4M at 2.5x discounted three years, at the $76.8M stack; burn multiple 8.3x FY2025, 4.2x FY2026E and 15.6x ex-stocking order; TAM $2.41B at eight panels and $368M at 1.22; $78.5M needs 5,150 sites at observed use or 528 at the model's; the two- and four-code Medicare cases ($17.23, $32.12); the $650 fee at 17.1 panels and 62 after the 2027 cut. What does not survive: the volume-to-revenue reconciliation (pass 1 Critical) and the two mis-scaled figures above.

items.issue: The volume the whole thesis rests on now has three incompatible statements inside the report. Business Model builds FY2025 revenue from 20,160 evaluation cartridges (and 23,952 research-use cartridges) at $33.40, i.e. a 1,680-a-month FY2025 run rate, and says the 58% margin 'closes only on the 2026-average volume'; Financials repeats 'today's 20,160 annual volume'; but the same sections also state 27,600 cartridges shipped in total since March 2024, 890 a month over 31 months, 567 a month before 2026. If 2026 January-September alone ran 15,120 cartridges, 27,600 cumulative cannot accommodate an FY2025 of 20,160 evaluation cartridges before it, and cannot accommodate 44,000 cartridges of any kind. One of the two figures is wrong by two to six times, and they set both the deciding utilisation number (1.22 panels per analyzer-day) and the FY2025 gross-margin bridge that was rebuilt this round. No section notices.
items.action: Reconcile the two series in one place: either the 20,160 and 23,952 are deck-disclosed FY2025 volumes (in which case the 27,600 cumulative is wrong and every '890 a month, 567 before 2026' inference is wrong), or the FY2025 line split is a reconstruction from the 2026 average (in which case say so in the table, drop 'bridge closes', and remove 'today's 20,160 annual volume' from Financials). Until a shipment ledger arrives, state in Business Model and the Executive Briefing that the observed 1.22 panels/day and the FY2025 line build cannot both be true and that the utilisation metric carries low confidence as a result.
items.evidence_request: Monthly cartridge shipments by site and by product line (evaluation versus research-use) from March 2024 to 2026-09-30; FY2024 and FY2025 revenue and direct cost by line; the deck page or workbook that defines the 27,600 cumulative total and the page that defines the 1,680 '2026 average'.

items.issue: The funding gap is computed on a clearance date the rest of the report has already rejected. Financials' base column keeps clearance in Q1 2027 (first information-request cycle) and derives the $8-10M shortfall; its stress column, a second request with clearance in Q3 2027, gives $25-40M and $55-70M in total. Thesis and Risk, however, put the base case at clearance in H2 2027 after one more cycle, with 45-55% probability of a decision later than June 2027. The executive briefing and scoring therefore carry '$40M needed against a $30M round' while the report's own base case implies $55-70M. A reader pricing a tranched cheque sizes it on the wrong branch.
items.action: Relabel Financials' columns so the base case matches the thesis base (one more cycle, H2 2027) and show the $8-10M branch as the upside; or state explicitly that the $40M figure assumes Q1 2027 clearance at a probability below 50% and that the base-case need is $55-70M. Carry one figure into the executive briefing and scoring, with the branch it belongs to.

items.issue: The competitor table's QuidelOrtho row has one cell too many ('Waived cardiac panel; EDTA blood' inserted as its own cell), so the menu reads as 'Troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin' in the Price column and '$599 per 25 tests' under Scale. The closest competitor's price and menu therefore sit under the wrong headers in the section's central table.
items.action: Merge the status into the product cell so the row has seven cells like the header and the Abbott and Boditech rows.

items.issue: The weighted-score sentence shows its own arithmetic summing to 3.85 (0.9 + 0.8 + 0.6 + 0.45 + 0.3 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.1) beside a headline composite of 3.9. Rounding is defensible but the two numbers should not appear in the same sentence without a note.
items.action: Write the sum as 3.85 and the composite as 3.85/10, or state that the displayed 3.9 is 3.85 rounded to one decimal.

items.issue: The rate-schedule item is only half-fixed. Business Model and Market now cite S154 (CMS's fee-schedule page) but alongside S160, which is a third-party lookup site (PayerPrice, accuracy medium) - the same class as the MedFeeSchedule pages retired this round. Business Model even says the amounts are 'republication'. Worse, the retired pages are still live elsewhere: ESG cites S82-S86 for the five national limitation amounts in two tables, and Risk cites S82 for the CY2027 cut analysis. S155, CMS's own MLN Matters MM14312 with the 2026 rate table, sits in the register unused, and so does S149's own 2026 base.
items.action: Cite CMS's file (S155 or the S154 data file) for the five amounts in all four sections, delete S160 from the tables where S155 covers the same figure, and replace S82-S86 in ESG's two tables with S154/S155. Recompute nothing if the amounts agree; where the third-party republication and CMS's file disagree, CMS wins and say so.
items.evidence_request: CMS CY2026 CLFS national limitation amounts for 84484, 83880, 83036, 82570 and 84132 taken line by line from MM14312 or the CMS CLFS data file, with the file date.

items.issue: Risk's waterfall paragraph cites S100, a blog summary of Cooley's Q2 2025 data, for a preference benchmark when Cooley's Q2 2026 report (S159) is in the register and used in Company Overview. The expected return is also stated over 4.5 years while the bull multiple it feeds is a five-year return, so two horizons are mixed in one calculation.
items.action: Cite S159 for the preference benchmark and state one holding period for the expected-return calculation, or show both (4.5 and 5 years).

items.issue: The price-war case is built on Boditech's cost base but names no Chinese or Indian immunoassay supplier. Getein Biotech, Wondfo and Snibe sell troponin and NT-proBNP immunoassays at cartridge prices well below $10 in Asia, the EU and Latin America, and any of them could file a US 510(k) with a waiver study. The report says an incumbent at $20-25 breaks Vantelle's economics without asking what a supplier with a $5 cost does to the incumbent.
items.action: Add one paragraph or table row to Competition: the named suppliers, what they sell, whether any holds US clearance or a waiver, and why the absence of clearance makes the threat a 2029-2031 financing risk rather than a 2027 one.

items.issue: The report quotes 34 of 37 sites reordering within 90 days and separately 41 sites, but never explains the three sites that did not reorder or why 37 rather than 41 is the denominator, and it does not say whether any site has been lost, declined to expand or reduced its fee. With zero conversions, those three sites are the only demand signal that points down, and the section's 'engagement, not demand' reading would be stronger with them.
items.action: State what happened to the three non-reordering sites and to the four sites outside the 37-site denominator, and say explicitly that no lost deals exist yet because no site can convert before clearance, so the first lost-deal evidence will come from the 300-site distributor pipeline.

items.issue: Market's top-down check misstates its own comparison: 'the $368M figure is still 60% of the smallest estimate'. $368M is 12.7% of the $2.89B Polaris estimate, not 60%; the 60% belongs to Abbott's entire global point-of-care line ($606M, $368M = 60.7%), which is a revenue line, not a market estimate. The same sentence computes 17%-83% correctly for the $2.4B claim, so the wrong figure sits beside a right one and inflates the report's own case fivefold.
items.action: Rewrite as: $368M is 12.7% of the smallest published US point-of-care estimate ($2.89B) and 60.7% of Abbott's global point-of-care revenue; keep the 17%-83% range for the company's $2.4B claim.

items.issue: The re-rating arithmetic is off by roughly a factor of three. On the stated weights, unit economics rising from 3 to 7 is +4 on a 15% weight, or +0.6 of a composite point, not 'roughly two points'; a clearance and accepted waiver pre-submission lifting regulatory from 3 to 6-7 is +0.6 to +0.8, not enough to carry the composite into a different band; and product and regulatory both falling to 2 is -0.4 and -0.2, or -0.6, not 'about a point and a half'. A reader is told the milestone moves the score three times as much as it does.
items.action: Recompute the three re-rating statements from the weighted table and state them in composite points (+0.6, +0.6-0.8, -0.6), or show the recomputed composite for each branch.

items.issue: The conditional cheque at $60-80M pre-money is justified on 1.40x over 4.5 years, a 7.8% IRR, and the report never states the hurdle that return has to clear. Its own exit section frames 3x (24.6%) as what the investment needs, and Risk says the ask fails because the return is below 'the venture hurdle and the risk-free rate' - but 7.8% is a bond-like return for equity risk, and at 30% worse the conditional cheque is back to about 1.0x. As written, the offer branch does not meet the standard the ask is rejected on.
items.action: State the hurdle rate the recommendation uses (e.g. 20-25% net) and show what price clears it on the 15/45/40 split; if none of $50-80M does, make Wait for milestone unconditional and present the $70M structure as a fallback rather than the action. One sentence in the recommendation card, one in Thesis.

Minors on reordering, lost deals and Asian suppliers are answered.

No decision-relevant gap is hidden by layout. The only residual is the wording slip above.

2.name: Claim verification
2.notes:
Claim verification. Register read (pages 1 and 5, 180 sources): every ID cited in the changed sections is registered, and the new primary sources are the right ones - S179/S180 are CMS's own CY2026 CLFS files (26CLABQ4, updated 2026-10), S159 the Cooley Q2 2026 survey, S176-S178 the Getein, Wondfo and Snibe product pages, S157 Boditech's 510(k), S127 Truvian K251058, S158/S156 Babson. No source appears that was not retrieved in this run and no company-material-only claim is left unlabelled: business_model, financials, market, technology_product and company_overview each carry 'company-reported and unverified' on the deck figures, and the CLFS amounts are now primary CMS in all four sections that use them.

The CMS line-by-line amounts reproduce: 12.47 + 39.26 + 9.71 + 5.18 + 4.76 = 71.38; four codes excluding 83880 = 32.12; troponin plus potassium = 17.23; 71.38 - 38.00 = 33.38 clinic spread; at the 15% annual ceiling, 71.38 x 0.85^3 = 43.84 and the spread 5.84. The 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month, 1.22 per operating day at 300 days and 41 cartridges per site-month are internally consistent with 1,680 across 55 analyzers and 41 sites.

The FDA series is now single-sourced (S97 FY2025 MDUFA: 127 days FY2023, 139 FY2024, 112-day FY2025 goal, cohort open), and market, strategy, risk and team tell the same story: late March 2027 at the 90-FDA-day floor, mid-May 2027 at the FY2024 average. The 175-day figure is labelled a database total time wherever it appears.

Stale or undated claims: none material. The 4.93% 10-year Treasury (S26), the 0.4x QDEL multiple and the 2026-10-30 price date are timestamped. The two residuals above are Minor and do not change the rating, the composite or any exit threshold.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes:
Missing competitors. The R2 gap is closed and the map now covers each substitute class the buyer actually has: direct (Abbott i-STAT, Siemens epoc, QuidelOrtho Triage, Roche cobas h 232, Radiometer AQT90), adjacent (Boditech AFIAS-6, Truvian TruVerus, Babson BetterWay), low-cost waived readers (Roche cobas b 101, Nova StatSensor), the Asian cost base that decides the 2029-2031 price war (Getein 1100, Wondfo Finecare, Snibe MAGLUMI, each with menu, waiver status and why no US clearance makes it a next-round financing risk), the reference laboratory as substitute and the transfer-or-call-later status quo. Geographic blind spots are stated rather than implied: EU blocked until CE marking after 2028, no staff in the Irish entity, US-only revenue.

Open source and academic spin-outs are not a substitute class here: the cartridge is a manufactured consumable with a licensed sealing patent, and no published platform was found that a clinic could run without an instrument. The one residual is Werfen, below, which matters less as a clinic competitor (GEM Premier is a blood-gas analyzer at the emergency-department bench) than as the acquirer exit names.

Comparative read: the report is honest that the wedge is packaging with a 12-24 month window, and it prices Abbott's matched $20-25 cartridge as the case-ending move rather than leaving it as a slogan.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes:
Product/market fit, the four questions and what the file now answers.

Hardest thing about selling: not the assay but the placement. The analyzer realises $1,160 on average against a $3,350 build, so each sale is a $2,190 cash subsidy, and three years of cartridge gross profit at observed use ($15,621) does not repay a $25,600-51,200 CAC. The report states this as the mechanism and prices it: 5.9 panels a day for 3:1 at today's $16.20 cost, 4.2 at the $7.50 target. Answerable and answered.

Budget owner: the clinic operator, not the clinician - stated from the $650 monthly fee and the CMS-claim arithmetic in market and business_model, with the added constraint that the natriuretic peptide carries $39.26 of the $71.38, so the two-analyte chest-pain order loses $20.77 a cartridge. This is the most decision-relevant finding in the file and it is priced into the market sizing ($222M-368M, not $2.4B).

Sales cycle: no data exists and the report says so - no conversion rate, no cycle length, no CLIA certificate type, no EHR interface, no payer enrolment, and no site can convert before clearance. U9/U10 name what would settle it. The 300-site pipeline is a non-binding letter of intent with no minimum purchase obligation.

Why adoption is not faster: investigational-use sites have no billing reason to run more (the honest counter-case is stated: a billing-enabled clinic could run several times more), the menu is moderate complexity until a 2028 waiver so hospital and reference laboratories are the end-2027 customer, and the 259 net adds needed in twelve months compare with 1.3 a month since March 2024 on nine commercial staff.

Lost deals: none can exist before clearance; the first evidence is the distributor pipeline, and the three non-reordering sites of 37 are stated as not disclosed rather than explained away. The 41-cartridge site-month reorder is correctly read as engagement, not demand.

No item: the section-level treatment is adequate for a private-company file, and the residual uncertainty is carried in the recommendation (tranche on clearance, waiver and a billing cohort above four panels).

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes:
Number stress-test. What reproduces, and what survives a 30% miss.

Waterfall (funding_valuation, exit): Series A = 36.0 + 23.75% x (exit - 9.4 - 76.8) reproduces every row to the decimal - 48.8 at 140, 62.3 at 197, 76.3 at 256, 116.7 at 426, 157.1 at 596. The $435M and $546M figures are gone.

Weighted return: 0.15 x 2.14 + 0.45 x 1.00 + 0.40 x 1.00 = 1.171 (1.17x), IRR 1.171^(1/4.5) - 1 = 3.6%; at $70M, 0.15 x 3.50 + 0.45 x 1.06 + 0.40 x 1.00 = 1.402 (1.40x), 7.8%. Both below the stated 25% hurdle, and the section now says so.

Utilisation: 1,680/55 = 30.5 per analyzer-month; x 12/300 = 1.22 a day; 1,680/41 = 41.0 a cartridge a site-month; $78.5M at 8 panels and $31 needs 1,055 analyzers (78.5/(8x300x31)); at observed use it needs 5,140-5,150 sites. FY2025 build: 20,160 + 23,952 = 44,112 against 27,600 cumulative; 1,680 x 9 = 15,120 leaves 12,480 over 22 months (567). The identity is now labelled a reconstruction and utilisation low confidence.

Reimbursement: 12.47 + 39.26 + 9.71 + 5.18 + 4.76 = 71.38; 71.38 - 38.00 = 33.38; 650/33.38 = 19.5 panels; 71.38 x 0.85^3 = 43.84 and 43.84 - 38.00 = 5.84, so 650/5.84 = 111 panels; four codes without 83880 = 32.12; troponin plus potassium = 17.23, a 20.77 loss on $38.

Stress: a 30% revenue miss gives 54.95 in 2029, worth 2.5x/1.25^3 = $70.4M, below the $76.8M stack, so 1.0x and common near zero - the thesis does not survive a 30% miss and the report says so rather than implying it does. Doubling CAC to $51,200-102,400 puts 402 analyzers at $20.6-41.2M of cost against a $30M round. The case that survives the stress is the optionality of a lower entry ($398M for 3x at $70M, $350M capped), not the ask.

Composite: 0.15x6 + 0.20x4 + 0.20x3 + 0.15x3 + 0.10x3 + 0.10x5 + 0.05x4 + 0.05x2 = 3.85.

Nothing here overturns the thesis: the thesis is that the ask is too high and the utilisation is unproven, and every number tested supports it.

final_memo:
# Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc.: Investment research report
Rating: Wait for milestone
Composite score: 3.9
Data as of: 2026-10-31

## Executive Briefing

Meridian should not lead Vantelle's Series B at $140M pre-money. The company has the strongest clinical wedge in the file — a five-analyte finger-stick panel aimed at clinics that cannot staff a laboratory, 41 paid evaluation sites and a 92% reorder rate — and a first-of-kind packaging position that incumbents would pay for. It also has the weakest operating proof: 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers — the January-September 2026 average on deck p.7, with the monthly series and FY2025 volume not disclosed — is 1.22 panels per analyzer operating day against the eight its 2028 plan needs; 27,600 cumulative shipments since March 2024 average 890 a month, so the 2026 rate is roughly double the programme average, and on flat per-analyzer use the $0.9M rise to $3.5M normalised FY2026 revenue has to come from more analyzers, research-use or development revenue, which the deck does not decompose; the financial section's FY2025 split of 20,160 evaluation and 23,952 research-use cartridges is a reconstruction from that 2026 average, and 44,112 FY2025 cartridges cannot coexist with 27,600 shipped to date, so the 1.22 rate and the FY2025 margin bridge carry low confidence until a shipment ledger arrives; troponin runs at 11.8% CV against the IFCC's <10% standard; the 510(k) is under an information request and a CLIA waiver has no cardiac precedent; and $6.9M of cash is six months at the current burn. Evidence confidence is medium on the regulatory calendar and low on the commercial plan, because every operating figure is company-reported and no public record of the company, its 510(k) or its patents exists [S1].

The price is the second problem. Five methods cluster at $50-100M with a $76M midpoint against the $140M ask and $170M post-money. The preference stack totals $76.8M — $30.0M senior B, $6.28M B-1, $36.0M Series A and $4.5M seed — and the Series A then participates at 23.75% of value above it, so the $30M Series B needs $596M of proceeds for 3x and $426M for 2x, while the April 2026 clearing price for a cleared, waived platform was $100M. The company's own 2029 plan, at 2.5x revenue, is worth $196M and returns the new money 1.0x. Only a strategic premium to $400-500M makes the bull case work, and that is 4-5x the clearing price [S126].

The consensus — the company plan, the $8M insider commitment, a Q1 2027 clearance and a 2027 waiver — is not the report's view. We differ on utilisation and price, not on the need: a first billing cohort above six panels a day and a waiver path accepted by FDA would re-rate the asset, while a second information request, a capillary troponin failure or a refused cardiac waiver would take most of the equity value. If Meridian wants exposure before the proofs arrive, the only defensible structure is a lower pre-money, a tranched cheque, a capped Series A participation and a capped or converted Corvia put [S72].

Three risks decide the outcome: utilisation staying near the evaluation rate, the capillary troponin study failing at the cutoff, and a waiver refused or deferred for the cardiac analyte. Each has an early warning in the sensitivity analysis and none is priced at the ask. The immediate financial risk is the runway against a close that still has to be signed, and a base case that consumes more than the round before breakeven.

Before any cheque, Meridian's diligence list should obtain the FDA letter and the pivotal protocol, the Corvia LLC agreement and its change-of-control clause, the Bluestem rate and covenants, the distributor's purchase terms, and the first billing cohort's panels per day and collected revenue per cartridge. Those items, not another meeting with management, decide whether the price is defensible or zero.

This single measure decides the case. At the observed rate the cartridge annuity never repays the cost of winning a placement, and the revenue plan needs several times the sites it targets; at the rate the plan assumes, the same site base supports a strategic exit. No other variable moves the level as much.

1. Do not lead at $140M: the ask is 40.0x normalised FY2026 revenue and needs a $596M exit for 3x, against a $100M clearing price for a cleared, waived platform [S1, S126].

3. If Meridian wants exposure now, its only defensible structure is a lower pre-money, a tranched cheque, a capped Series A participation and a capped or converted Corvia put on company-reported terms, unverified [S1, S126].

## Company Overview

Vantelle is investable at the parent level but not yet underwritable at the cap-table level. The Delaware issuer that would take Meridian's $15M holds patents VD-1 to VD-4 and is the FDA submitter; there is no VIE, offshore holding chain or founder super-voting stock. But the core sealing patent sits in a Texas affiliate Vantelle owns only 60% of, the CTO owns 22% of that affiliate and shares its 3% royalty, and the option overhang is 19.96% post-money — all company-provided and unverified. The buyer is an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital without a lab; 39% of US urgent-care centres are hospital-owned and send send-outs to a health-system lab. Vantelle places instruments and sells consumables: 41 evaluation sites, 55 analyzers, 1,680 cartridges a month and FY2025 revenue of $2.6M are unverified; scale depends on a 510(k) under an FDA additional-information request and a non-binding 300-site distributor LOI. [S99, S79]

The deck's "shares today" excludes the bridge conversion and the pool top-up, so the CEO's 17.6% is 14.89% pre-money (unverified). The bridge converts at $2.4423, 75% of the round price; the note is not disclosed, so those terms are unverified. [S99]

### The pool and the Series A preference decide who gets paid

Granted plus unallocated options equal 19.96% of post-money, against the 10% post-money pool this round itself creates; no primary NVCA or Cooley option-pool median was found, so the overhang is scored warn rather than critical. The top-up lifts the unallocated pool from 1,200,000 shares to 5,220,489, adding 4,020,489 shares — 7.7 points of post-money and $13.1M at $3.2564 — dilution borne entirely by existing holders inside the pre-money. $15M is 8.82% of the $170.0M post-money and 10.7% of the $140.0M pre-money; the refresh dilutes existing holders, not the new money. After the $9.4M Corvia put, the preference stack absorbs $76.8M of exit value on unverified share counts: Series B and B-1 take $36.28M senior and non-participating, the Series A $36.0M then 23.75% of the residual, and seed $4.5M non-participating. The founders receive $7.6M of a $100M exit (7.6%) and $29.9M of a $170M exit (17.6%); the $30M Series B returns 1.0x at $170M and needs $426M for 2x. Cooley's Q2 2026 survey of 166 financings found 96.4% non-participating preferred and 95.8% at 1x, so the Series A's 1x participation is a 3.6% structure and the largest mid-range claim. [S99, S159]

### The related-party royalty is small in percentage and large at exit

Vantelle pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales, of which the CTO receives 22%, or 0.66%, $0.52M a year on FY2029 plan revenue of $78.5M — company-provided and unverified. Corvia's 40% minority can put its stake at fair market value; 10x the FY2029 royalty implies a $9.4M put liability, an analyst estimate. Vantelle keeps 60% of the royalty, but the conflict is structural: the CTO is both technical key person and a counterparty paid per cartridge; no arm's-length opinion on the 3% rate and no Corvia LLC agreement is publicly disclosed. The board is better than the founder-control base case: two founder seats of six, one each for seed, Series A and Series B and one vacant independent seat; unlike Theranos, Holmes held super-majority Class B control until the SEC stripped it. The gap is an unfilled independent seat and no disclosed protective provisions, voting agreement or related-party approval process, so Meridian's power to block the Corvia royalty, new debt or a sale is unknown. ### Six months of cash, a loan amortising, no public paper trail

Cash was $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against $1.15M monthly net burn, a 6.0-month runway to 2027-03-31 against a 2027-01-29 target close (unverified). ## Technology & Product

The Q5 is an integration and manufacturing-cost play, not an assay-science advance. Its troponin I assay runs at 11.8% imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff — above the 10% CV that defines a high-sensitivity assay and more than twice Abbott's cleared point-of-care hs-TnI — and the evidence is a venous-blood study run by Vantelle staff at one urgent-care site. The package is five analytes from one finger stick, defensible only if the cartridge, cost curve, pivotal capillary study and a first-of-kind CLIA waiver hold; none is proven [S1, S68, S70].

**The troponin assay is not high-sensitivity by the standard its positioning implies.**

The IFCC definition requires total imprecision below 10% CV at the 99th-percentile limit and measurable values in half of healthy adults. Vantelle reports 11.8% CV at the cutoff and discloses neither its 99th-percentile value nor its detection limit; Abbott's cleared i-STAT hs-TnI is specified below 5.2% CV in whole blood with a 1.61 ng/L detection limit [S68, S70].

### How five analytes come out of one drop

A finger stick fills a capillary cartridge that meters a fixed volume, rehydrates dried reagents and runs each assay against an on-board calibrator; the VD-2 reader corrects for drift and a sample-volume check (VD-3) guards short fills (company description, unverified).

### Precision and capillary collection decide the label

At 11.8% CV a result on the cutoff carries a 95% spread of about ±23%, so a material share lands on the wrong side of the line — tolerable for a conventional rule-out troponin, not for the high-sensitivity pathways. The deck calls it high-sensitivity without stating the cutoff; on this data it is clearable, if at all, as a conventional cTnI. A Class II submission needs multi-level precision at the cutoff, limit of blank, detection and quantitation, linearity, haemolysis interference and a method comparison with slope, bias and total error; the study reports none. The 96.1% is categorical agreement; the direction of the five discordant results is undisclosed. The six excluded results were insufficient sample or cartridge error — exactly what the CLIA flex studies will stress. No capillary-versus-venous data appears in the deck: the four-site pivotal study — 1,150 patients, finger sticks run by clinic staff, results expected in Q2 2027 — is the first test of capillary collection and untrained operators. Potassium is the haemolysis-exposed analyte, biased upward into false hyperkalaemia; Abbott requires un-anticoagulated whole blood within three minutes. Finger-stick creatinine, HbA1c and potassium already exist from Nova, Roche and Siemens; the novelty is the five-in-one cartridge [S1, S13, S15, S16, S21, S68, S70, S74].

### The waiver is a second, harder validation

The application must reference a cleared product and carry flex studies and a clinical study in the hands of intended users; FDA's goal is 150 FDA days, and an additional-information request can add 180. A venous, staff-run, single-site evaluation is not that study. No point-of-care precedent exists: Abbott publishes a separate i-STAT waived-test manual for chemistry and blood gas, its hs-TnI launched on 2025-01-03 as moderate complexity, CMS ended the pandemic discretion for the older cTnI cartridge on 2026-03-30, and Quidel's Triage MeterPro troponin is moderate on the FDA-derived list. A waived five-analyte troponin panel would be first-of-kind, and a Q3 2027 filing decides in 2028 [S72, S104, S142, S145, S146].

### Supply chain and the antibody are undisclosed

What would settle it: the bills of materials with supplier sites, the antibody licence and supply agreement (including change-of-control and transfer rights), second-source qualification records, and the unredacted FTO opinion. The analyzer is a customer-acquisition cost, and the economics live in cartridge gross profit, which covers the instrument at observed use but not a direct sales force; readiness is uneven — troponin I and HbA1c at level 7 (submitted), NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium at 6 (pivotal enrolling), manufacturing at 5, with a leased plant, limited stability data and no ISO 13485 certificate. The open questions are the troponin cutoff and detection limit, what the FDA request asked, haemolysis in pivotal finger sticks, line yield and stability beyond the data held, and whether the waiver is filed alongside the second clearance [S1].

Confidence is medium-high: the analytical gap is visible in company data, while manufacturing, IP and waiver judgements rest on company disclosure and FDA's process.

## Market & Industry Analysis

The company's $2.4B US serviceable-market estimate is an arithmetic artefact of one unproven input: at the 1.22 panels per analyzer per operating day its own 41 evaluation sites delivered in the 2026 year to date, the same 13,200 sites and the same $38 cartridge support $368M of annual revenue, 15% of the claim and 60.7% of Abbott's entire global point-of-care revenue line. The need is real; the number is not. Both the $2.4B and the volume behind it are company-provided, unaudited and not independently confirmed [S1, S67].

The site count survives independent checks and is conservative. The Urgent Care Association counted 15,032 open centers in January 2025, 39% hospital-owned or affiliated and 67% open seven days a week; Definitive Healthcare counted 11,877 active clinics in June 2025; the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine reported 14,245 in September 2024. The deck's 11,400 urgent-care sites sits at the bottom of the range; 1,800 rural hospitals is plausible. Volume is where the file breaks. Deck p.7 heads its column "Cartridges a month, 2026 average": 1,680 across 41 sites and 55 analyzers, 41 a site on p.9, with figures as of 2026-09-30, a 2026 year-to-date average; FY2025 monthly volume is not disclosed. The same page states 27,600 cartridges shipped since March 2024, 890 a month over 31 months. Any FY2025 line split is a reconstruction from the 2026 average and cannot coexist with that cumulative total: 20,160 evaluation plus 23,952 research-use would total 44,112, and 20,160 plus the 15,120 implied by nine months at 1,680 already exceeds 27,600. A residual of 12,480 over the 22 pre-2026 months, 567 a month, follows only if 1,680 held every 2026 month; it is an inference, not a disclosure, and conflicts with the FY2025 line build. Across 55 analyzers, 1,680 is 30.5 cartridges per analyzer-month and 1.22 per operating day at 300 days, or 1.35 per site-day against the model's 8.0, a 6.5x gap that carries low confidence until a shipment ledger arrives. Either billing-enabled clinics run six times more than evaluation sites, or the company needs 1,800 sites at observed utilisation to reach $41.0M; it has 41. Its 52-clinic survey reports a median 14 send-outs a day, a different measure from cartridges used [S79, S80, S78, S1].
